News.title: Shocking moment yob attacks driver & hijacks bus before smashing cars into cars & ploughing down street
News.content:
Next

THIS is the shocking moment a bus driver is attacked in his cab before the crazed yob hijacks the vehicle and ploughs through a town centre.

The terrifying footage obtained by The Sun shows the thug lunging at the driver, yanking his beard and repeatedly smashing the bus’s cash register.



Horrified care worker Kymberlee Daley stumbled across the scene while she was walking to work.

She heard the horn on the 100 bus to Sutton Hill in Telford sounding and rushed over to help.



The 19-year-old filmed the video as she bravely tried to intervene as the panicking driver was attacked.

Kymberlee told The Sun: “It was terrifying what happened, the man held the cash register above his head and threw it at the poor driver.”

The horrifying scenes unfolded in broad daylight as the panicked driver could be heard caling for people to phone the police.

Bystanders reassured him they were already on the phone to officers as the man appeared to repeatedly try to headbutt him.



The yob then lunged into the cab and attempted to yank the driver’s beard.

He then appeared to grab the cash register and swung it towards the driver.

Kymberlee then told The Sun how she managed to distract the lunatic by heckling him and saying she was calling the cops.

With his attention on her, the driver then managed to climb through his smashed cab window and ran.

Kymberlee told The Sun: “The driver at this point then managed to jump out of the window and run away, we were scared because we didn’t know what this man was capable of.



“But I wasn’t going to let an innocent man get beaten up so I stayed to defend the driver and distract the attacker.

“It was my natural instinct to do that, in those fight or flight situations it is just one or the other and I wanted to help.”

But then things got worse as the attacker then climbed behind the wheel of the bus – and drove it away in scenes that could have been from Grand Theft Auto.

A further video taken by Kymberlee shows the crazed hijacker climbing into the cab and edging the single-decker towards a junction in the town centre.

But in a bizarre twist, the bus then comes to a standstill for more than a minute as crowds gather to watch the extraordinary spectacle unfold.



The engine can be heard revving loudly, with the man appearing to struggle to get the vehicle into gear.

Around a minute and a half later, with a huge queue of traffic building behind him, the bus finally starts moving.

The hijacker then drives through the town as shocked witnesses chase after the vehicle.



He allegedly drove along the wrong side of the road, sending terrified motorists and pedestrians scrambling to get out of his way.

One eyewitness, Tom Barnett, described the moment the bus came towards him on the wrong side of the High Street.

Tom told The Shropshire Star: “He came down at me when I was driving up the high street.

“I had to pull into the parking space by the old Charlie’s chip shop.

“He clearly wasn’t stopping for anyone, it happened so quickly.”



Another resident, Lorraine Rees, said she was concerned for the bus driver.

She commented: “Hope the poor driver is OK. He looked so scared.”

Cops were called to Court Street in Madeley at around 6.37pm after reports that a man had assaulted the bus driver.



During the attack, the driver was ejected from the vehicle before the bus was driven towards Park Way and the High Street.

The vehicle collided with multiple cars before officers eventually managed to stop it.

A man in his 20s was arrested on suspicion of robbery and dangerous driving and remains in police custody while enquiries continue.

The bus driver was treated for minor injuries by paramedics.

No one else is believed to have been injured during the incident.



Detective Sergeant Taigh Lannie said: “We understand this will have been an alarming incident for those in the area this evening.

“I’d like to reassure the community that officers responded quickly and a man has been arrested and remains in police custody.”

He added that officers were keen to hear from anyone who witnessed what happened or captured footage.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The road was closed for several hours while emergency services dealt with the incident before reopening at around 9.40pm.

Anyone with dashcam, CCTV, mobile phone or doorbell footage from Court Street, Park Way or the High Street is urged to contact police.

News.title: Youth carnage, private security guards & rampant shoplifting… the seaside town that has gone to war with the yobbos
News.content:
Next

SOUTHEND is a much-loved British seaside resort where families flock for fish and chips, funfair rides and the world’s longest pleasure pier.

But the Essex city has spent years battling a darker problem of yobs turning its streets into a playground for violence, intimidation and anti-social behaviour.



Residents have endured hundreds of youngsters descending on the area and causing anarchy – with much of the wild scenes ending up on TikTok.

Businesses have been forced to shut early as cops swoop to break up huge gathering crowds flocking along the seafront.



There have even been machete brawls as rival gangs use the town as a battleground – with fed-up locals telling The Sun the thugs “don’t give a f***”.

Others say the youngsters descend on the town simply “looking for trouble”, with the disorder now spreading beyond the seafront and into the city centre.

But Southend has now gone to war on the yobbos, with cops and the council deploying a string of new tactics to take back its streets.

Officers have been using stop and search powers, dispersal orders, high-visibility patrols and live facial recognition to target troublemakers.



The city also has private security Street Rangers and Community Safety Officers patrolling the centre.

And there are signs the crackdown is beginning to turn a corner.

Essex Police says crime across Southend has fallen – including a 20 per cent drop in violent and knife crime – while the force says it is solving three times as many shoplifting offences as it did three years ago.

Police also say there has been a 13 per cent reduction in anti-social behaviour and an 11 per cent fall in serious violence.

Home Office data showed Southend has the highest shoplifting figures in Essex over the last financial year, with 12 incidents per 1,000 people.



The latest weapon in the fight is live facial recognition, with Essex cops now celebrating its 200th arrest using the technology.

There were 26 LFR arrests in August alone, including suspects wanted over violent and theft offences, taking the total to 200.

Detective Superintendent Stephen Jennings said the technology allows cops to locate wanted people more efficiently, freeing officers to carry out visible patrols and engage with communities.

The system creates a watchlist of people police are seeking to locate, including those wanted for offences, subject to court orders or considered at risk of harm.

The crackdown has come after years of residents and traders dealing with the consequences of disorder.



Footage obtained by The Sun of one incident shows officers flooding the area to disperse vast crowds of youths.

And last month, Big News shopkeeper Hamza Zulfiqar, 24, was left with his wounds plastered up after a confrontation with a group of youths.

Hamza, who has worked at the shop just off the High Street for 11 months, said the gang had repeatedly stolen from his business.



He said: “For sometime now the same group kept coming in here and stealing things, we couldn’t do anything to prevent it.

“They would laugh at us when we said we would call the police. And then days later they would come back and do it again.

“I ended up saying I would publish a photo from CCTV of their faces on Facebook, they then came back and asked why we hadn’t and began making threats to kill me.

“Next thing you know several of them push through and one climbs on the counter and hits me. I punch him back in self defence.

“The shelf with sweets and chocolate went flying and me and one of the kids fell to the ground.



“They then all ran out of the shop. It was terrifying.”

Seafront business owner Valentina, 52, says the crackdown has made a difference, but traders can still pay the price when large crowds descend.

She has run The Boat House for nine years and believes police now have more control over the trouble.



But she says dispersal orders can still force businesses to close and leave traders struggling to survive.

Valentina told The Sun: “The issue of yobs has been worse in previous years to be honest, I would say the police have got more of a grip on them running wild, but it still happens.

“But when they do come here, the dispersal order officers put in place forces us to close and shut early.

“The council offers no relief when this comes into effect, and there is zero sympathy.

“They don’t understand how hard it is to run a business in today’s climate and the challenges we are all facing here. Yesterday I took around £280 and had two waitresses to pay.



“For some of us down here on the front we are just trying to make ends meet. Before the pandemic on a busy day we would take around £2,500/£3000, now it is about survival.”

The city has been hit by a social media-fuelled gathering craze, with officers previously forced to disperse crowds after calls to “get lit and cause trouble”.

Cops became aware of plans to cause trouble in Southend just a day after hundreds of teenagers gathered on Oxford Street amid a TikTok looting craze.

A similar social media meet-up was planned for Southend, according to 20-year-old Mia Cundy, who grew up locally.



Mia left for Colchester to study law and says she no longer wants to live in Southend because of the behaviour she sees there.

She said: “There are young kids running wild doing balloons, smoking weed, always getting into confrontations with security.

“The thing is there’s nothing for the kids to do, the amusements down here are a bit babyish for them.

“There needs to be somewhere for them to go, they see these homeless drunks and they want a bit of it.



“I don’t want to live here anymore. I am studying law at Colchester and even though it’s close it’s so much nicer there.”

Friends Brandy Baker and John Raftery also claim they were attacked by youths on the High Street.

John said the youngsters tried to snatch his bike before fleeing, with a Stanley knife allegedly falling from one lad’s pocket.

He said: “It is bloody terrifying, they smashed my bike in the ordeal, don’t know why they started on us but the kids are out looking for trouble.”

Brandy added: “There’s an influx of people from all over and they are struggling to integrate.



“The young kids here are animals, out of control. Every day there is something else crazy happening, and innocent people get caught up in it.”

Police say the difference is now being made by combining old-fashioned visible policing with new technology and tougher powers.

Dispersal orders give officers the power to direct people to leave an area where there are reasonable grounds to believe their behaviour could contribute to crime or disorder.



Southend also has a Public Spaces Protection Order covering the town centre, seafront and adjoining areas, with restrictions targeting behaviours including anti-social drinking, drug use and other nuisance activity.

Chief Inspector Jane Childs said: “Southend is safe and I am pleased that tens of thousands of people have travelled here each month this summer to enjoy the record-breaking hot weather.

“We’ve worked hard with our partners, including Southend-on-Sea City Council, British Transport Police, and the local traders, to ensure visitors can enjoy our fantastic city safely.

“Crime across Southend is down in the last years, including violent crime and knife crime, which has fallen by 20 percent. At the same time, we’ve secured 15 percent more knife crime related charges.

“So far this summer we have not experienced any significant violence or disorder.



“In fact, when we there was information about a group planning to come and cause trouble here, officers met them at the train station, turned them around, and sent them on their way.

“We know the impact shoplifting has on our hardworking local businesses and through the relentless focus of our officers, we’re solving three times the number of offences we did three years ago.

“We will always utilise the tools available to us to ensure residents, businesses and visitors are safe, and that includes dispersal orders.

“By using these powers, we’re able to tackle crime and anti-social behaviour and ensure businesses are able to stay open and people are able to enjoy everything Southend has to offer.

“Fortunately though, this summer we’ve not had to put these orders in place very often.



“We have a really good working relationship with the seafront traders and they have told me and my officers how positive they’ve been about this summer.

“Finally, I want to thank the vast majority of people in Southend who support the city and us.

“You will continue to see us visible in our communities so when you see us, please come and say hi.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Leader of Southend-on-Sea City Council Daniel Cowan said: “We work closely with Essex Police, local businesses and our community safety teams to keep Southend safe and welcoming, and anyone coming here intent on causing trouble should expect a robust no-tolerance response.

“But we won’t allow a tiny minority to define our city or dictate our summer: millions of people visit Southend every year.”

News.title: Lizzie Borden murder theories from poison plot to burned dress & why she got off as Netflix Monster revives mystery
News.content:
Next

THE new Lizzie Borden Monster series on Netflix opens with the alleged killer wielding an axe as she brutally murders her father and stepmother.

But the real-life case was nowhere near as clear-cut, with Lizzie acquitted by an all-male jury after Andrew and Abby Borden were found butchered inside their Massachusetts home in 1892.



Abby, 64, was killed first in an upstairs guest bedroom, suffering 19 blows to the face and back of the head, before Andrew, 69, was struck 11 times in the face while lying on a sofa downstairs later that morning.

Lizzie was accused of carrying out both killings, but more than 130 years later nobody has ever been convicted, with a burned dress, an alleged attempt to buy poison and a string of other suspects all becoming part of the mystery.



Despite the savage nature of the killings, there was one glaring problem with the case – not a drop of blood was found on Lizzie.

“She was examined very carefully by the police, and her clothing was examined and there was no blood on her,” leading Lizzie expert Dr. Stefani Koorey told The U.S. Sun.

Lizzie Borden NETFLIX'S MONSTER What you need to know about Lizzie Borden before new Netflix series

“She hadn’t just washed her face. She wasn’t, you know, wet from the water. She didn’t have any evidence of having committed the crime.”

Koorey, who has spent decades researching the murders, also highlighted the physical effort that would have been required to carry out both attacks.

“If you’ve ever picked up a hatchet and swung it above your head 19 times, it is a very strenuous activity,” she said.

“And then to sit and wait and do it again 11 more times. And these were people that she would have known and loved at one time.”



There was also a wild theory that Lizzie could have committed the murders naked, but there were no signs she had just taken a shower or washed herself afterward.

Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story, the fourth installment of Ryan Murphy and Ian Brennan’s Netflix anthology, is now putting the infamous case back in the spotlight.

The eight-part series, directed by Max Winkler, stars Ella Beatty as Lizzie alongside Vicky Krieps as maid Bridget Sullivan, Billie Lourd as Lizzie’s sister Emma, and Jessica Barden as stage actress Nance O’Neil.



Another bizarre strand of the case began the day before the murders when a drugstore clerk claimed Lizzie tried to buy prussic acid, a deadly poison.

Eli Bence said she asked for ten cents’ worth and claimed she wanted to use it on a sealskin cape, but he refused to sell it to her without a doctor’s prescription.

Lizzie denied trying to buy the poison and there was no evidence she ever obtained it, while tests carried out after the deaths found no poison and Bence’s potentially damaging testimony was ultimately excluded from her trial.

Yet it was another seemingly suspicious act that Koorey says resulted in Lizzie ever facing a murder trial at all.

Three days after the killings, Lizzie’s friend Alice Russell saw her preparing to burn a light-blue cotton dress in the kitchen stove.



Russell later testified that she saw Lizzie with the dress and heard her say, “I am going to burn this old thing up; it is covered with paint.”

Russell told the court she later warned her friend, “I wouldn’t let anybody see me do that, Lizzie.”

The following day, Russell said she confronted her again, telling her, “I am afraid, Lizzie, the worst thing you could have done was to burn that dress. I have been asked about your dresses.”

According to Russell’s sworn testimony, Lizzie replied, “Oh, what made you let me do it? Why didn’t you tell me?”

Russell’s conscience got the better of her and she eventually told investigators about the incident.



“If it wasn’t for the dress burning, Lizzie Borden would never have been indicted in the first place,” Koorey said. “She never would have stood trial at all.”

But there was evidence supporting Lizzie’s claim that the dress really had been ruined by paint.

“It definitely was a paint-stained dress, as we know, because there were witnesses who said that that dress existed, that it was paint stained,” Koorey said.



She said witnesses recalled Lizzie getting house paint on the garment before the murders, while a dressmaker also testified about the existence of the paint-stained dress.

“So is it the murder dress that she was wearing but was also paint stained? Who’s to say?” Koorey said.

“But … it caused her to be tried for murder. That dress.”

Police looked into workers connected to Andrew’s farm in Swansea as well as Lizzie and Emma’s maternal uncle John Morse, who had unexpectedly arrived at the Borden home the day before the murders and stayed overnight.

“He had an alibi, a great alibi, a kind of crazy, perfect alibi,” Koorey said.



Police even investigated reports of a man allegedly spotted with a bloody axe in the area.

“There were people who said, ‘Oh, I saw a guy with a bloody axe in Somerset on a farm,’ and they went and investigated,” Koorey said.

“And it turned out he was, like, killing some chickens.”

Koorey said investigators eventually eliminated the other leads and were “left with Lizzie,” but added, “If you read the trial transcript, you understand that there was no evidence to convict her.”

The murder weapon was also never found.



Lizzie was acquitted in June 1893, with Koorey saying the jurors spent approximately ten minutes deciding on their verdict before deliberately waiting longer to return to court because “they didn’t want to appear that they had already figured it out.”

“But she was acquitted pretty quickly. And they really believed her not to be guilty,” Koorey said, adding that the jurors later gave Lizzie a portrait of themselves that she kept.

Two months after her acquittal, Lizzie and Emma left the murder house and moved into a large Victorian mansion in Fall River’s wealthy Hill neighborhood, which Lizzie named Maplecroft.

But Lizzie was reportedly shunned by some members of local society and taunted by children as fascination with the murders followed her for the rest of her life.

The sisters later became estranged, with Emma leaving Maplecroft in 1905.



Lizzie remained there until her death in 1927 at the age of 66 and was buried in the Borden family plot alongside Andrew and Abby.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Emma died just nine days later, leaving behind a case that had divided the sisters’ hometown and a mystery that has never been solved.

To watch the full interview with Dr. Stefani Koorey, visit The U.S. Sun’s YouTube channel.

News.title: Brit tourist, 32, suddenly dies at hotel during holiday on Greek island after being found unconscious by horrified mum
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

ISLAND TRAGEDY Brit tourist, 32, suddenly dies at hotel during holiday on Greek island after being found unconscious by horrified mum







Next

A BRIT tourist has died suddenly in a hotel in Crete.

The 32-year-old holidaymaker was found dead in her hotel room by her horrified mum on the Greek holiday island.



She had been staying in Georgioupolis, ​​Chania, in the west of Crete.

Her mum, who had been sharing a room with her, found the woman unconscious.



The mother immediately told hotel staff and paramedics rushed to try and revive her daughter.

But the woman could not be saved and was declared dead at the scene.



Authorities said the tourist had no known health problems before her sudden death.

They launched an investigation into the death and ordered an autopsy.

The Sun contacted the UK Foreign Office for comment.

It comes after another Brit died after being pulled unconscious from the sea on the same island.



The 60-year-old had been holidaying on the busy beach of Kato Gouves, in the east of Crete.

The alarm was raised when he was spotted in the water and emergency services raced to the scene.

He was taken to the nearby Venizelio Hospital where he was pronounced dead.

The Heraklion Port Authority ordered an autopsy to determine the cause of the tourist’s death.

Just weeks earlier another Brit, 34, died after being pulled from the sea in critical condition in Greece.



He was rescued from the waters after getting into difficulty in Zante.

And in June a 17-year-old British tourist died after diving into dangerous waters in Crete.

The teen was swimming in the sea when they suddenly started screaming for help in Chania in June.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Six lifeguards rushed to the scene and managed to pull one of the boys out from the rough waters.

But the second boy tragically drowned before he could be rescued.

News.title: Our giant 30ft shark has triggered a planning war with moaning locals & internet trolls – we are baffled
News.content:
JAW BLIMEY Our giant 30ft shark has triggered a planning war with moaning locals & internet trolls – we are baffled







Next

STAFF at a crazy golf course have fiercely defended their beloved giant shark at the centre of a furious planning row.

The enormous 30ft plastic Great White has been caught in the middle of a campaign directed by critics who moan it is a “symbol of slaughter and destruction”.



Workers at Jungle Rumble Adventure Golf on Brighton Seafront have been left “baffled” by whining resident complaints about one of their most popular attractions.

The kids’ mini golf course is just down the road from Brighton Pier and is a stones throw away from the sea.



The fibreglass shark is named Bruce after the infamous antagonist of Jaws and leader of the “Fish are Friends” group in Finding Nemo.

The ocean view joint seems the perfect home for Bruce who became the city’s latest nautical resident in August last year.



But trouble started brewing when a witch hunt of environmentalists set their sights on the plastic beast, claiming he’s portraying sharks as “criminals” and giving them a bad name.

Jungle Rumble Adventure Golf applied for retrospective planning permission earlier this month.

But one keyboard warrior submitted an objection hoping to scupper the attraction’s centrepiece.

The complaint said: “It is ugly but also very offensive to have a marine animal being depicted as a criminal having been slaughtered for no reason.

“Sharks are a vital form of marine life and should be protected if we are to regain healthy seas which can help mend our planet.”



Since then the campaign against Bruce has snowballed with hateful comments online branding him “revolting, grisly and repulsive”.

But staff at the golf course say the shark is adored by customers who flock to the seaside attraction to compete underneath the huge fish.

Jungle Rumble manager Abby Parry told The Sun: “We started to see some stuff online that people were unhappy, but obviously we’re a kids’ mini golf place on the beach.

“We’re just baffled, it’s been blown up so big.

“It’s not like it’s our only animal themed thing here.



“I don’t really understand how having an animal on a children’s mini golf is portraying it as criminal, it’s not like there’s blood pouring out of it.

“Everyone that plays golf requests Bruce the shark’s Captain Hook course, we’ve had nothing but positive feedback.

“So it was disheartening to see all this slander online when we work hard to keep the business afloat and make sure people have a good time here.

“For them to drag the name of the whole venue is a bit disheartening.”

Even during The Sun’s visit on a murky and drizzly day customers battled through the rain to play golf on the course.



Players George and Marina were staunch supporters of the shark and said it was one of their favourite parts of the attraction.

George from Streatham said: “I think it looks nice, the complaints are because people haven’t got anything else to do, they need to go and get a job.

“When you’ve got people starving, talking about stuff like this seems irrelevant.

“I think it’s beautiful, sharks are beautiful animals.

“It doesn’t mean anything to the shark.”



Vintage clothes dealer Christopher Locke visits Jungle Rumble every day for his morning coffee.

He said: “I think it’s a great idea, it’s not tacky and is very well done, if it was lit up and said bingo or fish and chips then I don’t think it would be very nice.

“But it’s very tasteful, it’s a good idea for Brighton, it’s actually necessary because we need to try to have something a bit different.

“Brighton is different, it’s always been like that so I think it’s a positive thing.

“It’s wonderful.



“Jungle Rumble is very popular with people all over the country and some people will complain about anything.

“If it had neon lights all over it then it would be different but I think it’s quite cool.”

Bruce the shark hangs above the historic Volk’s Electric Railway which passes right next to the golf course.

Track worker Morris sees Bruce every day and is a big fan of the ocean beast.

He said: “I think it’s brilliant, I think the complaints are stupid and silly.”



Tied up in the same retrospective planning request as the shark is a toilet opened by the golf course which visitors to the nearby public playground can use free of charge.

But if the plastic shark is booted from Jungle Rumble by the council, it will mean the toilets have to go as well.

A heritage assessment notes the shark is “clearly visible” from the beach, Madeira Drive and Madeira Terrace.

It found that as Brighton seafront has historically hosted activities like mini golf, the new addition fits well with the area.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It said: “The works are therefore considered to represent contemporary additions associated with the established recreational use of this part of Brighton’s lower seafront without detracting from the significance of the East Cliff Conservation Area or the setting and significance of nearby designated heritage assets.”



Brighton and Hove City Council are set to decide on the application at a future date which will seal Bruce the shark’s fate.

News.title: Manhunt for driver after child knocked down in hit & run while crossing the road  before being helped by passerby
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

CRASH HORROR Manhunt for driver after child knocked down in hit & run while crossing the road before being helped by passerby







Next

COPS have launched a manhunt for a driver after a child was knocked down in a hit and run while crossing the road.

The horror unfolded in Clayton, Staffordshire, at around 3.20pm on Friday close to a nearby school.

Cops say a “small black car” collided with the child – whose age is unknown – while they were crossing the road.

The youngster was raced to hospital with head and leg injuries with his condition currently unknown.





A member of the public stopped to assist who officers believe wasn’t involved in the collision.

The car is then believed to have fled in the direction of the M6 motorway.

A spokesperson for Staffordshire Police said: “We are appealing for information after a non-stop collision where a child was injured.

“The collision happened on Clayton Road. A small black car collided with a child who was crossing the road.



“A member of the public stopped to assist but we do not believe they were involved in the collision.

“The small black car drove off towards Newcastle Road, in the direction of the motorway.

“The child was taken to hospital with a leg and a head injury.”

Any witnesses are urged to come forward to the police quoting incident number 514 of September 18.

News.title: Never-before-seen vid shows moment K2 climbers find dying porter at world’s most dangerous peak before leaving him there
News.content:
Next

THIS is the heartbreaking moment climbers find a dying mountain guide hanging upside-down and decide to leave him to continue a record-breaking ascent.

The never-before-seen footage shows the mountaineers finding the guide at 27,000ft on K2 in the dead of night.



A new documentary shows Norwegian mountaineering star Kristin Harila, 40, and her team as they tackle one of the world’s most dangerous mountain paths.

They were just metres away from reaching the summit and setting a new world record when they found the climber.



Pakistani porter Muhammad Hassan can be seen hanging upside down from his rope on the sheer snow-covered slope.

Footage shows the 2023 record-breaking climb as the team make the agonising choice whether to abandon their record attempt to do everything they can to bring him to safety.

They ultimately decide to leave him and continue to the summit, a decision that triggered months of scandal.

In the film Savage Mountain, Kristin said when they found Muhammad: “We saw there was something wrong with the rope around his legs.

“He was naked on his stomach and his back.”

She explained her team made desperate attempts to reach him in the dark.



Dramatic video shows one climber attempting to secure an ice screw and slipping as they try to get to Muhammad.

Kristin said: “People were worried about everything collapsing, so of course no one wanted to stay there.”

“I told Lama, we need to do something.”

Kristin’s cling partner Tenjen “Lama” Sherpa said: “People were scared. I clipped around 10 people to get closer to the accident.

“I picked him up and held his hand.



“We were on a big slope with very slippery blue ice. It was a very dangerous place.”

Kristin said her team managed to help Muhammad with a new rope but said it would not have been possible for everyone to turn back.

A huge avalanche then struck another part of the mountain, where part of Kristin’s team had gone ahead.

She and Lama went ahead to find the rest of the team, leaving Muhammad with her cameraman Gabriel.

Gabriel said the guide’s condition was already extremely serious when they found him hanging on the mountain.



He said: “He was completely frozen. No oxygen, no gloves, no down suit.

“I tried to warm him, to move his fingers, tried to give him hot water.

“Tried to give him comfort.”

He gave him his own oxygen bottle and stayed with Muhammad until he was told they had to leave him behind.

A viral video showed mountaineers climbing over his dying body the next morning to complete their climb.



Kristin said at the time she was the victim of “hatred” and death threats after celebrating her world record.

She wrote on Instagram: “This was no one’s fault, you cannot comment when you do not understand the situation and sending death threats is never okay.’

She said in the new film: “This [viral video] was filmed in the middle of the day, when it was light.

“We were there when he fell in the dark. We tried for hours to save him.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

An investigation into Muhammad’s death found his expedition company had not made proper checks on his equipment.



The company he worked for was forced to stop all expeditions for two years.

News.title: How soap stars’ favourite dog groomer was driven to suicide after trolls’ horror abuse – the sick texts that haunted him
News.content:
Next

LUKE Lister couldn’t believe his eyes as he looked through messages in a private WhatsApp group discussing sabotaging his nephew’s life, and then celebrating when he ultimately died by suicide.

Bailey Lister – known as Dr Doolittle – was an animal rescuer and dog groomer whose clients included Coronation Street stars, but behind the scenes a sick group of jealous trolls had banded together to take him down. The Sun reveals how a network of cowardly bullies systematically destroyed a talented young man’s life until he felt he had no other way out.



Poor Bailey was bombarded with constant abuse for months, with phone calls, social media posts and even bogus police and RSPCA visits before his sudden death on May 7, aged just 22.

Days earlier he’d been working for clients on the Manchester set of Coronation Street, and had previously appeared on TV, but behind the scenes the horrific bullying ordeal had left him broken.

Bailey had begun rescuing animals, including monkeys, snakes and porcupines, at the age of 14, and had gone on to launch a sanctuary as well as later run a grooming business.



However, success had seemingly nurtured a series of haters who would stop at nothing.

His uncle Luke has now made it his mission to expose those behind his nephew’s tragic death – and ensure they face justice.

He is also urging the government to provide more protection from online bullying, saying “the cruelty he endured became too much for him to carry”.

He added: “We must act decisively to put an end to this crisis.”

Sick messages, seen by The Sun, show how trolls hoped for Bailey’s death.



And in a secret WhatsApp group they had been using every day phrases like “chicken nuggets” – seemingly as bizarre code words while planning how to “sabotage” his work – before celebrating when they heard he’d died.

The campaign of abuse, which included lies being spread online that Bailey had been convicted of animal cruelty, had already led to a previous suicide attempt.

However, following an investigation, the police have said they can take no action against those responsible, the family claim.



Bailey’s uncle Luke told The Sun: “It was just disgusting what these people were saying – and Bailey couldn’t cope.”

Several Facebook groups, as well as the WhatsApp chat, seemed to have become hubs for abuse against Bailey, and even after his death were claiming he’d “taken the easy way out”.

Luke, 39, said: “I don’t entirely understand who these people were – or why they were targeting Bailey, but it was awful.”

He said he suspected there was jealousy around his growing social media presence, and success from a young age.

Prior to his death, Bailey’s mobile number had even been circulated and Luke says trolls were able to directly bombard him with calls and messages.



Luke said his nephew had first revealed to his family in December last year that he was struggling due to the unwanted attention.



“We tried our best to protect him from it, and encourage him to ignore them,” he explained.

“He shared the messages with me and they were disgusting.”

Bailey had recently been evicted from land in Hambleton, Lancashire, he used to run his charity Hugo’s Small Animal Rescue and Sanctuary.

He had previously been based at a different site in nearby Staining but amid a lack of funding had re-located.

At around 12.30pm on May 7, Luke was at work when he received a message out of the blue from Bailey’s mum Leanne telling him he had died.



“I went out into the hallway and called my sister,” he explained. “She said ‘can you get to the hospital?’

“I didn’t quite believe her, at first, I was just like Bailey’s done something to himself.”

You're Not Alone EVERY 90 minutes in the UK a life is lost to suicide It doesn’t discriminate, touching the lives of people in every corner of society – from the homeless and unemployed to builders and doctors, reality stars and footballers. It’s the biggest killer of people under the age of 35, more deadly than cancer and car crashes. And men are three times more likely to take their own life than women. Yet it’s rarely spoken of, a taboo that threatens to continue its deadly rampage unless we all stop and take notice, now. Papyrus, www.papyrus-uk.org, 0800 068 41 41

Samaritans,www.samaritans.org, 116 123

However, on arriving at the hospital, Luke was taken to the bereavement room.

“I was thinking, this isn’t right, what’s happened?” he said.

Bailey, just three days from his 23rd birthday, had been found hanged at his house that morning.



At his home, the animal lover had an aviary and two little monkeys he’d reared from birth – since closing the full sanctuary.

As a result, Bailey and his partner had been getting visits from the RSPCA due to bogus reports of animal abuse, Luke claims.

He said: “It was just as if these trolls were making up lies to make his life as difficult as possible before he died.”

It’s unclear why Bailey closed the full sanctuary, but Luke understands he was struggling to keep up with the rent and had previously been reported to the police for the conditions there, though no action had ever been taken.

“It just ruined him because he’d been running that sanctuary since he was a teenager,” said Luke.



“It was just a continuous battle,” he explained. “We just tried to protect him from it and they just kept on going.”



Luke said Bailey had started off by adopting a baby rat when he was 14, who he named Hugo and took to school in his backpack, and who became the inspiration for his later sanctuary.

“We called him Dr Doolittle because even from a young age he would be coming out with facts about animals, it almost felt like he could speak to them,” he said.

He rescued everything from pigeons and skunks to more exotic animals over the years.



Luke last saw Bailey a couple of days before he died.

“He was really excited about grooming dogs from the Coronation Street set… he would basically care for their dogs while they were filming,” he explained.

Luke added: “He seemed in a good place but obviously behind closed doors he was suffering.

“I think he was just putting on a facade for us.”

Following his nephew’s death, Luke said he “made it my mission” to get to the bottom of what had happened, and who was responsible.



He has since collected around one hundred pieces of alleged evidence of the abuse Bailey was enduring, much of which he’s sent to the police.

After an inquest was opened in July, Luke was approached by an anonymous woman on Facebook Messenger who told him she was part of a private WhatsApp messaging group set up to “sabotage” Bailey.

He was then sent screenshots in which participants appeared to use “code words” to mask what they were doing, including plans to steal items from the sanctuary.

“Then in the group chat, they’re laughing about lying to the police,” he added.

“Then when they found out that Bailey had passed away, they’re talking about, ‘I wonder what kind of noose he used.’”



The Sun has seen many of the exchanges.

Following his initial suicide attempt one person wrote “shame” and another added a laughing emoji.

They joked about getting the police out to his sanctuary, describing it as “all fun and games”, and how they’d been messaging Bailey’s donors encouraging them to stop providing him with money.

One message said: “Wow he needs a bullet the cruel f***!” and then in another message revealed Bailey had died before someone responded with “good” before adding: “Sounds bad that, doesn’t it?”

Another person said “bloody good” and “he was a waste of oxygen”.



One message then said: “I bet that childhood, then being a gay c****** through school would’ve battered his mental health.”

Someone else said: “Should have just drowned him at birth.”

However, other group members appear to have changed their tune after Bailey died, saying how much they admired him while turning on other trolls, with one writing: “It’s really sad he ended up that way… a big mess all round.”

A message from the whistleblower to Luke said: “I apologise deeply that I never stuck up for Bailey.”

He told The Sun: “It was all too little too late. What he suffered was horrible and they didn’t care what the outcome was.”



The Sun has approached Lancashire Police for comment.

Click here for Luke’s petition.

News.title: 'I'm telling the truth': Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about Charles in BBC interview
News.content:
Reacting to the rare statement from the Palace, Earl Spencer said: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"

Speaking to the BBC at his Althorp estate, he added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life.

"I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."

Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".

In response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."

When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."

Buckingham Palace declined to give a response to Earl Spencer's fresh comments.

The remarks may bring a renewed focus to the war of words between the Palace and the King's former brother-in-law.

News.title: Watch: Diana's brother says Charles 'went ballistic' in phone call after her death
News.content:
Princess Diana's brother said King Charles "went ballistic" during a phone call with him in the days after his sister's death.

Earl Spencer spoke exclusively with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg about claims he has made in a new book, alleging the then-Prince of Wales said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.

In a strongly-worded response to the book claims, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

Read more about Laura Kuenssberg's interview with Earl Spencer.

News.title: Billionaire Man United owner says he has lost confidence in the UK
News.content:
One of Britain's richest people, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, says he has lost confidence in the UK, describing the country as "on the slide".

The founder of petrochemical giant Ineos, who also owns a large stake in Manchester United, said the UK was in decline due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.

He told the BBC failing to invest further in North Sea oil and gas amounted to "insanity" and warned gas storage was so low that the UK could "run out of gas" if there was a cold snap this winter.

In response to the billionaire's criticism, the government said it was working to deliver growth and that business investment had increased in the last two years.

A spokesperson said they did not foresee any problems with gas supply: "We have a diverse energy mix and are confident in our security of supply."

Sir Jim, whose wealth is estimated to be around Â£15bn, has prompted controversy in the past with his comments on immigration. He was a supporter of Brexit but has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020.

The businessman's UK exit has been followed by other high-profile billionaires, including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos.

Sir Jim said the politics of envy was driving people away from the UK.

"In America they applaud people who create wealth," he said. "Unfortunately the UK has got a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment."

He said for him to return to the UK "things would have to get better".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will take a "pragmatic approach" to oil and gas, but one of the biggest decisions facing the government, whether to give the go-ahead to further development of the oil and gas fields at Rosebank and Jackdaw, is still waiting to be resolved.

Sir Jim criticised the hesitation and suggested high taxes on North Sea operators were threatening the sector's viability. Tax on energy company profits is being reformed, but won't be fully implemented until 2030.

Ineos operates the Forties pipeline which transports about 30% of the UK's North Sea oil.

"You would expect [the government] to exploit our natural resources and we're clearly not doing that. We're shutting it down.

"If you tax everybody to death, they're all going to leave. And that's what's happening."

Recent climate data combined with record heatwaves have given weight to the argument against further exploitation of fossil fuels. However, political pressure has grown on the government to proceed with Rosebank and Jackdaw to support UK jobs, tax revenues and boost energy security.

Sir Jim backed those calls, saying it was "absurd" to import more energy than necessary.

The government spokesperson said that oil and gas would play an important role in the UK "for decades to come", but they added: "The transition to homegrown clean power is the only way to deliver energy and financial security for families and businesses."

News.title: Michael Marra announced as new Scottish Labour leader
News.content:
He went on to thank his opponents, Joe Fagan and Monica Lennon, and praised them for their ideas about how the party needed to change.

He said: "Joe argued for a politics rooted in people and place, for less control in the centre and more control for local communities. That should be the case in our country and in our party.

"Monica was right to say we need to reconnect with the trade union movement that birthed the Labour party.

"Her record delivering change through parliament is also a template for how Labour should behave in opposition â robust in our criticism of the SNP, yes, but also making our own change."

Marra continued: "Scots know what we are against. They can't tell you what we are for... Social justice. Eradication of poverty. Good work. Good housing. Good public services. The good life for working people. An economy where everyone has a fair chance in life, which redistributes power, wealth and opportunity."

News.title: Bitter row over Diana book brings back unhappy times for royals
News.content:
At issue is Earl Spencer's account of a conversation with the then Prince Charles after the death of Diana, with the prince accused of telling Earl Spencer: "We'll forget her soon enough."

He is accused of sounding "giddily elated" and like a "lottery winner" after the news of her death.

Buckingham Palace hit back with a response, which although dressed in courtier-like politeness, was essentially saying the conversation had never happened like that.

The King was said to be "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways that others do not recognise".

Anyone who has lost someone knows how feelings can run high, people can hear different things about the same conversations - and families can fall out, or come together, in the wake of a death.

Psychotherapist Nick Hatter says he doesn't have a view on which version of events is correct, but he says that during traumatic events memories can be "distorted". A phone call doesn't have any of the visual clues or body language to give a fuller picture, he adds.

Hatter says there can be very different and unpredictable responses to grief, including a condition known as "bereavement mania" where someone can seem inappropriately hyper or even euphoric after the loss of a loved one.

The first opinion poll on who to believe has been published by YouGov - and it suggests a very split view, with 31% believing Earl Spencer's allegations, 36% suspecting it's not true and 33% saying they don't know.

Low thinks the book is unlikely to change many opinions, as "people have settled into their camps about how they regard Charles, how they look back on the Diana years".

There could also be a feeling that it's "tawdry" to rake up these claims so many years later, he says.

That's echoed by historian and author Sir Anthony Seldon who says Earl Spencer showed great courage at the time of Diana's funeral, but says his memoir is a "sad and unnecessary publication".

Royal commentator Richard Palmer says the book threatens to take the royals back to the difficult days of 1997.

"This book and the run-up to next year's 30th anniversary of Diana's death threaten to undermine the Royal Household's three decades of work to rehabilitate Charles and Camilla's image," he says.

Veteran broadcaster David Dimbleby, who led the BBC's coverage of Diana's funeral, said it seemed "odd" Earl Spencer would release the book now.

"Why 30 years later for God's sake you should do it... you have to ask him," he said on Radio 4's Today programme, adding he wished the appetite for the "cycle of gossip" would decline and instead that focus would shift to what kind of monarchy the country needed.

News.title: Daisy Edgar-Jones: I try and bury my emotion when it comes to love
News.content:
Daisy Edgar-Jones has been well cast in her new film.

She plays Elinor, the rational elder sister in Sense and Sensibility, opposite the younger, more romantic sister Marianne.

Speaking to the BBC, Edgar-Jones says that in her personal life, she really is like her character.

"When it comes to love, I think I am very much more Elinor in every sort of way," she says.

"I definitely lead a lot with my head and try and push aside, bury my emotion."

But she notes that one of the joys of the film is seeing Elinor learn to enjoy a "wilder, passionate side" of herself. "And I feel like I learnt to do that too," she says.

Best known for starring in hit TV series Normal People with Paul Mescal, Edgar-Jones, 28, is now taking on a lead role in the latest adaptation of Jane Austen's book.

Ahead of its release, sheâs been talking to me about whether we really need another Sense and Sensibility film (spoiler: yes. âThe more the merrier, in my opinion.â)

She also told me why young people today can still see themselves in Jane Austen's stories - and gave me her take on whether her friend and former co-star Mescal should be the next James Bond.

News.title: I found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and I want others to do the same
News.content:
Mary Timby was fed up with dating apps when she booked a trip to Ireland on a whim last summer - from the comfort of her Colorado couch.

The spur-of-the-moment trip was unlike her: Timby, 39, is a self-described "total planner".

But she'd always wanted to visit Ireland, and she found herself exhausted by the local dating scene while navigating a career transition. And then she remembered a few throwaway lines from a comedy series about a matchmaking festival in Ireland.

So she looked it up - and not only was the Lisdoonvarna Matchmaking Festival real, it was also taking place during the entire month of September, when she was scheduled to visit.

Now, a little more than a year later, Timby is reaping the benefits of that uncharacteristic last-minute decision: She's become a viral star. She's found love with an Irishman she met at a pub called The Matchmaker. And she's even started a new business venture - bringing others to Lisdoonvarna who hope to follow in her footsteps.

News.title: From 'fusty' to fashionable - is it cool to wear M&S clothes now?
News.content:
The retailer has been focusing on "newer styles and relevant trends" to attract younger customers, says Illis.

But she says that this has been achieved without compromising on quality which is what keeps M&S's core audience on board.

"They have created a modern version of everything we know and love - cashmere staples, knitwear and the lingerie department," says Nnadi.

Clark agrees that M&S has been nailing "funnel neck [styles] and barrel jeans, which are filtering down from high fashion".

M&S has perhaps been fortunate to rebrand at a time when consumer habits are changing, as young shoppers consider buying capsule wardrobes - a smaller number of staple pieces that can be styled in a variety of ways.

According to Clark, the idea of wear-it-once fast fashion has declined as people "are looking for [foundational pieces] to rotate".

This is something Perrie Sian, one of Britain's biggest fashion influencers, has also noticed. The 34-year-old tells the BBC: "The real height of fast fashion is behind us".

"As a group we've changed our shopping habits and M&S slots into that," she says. "In my content and with lots of other creators we're showing people how to wear things in multiple ways, how to look after them."

She added that she is noticing "people are willing to spend a little bit more" on wardrobe staples and items that "wash well and are made of cotton, not acrylic or polyester".

News.title: Parents could lose benefits or face prison for child's crimes, minister says
News.content:
Parents could lose their benefits or face prison sentences for their children's crimes under reforms to the youth justice system, a minister has said.

Youth Justice Minister Jake Richards told the Times newspaper the system "should hold parents to account in a proportionate way for ensuring that they play their role in keeping communities safe".

His comments come after the government set out plans in May to strengthen and expand Parenting Orders, which can currently compel parents or guardians to address their child's behaviour by attending counselling sessions or face fines.

Richards said prison sentences would only apply "in the most extreme cases" and would be up to judges' discretion.

He described the proposed changes in England and Wales as part of a "carrot-and-stick" approach.

"Parenting orders are going to make sure that parents are more involved in the process by which we try to turn around young offenders," Richards told the Times.

"Yes, that will have some stick. It could be custodial, or docking benefits - ultimately it will be up to a judge. But we want them to be more involved and that comes with responsibilities as well."

Critics of the proposals say engaging with parents on a voluntary basis is generally more effective in building trusting relationships and providing support.

Jess Mullen, chief executive of the Alliance for Youth Justice which represents more than 70 organisations that advocate for children, previously questioned how putting parents in prison would provide "stability or support for the child".

Andrew Neilson, director of campaigns at the Howard League for Penal Reform, told the BBC: "Reforming parenting orders in this way risks being ineffective at best and counter-productive at worst.

"Criminalising parents is unlikely to help children who need support, and putting them behind bars would only put further strain on a failing prison system that is already bursting at the seams."

When the government white paper was announced in May, then Justice Secretary David Lammy said that strengthening parenting orders would mean "there are real consequences for parents and carers who wilfully fail to support efforts to address their children's behaviour."

He told BBC Breakfast at the time that if a parent was struggling, then the "judge can intervene to make sure that the young person is getting the support that they need and the parent is doing the best that they can".

He also said he expected the power to jail parents to be used "very, very rarely".

Courts are currently required to consider issuing a Parenting Order where a child under 16 has been convicted of an offence.

They can also consider an order for 16 and 17-year-olds if they believe this would help prevent further offences.

The term of the order must not exceed 12 months and breach of a parenting order is a criminal offence with a maximum Â£1,000 fine, according to the Sentencing Council.

However, government statistics show the use of parenting orders has declined in recent years, from more than 1,000 orders in 2009/10 to just 33 in 2022/23.

The government's youth justice reform plans come after Phase One of the Southport Inquiry report found "catastrophic" failures by the parents of the Southport killer Axel Rudakubana and various agencies meant clear chances to prevent the 2024 child murders were missed.

In the interview with the Times, Richards also rejected calls from lawyers to raise the age of criminal responsibility from 10, saying it would undermine "public faith" in the justice system and it was "not a priority at all".

In June, the Bar Council, the representative body for barristers in England and Wales, said the threshold should rise to 14 due to criminalisation at such an early age not being an "effective, proportionate or just response".

The United Nations has previously pointed out the UK has some of the lowest ages of criminal responsibility in the world and that it should rise it to the UN recommendation of at least 14.

On Thursday, ministers met with local leaders and experts in Manchester to discuss how devolution could help reform youth justice.

Additional reporting by AndrÃ© Rhoden-Paul & Shelley Phelps, political correspondent

News.title: Temperatures could peak at 26C as summerlike warmth returns next week
News.content:
Temperatures could peak at 26C next week as late summer warmth returns to parts of the UK.

Southern areas will experience the highest temperatures, but most locations will be warmer than normal for late September.

Warmth could last all week for some in England and Wales, but it might only be a short-lived boost for Scotland and Northern Ireland.

The high pressure, which is responsible for the warmth, will also mean little rain for places continuing to experience drought conditions.

News.title: 'Fast, furious and dangerous' - a city's quad bike menace
News.content:
Sitting in his Birmingham city centre apartment, one resident says he can often hear them before he sees them.

The sound of revving engines is followed by groups of quad bikes and off-road motorcycles weaving through traffic, performing wheelies and riding through some of the busiest streets in the city.

"It's only a matter of time until something serious happens," he said.

Videos shared on social media over recent months have captured groups of riders travelling through areas including Hurst Street, Bristol Road and Corporation Street, often with faces covered and no visible number plates.

One video filmed by the resident showed a pedestrian narrowly avoiding being struck as a group rode through the city centre.

"I've watched them and they go through red lights, they just totally ignore the red lights," he said.

"People still cross when the pedestrian lights are green, but they don't even slow down to check.

"They're zigzagging in the middle of cars. No number-plates. It's bad because nobody sees any action happening and it's only a matter of time until something serious happens."

News.title: A village familiar with tragedy mourns Noah Woods
News.content:
Canon Yvonne Tulloch founded the charity Ataloss after the death of her husband in 2008. As chief executive, she campaigns for more support for those navigating grief.

She said that as a society, we are not good at acknowledging grief - preferring to convince ourselves that we will live until old age; because of this, emotions can be suppressed and come to the fore following high-profile cases.

"We assume it's next of kin who will be the grievers and, while that is correct, it is not the whole picture.

"There are these ripples, there will be people who will grieve who we wouldn't assume would be doing so.

"Because we've been so poor at understanding grief, what can happen even more is when there is a tragedy that is near to us it makes us think it could have been us - particularly when it involves a child and you're a parent who can relate to it."

Tulloch added this can be "confusing" because those removed from a tragedy can feel they do not have a right to grieve.

She said: "Those who helped with the search have done so because they felt helpless. Equally there will be those who did not help and feel they should have done more.

"In most cases people will have made their decision for sensible reasons and you have to release yourself from guilt and realise you did the best you could."

For the family, there is a balance between appreciating the community support, but not being overwhelmed by it, she said.

"The important thing is not to isolate the family because you do not know what to say.

"People fear saying the wrong thing, but it takes nothing more than acknowledging somebody and saying, 'I'm so sorry, I just want you to know I care'.

"It can mean even more coming from a stranger."

Annie Owen, who volunteers at Ipswich and East Suffolk Samaritans, said that in the modern world, the overload of information can anaesthetise people to many tragedies.

"But for this pure innocent child, there is nowhere to put our reactions or our grief," she said.

Owen said it was important that people do not "beat themselves up" over what they did or did not do.

"So if anybody can find the way of looking at themselves and just thinking, this hurts right now because I'm decent, because I'm caring, because I have a heart. And I think that's a way of easing ourselves through it."

If you, or someone you know, have been affected by child bereavement, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line

News.title: Politician who switched from Reform to Plaid 'lied about her beliefs', says Richard Tice
News.content:
Reform UK's deputy leader has accused the party's former Senedd Member Sarah Cooper-Lesadd of lying to them about her political beliefs before she defected to Plaid Cymru.

Richard Tice was speaking after a chaotic week for his party in which its Welsh leader resigned after being arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.

Helen Jenner, the party's deputy leader in Wales, is favourite to take over next week.

Tice insisted the events had not distracted the party from the issues it was tackling, saying there were good days and bad days in politics.

Plaid Cymru said Cooper-Lesadd had been "honest about her political beliefs" and had acknowledged her views had changed.

Sarah Cooper-Lesadd, who was elected to the Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg constituency, made the dramatic political move to Plaid Cymru, claiming Reform UK was "far more interested in division, opposition and headlines than in finding solutions".

As well as saying she was now a supporter of Welsh independence, she also revealed she had voted to Remain in the EU referendum a decade ago.

News.title: Police release CCTV of missing Lillia's last sighting
News.content:
The latest sighting at 10:36 at Piccadilly bus station on Monday follows a previous one earlier that morning when Lillia was seen boarding the number 36 bus from Salford.

Ch Supt Helen Critchley said: "Officers are making every effort to locate Lillia, and our team have been working through hours of CCTV footage and exploring every avenue to try and find her.

"I can now confirm that our last known current sighting was of Lillia at Manchester Piccadilly bus station at 10.36am on the morning of Monday 14 September.

"We can also share that she exited the number 36 bus at Piccadilly, with her boarding it in Salford.

"That bus service travels from Bolton through Salford and into Manchester city centre.

"If anyone has any information regarding Lillia's whereabouts or movements from this bus â or you were on the bus at the time she was also on there or when she got on in Salford or off in Piccadilly â please contact us via 101 or the Major Incident Portal below."

News.title: About 280 people evacuated after fire at seaside hotel
News.content:
About 280 people have been evacuated from a seaside hotel after a fire broke out overnight.

Kent Fire and Rescue Service said 26 fire engines were sent to the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone at about 01:05 BST. In an update at 08:30, it said 10 fire engines remained at the scene "dampening down any remaining hotspots".

Station manager Lawrence Pater said the "very severe" fire had raised concerns about the structural integrity of the building, and that it was seeking advice from inspectors.

Folkestone and Hythe District Council has set up a welfare centre at the Three Hills Sports Park and nearby residents have been advised to avoid the area of the fire and close windows and doors.

"We are supporting all emergency services involved in the response and their efforts to get people to safety", said the council.

South East Coast Ambulance Service said it assessed a number of people at the scene and one person was taken to hospital with minor injuries.

A spokesperson for Britannia Hotels Group, which runs the Grand Burstin, said it was "taking immediate action to ensure the safety and wellbeing of all guests and team members".

"Emergency services are on site and we are fully cooperating with the authorities to support those affected and assist with the ongoing response", it added.

Ross Honeycomb, 39, was staying at the hotel with his family and told the BBC they were woken by fire alarms at about 01:00.

He said: "I thought I was dreaming, it was horrifying.

"We looked out and there was smoke billowing from the underground car park. Later we started hearing explosions.

News.title: 'Our flat has been for sale for four years': Why is the market so weak?
News.content:
In 2015, thousands of people queued overnight in the rain to reserve and buy studio apartments selling for under Â£200,000 in Hounslow, west London.

It's in stark contrast to today's appetite for flats, with property portals reporting a slump in sales.

But why, when the country is in a housing crisis with a desperate need for affordable homes, are flats now struggling to sell?

According to the property site Zoopla, 88% of flats listed for sale in inner London on its website in 2025 did not find a buyer within six months. The company also says the gap between the value of a flat and a house is the widest it has been for 30 years.

Executive director Richard Donnell points to post-pandemic social changes with "people looking for space, prioritising houses, working from home".

He also points to higher mortgage rates, people concerned about "all the costs and liabilities of owning a property" including service charges and ground rents.

In September, nearly all the major mortgage lenders in the UK announced increases in the cost of home loans.

Donnell says flats in inner London are struggling in particular as they are more expensive, the service charges are higher, and "there's greater complexity - it's highly likely it's a bigger building, maybe more of a complex building, so less are selling within six months".

News.content:

Millwall goalkeeper Filip Marschall alleged that West Ham forward Taty Castellanos spat at him during the meeting of the London rivals at The Den on Saturday.

The incident came during the second half of the derby and as goalkeeper Marschall delayed releasing the ball from his hands while his side were leading 2-0.

The West Ham forward Taty looked to close Marschall down before he picked up the ball, before the players appeared to get involved in an altercation in the penalty area.

Marschall then appeared to point towards his jersey, gesturing that he was spat at, while Sky Sports reported that the fourth official confirmed an allegation of spitting had been lodged by Millwall staff. TV footage of the incident was inconclusive.

Lions boss Alex Neil confirmed the allegation afterwards, saying: “I believe so. Fil was saying to the referee throughout the game when that happened, at that point.

Millwall goalkeeper Filip Marschall speaks with referee Paul Tierney during the match against West Ham ( Getty )

“Obviously I’m so far away so it’s hard for me to see what happened, but I wouldn’t presume Fil would say that without cause, if you like, so I don’t know. I’m sure the referees and the authorities, whoever, will look at it and if it warrants that it needs dealt with, I’m sure they will.”

Hammers boss Nuno Espirito Santo said: “I didn’t see, so I’m not going to comment on any allegations. I didn’t see it. And that’s not what we should be speaking about [in] this game, this game has much to speak about, it was a very intense game for both fans.”

Millwall and West Ham were meeting for the first time in 14 years, following the Hammers’ relegation to the Championship, with a large-scale Metropolitan Police operation planned in east London.

Millwall dominated the first half at The Den and led the Championship leaders 2-0 when the flashpoint occurred.

Marschall had the ball in his hands when he was closed down by West Ham forward Taty. Confusingly, referee Paul Tierney then appeared to signal a corner after Marschall went over the eight seconds permitted to restart play.

West Ham quickly took the corner, with Taty crossing for fellow half-time substitute Pablo to finish into the empty net, but referee Tierney halted the play and summoned both captains to the penalty box and instead signalled for Marschall to restart play.

Argentine forward Taty then closed down Marschall for a second time, with the goalkeeper delaying the restart before picking the ball up, which is when the alleged spitting incident reportedly took place.

Sky Sports reported that Marschall delayed releasing the ball because he claimed that Taty had spat at him, with the Millwall coaching staff reporting the allegations to the fourth official on the touchline.

The incident was also something of a turning point in a pulsating east London derby, with West Ham recovering from an awful start to salvage a 2-2 draw at The Den.

West Ham’s Mohamadou Kante pulled one back from 25 yards in the 74th minute before Konstantinos Mavropanos grabbed the equaliser in the 80th minute when he headed in a cross.

Kante was then sent off for pulling down Millwall’s Kyrell Lisbie when he was the last man and Lisbie was through on goal, but the 10 men of West Ham held on to claim a point.

More follows

News.title: Brighton v Arsenal LIVE: Champions face early Premier League test against high-flying Seagulls
News.content:
Arsenal face high-flying Brighton in the Premier League ( Reuters )

Brighton host Arsenal in a clash between the Premier League leaders and Fabian Hurzeler’s high-flying side, with the Gunners looking to maintain their perfect start to the season.

The defending champions have recorded seven wins from seven games in all competitions so far this season, extending that record with a 2-0 win at Sunderland last weekend that featured plenty of drama as Mikel Arteta raged over the Black Cats being awarded a penalty - which David Raya went on to save.

Brighton meanwhile are fresh from a 5-0 drubbing of Coventry City in the top flight, with the highlight a long-range Lewis Dunk wonder-goal, and a 3-2 comeback win over Manchester United in an entertaining Carabao Cup clash on Wednesday night - inflicting a first home defeat from 2-0 up on United in 50 years.

This fixture sparked a war of words last season as Hurzeler criticised Arsenal for time-wasting at set-pieces, but the pair said prior to this match that they had smoothed over their differences and Arteta looked forward to “a beautiful game”.

News.content:

Gossip Girl star Kelly Rutherford was among the stars who joined the front row at London Fashion Week as the royal-approved designer Patrick McDowell made a case for falling in love with your clothes.

The American actress wore a plum McDowell design and sat alongside Leomie Anderson and British Fashion Council chief executive Laura Weir at the designer’s spring/summer 2027 show, titled simply Love, which explored the sentimental value of the pieces people keep returning to.

open image in gallery Kelly Rutherford wore a plum Patrick McDowell coat dress to their SS27 show (Lara Owen/PA)

McDowell’s profile has risen considerably since receiving the Queen Elizabeth II Award for British Design from the Princess of Wales in May 2025.

Having now dressed the likes of the Princess of Wales, Sarah Jessica Parker and Dame Helen Mirren, the designer transformed Yeomanry House, an army facility in central London, into an unlikely setting for a collection filled with wildflowers, a mirrored runway and blooming, romantic silhouettes.

open image in gallery The Princess of Wales (left) in Patrick McDowell in June (Chris Jackson/PA)

“Love is a complicated thing,” McDowell said.

“An emotion so strong it can bind you to someone or something for life.”

For the Liverpool-born designer, that feeling extends beyond relationships to the clothes people keep for years, long after they have ceased to be fashionable.

“I have always been fascinated by the power of clothes and how they have the ability to communicate to the world who we want to be,” they said.

“They can give us the ability to face the days that feel impossible. A good outfit is not to be underestimated.”

open image in gallery Dame Helen Mirren wearing AW26/7 Patrick McDowell to The Olivier Awards in April (Ian West/PA)

The collection, they explained, was a selection of special pieces “designed to make you feel good, look good and embrace love”.

As guests arrived at the military venue, they were greeted by an artist drawing portraits of McDowell-dressed attendees while Aspinal of London keyrings emblazoned with the word “Love” were placed on seats, offering a touching reminder of the collection’s theme.

Inside, the sound of running water accompanied a silver mirrored runway, with wildflowers blooming at one end and reflected across the floor like a lake.

The soundtrack was equally romantic, opening with Etta James’s At Last mixed with Rihanna’s Umbrella, before moving into strings.

It was an eclectic combination, but then love has never been particularly concerned with consistency.

open image in gallery Models on the catwalk at the Patrick McDowell show at Yeomanry House, London, during London Fashion Week. Picture date: Saturday September 19, 2026.

The clothes began with green – not the acid shades that have appeared elsewhere this fashion month, but lush, botanical tones reminiscent of new growth.

Flowers appeared throughout the collection, from overt appliqué roses to silhouettes that seemed to mimic the shape of an upside-down bloom.

One of McDowell’s personal favourite pieces, the Sylvia jacket, opened the show, reworking classic tailoring in green-striped silk-wool georgette, with a structured shape, peplum waist and silk roses.

It captured much of what the designer does well – taking something familiar, such as a blazer, and making it feel special enough to hold on to.

open image in gallery McDowell’s favourite ‘Sylvia jacket’ on the runway (Yui Mok/PA)

There was a strong sense of the 1930s and forties throughout, decades McDowell frequently returns to for inspiration.

Waists were drawn in with a nod to Christian Dior’s post-war New Look while shoulders were carefully structured and skirts fell just below the knee, creating a cool, mid-century silhouette.

A powder-pink skirt suit, with its asymmetric collar, jewelled buttons and sharply-pleated midi skirt, looked as though it could have been lifted from the wardrobe of a forties film star.

open image in gallery Powder pink peppered the collection (Yui Mok/PA)

Elsewhere, a pale-blue shirtdress was given a more theatrical touch with a dramatically wide, flat-brimmed black hat, while a white skirt suit offered a cleaner interpretation of the same ladylike silhouette.

open image in gallery Classic McDowell designs were also present (Yui Mok/PA)

The palette gradually moved from green into sky blue, with black providing sharper accents to contrast the softness.

One high-low skirt – a 2010s trend set to return to fashion – combined a busy floral print with an exaggerated pale-blue hem and layers of black tulle. Paired with a sleeveless black top, it brought a slight edge to a collection otherwise preoccupied with the prettiness of flowers.

open image in gallery ‘High-low’ skirts seem to be a returning trend this season (Yui Mok/PA)

The collection offered a rather more glamorous take on the 2010s return of business casual, a decade in which McDowell exclaimed “are back” before the show.

Across New York and London Fashion Week, designers have been revisiting office staples, from pencil skirts to cropped-sleeve blazers and capri trousers.

McDowell’s version was considerably more feminine, with sculpted peplums, ruffled tulle and three-quarter-length trousers that appeared more suited to a long lunch than a Monday commute.

open image in gallery Models on the catwalk at the Patrick McDowell show at Yeomanry House, London, during London Fashion Week. Picture date: Saturday September 19, 2026.

McDowell’s collaboration with Aspinal of London was evident in the accessories, as with floral handbags reinforcing the collection’s central motif.

One compact pale-blue bag accompanied a brightly-coloured floral shirtdress, its pink, blue and green print offering a less formal way into the collection’s otherwise highly polished approach to dressing.

Flowers have become something of a signature for McDowell, but this season they felt less nostalgic and more personal. The collection was not simply about dressing romantically, but about finding something worth keeping.

open image in gallery A jacquard floral white gown on the runway (Yui Mok/PA)

To round off the show was the McDowell bride, who stepped out in a strapless, double-layered bubble-hem dress with an tightly fitted headpiece.

It was a striking departure from the traditional lace and tulle veils, bringing a modern quality to the collection’s otherwise traditional symbols of romance.

The look also demonstrated how McDowell expertly grapples with volume in their designs. With a focus on the waist once again, rather than simply making a dress bigger, they manipulates its proportions until the silhouette itself becomes the decoration.

For all its talk of love, this was not a collection concerned with dressing for someone else. McDowell seemed more interested in the relationship we have with our own wardrobes, and that the most enduring love affair might be with the clothes we never want to part with.

News.content:
