Four in 10 Brexit backers think Andy Burnham should strengthen defence ties with Europe, new polling a decade on from the EU referendum shows.

Overall, half of all voters want to prioritise stronger security links with European allies, while only a tiny number, one in 10, believe the UK should co-operate more with the US.

The findings, from pollsters Savanta, show that with an “aggressive Putin and an unpredictable Trump” undermining global security Mr Burnham cannot stick to Labour's Brexit red lines, the Liberal Democrats, who commissioned the polling, said on the first day of their annual conference in Brighton.

open image in gallery Support for rejoining the EU has never been higher ( AFP/Getty )

Mr Burnham has vowed to honour Sir Keir Starmer’s decision to rule out rejoining the customs union and single market or allowing free movement of people, despite saying he wants to be “bolder” than his predecessor in resetting relations with the bloc.

But the Lib Dems said the policy is a “risk to our national security”.

The party has called for a new ‘growth and defence partnership’ with Europe, to both protect the continent in the face of Russian aggression and give a welcome boost to the UK's economy.

It would include membership of the single market and a new security council, in a move that would help protect the UK’s border and boost British industry, supporting high-skilled jobs in areas like shipbuilding and aerospace, the party said.

Among those supporting prioritised defence links with European allies were 25 per cent of Reform UK voters, the poll found.

Lib Dem Europe spokesperson Al Pinkerton said: “Ambitiously rebuilding our defence and trade ties with Europe is the biggest step this government could take to turbocharge economic growth and bolster Britain's defences.

“The public sees this clearly – yet Starmer stuck his head in the sand, and Burnham now risks becoming continuity-Keir.”

He called on No 10 to put a Growth and Defence Partnership “on the table, which includes a new UK-EU defence pact and the UK joining the single market. With an aggressive Putin and unpredictable Trump undermining global security, sticking to outdated red lines is no longer just timid; it is a risk to our national security”.

Mr Burnham is facing growing pressure over his decision to keep to Sir Keir’s red lines.

In an exclusive interview with The Independent, former Labour leader Neil Kinnock said the new prime minister should not be “constrained” by them, adding that those who “love their country” will want to return to the European Union.

And earlier this month former Tory chancellor George Osborne told this publication that Britain’s economy had “fallen off a cliff” since Brexit and that rejoining the EU’s customs union would be the swiftest route to recovery.

It comes as polling guru professor Sir John Curtice told The Independent that support for rejoining the European Union was now at its highest level since the Brexit vote. But he warned political leaders needed to seize the opportunity or it will all come to nothing.

Savanta interviewed 2,376 UK adults between 4 and 7 September.

A government spokesperson said: “Europe faces the most dangerous security environment since the Cold War, and we are stepping up alongside our allies to build a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO.

"That is why we are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will improve our security and unlock good growth in every postcode."

Jakob Ingebrigtsen put in a late surge but was unable to hold on for gold in the 5000m at the World Road Running Championships, with the Norwegian pipped to the line by Eritrea’s Dawit Seare.

A quick race was led out by Frenchman Flavien Szot, with the lead chopping and changing until Ethiopia’s Mezgebu Sime charged to the front with around a kilometre to go in Copenhagen.

He strung out the field behind him but Seare was quickly onto his shoulder and stormed clear – but Ingebrigtsen, in scenes reminiscent of his charge to 5000m gold on the track at the European Championships last month, made up a huge gap to the 21-year-old.

He came around Seare in the final 200m and victory looked inevitable but he faded just 100m later and Seare pounced, reeling him back in and celebrating by pointing to the sky as he crossed the line in a national record time of 12:56. Ingebrigtsen’s silver medal came with a consolation prize of a national record of his own, 12:59.

Seare’s compatriot Saywon Amanuel was third in a personal best of 13 minutes flat, while France’s Jimmy Gressier, who had run a world-leading 12:51 earlier this year, was 14th in 13:17.

Ethiopia’s Likina Amebaw continued a brilliant end to her season a week after clinching Ultimate gold in the 5000m, sprinting clear of the field to win the women’s 5k in a season’s best time of 14:41.

She was seven seconds clear of Kenya’s Caroline Makandi Gitonga, with Rose Davies of Australia completing the podium in an area record 14:50. Britain’s Hannah Nuttall was down in 10th but nonetheless finished strongly in a personal best 15:08.

open image in gallery Seare pulled away from Ingebrigtsen in the final 100m ( AP )

Earlier on Saturday Agathe Guillemot won the women’s mile with a stunning run to overhaul frontrunner Freweyni Hailu – who had stretched out the field – in the closing couple of hundred metres.

The Frenchwoman stuck with her before powering away to win the world title in a world-leading time of 4:22.74, with Hailu unable to respond to her kick. She dropped to the ground and screamed in delight and shock before she was congratulated by her rivals.

Ethiopia’s Hailu took silver in a season’s best time of 4:24.35, with Kenyan Mirriam Cherop third in a season’s best 4:25.71. Home hopeful Annemarie Nissen was delighted as she finished fourth in a new personal best of 4:26.78.

There was a shock in the men’s mile as the USA’s Yared Nuguse led from the start but was reeled in by Germany’s Robert Farken in the latter stages, winning in a world-leading 3:51.80, with Nuguse forced to settle for silver in a season’s best 3:52.33. Luxembourg’s Ruben Querinjean set a new national record as he took bronze, 3:52.77.

Britain’s Jake Heyward was 11th in a new personal best, 3:55.76.

News.title: GPs summoned in Frankfurt as third malaria death reported
News.content:
While malaria is treatable if caught early, the patients were likely not considered to have the disease because they lacked travel history to countries where malaria typically circulates, meaning treatment was delayed.

“This is why we alerted the medical people in Frankfurt, if you have odd cases presenting at your clinic, please also consider that there might be malaria around,” Dr Tinnemann said.

“There is this assumption that people who get sick with a nasty fever in places like Frankfurt and elsewhere that have not travelled cannot have malaria, and we don’t bother to investigate. That’s got to stop. That’s why these people die,” Joe Lines, Professor of Malaria Control and Vector Biology at the London School of Tropical Hygiene and Medicine, told The Telegraph.

Before the two cases in Schwanheim – both of which occurred at least 3 miles from the airport where the first malaria cases were reported – investigators were working on the hypothesis that just a single mosquito was responsible for the outbreak, but the new cases have cast doubt on that theory.

“We expect mosquitoes to live between one and three weeks on average,” said Dr Tinnemann.

“We had five cases in the beginning of July, then another in August - at that point, there was a good chance that potentially it could just be one bug. But now it seems at least there must be one other,” he said.

Frankfurt’s public health board have now shipped blood samples from all eight patients to a specialised lab in Antwerp, Belgium, where scientists can carry out DNA analysis to indicate if the infections came from one or multiple mosquitoes, and are awaiting results.

As temperatures warm, experts fear that several tropical mosquito-borne diseases – including malaria, dengue fever, Zika virus, and chikungunya could become established across Europe.

Earlier this month, a colony of Aedes aeypti mosquitoes – the bugs responsible for transmitting dengue and Zika virus – were found breeding in a residential area in East London for the first time.

Airfinity, the disease-monitoring company, said of the malaria outbreak in Frankfurt: “the risk to the wider public remains low but non-zero.”

“Continued vector surveillance, rapid diagnosis, and ready access to antimalarials are critical to prevent further severe outcomes.”

News.title: Global fund utilises AI to tackle malaria, TB, and HIV amid aid cuts
News.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is helping to soften the blow from aid cuts, according to one of the world’s biggest development funds.

The Global Fund, which raises and invests billions of pounds to reduce the burden of HIV, tuberculosis (TB) and malaria globally says new AI-driven products like portable pregnancy scanners are helping to mitigate the funding gap.

“[We] have adapted pretty quickly to the changes in the funding environment; it has undoubtedly had negative impacts on health outcomes [...], but in some ways, the resilience of life-saving services has been remarkable,” Peter Sands, the executive director of the Global Fund, told The Telegraph.

The Global Fund is managing a $6 billion (£4.4bn) shortfall for the period 2026 to 2028 and has been forced to make difficult decisions to continue their work, it confirmed this week.

The gap comes as Western governments shift money from foreign aid to defence. The UK reduced its contribution to the fund by 15 per cent last year to £850 million, down from £1 billion.

But Mr Sands said investments in tools to tackle infectious diseases – including those driven by AI – are starting to pay off.

“Innovation is absolutely part of the answer when money is short. One of the few ways you can get to make the money go further is to have a better tool, a better way of doing things,” Mr Sands said.

News.title: Thomas Tuchel faces fight to win trust of England players
News.content:
Thomas Tuchel faces a fight to regain the full trust of his England players, despite claiming that “99.9 per cent” of supporters do not talk about the semi-final defeat by Argentina.

Telegraph Sport reported that players were shocked and disappointed by Tuchel’s approach to the final 30 minutes of the World Cup semi-final.

It can now be revealed that doubts linger among England players over Tuchel’s ability to get the best out of his squad and ultimately lead them to glory in the next European Championship.

There is also some lasting unhappiness over Tuchel’s perceived unwillingness to take ultimate responsibility for England’s World Cup exit and his claim that ball possession was not in “the DNA” of the nation’s players.

Tuchel has spoken of fostering a “brotherhood” within the England squad, but a source told Telegraph Sport: “He still has work to do to get all the players fully behind him again. What happened at the World Cup and some of his comments caused some damage that has not just disappeared.”

Tuchel has no concerns over the commitment of his players and said: “I have no doubt how keen they are. No doubt. I know them, I was seven weeks with them. We had a qualification campaign together, we are 18 months together, I have no doubt that we step up and produce performances in the next cycle. I’m responsible for that.”

One player who did not travel to the World Cup and is not part of Tuchel’s latest England squad for four Nations League games is Morgan Gibbs-White. His partner, Britney De Villiers, took a swipe at Tuchel by posting an image on Instagram that referenced the fact the Nottingham Forest man is the only Premier League player to have created five or more chances in every match he has played this season.

News.title: Fiji declares national crisis as HIV epidemic escalates
News.content:
“The rollout has been slow and frustrating, and Fiji will pay for it in terms of lives lost,” said Prof Lisa Maher, an epidemiologist at the Kirby Institute in Sydney who is supporting Fiji’s response. “This is the only thing that will turn the epidemic around and stop people dying, and stop onward transmission of HIV to the general population.”

But the emergency declaration should provide political cover to introduce the needle and syringe programme, with a Cabinet subcommittee now created to remove barriers to action.

“The government is signalling that it is prepared to act in this particularly important and controversial area,” said Prof Maher. “It’s not coincidental that the draft bill [to legalise the distribution of needles and syringes for certain groups] now looks likely to go before parliament, after being blocked for 10 months… So it’s not just symbolic.”

Dr Jason Mitchell, head of Fiji’s HIV taskforce, added: “Since the government announced [the crisis], it has followed with some very rapid actions in progressing the needle and syringe programme. So that is being fast tracked through the necessary channels, and the government is determined to get that out in the next couple of weeks.

“We’ve gotten to the point where we really needed to take some really strong action,” he told The Telegraph. “This is the government realising that there have been challenges, and they need to step it up.”

It is hoped that the declaration will also turbocharge other elements of the response – for instance the scale-up of the post-exposure prophylaxis (Prep) scheme, which was introduced in May – as the virus gains a foothold in the broader population.

Although there has been a major focus on testing, treatment and education, UNAIDS still estimates that only 39 per cent of an estimated 9,100 people living with HIV in 2025 knew their positive status. Just 22 per cent were accessing antiretroviral treatment, and 117 people died in 2025, compared to 25 in 2021.

News.title: Floyd Samba’s Man City debut double has father Chris dancing
News.content:
There was very much a Samba beat to this Manchester City victory – and it almost had a famous father in the crowd up dancing.

This was a night when Brazilian Allan Elias scored his first goal on an enterprising first appearance for City.

But it was another debutant who stole the show as the Carabao Cup holders sailed past Norwich City to set up a fourth-round meeting with Brighton.

Floyd Samba scored two fine goals and had a hand in another on a dream debut that had his beaming dad up off his seat and thrusting his arms in the air as if ready to party.

If the Samba surname feels familiar, that is because Floyd’s father Christopher played more than 200 games for Blackburn Rovers, Queens Park Rangers and Aston Villa.

In fact, it was very much a family affair as Floyd’s brothers Tyrone and Emerson, who are also in City’s academy and hoping one day to tread a similar path, joined in the jubilant celebrations alongside their mother, a visibly emotional Theresa.

News.title: Banton shows his worth as England cruise to series victory against Sri Lanka
News.content:
A patchy Test team and a one-day international side learning on the job should not obscure the fact that under Harry Brook, England have built a formidable T20 outfit.

Missing a slew of first-choice players, they dispatched Sri Lanka with a game to spare and an emphatic show of their depth in the format, with Sonny Baker and Tom Banton – two men still finding their feet in the side – to the fore. England have now won 20 of the 23 completed T20s since Brook took over last year, and six matches in a row this summer. It is easily their best format and, as Liam Dawson said, they have “match-winners throughout” and plenty of “freak” performers.

In this six-wicket win, Baker’s one for 15 limited England’s target to a paltry 146, which Banton, a natural opener who is being recommissioned in the middle order, helped knock off with 47 balls remaining. “Tonight was a special performance, very clinical,” said Brook.

News.title: Interest rate increase ‘likely’, warns Bank of England
News.content:
Andrew Bailey has said that interest rates are likely to rise if the Middle East war rages on, warning inflation is now on course to hit 4pc.

The Bank of England opted to hold borrowing costs at 3.75pc on Thursday, the sixth time in a row it has left them unchanged.

However, the Governor said a “material” increase in energy prices since July would push up inflation to twice the Bank’s 2pc target.

He warned the outlook for inflation “continues to be on the upside” and criticised the “seeming loss of urgency to find solutions” to the war in Iran.

Oil prices are back above $100 a barrel and analysts expect average gas and electricity bills to rise above £2,000 this winter as the conflict continues.

Mr Bailey said: “So far, higher global energy costs have had a limited effect on price and wage setting in the UK.

“But the longer this volatility persists, the bigger the impact it will have on inflation, and the more likely it is we will need to raise Bank Rate to ensure that inflation falls back to our 2pc target.”

Investors expect the Bank to raise interest rates as soon as November, which has pushed average mortgage rates to their highest level in three years.

The average five-year fixed mortgage deal has risen to 5.87pc, according to Moneyfacts, which is the highest level since November 2023 and up from 4.95pc before the Iran war.

Thursday’s rate hold leaves the Bank out of step with central banks around the world after the US Federal Reserve and European Central Bank voted to raise borrowing costs this month.

However, economists said there had been a change in tone from policymakers over the threat posed by energy prices and whether this would feed into the wider economy.

The Bank of England predicted that inflation would hit 4pc early next year, just as most workers are negotiating pay rises.

Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said: “It seems as though a majority of the MPC is on the cusp of wanting to tighten policy.”

In a warning on the impending pain facing households, Mr Bailey told the Chancellor that energy bills would rise by 24pc early next year under the Ofgem price cap.

This will push up annual average bills by £413 to £2,136, which the Governor blamed on the war in the Middle East.

The Governor is required to write a formal letter to the Chancellor every time inflation is more than a percentage point above its 2pc target.

Official data showed inflation rose to 3.1pc in August.

Mr Bailey said: “The energy price shock has been the most important factor driving recent short-term movements in inflation.”

Despite expectations of higher rates, the FTSE 100 rose on Thursday at its steepest pace since July, climbing more than 1pc, as the Bank of England eased the pressure on the UK bond market.

Policymakers also confirmed a Telegraph report that the Bank will stop selling the long-dated bonds it amassed during the financial crisis and lockdown.

The Bank will continue actively selling £20bn of government bonds per year until the rest of the stockpile is wound down to zero in 2034.

The announcement triggered a sharp fall in the cost of borrowing for the Treasury, with the yield on 30-year UK gilts falling at the fastest pace since May.

News.title: Next-generation antivenom fights India’s deadliest snakes
News.content:
The process to make antivenom has barely changed in a century: snakes are milked, their venom is injected into horses, and their antibodies are harvested to form the basis of the product. The resulting treatments are difficult to administer, can trigger severe side effects, and the quality varies from batch to batch.

“The big four snakes contribute to 70 per cent of poisonous bites [in India]… so 30 per cent of poisonous snakes are not covered, even to begin with,” said Dr Yogesh Jain, a public health physician in Chhattisgarh state and a member of The Global Snakebite Taskforce.

“But there are huge quality and efficacy issues even against these 70 per cent of bites. We’re relying on a 100-year-old technique of getting antivenoms, and at least 50,000 people are dying every year,” he told The Telegraph.

“There’s a real need for new technology. We don’t have a safe and appropriate antivenom for the largest majority of people in rural India.”

Now, scientists are hopeful that they have developed a potential alternative.

In the latest study, published last week, researchers showed that an experimental antivenom cocktail with five components protected mice against lethal doses of antivenom in Indian cobras, even when delayed by up to 20 minutes – a scenario that mimics the real-world lag between a bite and treatment.

“If you go 10 years back, people didn’t think you could make sufficiently simple products with new, modern biotechnology that could cover all these different snake venoms,” said Prof Andreas Laustsen-Kiel, head of the Section of Biologics Engineering at the Technical University of Denmark and co-author of the paper.

“People simply believed it was too complex, too expensive to manufacture, and so on… But the data we are gathering is convincing enough to say this is something that could make a huge dent in the lost lives and limbs snakebite causes every year.”

The antivenom itself was based on lab-made nanobodies – antibodies derived from a group of animals including camels, llamas and some species of shark. Scientists believe their structure means they could be a more potent, more precise, more temperature-stable alternative to man-made monoclonal antibodies – and cheaper to manufacture.

“The latest study builds on an earlier discovery of nanobodies that can protect across a broad spectrum of African snakes,” said Prof Nicholas Casewell, director of the Centre for Snakebite Research and Interventions at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, who has previously collaborated with Prof Laustsen-Kiel.

“In this paper they have iterated and demonstrated that a narrow number of nanobodies can protect against Indian cobras and king cobras. This demonstration brings the nanobody technology closer to market,” he added.

But that is likely still years away, depending on how much funding the researchers can attract. The next steps – a larger animal study, scaling up manufacture, and launching human trials – are expensive.

“If money was no issue, we could probably be testing in humans in 1.5 to three years from now,” said Prof Laustsen-Kiel. “But since money is a big issue, it is more likely that human trials won’t be able to start until 2.5 to four years from now.

“But I really think that this [study shows] there’s no doubt that biotech can deliver better antivenoms. The question is whether people are willing to fund it,” he said.

Sports.title: ‘Is this in our DNA?’ – Thomas Tuchel admits he may never be able to fix England’s biggest issue over lack of ‘heritage’
Sports.content:
Next

THOMAS TUCHEL has claimed he “doesn’t have time” to coach England how to keep the ball and claimed possession play might not be in their “DNA”.

The German is preparing for England‘s first set of games since getting knocked out of the World Cup semi-finals by Argentina.



Tuchel came under fire in that game over his tactical choices having switched to a defensive set-up after going 1-0 up.

After announcing his latest England squad, it was put to Tuchel that it was his job to help the players keep control of games.



But the ex-Chelsea boss took issue with the question and said English fans wanted to see teams attack and entertain.

He said: “I should be coaching them to keep the ball? That’s my job? I’m not sure that I have the time to coach them to (keep the ball).



“I’m just wrestling with this myself because even if a team control matches in the Premier League, how many English players are there in these teams?

“Is this in our DNA? Do we really value control? Is this something that makes us feel good in a match? Is this something that comes easy to us?

“Do we even realise: “Oh, we’re controlling a midfield, everything is fine?”

“I don’t think that an English supporter goes to a Premier League match and wants to see a controlled match and a 1-0 late win.”



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Tuchel said there was “no heritage of control” of building up play in English football and insisted fans wanted to see fast attacks.

England put on a show for supporters by beating France 6-4 in the World Cup third-placed play-off and Tuchel said he wanted to see similar displays in future tournaments.

He added: “I think deep down in the core, English players – and it’s a beautiful thing – and the spectators want to go for it.

“Let’s go. Let’s play for 6-3, let’s play for 4-3. Let’s not play 1-0. Bring this ball into the box. Let’s play in the box.

‘I think there is no heritage of control around the middle line. No heritage of: “Oh, let’s do a deep build-up and then bring them out”.



‘It’s just like: “Okay, come on, let’s kick the ball into the opponent’s box and fight with them”. And this is what I feel now that I have a tournament as an experience.”

England have upcoming Nations League games against Spain, Croatia and Czechia over the next few weeks and Tuchel has refreshed his selection.

NINE of his World Cup stars are missing – including Noni Madueke, Ollie Watkins, Ivan Toney and Reece James.

Sports.title: Non-league manager, 35, quits to take charge of opposition just hours before FA Cup clash
Sports.content:
Next

BRETT MUNYARD has sensationally quit Aveley to take charge of their FA Cup opponents Brentwood Town, just days before the two clubs meet.

The 35-year-old left Aveley after a year in charge to become Brentwood’s new boss ahead of Saturday’s second qualifying round clash.



And Aveley chairman Craig Johnson admitted the timing of the shock switch “could not have been worse”.

Munyard informed the club on Thursday evening that he was leaving, with the Millers due to face his new side at Parkside just 48 hours later.



It means Munyard will have to watch on as Brentwood take on the club he has spent the past 18 months working to build.

The manager enjoyed an impressive campaign with Aveley last season, guiding them to second place in the Isthmian Premier following their relegation from the National League South.

But it was Brentwood who ended Aveley’s promotion hopes with a 4-1 play-off semi-final victory.

The Blues eventually lost 2-1 to Billericay Town in the final, but their victory over Aveley proved a major blow to Munyard’s side.

Now, the two clubs will meet again with Munyard at the centre of one of the most unusual managerial switches in non-league football.

Johnson did not hide his frustration at the timing of the move.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

He said: “Disappointingly Brett called me this evening, just prior to training commencing and ahead of our important FA Cup tie with Brentwood on Saturday to tell me he was leaving to join our opponents.

“The timing could not have been worse.”

Johnson confirmed that Adam Bailey-Dennis will take charge of Aveley for the cup clash and called on supporters to rally behind the team.

Meanwhile, Brentwood had been searching for a new manager after Keith Rowland left the club with assistant Steve Butterworth on Wednesday.

Rowland had enjoyed considerable success, guiding Brentwood to the Isthmian League North Division title in his second season before another play-off final appearance last term.



Munyard now takes over with Brentwood looking to halt a miserable run of six straight defeats after winning their opening game of the season.

The new boss said he was “delighted” to join Brentwood and insisted the club’s ambition matched his own.

He said: “I’m an ambitious person and I want to be part of a club that wants to keep progressing, improving and pushing forward.”

Munyard also issued an emotional farewell to Aveley, admitting his decision to leave had been “hugely difficult” for him.

Sports.title: Meet Premier League’s rising stars with famous parents including David Haye’s son, Kai Rooney and England icon’s boys
Sports.content:
Next

BECOMING a professional footballer takes an incredible amount of natural ability, hard work, and perseverance.

However, it also helps to have a bit of magic already in your genes.



Erling Haaland is just one example of a superstar born to a former pro, and the Premier League’s academies are littered with young stars hailing from famous parents.

And it is not just retired footballers breeding the next generation, but athletes from other sports too.



Here, SunSport takes a look at a handful of wonderkids born to big-name parents who are now looking to make a name for themselves…

KINGSTON HAYE

The son of boxing legend David Haye, Kingston is making waves at Arsenal as part of their youth system.

The prodigy, 12, joined Hale End last year from Sutton after impressing scouts to earn a switch to the top-flight academy.

His technical ability, vision, and ball control earned him a reputation as a highly promising talent, leading to his move to North London.

Kingston is not the only one of Haye’s kids to impress in sport either. Older brother Cassius, 18, previously made waves on the Spanish junior tennis circuit.

BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK



KAI ROONEY

Some youngsters have a massive name to live up to, and Kai Rooney is certainly one of them.

Kai, 16, is the eldest son of Wayne and Coleen Rooney and is following in his father’s footsteps by trying to make the grade at Manchester United.

The forward-thinking winger penned scholarship terms at Old Trafford earlier this year and has been tipped for a bright future at United.

In seven games for Man Utd U18s last season, Kai netted two goals and registered another assist.



The teenager has recently claimed he models his game off former Arsenal winger Gabriel Martinelli, but will know that he will always be compared to his superstar dad – not least because his middle name is Wayne.

REIGAN & JADEN HESKEY

Rooney isn’t the only former England striker trying to breed the next generation of stars, with Emile Heskey also doing the same.

Heskey’s sons Reigan and Jaden have both been making splashes in the Manchester City academy system.

Jaden, 20, is highly thought of in Manchester and was sent out on loan to Sheffield Wednesday this season after impressing in a short spell there last term.

Reigan, 18, left City permanently this summer in search of the next step in his career, joining German club Cologne.



Reigan will be hoping to follow in the footsteps of young English talent like Jadon Sancho and Jude Bellingham who excelled in Germany during their early development.

PHOENIX OFFIAH

A step removed from the footballing world, Phoenix Offiah is the son of rugby league legend Martin Offiah.

Phoenix, 16, is part of the Tottenham academy and has been tipped for an England youth call-up after impressing for the North London club.



The 6ft 2in striker netted all four goals in a 4-1 win over Wolves last month and has trained with Roberto De Zerbi’s first-team squad.

In an exclusive interview with SunSport, dad Marin said: “Phoenix wasn’t really on anyone’s radar at the start of last season — but he certainly is now.

“He scored four in a 6-0 win over West Ham last September and never looked back since.”

GABRIEL ARTETA

There could soon be a father and son duo representing the same team, with Mikel Arteta’s son Gabriel currently in the youth ranks at Arsenal.

Gabriel was made a first-year scholar this summer and has already played for Arsenal’s U18s.



The youngster previously travelled to Arsenal‘s first-team pre-season training camp in the United States a couple of years ago.

Aged just 14 at the time, he did not take part in any sessions and instead watched from the sidelines with the coaching staff.

STELLA AND ESTERE CICCONE

It is not just the men’s game that has rising stars connected to celebs in the youth ranks.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Stella and Estere Ciccone, the adopted twin daughters of pop superstar Madonna, are both enrolled in Tottenham Women’s youth ranks.

The 14-year-olds even attended a WSL game with their mum last season, watching from the stands as Spurs lost 2-0 to Chelsea.

now 09.25 EDT 90 min: Seven added minutes. I can’t help but think of that Simpson’s meme. The “stop, he’s already dead” one. Share

1m ago 09.23 EDT 88 min: Jackson is off. What a game he had. Not just the goal, but he was full of running, led the line, really top work. On comes Abraham. Buendia, meanwhile, wins a freekick inside Spur’s patch after some nifty footwork and relentless running. My player of the match. Share

3m ago 09.22 EDT Was it an own goal? It counts all the same. Good work from Kudus down the right as he burst into the box and found the byline before cutting the ball back in. Gallagher got there and hacked it towards goal. Was that strike on target before it took a deflection off Cash? Not sure. Either way, the ball settled in at the back post and Spurs’ long wait for a league goal is over. Share

4m ago 09.21 EDT GOAL! Tottenham 1-3 Aston Villa (Gallagher, 86) The duck is broken! It won’t matter much in the context of this game, but at least Spurs have scored. Share

5m ago 09.19 EDT 85 min: Emery is still barking orders on the touchline. He wants this clean sheet. De Zerbi, meanwhile, looks like a man drifting on a lifeboat alone in the middle of the Atlantic. Share

6m ago 09.18 EDT 84 min: A double switch for Villa. Barkley and Mbaye on for McGinn and Kamara. Bentancur and Tonalie are off for Spurs, replaced by Bergvall and Gallagher. Even more fans are leaving now. Share

7m ago 09.17 EDT 83 min: A reminder that Spurs could have been 3-0 up in the first half, and would have been were it not for the brilliance of Suzuki. But Villa have held firm and shown quality that looks beyond this Spurs side. Now the visitors are in complete control, knocking the ball around as if on the training pitch. Oles ring out from the away stand. Share

9m ago 09.16 EDT Justin Kavanagh points out: double quotation mark If they don’t score today, Spurs will have gone over 8 hours without doing a goal. That’s long enough to read a lengthy novel. If I was a Spurs fan walking out early today, I’d head for Waterstones and spend the next few weeks perusing something more convincing than this fiction that Spurs are still a functioning football club. Share

10m ago 09.15 EDT Oh my word, the second viewing is even better! Just an incredible strike. Joao Gomes ran from midfield and fed Hemmings on the right. The pass came back infield to Buendia who puts his foot through it and rifled it into the top corner. That has sparked a small exodus from some Spurs fans. Share

11m ago 09.14 EDT GOAL! Tottenham 0-3 Aston Villa (Buendia, 80) STUNNER! He did it in the Europa League final and this one might be even better! Smashed into the top corner and that is that! View image in fullscreen Buendia lets rip to make it three! Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/Reuters View image in fullscreen Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/Reuters Share Updated at 09.18 EDT

12m ago 09.12 EDT 78 min: Maddison runs back to dispossess Hemmings around halfway with a sliding tackle. But there’s a real lack of quality on the ball. Credit to Villa. They’ve been well organised and look totally comfortable. Share

13m ago 09.11 EDT 76 min: Gray draws a foul out in the right channel. Spurs will get a chance to whip a cross in. Did anyone catch Jackson’s celebration? Got to say I missed it. Michael Cosgrove didn’t: “Whatever else, I thought Jackson’s post second goal ‘celebratory’ throat slitting gesture was way beyond the pale.” The cross from the free-kick comes to nothing. Spurs seem to have lost their oomph (if they had any to start with). Share

15m ago 09.10 EDT 76 min: The crowd is really on top of Spurs now. They win the ball in midfield but don’t move it fast enough to take advantage. Marmoush has it on the edge of the area and shoots, but he’s well smothered by Lindeloff as the ball bounces away for a corner. Suzuki punches it away to Kudus who can’t direct his shot towards goal with any menace. Share

16m ago 09.08 EDT 74 min: Savio has been the driving force this half. He charges into the centre and feeds Kudus on the right. The cross is whipped in but Suzuki makes another claim. Manzambi is off for Hemmings. Share

18m ago 09.07 EDT 72 min: Good work from Cash – who has been neat since he came on – who heads clear at the back post from a chipped cross. But Spurs come back at them and how on earth did Robertson miss from there! He’s well off-side so wouldn’t have counted as he got himself free down the left inside the Villa box, but he scuffed it with his left foot, skewing it across the face of goal as if he was squaring the ball. Share

20m ago 09.04 EDT 71 min: Tonali unfurls a wonder strike! It’s about 30 yards away as he whips his foot around and it almost finds the top corner. That wasn’t far off. Spurs need a spark of brilliance from someone. Share

21m ago 09.04 EDT 70 min: There are no midfielders on the park. it’s really like a basketball game at present with both teams throwing attacks against each the other. Savio is doing some running, Jackson gets a chance to run himself. It all ends with Ruggeri skewing a clearance kick out for a corner. Share

23m ago 09.02 EDT GOAL! Tottenham 0-2 Aston Villa (Jackson, 67) Brilliant from Jackson and Spurs are sinking! Wonderful feet from the striker. He plays a quick one-two with Manzambi off a long kick, then flicks it over van Hecke before keeping the ball low to the corner with a (not) volley strike. It’s saved, but only half as it trickles in off the far post. View image in fullscreen Nicolas Jackson makes it two for Villa! Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/Reuters View image in fullscreen Photograph: Alex Pantling/Getty Images Share Updated at 09.08 EDT

24m ago 09.00 EDT 66 min: Savio wins a corner which he takes himself on the right. It’s a little floaty and Solanke can’t steer it back towards the danger area from the far post. That’ll be Solanke’s last act as he’s replaced by Maddison. That’ll push Marmoush further forward. Share

26m ago 08.58 EDT 64 min: In the end it was pretty tame. It was indeed a Robertson dinked cross, but Suzuki seemed to be the only player paying attention as he came off his line to grab it. Share

27m ago 08.58 EDT 63 min: Marmoush wins a free-kick having cut inside just beyond the Villa box. It’s certainly within range. Angle might be a touch tight, but could be a shot. My money is on a Robertson cross to the far post. Let’s see… Share

28m ago 08.57 EDT 62 min: How unlucky. But Spurs can’t let that get them down. They need to keep going. Villa are dropping deeper while maintaining a well held high line. So there’ll be chances. Of course, Villa also pose a threat on the counter. Maddison warming up for Spurs on the side. Share

29m ago 08.55 EDT NO GOAL! Tottenham 0-1 Aston Villa The drought continues! Robertson was half a yard off-side as he had the beating of McGinn down the left. The cross was half blocked before it was swept in by Kudus from close range, but there’s no doubt the left back was off-side. Share

30m ago 08.54 EDT Oh no! Was Robertson off-side? I think he is. Hang tight…. Share

31m ago 08.54 EDT GOAL! Tottenham 1-1 Aston Villa (Kudus, 60) They’ve done it! The duck is broken! Share

33m ago 08.52 EDT 57 min: Savio does well on the right of Villa’s box. He feints to go down the byline before shifting back onto his left foot. He dinks a cross to the back post but Suzuki gets on his bike (sorry) and claims it. Up the other end, Jackson’s shot is blocked. End to end now. Share

34m ago 08.50 EDT 56 min: Ruggeri flattens Savio in a 50/50 challenge. That sparks a counter that ends with Jackson firing a shot after cutting infield onto his right boot. Spurs are bossing the ball but every time Villa break they’re creating something. Share

36m ago 08.48 EDT 54 min: This will be the pattern for the rest of the game: Villa defending deep and looking to counter with Spurs trying to work the space against a low block. Was Savio blocked earlier when he tried to run onto a Tonali cross? I’m not so sure. Share

37m ago 08.47 EDT 52 min: Kinsky makes a big save! Jackson exploded away from his marker and was first to the ball from Manzxambi from the left back towards goal. Jackson hit it first time rather than try and take it round the onrushing Kinsky. Still, the shot was on target and needed saving. Sharp but not quite clinical from Jacskon. Share Updated at 08.51 EDT

39m ago 08.46 EDT 52 min: The crowd is growing restless. They’re not happy that another Spurs move fizzles to nothing, but they do keep the ball and send it right then left. Villa are defending very deep. Solanke gathers a Tonali ball but he’s repelled. Still, they keep the ball. Tonali seeing a lot of it in the second half. Share

40m ago 08.45 EDT 50 min: Spurs win a free kick that van hecke takes quickly. Oh brilliant from Manzambi after Villa win it back, the new signing spins out of a tackle. He’s back on the ball inside Spurs’ box. Then he’s bundled over on the edge but he was looking for it. Play on. Share

41m ago 08.44 EDT 49 min: Van de Ven is sporting a huge shiner on his face. Anders Vad Bruun has written a strongly worded email questioning my claim that the cenbtre-back’s absence was the reason for the goal. He makes a point that perhaps Robertson’s decision to keep the ball in play and not concede a corner had to do with a lack of the centre-back. But then he’d have been allowed to come back on? In the words of Kanye, I guess we’ll never know. Share

43m ago 08.42 EDT 48 min: Tonali runs from deep. Defintiely an extra yard in his step. But the move comes to nothing. More direct. More accurate. Just more from Spurs is what’s needed. Share

44m ago 08.41 EDT Second half Changes for both teams. Wan-Bisakka is off for Cash at right back. Kudus slots into Spurs’ midfield – at the 10? – in place of Fernandes. Share

45m ago 08.40 EDT I’ve said that Spurs probably deserve a lead but not according to xG. Spurs’ xG is 0.59 despite four excellent Suzuki saves. Meanwhile, Villa’s is 0.83. Probably because the goal was pretty much a gimme right in front. Spurs haven’t made a single successful cross. Share

55m ago 08.30 EDT Should note that Villa’s goal came with van de Ven off the pitch. Not saying that was the reason, but it’s worth noting. Share

1h ago 08.26 EDT Half-time: Tottenham 0-1 Aston Villa Boos, half hearted at best, ring around the stadium. Spurs bossed it but still don’t have a goal in the league this season and are staring at another defeat. Share

1h ago 08.25 EDT 45+7 min: Shaky for Spurs at the back as Buendia is given too much time on the ball on the edge of the area. Manzambi tries to shoot but its deflected and Jackosn scuffs wide. Share

1h ago 08.24 EDT 45+5 min: Van Hecke clatters Jackson on halfway and gets a yellow card. But was there a shove in the back moments earlier on Fernandes just as the Spurs player was about to shoot inside Villa’s box? I think so. It definitely put him off balanced. Oh, it was just outside the box but Gomes definitely put his hands on Fernandes. Share

1h ago 08.22 EDT Good work from Villa there. McGinn benefited on the byline after Robertson’s lapse. Then he played in Kamara who slipped it on for Manzambi right in front of the goal. So credit to the visitors. But that was almost an own goal from Robertson who was trying to do his best for the team, but really should have just let it bobble out for a corner. Share

1h ago 08.21 EDT GOAL! Tottenham 0-1 Aston Villa (Manzambi, 45+4 Can you believe it! After dominating the half, Spurs are down! Sloppy from Robertson who inexplicably kept the ball in play after Bentancur’s header was destined for a corner. Instead the left-back kept it alive and it fell for a Villa player who played it across for Manzambi who couldn’t miss from right in front. View image in fullscreen Johan Manzambi prods home the opening goal. Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters View image in fullscreen Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters Share Updated at 08.30 EDT

1h ago 08.19 EDT 45+2 min: Van den Ven is up but that is a mighty gash and bruise under his right eye. They’re showing replays of Suzuki’s two biggest saves. That one from Gray, I didn’t realise how close it was to a goal. Gray fired from an angle and the ball almost went through the keeper’s legs, but took a deflection off the instep of his left foot and scooted across the face of goal. Share

1h ago 08.17 EDT 45 min: Van den Ven is actually bleeding from his face. Looks like he’s been cut on the right cheek just below the eye. We’ll get at least five added minutes but it could well be more as a result of this stoppage. Share

1h ago 08.16 EDT 44 min: It’s a great ball that Mings attacks, but a combination of van den Ven and van Hecke clear the danger. Think it was van den Ven who made contact with the ball just as he got clattered in the back. He goes down having won the free kick and requires a bit of medical attention. Share

1h ago 08.15 EDT 44 min: Wan-Bissaka gets the ball in acres of space down the right. He takes on Tonali then shifts back to Manzambi infield who draws a soft foul. Not in range and on the angle, but a chance for McGinn to whip one in from the right with an inswinger. Share

1h ago 08.14 EDT 43 min: Van den Ven makes a great intervention to a Buendia pass against the grain. If that went on then Jackson was away and possibly in a 2-v-1 with Manzambi in support. They’ve been by far the better team, but Spurs will know that just one moment could see them chasing the game. Share

1h ago 08.12 EDT 41 min: Nothin’ doin’ from that Villa corner as Solanke heads clear. Villa go all the way back to Suzuki and eventually lose possession. Share

1h ago 08.11 EDT 40 min: Solanke gets Tonali’s pass inside the box, but he’s facing the wrong way. He tries to turn but is smothered by two Villa defenders. “Perhaps today we’ll witness the advent of the minus value XG rating?” That’s from Justin Kavanagh. Thing is Spurs could have scored three! But they haven’t, of course. Villa win a corner. McGinn to take it from the left. Share

1h ago 08.10 EDT 39 min: Tonali picks Manzambi’s pocket and launches a move down the left where Robertson is on the ball, running at pace. His crosses but it’s blocked away for a corner. Spurs get a rare corner from the left. Can they do anything with it? Nope. Mings biffs a strong header clear. Share

1h ago 08.09 EDT 37 min: Suzuki is showing off now. He explodes off his line as Robertson spots Marmoush galloping upfield into space. But the Villa keeper is quickest to react as he controls the ball with his chest outside his box. Share

1h ago 08.07 EDT 36 min: Manzambi, who has had a lively game, full of confidence, is down having copped a blow. Short delay. I don’t think he’ll have to leave. Is this the part where I say, ‘Welcome to the Premier League’? Share

1h ago 08.06 EDT 35 min: Two blocks inside Villa’s box. At the back post Solanke’s header is smothered by Wan-Bissaka and then Tonali’s effort is redirected by Buendia. Appeals for a hand ball are ignored. Share

1h ago 08.04 EDT 32 min: Van Hecke dinks a wonderful long pass for the onrushing Marmoush who times his run perfectly, but the touch is very heavy and it bobbles for Suzuki. A better touch and he was clear. Then Suzuki makes a brilliant diving save down low to a shot from Tonali who had to get his head over the bouncing ball. Or did he? Replays show there was no save and it bounced wide. Let’s hope there’s no goal from this corner. There isn’t. Instead we’ll get another corner as Robertson’s low driven cross is blocked. Share

1h ago 08.02 EDT 31 min: Suzuki, comfortably the player of the match so far, shows some slick feet as he receives a hospital pass but he deals with it comfortably. At the other end, Jackson and Buendia combine before Manzambi has the ball. He fires from a different post code into row R when a pass for McGinn on his right was perhaps the better option. Share

1h ago 08.00 EDT “How about Unstoppable Farce vs Risible Project?” That’s Gary Naylor. Spot on. Share

1h ago 08.00 EDT 28 min: Brilliant from Jackson on the end of a Villa counter. Loose from Spurs around halfway allows Manzambi to spark the attack. McGinn involved and the ball to Jackson on the edge of the area is well controlled before the striker spins and makes the space for the shot. Perhaps he thought he had less time than he had as he pulls it from the middle of the goal well wide to the left. 10/10 for the first part. 0/10 for the shot. Share

Sports.content:
now 09.24 EDT GOAL! Tottenham Hotspur 1-3 Aston Villa (Gallagher 86). Another 86th-minute goal for a Gallagher … Conor this time. Which means Spurs have finally scored a Premier League goal after nearly five-matches-worth of asking! Although it might be an own goal, Matty Cash having touched the ball last. Not 100 percent anyone involved with Spurs will care too much either way right now. Tottenham v Aston Villa: Premier League – live Read more Share

3m ago 09.20 EDT GOAL! Stoke City 2-1 Sheffield United (Gallagher 86). Stoke have turned it around late, Sam Gallagher doing the business with full-time looming. Share

He’s the last man, so allowing himself to be charged down by Kyrell Lisbie is a disaster. The Millwall striker tears clear. Kanté has no option but to take one for the team, hauling Lisbie down and earning himself a red card. There will be five additional minutes at the very least. Share

It follows earlier goals from Johan Manzambi and Nicolas Jackson, and Roberto De Zerbi’s post-match interview is going to be appointment viewing. His coat on a shoogly peg. Sports.title: Andoni Iraola makes Bournemouth return still learning on the job at Liverpool
Sports.content:
Alisson made little attempt to sugarcoat Liverpool’s unbeaten start to the season under Andoni Iraola when analysing the draw against Fulham with the club’s in-house media. “Unbeaten with three draws is not something to celebrate too much with this shirt,” said a peeved Liverpool goalkeeper. “We take the clean sheet but we are not happy at all. We need to aim for big things.”

Big things are the target and big things are expected from a Liverpool side containing three £100m-plus forwards. But the learning curve under the new head coach is proving challenging. As it is for the new head coach, too. Big decisions appear unavoidable.

When Iraola faces his former club Bournemouth on Sunday for the first time since ending his impressive three-year reign there last season, he is likely to know more about the opposition players than his own. “It’s going to be a tricky one because they know very well what we try to do,” Iraola said. “But I also know their strengths and weaknesses. It’s going to be strange for me.”

Iraola spent more than two hours debriefing Marco Rose, his successor at the Vitality Stadium, on the Bournemouth squad and staff in June. They had time for a smooth handover because, as Iraola put it, his exit from the club “was so clean” and he decided to stay on the south coast while his two young children finished school. Whether they discussed how Bournemouth became the draw specialists of last season remains private.

No coach or manager oversaw more stalemates in the Premier League last season than Iraola, whose Bournemouth team were held a remarkable 18 times. It was a league high by a comfortable distance. Leeds in second had 14. Ten came at the Vitality, 52.63% of their home league fixtures, and Bournemouth ultimately missed out on the fifth and final Champions League spot by three points from a Liverpool team that stumbled over the line under Arne Slot.

Over the course of his last 38 league games, Iraola has drawn 21 times. That is a joint record in the Premier League alongside Mark Hughes, whose identical run across 38 games came with Manchester City and Fulham between October 2009 and February 2011. Hughes had a seven-month break between those two jobs, however, making Iraola the first Premier League coach to draw 21 of 38 matches in a continuous sequence.

The sample size at Liverpool is too small for conclusions, admittedly. Iraola is also still searching for balance and assessing his options, as changes in both full-back positions and central midfield have demonstrated regularly. But the 44-year-old knows full well that a draw with Liverpool is far more damaging to his current employer’s aspirations than his previous one. Three from four league games so far have enabled Arsenal and Manchester City to quickly establish an ominous six-point gap over the 2025 champions. The audible groans that greeted the home draws against Nottingham Forest and Fulham confirmed Anfield’s patience has not recovered from last season’s travails.

“That’s totally fair,” Iraola said of the contrasting reactions to a draw at Liverpool and Bournemouth. “But it’s something that I knew before coming here. When you draw 2-2 at Newcastle with Bournemouth it is probably a good result, but I understand that with Liverpool it is not a good result. The goals of the team are different and the expectations are different as well.”

Fulham was a step backwards, according to Iraola, after two steps forward against Ipswich and Atlético Madrid. A younger, fresher Liverpool team restored momentum with Tuesday’s Carabao Cup win over Tottenham. Elements of that performance were as timely for Iraola as the result. Having demanded greater effort from his forward line following the Fulham draw – and then rested Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz against Spurs – youngsters Lewis Koumas, James McConnell, Rio Ngumoha and Trey Nyoni all made tireless contributions to the cup win in their absences.

View image in fullscreen Rio Ngumoha, in action against Atlético Madrid, has has shown his quality as one of Liverpool’s rising stars. Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Academy players appeared more attuned to Iraola’s methods and instructions than their expensive elders. With Liverpool’s midfield balance also under scrutiny and Wirtz following a good Champions League performance with an indifferent Premier League display, as was often the case last season, Iraola may spend the extended international break wrestling with some big calls depending on how his Bournemouth return unfolds. He has shown himself unafraid of making them.

“For me the demands on the players and positions are the same,” Iraola insisted on Friday. “I don’t give different instructions to one player because he is more expensive than another player who has cost us less money. The demands are always the same. But I also have to adjust to the things that some players can do and others cannot do.

“The strengths and weaknesses of players are different, so we have to always adapt the team to try and maximise the collective side of this. In Bournemouth we had players who could run forever and other players who could not do it. It was not like everyone in Bournemouth was running. Some of them were faster, others were slower, some of them scored more goals, some are good at set pieces. There is no standard player. I feel all the players here are doing everything to try to win and to try and get where we want as quickly as possible. But sometimes I need to adapt too to the players that we have.”

Iraola was asked if he would love 11 players with the mentality of Koumas. “That is a cheating question,” he said, laughing. “I love the desire of Koumas, I love what he gives, but every player has different weaknesses and strengths. He is a good example especially for the players coming from the academy, he is grabbing his opportunity and doing everything to try to gain minutes. But I also have to work with Koumas a lot in other areas. There are things he has to improve.”

Everyone at Liverpool, it seems, is learning on a job that demands the finished article.

Sports.title: Brentford blitz Chelsea as Fábio Carvalho caps stunning second-half display
Sports.content:
Those early-season thoughts that Chelsea might be the team best-placed to challenge Arsenal are beginning to look extremely over-optimistic. The two chaotic wins with which they began were always difficult to read: they might have been useful points picked up on the way to a more solid structure, or they might have represented evidence of significant problems. After three games without a win, and 12 goals conceded in five games this season, it’s beginning to look like the latter.

At the final whistle, Keith Andrews tipped his head back and roared at the sky, celebrating Brentford’s first home win over Chelsea since 1938. They remain unbeaten, coherent and disciplined, and moved up to third in the table. The comparison is impossible not to draw: as one side flail in an orgy of structured spending, their far less wealthy neighbours thrive with a clear plan and sense of direction. “It was a performance I felt was bubbling,” said Andrews. “I could see it in the players’ eyes over the last two days. They were very focused, very determined.”

Such is the state of perpetual flux at Chelsea that the usual homilies about the benefits of stability always seem a little redundant when applied to them. With 11 new signings this summer maintaining the sense of the club as a trading hub, learning the names of everybody in the dressing room has probably been a greater priority than worrying too much about boardroom wrangling. But, still, their first game since Todd Boehly and Mark Walter agreed to sell their 12.8% stake in the club to the major shareholder Clearlake Capital felt significant. At the very least, a more harmonious boardroom should be beneficial.

Boehly, the great disruptor, who arrived blithely telling English football it was doing everything wrong, has departed having achieved very little other than splurging £300m on players who didn’t fit and giving Raheem Sterling a £325,000-a-week contract in his shambolic spell as de facto sporting director. Four years on, after 60 arrivals, do Chelsea look any more like title challengers than they did then? It was, in truth, very hard to say what this looked like, other than a team that is every much still under construction. Jordan Henderson made his full Chelsea debut at his former club, while Danny Welbeck, Pep Chavarría and Valentín Barco made their first league starts.

Barco, whose overenthusiastic celebrations after Argentina’s winner against England at the World Cup earned him a post-match slap from Jude Bellingham, was booed with impressive consistency from the home fans. The lesson was clear: if you’re going to be a major irritant while in possession of a distinctive shock of hair the colour of burnished copper, there will be consequences. Emí Martínez was jeered as well for the crime of being Argentinian. Henderson, by contrast, was treated relatively gently, his booing as a returnee more sporadic and muted, tending to the perfunctory.

View image in fullscreen Jaidon Anthony rises to head Brentford in front. Photograph: David Klein/Reuters

The pattern for Chelsea was a familiar one: a fast start, fading to something a little scratchier. The opening, for the second successive game, did not produce an early goal, although Pedro Neto would have given them a ninth-minute lead had it not been for a sharp save from Caoimhín Kelleher.

“We have dropped our consistency, our competitive mentality in the second half,” said Xabi Alonso. “We have not been able to keep our level. When you lose shape you are out of control. To be able to understand and know what it takes to be competing to the end, it’s a process and it takes time.”

The longer the game went on, the less assured Chelsea looked and a Brentford opener arrived just after the hour. Perhaps inevitably, it came from a dead ball; the stats had suggested that Brentford this season had been creating significantly more chances from set plays than they had converted. As modern corner routines go it seemed very straightforward, Jannik Schuster climbing above the diminutive Barco to head Mikkel Damsgaard’s corner back across goal, where Jaidon Anthony nodded in from close range, his first goal since his summer move from Burnley.

View image in fullscreen Fábio Carvalho fires Brentford into a three-goal lead in injury time. Photograph: David Klein/Reuters

Chelsea belatedly applied some pressure but, although the final minutes were played largely in the Brentford half, they created little beyond corners, as Brentford maintained their composure and structure.

The second goal arrived seven minutes from time. Damsgaard, perhaps the tidiest player in the league, led the break, playing in Kevin Schade. Martínez saved his side-footed effort but Igor Thiago guided an awkwardly bouncing ball inside the post for his first goal of the season. Fábio Carvalho made it 3-0 in added time, slamming in a cross from Schade, who had been left inexplicably unmarked on the left after a long throw was half-cleared.

As Brentford begin to consider that European qualification is a real possibility, Chelsea remain what they have been since the takeover: a work in progress – and, particularly at the back, it feels that progress has a long way to run.

Sports.title: Harry Kane smashes record for fastest to 100 Bundesliga goals in 98th game
Sports.content:
Harry Kane smashed the 49-year-old record for the fastest player to score 100 Bundesliga goals in Bayern Munich’s 7-0 victory over Union Berlin, his 98th league game for the club.

Cologne’s Dieter Müller set the previous mark in 1977, but it took him 129 matches and, with the England captain scoring at better than a goal a game, a new record had been inevitable for some time. Since his arrival in 2023 Kane had been averaging a Bundesliga goal every 78.5 minutes and has now scored 152 in 154 appearances in all competitions, including 61 in 51 games last term.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

He blasted home a 39th-minute penalty to take the record before nodding in a Michael Olise cross early in the second half to send Bayern top of the table before the other weekend matches.

The feat stole the spotlight from Olise, who scored his first Bayern hat-trick, and Jamal Musiala, who also scored a goal worthy of winning any game.

“I’m very proud to have now scored 100 and 101 Bundesliga goals. I haven’t been around that long. I’ve loved every second of it,” Kane told Sky Germany. “With Michael, Lucho [Luis Díaz] and Jamal I naturally get chances and today was no exception.

“So I just want to thank the team, the club, the coach, and the staff – everyone who has helped me achieve this. Let’s keep going like this. Scoring more goals in games is obviously a big step. Of course, there have been many important goals among them. I can only say that I’m enjoying every minute of it. Just like today.”

Sports.title: Heat is on Carrick but Wilcox must share blame for Manchester United’s woes
Sports.content:
There was a mix of boos and apathy as Manchester United slumped out of the Carabao Cup on Wednesday in their latest depressing act in domestic cup competitions. A solemn Michael Carrick and his players were the target for the jeers. The director of football, Jason Wilcox, looked unamused on his way out of the directors’ box but he and the hierarchy need to accept responsibility for their actions.

This is the natural course of football, where supporters know what is good or bad and give a rapid opinion to those whose wages they deem they pay. Carrick and his charges are the face of the club, the ones put up to speak with journalists and sent to promote the wares of sponsors.

The head coach is often viewed as accountable for everything, from tactics to transfers, but the picture is more complex.

Carrick returned to United in January, but others have overseen the long-term strategy, within which the head coach sits. Pressure comes with his job, though, and a loss at Fulham on Sunday would significantly increase it.

United’s fanbase is fully aware of those running the club, with regular protests against the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe. They realise not everything happening over 90 minutes is the fault of the head coach and those wearing the shirt. The boos are for the one-off performance, the apathy for the bigger picture. It is tough for United supporters to see their club, back in the Champions League, outspent in the summer by promoted sides but this is the reality after years of financial mismanagement. It means the funds available have to be spent wisely.

United being two goals ahead against Brighton after 10 minutes and deservedly losing a game they were barely involved in for the remaining 80 is a strong indication things are not right within the team but Carrick knows this. Brighton were much changed but possess an exciting array of talent acquired from all over the world thanks to clever scouting and recruitment. They signed players from clubs in seven countries this summer, while United made four acquisitions from fellow Premier League clubs. Calculated risks and dynamism are part of the job but rarely seen at Old Trafford. It is somewhat ironic considering the most successful acquisition last summer was Senne Lammens from Royal Antwerp, in terms of price and consistency.

Carrick and Wilcox cannot truly be analysed until the most expensive of the three summer buys, Carlos Baleba, is available because his attributes should solve the lack of mobility. Targeting central midfielders was logical after the exit of Casemiro and inadequacy of Manuel Ugarte, but it was not the only area requiring attention. The overall deficiency of the squad was acknowledged internally but the lack of variety in strengthening felt naive and is proving to be so.

View image in fullscreen Senne Lammens was Manchester United’s most successful signing last year, yet the club chose to invest mainly in Premier League players this summer. Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA

Buying players from other Premier League clubs is rarely cost-effective but there is a logic to limiting the adaptation time. Given the left-back shortage and Joshua Zirkzee’s inadequacies, sourcing a cheaper midfield option than the £50m Andrey Santos could have been advantageous for the wider health of the team. Someone needs to alleviate the pressure on Carrick by explaining why it was deemed best to spend £155m on three players in the same position. The outside world is left to pontificate, while Carrick creates a plan B when Luke Shaw, as many anticipated, has time out injured.

Wilcox has carried out internal media duties. On 30 October 2025, after three consecutive wins, he discussed the long-term plan, which was derailed by sacking Ruben Amorim just over two months later. Matters were going well when Wilcox opened up to United’s editorial staff but, apart from statements on sackings, he shows no appetite to speak amid downturns.

In Europe, sporting directors talking to the press is normal but the Premier League is yet to catch on, and the silence mounts at United with the team 13th.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Wilcox arrived, originally as technical director, from Southampton in 2024 and helped oversee the retention of Erik ten Hag after an eighth-placed finish. Ten Hag was belatedly dismissed for a poor start to the next season. Amorim was hired from Sporting despite his tactics not matching up with the squad available and a lack of finance to provide the overhaul required. United ended 15th and endured a meek Europa League final defeat by Tottenham. When Amorim was dismissed for his shortcomings after 14 months, Wilcox was permitted another chance to rectify the situation.

Carrick is not absolved of criticism; this United team are underperforming and pummelling promoted Ipswich and the Azerbaijan side Sabah cannot mask the disappointing start.

The defence has struggled, conceding seven goals in four Premier League games, and against Brighton the pairing of Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven was bordering on inept. The forward line has looked disjointed.

Wilcox was well respected when working as Manchester City’s head of academy, and those who dealt with him thought he was exceptional and suited to a role at that level. He is scrutinised and criticised for his work at United after moving up the chain. Many on the outside will be frustrated if JJ Gabriel departs but Wilcox would not be culpable, having worked hard to convince the player to stay, including via the teenager’s inner circle.

With power comes great responsibility at United but only Carrick is forced to embrace it. Ten Hag and Amorim have fallen for their failures, while others have been allowed to carry on. Carrick and Wilcox are equally invested in the success of the team but it seems only one will feel the consequences if things do not improve.

Sports.title: Manchester City scramble to dramatic WSL win over Liverpool with two goals in added time
Sports.content:
Manchester City continued their winning start to the new Women’s Super League season but the defending champions needed a 90th-minute own goal from Grace Fisk to help them edge past an ever-improving Liverpool side after an entertaining game in which Lauren Hemp scored twice.

Fisk inadvertently turned Grace Clinton’s dangerous cross into her own net to put City 3-2 up and then – with Liverpool searching for an equaliser and committing players forward deep in stoppage time – Hemp added another on the counterattack to make it 4-2 and widen the margin of victory, but that slightly masked how well the visitors had played.

Gareth Taylor – against his former side – will have taken significant encouragement from his Liverpool team’s performance, on a night when they made the league leaders dig deep.

“Playing that way, we believe we’ll win a lot of games this season,” Taylor told Sky Sports, as he praised his team’s effort. “What you saw was a more improved version of what we were towards the end of last season.”

That certainly seemed the case. Nevertheless, the result ensured that City, who had already been the only WSL side who held a 100% winning record after the opening two rounds of games and now will certainly stay top of the table for at least another week, have still not dropped any points in home league fixtures since Andrée Jeglertz took charge in the summer of 2025.

It had looked as though Jeglertz’s City were set for a routine evening when Hemp met Carlotta Wamser’s incisive inside ball and sent a controlled, low finish into the far bottom corner. It was Hemp’s first goal since scoring for England in a victory over Spain in April, her first club goal since scoring in the FA Cup in February and her first WSL goal since last November’s Manchester derby.

Moments after Hemp’s opening goal, with 13 minutes on the clock, the entire crowd rose to applaud the late Matt Beard, the former Liverpool manager, in reference to the year 2013, when he won the first of two consecutive WSL titles with Liverpool.

Supporters of clubs across the WSL and WSL2 have been invited to applaud at the same time in games across this weekend, to mark a year since Beard’s death on 20 September 2025. He was a much-loved character and hugely successful coach at Liverpool, whose performance – particularly in the remainder of the first half – would have done him proud.

View image in fullscreen Vivien Endemann puts Liverpool 2-1 up against Manchester City. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

The away side deservedly struck back and found themselves 2-1 up before the half-hour mark, as their pressing gave the defending champions a headache. First a misunderstanding between Wamser and Alex Greenwood allowed Vivien Endemann to set up Alice Bergström for the equaliser, which she calmly tucked past Ayaka Yamashita.

Soon afterwards, after City failed to clear a cross, Endemann – who had opened her Liverpool account with a debut goal at Charlton on the opening weekend – fired in a shot that Yamashita got a hand to but could only help into the net.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Khadija Shaw struck a post from a difficult angle after rounding Khiara Keating, but Shaw eventually did equalise after a goalkeeping error shortly before half-time. Keating – returning to face her former club after her summer move to Liverpool – did well to block Hemp’s strike but was unable to prevent the ball trickling into the path of the onrushing Shaw, who gratefully poked home.

Keating impressed in the second half with a fine reaction save, keeping out a Shaw effort that had looked destined for the top corner at her near post. But the hosts began to build pressure and the introduction of the lively Clinton inside the final 15 minutes boosted their attacking threat.

Her near-post cross proved too difficult for Fisk to clear and – just as they did on countless occasions last term – City lived up to Jeglertz’s mantra of “we will find a way to win”, a message that has been imprinted on the walls of their training base.

Jeglertz hinted at that again as he told Sky Sports: “I’m very pleased with the mentality of the group. They never stop believing, they keep on going and – in the end – we are winners.”

Sports.title: Oxford United apologise for launching ‘United 93’ clothing range around 9/11 anniversary
Sports.content:
Oxford United have abandoned a new range of American style-sportswear after it inadvertently referenced the tragedy of September 11.

The League One club launched their new “Campus Collection” on Friday morning but had removed it from sale by lunchtime, after clothing designs were revealed to bear the slogan “United 93”. The U’s immediately published an apology that admitted to a lack of understanding of “the historical context and associations” related to the branding and made “sincere apologies for this error and any offence caused”.

“Inspired by the style and culture of American sports,” the club originally trailed the Campus Collection as launching on 11 September of this year, the 25th anniversary of the atrocity that killed nearly 3,000 people. Concerns over sensitivity saw the launch then delayed, but when the online collection was finally made available for sale on Friday, images showed models wearing an NFL-style shirt with “United 93” on the chest, in recognition of Oxford being founded in 1893.

United 93 was one of four domestic passenger jets seized by al-Qaida terrorists on 11 September 2001. A mutiny by passengers prevented hijackers from using the plane to destroy a government building in Washington DC, and it ultimately crashed into a field, killing all 44 people on board. A film titled “United 93” was also made about the tragedy.

The Campus Collection was live for approximately two hours on Friday before the webpage was deleted by the club after they realised the meaning of the phrase. “The range was released without understanding of the historical context and associations,” the club statement read. “It should not have reached the point of sale and we take full responsibility for not undertaking proper due diligence.

“We have removed the collection with immediate effect and are reviewing our approval processes to ensure nothing like this happens again. Once again, we would like to put on record our sincere apologies for this error and any offence caused.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Opinion was mixed among Oxford fans, with many outraged but others inclined to forgive the error. One user of the Yellows Forum called it a “monumental cock-up that I would expect to be sacked for if I’d signed off on it”. Another wrote: “Whilst not ideal … everyone who sees this realises there’s no malicious intent. Ultimately there was just no consideration to it at all.”

Sports.title: Millwall celebrations leave reporter stunned as West Ham rivalry reignited
Sports.content:
West Ham player accused of spitting at Millwall goalkeeper in first clash for 14 years

Millwall goalkeeper Filip Marschall accused West Ham player Taty Castellanos of spitting during the Championship clash on Saturday.

There was confusion in the second-half of the Dockers Derby as the Lions shot-stopper appeared to hold onto the ball for too long.

2 Castellanos found himself at the centre of a row during the lunchtime clash Credit: Getty

Thinking the Hammers had a corner, Castellanos took it quickly and created a goal, before it was ruled out and Millwall given an uncontested drop-ball by referee Paul Tierney.

Moments later, a replay showed Marschall wiping his head and suggesting he had been spat at by Castellanos.

Sky Sports later confirmed the accusation after conversations with the Millwall bench and the fourth official, moments before West Ham completed a comeback from two-goals down and drew level.

Fiery atmosphere

The high-profile London rivalry was reignited for the first-time in 14 years on Saturday.

A fierce atmosphere erupted from the moment it kicked off - with Millwall’s opening goal met with a deafening explosion of noise.

The Den rose to its feet when Caleb Taylor fired the Lions ahead in the 16th minute of the much-anticipated dockers derby.

It was all one-way traffic in the early exchanges and Millwall deservedly broke the deadlock thanks to Taylor’s close-range finish in front of the travelling away support.

The decibel levels were ramped up compared to usual as Taylor was mobbed by his teammates in the celebrations that followed.

And the noise was felt in the press area at The Den with talkSPORT reporter James Fielden left stunned by what he had experienced.

“The Dockers Derby has just absolutely exploded,” Fielden belted out on air. “The Hammers can’t say it hadn’t been coming.

2 Caleb Taylor's opener saw The Den explode into a cauldron of noise Credit: Getty

“Caleb Taylor with the goal as he scrambled it in from close range.

“I haven't seen celebrations like that inside a stadium for a long, long time.”

The Lions continued their dominance as the half drew on and rewarded themselves with a two-goal cushion.

Just moments after Mark Sykes’ thunderous effort from range came crashing off the crossbar, Camiel Neghli fired home from five yards out, leaving the Hammers with a mountain to climb in the second half.

However, the visitors scored twice in quick succession to draw level through Mohamadou Kante and Konstantinos Mavrpanos.

West Ham were reduced to ten men late on when goalscorer Kante was shown a straight red card for a professional foul.

This is a developing story and is being updated.
