talkSPORT cares about getting it right, not just getting it first and because this is a developing situation, details will change. We will be updating this page constantly with verified info, expert takes, and official statements.

Stay tuned for further developments as this story continues to break.

Sports.title: Arsenal open to Max Dowman loan in January after EFL request
Sports.content:
Arsenal could allow Max Dowman to leave the club on loan, but only if it supports his development.

The 16-year-old impressed in the midweek Carabao Cup win at Ipswich, scoring twice in a 4-2 win for Mikel Arteta’s side.



3 Max Dowman put in a superb performance in the midweek win at Ipswich Credit: Getty

Dowman became the youngest player to score in Premier League history last season when he opened his account for the Gunners against Everton.

The teen prodigy was left out of the squad for last weekend’s win at Sunderland with competition for places as fierce as ever at the club.

Earlier this week, Luton Town scout Mick Harford told talkSPORT that the League One club had enquired about taking Dowman on loan ‘a couple of times’ but their advances were rebuffed by Arteta.



Luton are managed by ex-Arsenal star and former Gunners Under-18 head coach Jack Wilshere who has kept a close eye on the star’s development.

But it now appears that Arteta is open to the idea of a loan with the club set to regularly evaluate the player’s needs.



The Dowman plan

"We will evaluate every six months where we are and what is the best thing for him to do and then make the right decision," Arteta said.

"It depends on a lot of factors. What he needs, and what the team needs as well, the availability we have in the squad, the minutes that he is playing and the qualities of those minutes.



"We have to be open, but now the focus is to be here and to impact the team."

Dowman is unable to complete any loan move until he turns 17 on New Year’s Eve.

That falls just one day before the winter transfer window opens and that could see Wilshere try his luck once more.

3 Arteta will play a key role in where Dowman goes if he does leave on loan Credit: Getty



"We haven't really listened to any of the possibilities because we were crystal clear that we wanted to have Max in the squad, that we wanted him to be part of the pre-season and then start to see where we are from there," Arteta added.

Dowman made 13 appearances for Arsenal last season, picking up a Premier League title medal.

And with such promise shown at a young age, Arteta took a high-protective approach over the academy graduate.

A cautious approach

"There have been many cases of that age when they have gone out and been successful and others not," Arteta added.



"In my particular case, I was 17 when I went to Paris [Saint-Germain]. It depends on the atmosphere that you find there, and how much the coach believes in you as to whether you go there just to be part of a squad or play minutes.

"Which country, it depends. But now he is in a good place, let's keep him here."

3 Ex-Arsenal player and coach jack Wilshere may try again in January to bring Dowman to Luton Credit: Getty

Dowman’s heroics at Portman Road would have done his hopes of breaking into the starting XI no harm.



His superb two-goal haul has certainly provided Arteta with some food for thought over the coming months.

"The best way to knock on the door is to do it on the pitch, not in the office," Arteta said when asked whether Dowman could feature against Brighton this weekend.

"Then you just leave out the arguments. When a player delivers constantly on the pitch, every single day in training, that's the best way, that's the best signal for the manager. That's the best signal for his team-mates, too.

"And what Max did the other day, alongside all the other players as well that haven't played many minutes this season, was really impressive."

Sports.title: ‘I’ve not spoken to him’ – Thomas Tuchel admits he ‘didn’t like’ England veteran’s behaviour
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel has admitted Harry Maguire’s reaction to his World Cup omission 'didn’t help' in a telling message about his England future.

The Manchester United defender was once again overlooked by Tuchel in his 27-man squad for the Three Lions' upcoming Nations League fixtures.



4 Harry Maguire's omission earlier this summer saw him miss out on a third straight World Cup with England Credit: Getty

His continued exclusion came despite England being thin on the ground defensively, with World Cup stars John Stones and Dan Burn both not in the latest squad due to injury.

However, instead of recalling Maguire, Tuchel picked Everton's Jarrad Branthwaite in his first call-up since June 2024.

The move is a strong hint over Maguire's international future, following his public criticism of Tuchel for leaving him out of his World Cup group.



Maguire broke the news of his exclusion last May before the official announcement and told talkSPORT he had been left 'shocked' by it.

His mother, Zoe, also fumed at the decision on social media, tweeting that she was 'absolutely disgusted' by Tuchel's call.



Tuchel's honest Maguire reaction

Following Maguire's latest omission, Tuchel has now admitted he was not a fan of his behaviour earlier this summer.

Asked about the centre-back's public response to his World Cup snub, the German responded: “It does not help.



"I will not hold it against him for the rest of his life, because I’m not that type of person. I can forget easily and quickly.

“But I didn’t like it and it doesn’t help. I’ve not spoken to him since.”

After a resurgent 2025/26 season, Maguire has remained a regular starter for Man United in their difficult start this term.

4 Thomas Tuchel didn't appear to have given a Maguire recall much thought Credit: Getty



4 Maguire's World Cup snub saw him miss out on a second consecutive major tournament with England Credit: Getty

He has started in all four of the Red Devils' opening Premier League games, which has seen them win just once and lose twice - including last weekend's controversial Manchester derby defeat.

Alexander-Arnold given clear instructions

As well as Maguire, another major talking point from Tuchel's squad announcement was Trent Alexander-Arnold's return to the fold.

The right-back had fallen out of favour following his move to Real Madrid in the summer of 2025, and was subsequently left out of the World Cup squad.



But after World Cup stars Reece James and Djed Spence were both ruled out of the upcoming internationals through injury, Alexander-Arnold has now been handed a second chance.

With Tuchel appearing not to trust the attack-minded full-back defensively though, the England boss admitted he must showcase his ability without the ball.

He warned: “I am not sure a lot of things have changed.

4 Trent Alexander-Arnold is back with the Three Lions for the first time since June 2025 Credit: AFP

“I know what he is capable of. I know about his talent. He is desperate to play for England and he will fight for his shirt.”



Tuchel added: “It’s a long camp and it’s a good moment to show up.

“But now he has to offer enough defensively, he has to. It’s necessary. My conviction is that he will but he has no choice.”

The 53-year-old also insisted Alexander-Arnold would play as a right-back for England, despite starting in central midfield for Real Madrid in their Champions League win over Inter Milan earlier this month.

Alexander-Arnold has made five appearances for the Spanish giants this season, starting three out of their seven games.

And Tuchel said: “He had a good start in two positions for Real Madrid and he comes as a right-back for us.”

Sports.title: I’m 44 and Man United will not win another Premier League title in my lifetime
Sports.content:
I’m 44 and Man United will not win another Premier League title in my lifetime

Manchester United fans have been dealt a brutal reality check.

In a season that initially offered so much hope, the same challenges have once again emerged without warning.

5 Manchester United have made another underwhelming start to the season Credit: Getty



Two home defeats in the space of four days did little to enthuse supporters who may otherwise have fallen into a false state of security following the 4-0 Champions League destruction of Azerbaijani minnows FK Sabah.

Last weekend’s controversial 1-0 defeat to ten-man Manchester City left United in 13th place and already eight-points off the top.

Their cataclysmic collapse in midweek, throwing away a two-goal lead before being dumped out of the Carabao Cup by Brighton, felt like the needle mover.

Not because United fans haven’t become accustomed to the inexplicable over the last decade, but instead due to the same mistakes being repeated.



Millions invested in the team, a plethora of managers all hoping they can be the one to turn the Old Trafford tide, but ultimately, the same end result.

Boss Michael Carrick, a man who contributed to the club’s glory days, is now firmly in the firing line while fans have again slipped to a low ebb.



For talkSPORT’s chief football correspondent Alex Crook, the chances of the Red Devils lifting another Premier League title are minuscule, regardless of who is in the dugout.

The Manchester United fan provided his sobering reality on the latest episode of talkSPORT’s Fiery Fridays podcast.



The glory days are over...

"So the realisation for me and my hot take this week, I'm 44 now, probably not going to live until I'm 100, realistically,” Crook began.

"Even if I did, I don't think United are going to win the title in my lifetime, I don't think it's going to happen.

5 United's last league title came in 2013 and they have come nowhere close to repeating the feat ever since Credit: Getty

"My big wish now, I've been there and seen it, I've had the glory days, I want us to win something significant so I can share the moment with my two lads who I've forced into following in my footsteps.



"But I don't think that's a realistic ambition anymore, I just think they're so far behind.

"All the time the players are in situ and INEOS and Sir Jim Ratcliffe come in and make the situation worse in my opinion, and not better.

"They've put people like Jason Wilcox and Omar Berrada in positions that their CVs don't really warrant.

“They've destroyed the morale of the football club, the fans hate INEOS and Ratcliffe as much as they despise the Glazers.”



Asked how the 20-time top-flight champions return to competing for Premier League titles and the Champions League, Crook provided fans with a huge dose of reality.

5 Man United fan Crook has resigned himself to eternal Premier League failure

"We're going to have to cherish that win over Sabah because we played a pub team,” he added.

"We're not going to play anybody else as bad as that for the rest of the season and I fear we're not going to get out of the Champions League, League phase.



"How embarrassing would that be if we ended up getting knocked out and not even qualifying for the extra round at the end of it?

'The club is broken'

"I'm just really down about the club, it's completely broken to me, I know it was 26 years between titles last time around, it has been 13 already, so we're halfway there.

"I'm not sure there's a genius in the surrounding areas who's going to come in and save us.

“There's not an Eric Cantona coming over the hills to completely rewrite the history of this football club.



5 The rot has long set in at Old Trafford and Crook believes minority owners INEOS are not helping the cause Credit: Getty

"And actually, only three men [managers] have ever won the league title at Manchester United, I don't think there's going to be a fourth."

Voice of talkSPORT Adrian Durham concurred with his broadcast colleague’s desperate monologue.

He quipped: "I think you are going to live forever, Crooky, to be honest with you, the way you live your life and there's no consequences, you are going to live forever.



"So, Man United are never going to win the league again, I cannot see that happening any time soon and even after that, you've got to rebuild a squad, others will be growing at the same time

"The scary thing about it is, Arsenal are incredibly well run, it's incredibly stable, they've got about three players for every position, and I don't even think Man City are going to get that close to them this season, even though they've started well.

"So, yes, Man United are absolutely miles off it, I make you absolutely right."

5 Man United's last trophy came in the 2024 FA Cup final Credit: Getty



Having the final say, United fan Angelina Kelly then joked: "We don't know how long Crook will live, I was trying to give him at least another 40 years for argument's sake

"United had to wait 41 years before, so maybe it'll be similar, who knows?

"But I agree as well, the ownership's lack of ambition is clearly the problem and they're never going to turn things around if they don't actually sort out the root of the issues."

Manchester United head to Fulham on Sunday needing a win to get their domestic campaign back on track.



Following the three-week international break, a crucial run of fixtures await Carrick's side.

United face key clashes with Tottenham, Leeds and Chelsea, with trips to Atletico Madrid and Como up next in the Champions League.

Sports.title: Chelsea told they’re ‘definitely not’ title contenders as Xabi Alonso sets unwanted record
Sports.content:
Chelsea are not going to be in the Premier League title race this season - there is so much wrong with the 'crazy club'.

Those are the thoughts of Adrian Durham, who watched on as the Blues were beaten 3-0 by Brentford on Friday night.

3 Chelsea were easily beaten by Brentford on Friday, losing away to the Bees in the Premier League for the first time Credit: Getty

Keith Andrews outclassed Xabi Alonso at the Gtech Community Stadium as his side moved up to third in the table.

Meanwhile, Chelsea dropped down to seventh after being handed their second loss of the season in just five games.

The teams went in goalless at half time, but Brentford came out the much better side in the second half, opening the scoring just after the hour mark through Jaidon Anthony.

Igor Thiago then made it two with nine minutes to go and ex-Liverpool man Fabio Carvalho added the third in stoppage time.

The impressive result handed the Bees their first-ever Premier League home victory over Chelsea.

They were winless in five meetings beforehand, but now Xabi Alonso is the first Blues manager to lose on the road against them.

Chelsea out of the Premier League title race

A 3-0 loss for Chelsea has them sitting on seven points after five games and already five points off the top of the table.

That could increase to eight if Arsenal or Manchester City win their matches across the upcoming weekend of action.

And talkSPORT's Durham has already ruled them out of challenging for the Premier League title this campaign.

Speaking after the full-time whistle, he said: "So many questions about this Chelsea performance...fundamentally, they are definitely not Premier League title contenders, we can see that.

3 Alonso has lost two of his opening five league games as Chelsea boss Credit: AFP

"I think there's so much wrong with them."

Arsenal legend Martin Keown added: "It's extremely disappointing from a Chelsea point of view, we were never really convinced.

"The wealth that the club has and the players they buy, but then you see that tonight...it wasn't particularly convincing."

He later continued: "That is a wake-up call for Chelsea."

And Durham then concluded: "They're a crazy club, Chelsea. They started with a 36-year-old in midfield and finished with a 16-year-old in midfield. That's how crazy they are."

Jordan Henderson, formerly of Brentford, made his first start for Chelsea before academy prospect Madhi Nicoll-Jazuli was brought on to join him for the final stages of the match.

3 Brentford outclassed Chelsea to leave the Blues well off the pace in the Premier League Credit: Getty

Jason Cundy's comments come back to bite him

Chelsea superfan Jason Cundy would have been watching their defeat to Brentford behind his hands on Friday.

Not only because of the poor performance, but because just before the season started, he predicted the Blues to win the title.

“I’m going to make a statement now. There is no reason why Chelsea cannot win this title. In fact, I’m going to say it. Chelsea will win the title," Cundy said at the start of August.

“There is something about Chelsea. We have got a cheat code. I’m not proud of it, but we can win the title for a number of reasons.

“Have you seen our front three? Joao Pedro, Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer - Palmer’s had a rest, Joao Pedro’s had a rest.

“Our midfield, the recruitment at the back. It almost certainly looks like we could be playing three at the back with someone in Xabi Alonso, who knows how to win a title.

“One game a week, we saw how beneficial that could be when Antonio Conte came in, went to three at the back. Win the title. History is going to repeat itself."

But after losing in such a fashion, it seems Cundy's title shout may have been a little bit too ambitious.

And Jamie O'Hara has made sure to rub it in, posting an edited image of Cundy dressed as a bee and writing: 'Up the Bees'.

Sports.title: Millwall's home becomes cauldron of hate as English football's nastiest rivalry is reignited with West Ham entering enemy territory at The Den
Sports.content:
Millwall and West Ham reignited their rivalry with the London foes facing off for the first time in 14 years on Saturday.

The Hammers - captained by Dani Dyer's footballer husband Jarrod Bowen - have entered hostile ground in South East London, with the team receiving a volatile reception as their bus arrived before kick off.

The Docker Derby is widely regarded as one of the nastiest rivalries in English football and the Met Police have acted accordingly to ensure the match passes off safely, with approximately 400 officers on duty for the game.

In the build-up to kick off, Millwall fans set the tone by booing and shouting at the Hammers as they arrived at The Den.

One fan could be heard yelling: 'You f***ing n**heads' as the team bus pulled in. Others shouted 'f*** off' and directed x-rated hand gestures at the coach. Inside the ground, fans of both teams hurled abuse at one another

Rival fans hurl abuse at one another as the atmosphere intensified before kick off

A Millwall fan is held back by a steward while pointing at a West Ham supporter on Saturday

Millwall fans shout and point at West Ham's players during the warm up ahead of kick off

On Friday night, police cracked down on an organised fight at The Carpenters Pub in Stratford - with Millwall fans filmed being apprehended by officers.

It is the first time in 14 years that the two sides have met, and Hammers boss Santo urged fans to refrain from violence ahead of kick off.

He said: 'What we want most is that everything goes well, both fans supporting their teams and no conflict. We have people inside the club who are taking care of that. We have to focus on our tasks.'

The rivalry originated in the late 19th century between competing dockworkers and exploded in the second half of the 20th century with the rise of football hooliganism.

There was a large police presence inside The Den to help ensure the match passes safely

West Ham players received a hostile welcome from Millwall supporters on Saturday morning

A Millwall fan aims an x-rated hand gesture at West Ham's bus as it arrived at The Den

The Millwall Bushwackers and West Ham's Inner City Firm were two of the most notorious football firms in England. A Millwall fan died in 1976, while a West Ham supporter was murdered in 1986 as a result of fan disorder.

The Upton Park riot of 2009 was another dark day for English football. The Carling Cup contest between West Ham and Millwall was interrupted by three pitch invasions, while a Millwall fan was stabbed outside the ground.

Following that contest, West Ham were fined £115,000 after being found guilty of 'violent, threatening, obscene and provocative behaviour' and of 'failing to prevent fans entering the field of play'. Millwall were cleared of all charges.

More to follow.

Sports.title: Billionaire Sir Jim Ratcliffe says he has lost confidence in the UK and is not surprised the super-rich are fleeing a country 'on the slide'
Sports.content:
Billionaire businessman Sir Jim Ratcliffe says he has lost confidence in the UK and is not surprised the super-rich are being driven away from a country 'on the slide'.

Outspoken Sir Jim, the co-owner of Manchester United and one of Britain's richest people, warned the decline was down to Labour's failure to tackle welfare and immigration and blamed high taxes.

And he said no politician was 'tough enough' to do something about it and act in the best interests of the country 'instead of their party'.

'Nobody's tough enough to deal with the immigration problem. Nobody's tough enough to deal with the benefits problem. But somebody needs to do it or it ends in a bad place,' he said.

Also highlighting 'the crime on our streets', Sir Jim, who made his fortune in the energy and chemicals sector, said: 'The UK was a fantastic place with the greatest empire in the world. We won two world wars. We were good, honest folk,' warning it was now 'difficult to see how we could arrest' the decline.

He also slammed the government's failure to exploit the UK's own oil and gas supplies and allow and encourage new domestic oil and gas production as 'insanity'.

Brexit supporter Sir Jim, who is said to be worth £17billion and has previously drawn criticism for saying the UK had been 'colonised by immigrants', said the UK could even 'run out of gas' this winter 'in a cold spell' because gas storage was so low.

The businessman left the UK for Monaco in 2020 and said 'things would have to get better' for him to return.

Billionaire businessman Sir Jim Ratcliffe says he has lost confidence in the UK (Pictured last night with wife Catherine Polli at the 20th Anniversary Gala Of the Prince Albert II of Monaco Foundation in Monaco)

'Nobody's tough enough to deal with the immigration problem' Sir Jim told the BBC

He is not the only high-profile billionaire to quit our shores. Others who exited the UK include steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and hedge fund boss Chris Rokos.

In a major blow to confidence in the government, hedge fund billionaire Mr Rokos, Britain's third largest taxpayer, paying £330million alone last year, announced this month that he was leaving the UK for Greece, which has generous tax rules to attract overseas business leaders.

Sir Jim, who founded petrochemical giant Ineos after rising through the ranks from a humble working-class background in Greater Manchester, also hit out at the jealousy aimed at the wealthy in the UK.

He said the politics of envy was driving people away from the UK, contrasting the positive attitude in the US to wealth and said the wealthy should be encouraged to stay because they clearly 'spend in the economy they reside in'.

'In America they applaud people who create wealth,' he told a BBC podcast. 'Unfortunately, the UK has got a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment.'

Sir Jim, who runs the Forties pipeline which transports about 30 per cent of the UK's North Sea oil, also lashed out at the government's 'horrendous' high taxes on North Sea operators meaning they were closing down rigs.

'If you tax everybody to death, they're all going to leave. And that's what's happening,' he said.

Andy Burnham has delayed a decision on whether to grant new licences for domestic oil production with Sir Jim criticising him for 'promising to do something about it' but not 'doing anything'.

Sir Jim says further development of the oil and gas fields at Rosebank and Jackdaw – unpopular with Net Zero zealots such as former energy secretary Ed Miliband – must go ahead to save the industry.

Instead of 'exploiting our natural resources' which you would 'expect,' he said, we are 'shutting it down' and 'risk running out of gas this winter'.

He even warned industry 'could be switched off' if reserves ran out because we are competing with China 'which can pay more' for importing energy rather than producing our own which was 'absurd'.

And he said storage facilities which were already smaller than those of our European neighbours because of lack of investment were already not full.

Energy specialist consultancy Cornwall Insight said that current gas storage levels in the EU were at about 69 per cent, when typically they would be at 85 per cent at this time of the year.

Ineos has invested in the EU's first carbon capture project in Denmark which is being subsidised by the Danish government and the EU.

Sir Jim said he had hoped to develop the technology in the UK but there had not been enough government support.

Critics say carbon capture is expensive and the money could be better used to invest in renewables rather than supporting continued fossil fuel use.

Defending its record, a government spokesperson said oil and gas would play an important role in the UK 'for decades to come' but insisted that the 'transition to homegrown clean power is the only way to deliver energy and financial security for families and businesses'.

Earlier this year, Sir Jim was called 'wrong and offensive' by then PM Sir Keir Starmer for his comments on immigration for which he later apologised.

Sports.title: Jordan Henderson embroiled in tense on-field spat with Emiliano Martinez: Chelsea star exchanges words with new team-mate after first Brentford goal in shock 3-0 defeat
Sports.content:
Jordan Henderson embroiled in tense on-field spat with Emiliano Martinez: Chelsea star exchanges words with new team-mate after first Brentford goal in shock 3-0 defeat

Chelsea new boys Jordan Henderson and Emiliano Martinez were involved in a war of words after Brentford's first goal on Friday night.

The Blues were schooled in a 3-0 rout away at Brentford as second-half goals from Jaidon Anthony, Igor Thiago, and Fabio Carvalho left them for dead.

Club legend Gary Cahill blasted them as 'soft' in the aftermath, with Chelsea having conceded 12 goals in their five Premier League games so far.

Martinez was signed from Aston Villa for £7.5million late in the window to seemingly fix their goalkeeper issue. Former number one Robert Sanchez conceded three on the opening weekend against Fulham and is now on loan at Como.

But the 33-year-old Argentinian has struggled to have the desired impact so far and Henderson voiced his frustration after Anthony's opening goal.

Brentford scored far too easily from a corner, with Mikkel Damsgaard's cross being whipped towards the back post before it was headed back across to an unmarked Anthony.

Jordan Henderson and Emiliano Martinez got into a heated exchange after conceding

Chelsea lost 3-0 against Brentford - and Jaidon Anthony's opening goal was far too easy

Anthony was only loosely marked and Martinez was nowhere near as the forward headed in

Martinez was fairly static throughout the set-piece and Henderson appeared annoyed that the goalkeeper had not come for the ball.

But the fact that Anthony had found space to head home with three defenders in his vicinity raised alarm bells.

Henderson, meanwhile, had been marking nobody.

The midfielder, who was signed from the Bees for his experience and leadership qualities, also remonstrated with defender Maxence Lacroix at another point.

This was Henderson's debut for Chelsea, having signed while he was recovering from a broken arm sustained on England duty.

Brentford now sit third in the Premier League and are still unbeaten, while Xabi Alonso's side are seventh - and you can expect them to slip with nine matches still to come this weekend.

Former Chelsea captain Cahill told Sky Sports at full time: 'There is a certain element of fragility.

'Once they’ve conceded that set piece, you don’t want it to be a mindset but it is a "here we go again" type scenario.

Henderson and Martinez did appear to comfort each other in their full-time disappointment

'I’m sure the manager will address it in videos and on the training ground. Obviously, as a goalkeeper and a back four, you feel a big responsibility when goals are going in.

'The only way you can get out of that is by working hard together and making sure you’re harder to play against, and be more ruthless.

'There just seems to be a kind of softness at the minute in terms of the way they concede goals. You have a few weeks now during the international break, although some of them won’t be there, but they will have time.'

Alonso is attempting to implement a back three with wing-backs, a system which has often been a risk in the English top flight.

Ruben Amorim, for example, could never get his back-three structure to work at Manchester United.

It does have precedent as being successful for Chelsea - fans will remember Antonio Conte's 2016-17 title-winning season fondly.

The Blues were 3-0 down at half-time against Arsenal in their sixth game of that season, prompting Conte to switch to a back three, which he had never drilled.

They then went on a remarkable 13-game winning streak in the league, and won the title by seven points, proving that flexibility can be a key trait for a manager.

Sports.title: RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: It's all very well Howard Webb sending his VAR bunglers to the naughty step - but those that know him tell me 'back-stabbing' referee supremo must look in the mirror
Sports.content:
RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: It's all very well Howard Webb sending his VAR bunglers to the naughty step - but those that know him tell me 'back-stabbing' referee supremo must look in the mirror

Matt Donohue and Blake Antrobus will have a sharper grasp of what it means to interfere with play this weekend. On account of their VAR blunders at the Manchester derby, Howard Webb has decreed they won’t have that option in the Premier League for the foreseeable future.

We know enough by now about their journey to the naughty step. But what about their boss? What about Webb?

How many of these malfunctions need occur before the guy in charge of refereeing takes a look closer to home?

He gave his opinion on Tuesday, which is to say he took a dim view of how his best official, Michael Oliver, saw a correct decision to disallow Erling Haaland’s winner overruled by his eyes in the sky. When Webb reviewed it all, he blamed Donohue’s ‘tunnel vision’ on Haaland and Antrobus was guilty of following Donohue down the same hole.

Neither of them factored for the obvious, that Enzo Fernandez was offside and interfering, and each of them will spend some time below ground as a consequence.

‘They'll not be officiating again until after the international break,’ said Webb.

Howard Webb may have a few questions of his own to answer if the Premier League refereeing standards keep slipping

Enzo Fernandez clearly interferes with play in the Manchester derby but it was missed by the VAR officials, who have now been stood down by Webb

I chatted over a few of these sentiments with a former Premier League referee on Friday and there was no disagreement about standing down the officials. Donohue, the VAR, and Antrobus, his assistant, had committed a cock-up in a high-profile game. Of course they should be benched for a while, we agreed.

But the issue was the man whose organisation put them there in the first place. That being the man who was also responsible for the training and refinement of Michael Salisbury, Lee Mason, John Brooks, Darren England and Dan Cook.

What do they have in common? They have all been in the VAR booth since Webb took over at what was then known as the PGMOL in late 2022 and they have all sat on that naughty step for human errors in their handling of the machine era. Salisbury has visited it more than once.

Errors will happen. That is fine. And it is also fine to view VAR as the worst encroachment in the recent history of the game; a joy-sucking, time-wasting, immensely flawed attempt to find a level of perfection that sport never needed and won’t be delivered. That’s my view and immediate abolition is my wish.

But so long as it exists, where is the accountability from Webb for its botched application in the Premier League? How many people have to be stood down for huge mistakes on his watch before Webb himself stands down?

To follow my conversations with those who have worked with him is to construct a complicated portrait. ‘He’s a clever man and he can be very charming,’ one former official tells me. ‘He can be very impressive, but he is also a master politician and will stab you in the back if it suits him.’

We can take those thoughts or leave them – refereeing is a competitive world. They can bitch and moan about a colleague as well as the best of us.

But other observations go deeper, namely around his key appointments, which include the import of Kevin Blom from the Dutch Eredivisie as performance coach and Hugh Dallas as manager of Pro Ref’s select group.

Erling Haaland celebrates the goal that should not have stood but that won the Manchester derby

Referee Michael Oliver takes his instructions from the VAR in Stockley Park

Dallas was fourth official in the 2002 World Cup final, so his credentials have merit; Blom is perhaps more famous in Scotland over a bad penalty decision that favoured Czech Republic in a Euro 2012 qualifier.

The latter is part of the tit-for-tat of football, but there is a perception in some quarters that they do not pose enough of a challenge to Webb’s leadership. In other words, who is keeping the boss in check?

As a former Premier League referee put it: ‘As ex-referees, we are asking: “Really, are you really surrounding yourself with these people?” It’s so Howard can be comfortable. I think he will always want people who he can be above.’

Only Webb will know if that’s true. But it is hard to deny that a vast amount of Premier League expertise has been lost to the migration of officials elsewhere once they leave the frontline.

Martin Atkinson refereed in the Premier League for more than 20 years, and then led the select group, but he is now the VAR manager for the Scottish FA. Jon Moss oversaw almost 300 top-flight games and left Webb’s PGMOL in 2024 – he is now head of refereeing at Football Australia. Mark Clattenburg presided over a Champions League final and today works on Gladiators.

All of them will have their reasons for being where they are and all of them dropped the occasional clanger. That’s football. That’s refereeing.

But it also looks a little like a drain of know-how that would doubtless help in the English game, where the quirks and rhythms are a unique challenge to officials.

I tend to doubt the idea that the VAR system is better implemented abroad, because statistics around the error rates across the major European leagues are fairly consistent.

Why is former referee Mark Clattenburg working on Gladiators and not helping out in the Premier League?

Martin Atkinson refereed in the Premier League for more than 20 years but he is now the VAR manager for the Scottish FA

I would also suggest that Webb is hardly the face of gross incompetence – one former colleague of his says that he is a better manager than his predecessor, Mike Riley, and worse at training referees.

Equally, some applaud the greater transparency he has pursued with video analysis on television; others say the referees ‘hate’ it.

It’s a tricky picture to study. It’s certainly far tougher to interpret than the one showing Enzo Fernandez interfering with play in front of the Manchester United goalkeeper. But one thing is clear – Webb cannot persist with the charade of blaming everyone except himself.

Sports.title: Goalkeeping icon reveals SIX secrets to David Raya's success: The Arsenal No 1's 'K-block', his spring, how he compensates for his height, the area he's always prided himself on... and where he can still improve
Sports.content:
Gravity-defying leaps, match-winning blocks, brilliant distribution and calming catches are just some of the attributes that have helped David Raya become one of the most important lieutenants in Mikel Arteta's Arsenal.

The Spaniard has won three consecutive Premier League Golden Gloves (awarded to the goalkeeper with the most clean sheets) and was instrumental in last season's title glory.

Only Petr Cech and Joe Hart have more Golden Gloves, on four apiece, and Raya is hunting them down. He is also in the running for the Yashin Trophy – the Ballon d’Or for goalkeeper of the year.

Daily Mail Sport has enlisted the help of Asmir Begovic, the former Chelsea Premier League-winning goalkeeper with more than 300 appearances in the top flight, to break down Raya’s strengths, weaknesses and development across six key areas.

The result is a portrait of a goalkeeper whose game is not simply about spectacular saves, but about making the right decision, at the right time, again and again.

Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya is a three-time Premier League Golden Glove winner

Raya's consistency has seen him become one of the key lieutenants in Mikel Arteta's Arsenal

ONE-ON-ONES

There is probably no better example of Raya’s proficiency at this element of goalkeeping than his wonder save against West Ham in May. With the score at 0-0, Mateus Fernandes was one-on-one against Raya with plenty of time on his side and a huge portion of the goal to aim at.

Yet Raya refused to commit early, standing tall and making himself as big as possible, forcing Fernandes to take the near-post option. When the shot finally came, Raya reacted brilliantly at point-blank range to block it with his body and keep the scores level.

It was that save that sent Arsenal on their way to the title, a stop made under intense pressure. Rather than gambling on where a striker will finish, he stays patient to narrow the angle and make the attacker beat him.

‘This is where he comes to life,’ says Begovic, who runs a goalkeeping academy specialising in coaching and educating young keepers.

‘He’s very good in terms of his decision-making, which techniques to use, when to go out, how to go. He's excelled in this part of the game. You can use different techniques. You can use a full spread: a smother where you throw your body and chest at the ball and go with your hands first.

‘You can use the K-block, which is something some goalkeepers use when you get really close to an attacker – when a keeper goes on his knee and puts his arms out like a K sign.

‘There's different ways you can challenge the attackers in a one-v-one situation. He has all those techniques. He's really good and selective as to when to use them.

‘The best (keepers) have different strings to their bow and are able to use different techniques and use them really well in times they need to.’

Begovic's verdict: 9/10

Raya pulls off his crucial one-on-one save against West Ham's Mateus Fernandes last season

Asmir Begovic, a Premier League winner with Chelsea, is hugely impressed by Raya's all-round game

SHOT-STOPPING

Raya’s reflexes are super sharp. And there are plenty of examples. There’s the save against Atalanta in the Champions League in September 2024 where he first sprang low to his right to parry Mateo Retegui’s penalty before somehow scrambling back to his feet and throwing himself in the opposite direction to claw the striker’s header off the line from the rebound. It was a remarkable display of agility and recovery.

Most recently, of course, he denied Enzo Le Fee from the penalty spot against Sunderland, diving sharply to his left and pushing the midfielder’s effort on to the post.

‘His shot-stopping has been one of the best (in the world), absolutely tremendous,’ says Begovic. ‘When you play for a team like Arsenal, it's not so much multiple shots a game, it's about having to make that one save.

'And he's been able to do that. He's showed up in big moments and helped them win many, many games.

‘There's many things in shot-stopping. Of course, years of practice and training, your physicality, your power, your speed. So I think balance, technique, many different factors go into it.

‘In particular, if you look at his power, his spring is able to really cover the goal. That's what's needed. If you look at goalkeepers (like Raya) that are slightly shorter in height, then they need a lot of power and push to be able to go and cover the goal.

‘Goalkeepers that are a bit taller, bigger, they have a bigger wingspan, they can get away with maybe not having as much power. So his spring and power is second to none. You have to compensate.’

Begovic's verdict: 9/10

Raya makes a remarkable double save against Atalanta in the Champions League

And he gets down brilliantly to tip Enzo Le Fee's penalty on to the post in last weekend's win over Sunderland

AERIAL ABILITY

Of Raya’s many strengths, it’s in the air where a chink in the armour can be found. He is still very good, no doubt, just not superhuman like he is in most other categories.

At 6ft tall, he is one of the smaller goalkeepers in the Premier League, so can’t easily rise above everyone else on crosses and corners to steal the ball away from giants trying to score. Rather than simply plucking the ball out of the air, Raya often has to rely on his positioning.

‘He copes well but it’s the trade-off,’ says Begovic. ‘If you're at a certain height, and obviously you can't do everything, you have to rely on your team-mates to help in the air.

‘He competes, he punches, he uses different techniques. He might not be able to catch often because he might not be able to reach a certain place (due to his height), but he certainly makes good decisions as to when to go, when not to go for crosses.’

His size does, however, force Raya to compensate in other ways. It leaves him making use of his goalline more, instead of always coming out to catch the ball. ‘His main strength will be on the goalline and that's where he'll always look to revert to and make the save as and when he needs to,’ Begovic says. ‘People might assume that is not being aggressive, but actually sometimes it's being more sensible.

'Because if you can't get the ball, you still give yourself a chance to make a save if you stay on the line. But if you go out and miss it, then you're usually in a world of trouble.

‘The best thing about Arsenal is they've built that relationship over time where they know what Raya’s strengths are and what they aren't, and when he's going to do things. He knows when to rely on his defenders (on aerial balls), and help them out in different ways.

‘It's very difficult to find goalkeepers who do absolutely everything. You have to pick and choose your battles.’

Begovic's verdict: 6/10

At 6ft tall, Raya is one of the smaller goalkeepers in the league, so can’t easily rise above everyone else on crosses and corners

DISTRIBUTION

Raya is amazing at distributing the ball quickly to set up counter-attacks through long throws and pinpoint kicks down field.

It helps make Arsenal deadly in transition. Raya can turn a defensive situation into an attacking opportunity within seconds. His long throws are particularly useful after corners, allowing Arsenal to bypass the first line of pressure and release players into space before the opposition can reorganise.

His solid distribution extends to a confidence in playing short passes under pressure, making him an important part of Arsenal's build-up from the back when they don't want to go long.

Begovic sees this as a real strength of Raya’s. ‘Making sure his distribution is spot on is something he's always prided himself on,’ he says.

‘He doesn't get into too many uncomfortable situations because of Arsenal’s backline but when he does, he has the different range of passing, which he also had at Brentford and Blackburn. It was always one of the strengths of his game.

‘There's the distribution with your feet, out of your hands, goal kicks. Obviously then in live play there’s dealing with pressure and dealing with different presses. Looking at his body type and the way he presents himself, it's something that he's quite comfortable in doing.

‘If I look now at Raya and Aston Villa’s Zion Suzuki and Jordan Pickford. They are very, very good at distribution. But Raya is right up there.’

Begovic's verdict: 9/10

Raya's distribution with his feet is superb and he often starts Arsenal's attacks with pinpoint passing

PERSONALITY

Raya is not a goalkeeper who hides from the spotlight. He is an assured and vocal presence behind Arsenal’s defence, demanding concentration from those in front of him while taking responsibility when the pressure is on.

He is also highly competitive and animated, his frustration quick to rise when things go wrong. Most importantly, Raya has shown a strong mentality when he has made mistakes, continuing to demand the ball and play out from the back, for example, rather than allowing errors to affect his confidence.

Begovic says: ‘He seems really well-balanced in how he approaches the game, great composure. He's been so reliable and that's the sort of presence you need at any club, but especially at a big club.

‘It's important to convey that sense of calmness. We call it being almost emotionally neutral, never get too high, never get too low, being consistent. They (the backline) look around and see you're very assured in what you're doing, very safe, very comfortable and that gives a lot of confidence to the other players.’

Begovic's verdict: 8/10

‘Raya seems really well balanced in how he approaches the game, great composure,' says Begovic

THE 'BIG' MOMENTS

From all of Raya’s strengths, there is one area Begovic believes the Spaniard has improved most in.

‘That ability to make the big saves,' says Begovic. 'In Arsenal's progression, he's not had to make as many saves, but we can look at many games where he makes those big, crucial saves.

‘That's a skill because it takes concentration, it takes focus, a save that happens in the 75th minute after maybe not having had an awful lot to do. So that's definitely something where he's progressed his game and again, it shows why he’s one of the world's best. The other thing is consistency. His consistency at the highest level has definitely improved.’

For Begovic, Raya should win the Yashin Trophy. ‘Yes, he’s been the best all-round goalkeeper in the season and the most consistent in his performances,’ he says.

Raya will certainly have earned the accolade.

Begovic's verdict: 9/10

Follow this link https://ab1academy.com/ to find details of Asmir Begovic’s goalkeeping academy which has five centres in the UK and is inspiring the next generation of keepers

Sports.title: Inside the Lancashire civil war: Why the actual cricket has been 'neglected', the tone-deaf powers-that-be, a pre-season fiasco, 'disgraceful' commercial decline, fury at 'c**p' outground and Dame Sarah Storey's Strictly saga
Sports.content:
When an institution collapses into civil war it is, perhaps, wise to seek the view of an outsider if attempting to identify where the blame lies.

‘Lancashire?’ a board member at a rival county tells me, ‘that’s the events-hosting business with the s**t works cricket team attached to it, isn’t it?’ The executive in question is not from Yorkshire but he is only half-joking.

At this early stage I will declare a depth of feeling and perhaps the possibility of over-emotion because this is my county and, in the words of Manchester band James, if I hadn’t seen such riches I could live with being poor.

But few would argue with this statement: Lancashire, proud Lancashire, are currently an absolute laughing stock. Consider this as they face up to arguably their worst season in 162 years of existence: in their last nine County Championship innings – over a pathetic run stretching back to June – the Red Rose have failed to post a score of 200 runs or more.

When they last scored 300 we were in April, wondering if we were in for a decent summer and yet to welcome a Lancashire supporter to No 10.

That, sadly, is not the least of it on a depressing charge sheet as long as Brian Statham Way. A club that should not be in the Second Division, let alone in grave danger of propping the rest of it up, have now lost eight of their last 10 matches and a shameful first wooden spoon is a distinct possibility.

As for the white-ball efforts, Lancs failed to make it out of the group stages of the Vitality Blast and fell at the Metro Bank One-Day Cup quarter-finals, with a team admittedly decimated by call-ups to the Hundred. The women’s side finished bottom of the Blast ladder. They also failed to make the One-Day Cup knockout stages.

Clouds have been gathering over Lancashire and Old Trafford for some time with the team struggling in Division Two of the County Championship

Sir James Anderson has been one ray of sushine with 50 Championship wickets this season

All that is left now, in this Pendle Witch of a year, is the battle to avoid bottom place. Although coming last would ensure at least that next year could not be worse.

In bad light, as there often is in these parts, there remain some rays of sunshine. Enduring humour is one. Amid widespread allegations that those charged with running Lancashire care only for the commercial side, one wag suggested they might now wish to consider a sponsorship deal with a well known pizza delivery firm after 81 for 0 turned into 161 all out during the latest forlorn tale at Canterbury.

The wickets tumbled at such a rate that the club’s own X account appeared to fail to keep up and stopped posting each time one fell. Speaking of social media, earlier this week the 15th anniversary of Lancs’ last County Championship Division One triumph came and went without any mention.

Perhaps they were, understandably, wary of the comments such a post would trigger from a fanbase that is up in arms.

What was posted during the carnage, presumably at the request of the tone deaf powers-that-be, was an advert enticing punters to ‘watch our 2027 major matches @EmiratesOT in style’ accompanied by a video tour of one of the ground’s hotel rooms with a panoramic view of the field of misery.

Some joked that you’d only need to stay for one night to watch a County Championship match, while others pleaded – with some irony – for them to ‘read the room’. ‘This is why you’re stuck in Division Two – it’s always money over cricket,' one added.

That final observation is one that has been shared many times to Daily Mail Sport for this report. And it is one that appears to carry considerable weight. Lancashire, put simply, are a cricket club that have lost sight of what being a cricket club entails.

A name is often offered when you ask those inside and outside the club who is behind this perceived relegation of sport: Daniel Gidney.

The 14-year chief executive is the prime suspect in this crime against cricket. He will leave at the end of the season and may well point to a club not far away from going bust when he arrived to one in a redeveloped ground (albeit an aesthetically underwhelming one) with an extended hotel and top-tier conferencing facilities that have transformed how they generate revenue, and how much revenue they generate.

He may also make the valid point that a cricket club cannot survive on cricket alone and he would be right to do so. But there is no need for one to suffer at the hands of the other, and it is hard to make an argument that this is not what we have witnessed.

Old Trafford has an extended hotel and top-tier conferencing facilities that have transformed how Lancashire generate revenue

But chief executive Daniel Gidney (right), pictured with Mike Atherton and Anderson, has been accused of putting commercial interests ahead of cricketing ones

‘The core business – whether Gidney likes it or not – is cricket,’ explains one well-placed source. ‘The clue is in the name, Lancashire County Cricket Club. Cricket has been neglected. You need business and finance, absolutely, but you must never lose track of the fact that you have to win cricket matches.’

In what is a small but perhaps telling anecdote, one source discloses that current coach Steven Croft got a glimpse of the priority not long after taking the reins.

Ahead of the season the playing staff, the story goes, wanted to go to Spain’s Desert Springs, with its state-of-the-art, warm-weather cricket facilities, with staple Dubai out of the question due to the conflict in the Middle East.

‘The chief executive was resistant,’ the source recalls. ‘He said that there was no commercial value in going to Spain and suggested they should go to India because of the tie-up with Emirates Airlines and the Manchester Super Giants franchise (which is now Indian owned). They eventually ended up in Spain but it spoke volumes about what was important.’

Another gripe among some of the members is the addition of a new, first-team ground at Farington, on the rural outskirts of Preston. Some see it as an attempt to take more cricket away from Old Trafford and free it up for more concerts (although those have been banned by the local council since a member of the public was injured at a Red Hot Chili Peppers gig in 2022).

‘It’s c**p,’ says one member, bluntly, after it made its bow this summer. ‘Middle of nowhere, no shelter, basic facilities. Give me Blackpool, Southport and Liverpool any day.’

It would appear that some in the dressing room share that feeling, amid a bemusing allegation that players and coaching staff were not consulted over the designs for the site.

Club officials say that director of cricket Mark Chilton was involved in the planning, improvements are on the way, and add that they believe the facility is the envy of many other counties, with Surrey looking at following suit.

Perhaps in a nod to the old saying that while success has many fathers, failure is an orphan, it was difficult to get a straight answer to the next question. But if the assumption is that the director of cricket performance directs the cricket performance then it has to be assumed that Chilton was responsible for a managerial decision so staggeringly stupid that it would even make the folks at the other Old Trafford wince.

It was in 2023, when someone saw fit to make Dale Benkenstein the men’s first-team head coach. The South African had taken over at Gloucestershire in late 2021 and in 2022 promptly guided them to bottom of Division One. He repeated the trick in 2023, with Gloucester failing to win a single one of their 14 matches in Division Two. And then he got the Lancashire job.

‘It’s c**p,’ says one member of the new outground Farington, after it made its bow this summer. ‘Middle of nowhere, no shelter, basic facilities'

Dale Benkenstein led Gloucestershire to bottom of Division One in 2022 and repeated the trick in Division Two, with his side failing to win a single match. And then he got the Lancashire job

‘With no disrespect to Gloucester, in football terms it was like finding someone who had failed in League Two and giving them the Manchester United job,’ one onlooker comments.

Benkenstein did, at least, manage to avoid a hat-trick of bottom-placed finishes in his first season at Old Trafford. Instead, he led Lancashire to second bottom and relegation.

In his second season, he was finally shown the door after a winless first two months, leaving many asking what on earth those in charge thought was going to happen when they made the appointment. Chilton, a former Lancashire player, turned to Croft, a former Lancashire player.

On the subject of appointments, Dame Sarah Storey arrived as chair late last summer, installed by the board, to replace the outgoing former Manchester United and British Olympic Association executive, Andy Anson.

Great Britain’s most successful Paralympian of all-time did not create this firestorm, but according to some she has done little to extinguish the flames.

On day two of the season opener at Northampton, all the players were told to gather on the field for an address from the 48-year-old Mancunian. Some wondered why they needed the address and why – if it was necessary – it had not taken place before now, and behind closed doors.

‘Then cameras started clicking and they all felt like they’d become part of some kind of self-promotional photo opportunity,’ says one insider.

Club officials insist the above description is misleading and that Storey, as she had done with the women’s team, had simply wandered out to the outfield to chat to players as they warmed up in her capacity as chair.

Storey’s decision to take part in this year’s Strictly Come Dancing has done little to dampen concerns. While chair is an honorary position, given the disastrous state of the club it is safe to say that eyebrows have been raised at what may well be a time-consuming, alternative pursuit.

New head coach Steven Croft, a former Lancashire player, has done little to improve results

Dame Sarah Storey became the club's chair late last summer but her decision to take part in this year’s Strictly Come Dancing has done little to dampen concerns around the place

It would also be wrong to absolve the players from blame. This is not a story of under-investment, or of a county whose league position represents precisely where it sits with regards to money spent on wages.

There are those who are exempt, a small list that obviously includes Sir James Anderson, who continues to presumably put his 44-year-old body through torture and who has picked up 50 wickets in 11 games. But at some stage, despite a perceived lack of direction from above, it has to be accepted that this is a group which continues to grossly underperform.

The picture is one of a county that continues to punch itself in the face, and I had my own glimpse earlier this week.

On Wednesday, as the men’s first team limped to the latest surrender at Kent, I was due at the other Old Trafford, where Manchester United (speaking of limp surrenders), were hosting Brighton in the Carabao Cup. Given I was in the area, I thought I would nip into the Lancs club shop to pick up a couple of bits and show some token support, in these miserable times.

The car park is heaving and the place is a hive of activity. As it often is when United are at home, the hotel is sold out and they are preparing themselves for the arrival of the hundreds of corporate guests who are wined and dined before making the short journey to the football ground.

When I tell the fluorescent-jacketed stewards I am trying to get to the club shop, they look at me like they had never heard those words before. Eventually, a senior official comes over. They tell me that the club shop is closed and now only opens on matchdays. When I joke that this place used to be a cricket club they laugh, roll their eyes and add for good measure: ‘They’re idiots, aren’t they?’

When I make the point to a member, they say that Lancashire’s retail income last year was £57,000 compared to £382,000 the year before. ‘Watching the decline is bad enough,’ they say, ‘causing it and then congratulating yourself – that’s the real disgrace’.

There is, according to some, hope. If nothing else, things can hardly get worse – even if top-of-the-table Durham are up next.

Arav Shetty is bowled by Ollie Price against Gloucestershire back in April. Lancs have not reached 300 in a first-class innings since that month

The talented Rocky Flintoff, son of Andrew, provides a reason to be cheerful about the future

The county’s conveyor belt continues to churn out talented young cricketers, with great things hoped for Joe Moores and Rocky Flintoff, who have both been involved with England Lions this year. Whether they will remain with Lancashire, who have sadly developed a reputation for failing to develop talent, remains to be seen.

On one side of the civil war sits a group of club greats including David Lloyd and Paul Allott, big beasts who continue to lead the calls for change. The new chief executive, Richard Kenyon, is a Lancashire supporter who has widespread experience in the world of sport following a long stint at Everton. Kenyon heads west from Nottinghamshire, who are seeking back-to-back titles.

There have been positive arrivals to the board of late, and it is understood that Sir Clive Lloyd and Mike Watkinson will be heavily involved in an end of season review into what has gone wrong. It may take them some time to complete.

Membership numbers have, perhaps surprisingly or perhaps thanks to the introduction of cheaper five-day options in 2023, held up, with 6,364 at the last count. The widespread joking is a deflection tactic of a fanbase that still cares deeply.

And, perhaps above all else, the solution is also relatively simple, despite how hard the current regime is making it look. I ask the straight-talking member who described Farington as ‘c**p’ what needs to change. Again his response is sharp and to the point. ‘Just win some b****y cricket matches,’ he says.

Sports.title: 'At a big club it's our house, our rules': Inside the challenge Andoni Iraola faces in making the leap to Liverpool, as sources reveal the fatal errors made by Hodgson, Frank and Moyes - and the shocking player power they were up against
Sports.content:
When Roy Hodgson made the step up from Fulham to manage Liverpool, he was reigning Manager of the Year and understandably sure of himself as a coach.

His reputation for tactical knowledge and intelligence had been built across two-and-a-half decades and more than half-a-dozen countries. What he was not prepared for was working at a club like Liverpool.

‘He didn’t understand it when he walked in and he still didn’t fully understand it when he was asked to walk out again a few months later,’ a source who was there at the time tells Daily Mail Sport.

‘It’s different at a really big club and it’s especially different at a club like Liverpool. It’s not just about the football. It’s about what you do, what you say and how you carry yourself.

‘It’s nuanced and every part of it matters. That sounds daft and exaggerated. But it’s true. Roy thought his football pedigree and coaching was all that mattered and he was wrong.’

As Liverpool manager, the spotlight is on Andoni Iraola in a way he will never have experienced before

Roy Hodgson could not handle the Liverpool job despite his vast experience. ‘He didn’t understand it when he walked in and he didn’t understand it when he walked out,’ a source tells Daily Mail Sport

Taking the step up in football management always feels like a defining moment in a career. Sir Alex Ferguson at Manchester United managed it, eventually. So did Arsene Wenger. Eddie Howe’s switch from Bournemouth to Newcastle was seamless.

Others, more recently, have struggled.

Graham Potter fell on his face at Chelsea after leaving Brighton. Thomas Frank’s transition from Brentford to Tottenham proved too much. Ruben Amorim swapped Lisbon for United and drowned.

And now it’s Andoni Iraola’s turn. The 44-year-old Spaniard returns to his old club Bournemouth on Sunday still feeling his way as manager of Liverpool. Three wins and three draws from six opening games is an acceptable return but the size of the step up cannot be overstated.

For Liverpool’s opening pre-season game against Sunderland in Nashville – Iraola’s first as manager – there were 25,000 fans present. That’s twice as many as ever watched Bournemouth at their tiny stadium on the south coast. The level of expectation and scrutiny is incomparable.

‘That’s the key difference,’ says a source who watched Frank’s struggles at Tottenham closely. ‘At Brentford, every Premier League win Thomas gave them was a gift. They were grateful. It’s a bonus.

‘At Tottenham and other top clubs, it’s not like that. Three points are a minimum requirement. And then you have to play the right kind of football and say the right things. By the time Thomas started to get to grips with that, it was too late.’

For Liverpool’s opening pre-season game against Sunderland in Nashville – Iraola’s first as manager – there were 25,000 fans present

Thomas Frank could not make the step up from Brentford to Tottenham and eventually lost his job

Iraola is a well-respected and talented coach. His two previous postings have been successful, at Bournemouth – who he took into Europe – and Rayo Vallecano in Spain.

On that tour of America, Liverpool players were impressed with his sessions and expressed surprise at just how much time he spent with them on the grass, ball in hand and whistle in mouth.

Those on the trip talk of an easy charm and natural sense of calm. What is yet to emerge – simply because it hasn’t had to – is the depth and strength of his personality, steel and emotional intelligence.

‘There are some strong characters in that Liverpool dressing room,’ explains one agent to a first-team player. ‘There are egos. Others may use stronger words.

'Look what happened between Mo Salah and Arne Slot. That’s where the power balance can shift. At Bournemouth his word will have been law. Here, he may have to earn that right a little bit.’

Players are more powerful than ever in modern football. What they say and do matters more than it ideally should and they are not always rational judges.

Frank, for example, asked one first-team player to apologise for being late to a Champions League team meeting last season only to be met with refusal. At Chelsea, some of the club’s bloated squad called Potter ‘Harry’ behind his back.

On one occasion, a member of the Stamford Bridge ownership tried to pick the team for a talented coach. He had never even attended a Champions League match before selecting a Chelsea XI for one.

In the post-Ferguson era at United, meanwhile, David Moyes – hired from Everton – was suffocated by a combination of player scepticism, modest results and a lack of understanding of how you were expected to talk and behave at the biggest club in the land.

At Chelsea, some of the club’s bloated squad called Graham Potter ‘Harry’ behind his back

At Old Trafford back in 2013, players used to joke that the infamous Portuguese flop Bebe had more medals than the new manager. On a plane back from a European game, meanwhile, they chuckled when they saw Moyes reading a book on management.

‘The players were in charge,’ left back Patrice Evra told Daily Mail Sport at his book launch five years ago.

These things really shouldn’t matter but unfortunately they do and to what extent depends in part on the standing of the manager who came before. Iraola is replacing Slot who was sacked but only after winning the Premier League. The memory of Jurgen Klopp still lingers, meanwhile.

Klopp possessed a charisma, turn of phrase and political outlook that fell neatly in step with those on the Kop. He was smart, too. One of his first tactics, for example, was to reduce the very size of the football club in his head by learning the name of every single person who worked at the training ground. That was for them. But it was for him, too.

Again the contrast with the unfortunate Hodgson – sacked after taking 25 points from a possible 60 in the 2010-11 season – is stark. Hodgson, remember, was no ingenue. He had previously managed Inter Milan and the Swiss national team and had taken Fulham to the final of the Europa League only weeks before his appointment. He was an elite coach. Liverpool, however, is just different.

‘Klopp just understood the club and its quirks,’ explains another source. ‘Rafael Benitez – Roy’s predecessor – did too. And indeed Brendan Rodgers later on. At Liverpool, the media need to be indulged, as do certain fans’ groups. Your language needs to reflect that, too.

‘Iraola, for example, will be examined in a different way to how Enzo Maresca will be by Manchester City fans. Even though his job is, on the surface, a significantly harder one.

‘How many people were listening to what he said at Bournemouth? At Liverpool, everybody is listening to it. Every word of it. And they will soon be dissecting it on podcasts and looking for hidden meanings that often are not even there.

‘One of Roy’s most memorable errors came when Ferguson accused Fernando Torres of diving and he didn’t bite back. He basically said he wasn’t getting involved. Torres was his best player and a Kop idol. To the fans, Roy left him hanging there after a verbal assault by our greatest rival. As Liverpool manager you just can’t do that.’

David Moyes found the step up from Everton manager to boss of Manchester United too great

Manchester City fans call on United to keep the faith with Moyes - for their own selfish reasons

Liverpool’s style of football will also be interesting to observe under Iraola. At Bournemouth, his team were smart. Counter-pressing became an art form and they were, at times, comfortable not to have the ball even at home.

His team’s average possession, for example, was less than 50 per cent. That’s OK for a club looking to punch above its weight by way of its results. It’s not for a club like Liverpool. Klopp’s teams averaged 62 per cent while Slot’s sat at 59 per cent.

So far Iraola’s metrics are good. Only in the 2-1 home win over Atletico Madrid did the number drop below 50 per cent while even in draws against Newcastle and Nottingham Forest they were comfortably on the right side of 50 per cent.

This was one of the things that did for Frank at Spurs, according to those close to the club. ‘The players liked Thomas,’ says a source. ‘It’s impossible not to like Thomas. But they thought his football was too often built around what he thought the opposition would do.

‘Sometimes his team’s xG (expected goals) was almost minus. That may occasionally be OK at Brentford but never at Tottenham. At a club like this one you have to get on the front foot. Our house, our rules.’

Iraola seems to have avoided any obvious banana skins so far but he has not yet been placed under real pressure.

When asked about the step up in Friday's press conference, he said: 'For me the demands on the players are the same. I don’t give different instructions to one player because he is more expensive than another player because he has cost us less money.

'The demands are the same. The strengths and weaknesses of players are different, so we have to always adapt the team to try and maximise the collective side of this. In Bournemouth, we had players who could run forever and other players who could not do it.

'When you draw 2-2 at Newcastle with Bournemouth, it is a good result, but I understand that with Liverpool it is not. The goals of the team are different and so are the expectations.'

Last season under Slot was so miserable that his successor is working with some afforded leeway. That will only last so long. Two or three poor results would soon change the atmosphere and narrative, especially given the fast start made at the top of the Premier League by Arsenal and City.

It was interesting to hear Iraola say how hard it was for his team to face Fulham on Saturday having played in Europe in midweek. As we know, that is the way of life at the sharp end of our game. It simply will not wash as mitigation.

It was interesting to hear Iraola say how hard it was for his team to face Fulham on Saturday having played in Europe in midweek

Tottenham fans show their frustrations at the club during Frank's time in charge

There are always uncontrollable reasons contributing to failure, of course. Managers by and large inherit problems.

Potter’s Chelsea was a madhouse while Frank’s Tottenham finished 17th the season before. This season’s Spurs manager – Roberto De Zerbi – has been given £300million of new players for a reason.

Back in the day at United meanwhile, Moyes was dealt an almost impossible hand once Ferguson left the building with all the club’s recruitment processes buried in the back of his head. Some experienced players simply didn’t try hard enough while Old Trafford executives have since acknowledged they failed the Scot.

‘We should have helped him more,’ said former CEO Ed Woodward and it’s not by co-incidence that Moyes and indeed Hodgson have gone on to prove their enduring worth elsewhere.

Undoubtedly, though, there were some spectacular errors. Moyes’ decision to lead his squad for a walk on Sydney’s Bondi Beach on his one and only pre-season tour was taken despite warnings of impending chaos by club security.

‘It’s fine, I did it with Everton,’ said Moyes. By the time the United party had required a hastily-convened police escort to get them safely back to the team hotel, Moyes had come to understand that Everton was one kind of football club – with one kind of global standing – and United was quite another.

Such colourful tales make for great podcast chat and help to sell books. Equally, they matter. Perception matters.

Still with United, the recently departed Ruben Amorim couldn’t understand why he was required to do so many media interviews each week. Hodgson, meanwhile, once bit back at a young journalist asking about his tactics with all the patience of a surgeon who had just been told he was holding his scalpel the wrong way.

At United, Moyes was dealt an almost impossible hand once Sir Alex Ferguson left the building with all the club’s recruitment processes buried in the back of his head

Ruben Amorim couldn’t understand why he was required to do so many media interviews each week while he was manager of Manchester United

‘I just don’t understand what it has to do with them,’ he subsequently told a staffer. And that’s the point. You either instinctively get it at a big club or you don’t. And if you need to learn, you must do so quickly.

Potter – still coming to terms with what happened at Chelsea and indeed West Ham if some of his recent social media exchanges are anything to go by – said philosophically recently that: ‘You are never quite as good or quite as bad as people say.'

He is absolutely right about that. But how a manager goes about influencing those judgments at a big club really does matter.

Slot – endlessly respectful of his predecessor’s achievements - got it right for a while at Liverpool. It was his results that got him in the end and they will be the prime metric for Iraola. But Hodgson departed a decade-and-a-half ago lamenting that he never got to feel the famous love from the Kop.

The point is that you have to know how to earn it.

Sports.content:
West Ham star accused of SPITTING by Millwall goalkeeper during derby clash

Referee Paul Tierney stopped play during the clash between Millwall and West Ham following an allegation of spitting made by Filip Marschall against Taty Castellanos

View Image The allegation was made against Taty Castellanos (Image: Richard Pelham/Getty Images)

Millwall goalkeeper Filip Marschall has accused West Ham striker Taty Castellanos of SPITTING at him during Saturday's Dockers Derby. The incident occurred midway through the second half with Millwall leading 2-0 at The Den.

‌



Referee Paul Tierney stopped play to speak to Marschall. His allegation was then reported to fourth official Lewis Smith by Millwall's coaching staff.

‌



When play restarted, West Ham mounted a comeback. The away side made it 2-2 by scoring two goals in quick succession through Mohamadou Kante and Kostas Mavropanos.

Sports.title: Ayr Gold Cup under threat after 40-minute deluge of rain leaves standing water on track
Sports.content:
Ayr Gold Cup under threat after 40-minute deluge of rain leaves standing water on track

The ground at Ayr Racecourse was changed to heavy after 8.5mm of rain fell and caused water to build up on the course ahead of Scotland's biggest meeting on the Flat

View Image Jockey Paul Mulrennan (left) inspecting the ground conditions at Ayr Racecourse (Image: Steve Welsh/PA Wire)

Horse racing's big Saturday meeting at Ayr is under threat after a deluge of rain at the track this morning.

‌



A total of 8.5mm fell in 40 minutes and turned the ground heavy, causing standing water around half-a-furlong from the winning post. The area is unavoidable and will need to be crossed the the horses and jockeys on the final day of three at the Ladbrokes-sponsored festival.

‌



Jockeys including St Leger heroine Saffie Osborne and top northern rider Paul Mulrennan went out to check conditions at 12.20pm and a decision was made to push the first race to 2.30pm. However the seven-race card, which had the feature £180,000 Ladbrokes Ayr Gold Cup scheduled for 3.40pm, has to pass a second inspection at 1.45pm.

‌



Prior to the call being made, Racing TV presenter Gordon Brown suggested there is a "40 per cent chance of racing." "There's slight odds against racing taking place," he said.

"The problem area is about half-a-furlong down from the winning post. The rain that fell was of biblical proportions, really heavily and quickly. Lots of the car parks were flooded, the way I have come in all the roads were flooded and there is a showery forecast this afternoon.

‌



"The jockeys have had a look at this area. It's all the way across so it's unavoidable. You can't come past it on the round or straight course and we have two big fields today for the Gold and Silver Cups."

Trainer Jim Goldie said on ITV he thinks officials could "probably" give the event the green light if it stays dry. "It's up to the jockeys if they decide it's not safe," he said.
