World.title: US and Denmark reach deal over Greenland after Trump annexation threats
World.content:
The US and Denmark have announced a deal on Greenland's security, resolving a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Donald Trump's threats to seize it by force.

Trump said the agreement would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs" in the semi-autonomous Danish territory.

The leaders of Denmark and Greenland welcomed the deal to "strengthen security" in the region, which they said was expected to be signed next week, but did not outline its contents.

The announcement comes after months of threats by Trump to "take" Greenland over national security concerns, citing its strategic location for defence purposes and its mineral wealth.

No text of the agreement has been released. Trump said the deal came with "no cost to the United States" and would grant it the ability "to do what is necessary" to "secure and defend the security of Greenland", in a post on Truth Social.

He said it included a rule that no US adversary could maintain a military presence in Greenland or "make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval".

Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties, which was expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week.

The deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognising "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination", she said in a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.

The agreement would still need to go through "the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force" once signed, the statement noted.

Nielsen said it was "gratifying that we are about to enter into an agreement that ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western alliance".

"The agreement recognises Greenland's interests and our place in international co-operation. It is for the benefit of us all," he said.

A Nato spokesperson said the military alliance welcomed the deal, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region".

World.title: Trump says he is banning CNN and Politico from White House
World.content:
Since returning to office in January 2025, Trump and administration officials have repeatedly clashed with members of the White House press corps. In his second term, Trump has also moved to bring conservative bloggers, influencers and other media into the press room, arguing it is necessary to provide diverse perspectives to the American public.

In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.

The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America".

AP swiftly filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.

The president has frequently clashed with reporters in the Oval Office on Air Force One and during White House events, often referring to them as "fake news" and "rude".

In his first term, Trump also banned CNN correspondent Jim Acosta from the White House, although his credentials were restored after CNN sued.

CNN is one of only five US news outlets that film video for the pool. The pool refers to an outlet or reporter sharing material from a presidential event with other media outlets. The BBC contributes to the White House radio pool.

The announcement was immediately criticised by leading advocacy organisations for freedom of the press.

In a statement on Friday afternoon, the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University said that "with so many courts having ruled against him on exactly this point, you'd think President Trump would have learned this lesson by now".

"If President Trump means to expel these news organizations from the White House press pool, his action is doubly unconstitutional because the press pool is a 'public forum' under the First Amendment, which means the president can't exclude journalists from it on the basis of their viewpoints," said the institute's executive director, Jameel Jaffer.

A major group that provides legal services to the media - the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press - said it expected Trump's ban to be struck down quickly by the courts because it was "flatly unconstitutional".

"The First Amendment is clear that once the White House invites in some journalists, it can't ban others because it doesn't like their reporting," said the group's president Bruce Brown, calling the potential ban "textbook viewpoint discrimination".

The Freedom of the Press Foundation also said it was illegal, adding: "It's also hard to imagine a dumber move".

Trump "has been retaliating against the press for years, but it hasn't helped him," it said, saying "these outrageous attacks only demonstrate how scared he is of an informed public".

Trump has pursued legal action against a number of US and international news outlets, including The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times and the BBC.

Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multimillion dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.

World.title: Google's Gemini AI hacked three companies in security test
World.content:
Google's AI model Gemini autonomously hacked into three companies during a test of its cyber-security capabilities, the company has said, in what is thought to be the first known case of it carrying out such an act.

Gemini found "public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test", a Google official told the BBC, noting that in each instance "the model stopped".

The affected companies have been informed about the breach.

It comes after renewed public scrutiny over the pace of AI development, with some tech firms calling for a slowdown as they raise concerns over its potential threat to humanity - though not all companies agree.

The hacks first reported by the Wall Street Journal, occurred in May during a test conducted by an independent company that carries out cyber-security evaluations.

Heather Adkins, vice president of Security Engineering at Google, told the BBC in a statement: "We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they've now made to their testing processes."

She added: "These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly."

Other AI systems have recently reported similar instances of breaches.

In July, Anthropic's Claude escaped its test environment to hack three organisations on its own just days after OpenAI said its models had carried out cyber-attacks against several "publicly available services".

As public debate continues to grow over the safety of developing the tech, so too does conversation around regulation.

Both Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang and OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman are expected to attend a White House state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping next Friday. Altman will then brief the UN Security Council next week.

On Friday, Huang told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, "we should go as fast as we can" with AI development.

World.title: Trump signs sweeping Russia sanctions bill
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has signed a sweeping sanctions bill, taking aim at Russia's economy by punishing major purchasers of its oil and gas.

The bill, passed by the US House of Representatives earlier this week, gives Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas â most significantly China and India.

At Trump's behest, the bill also extends to Iran's energy and weapons sectors.

The bill is named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Ukraine's staunchest defenders in Washington before his death on 11 July.

The 48-page bill, formally titled the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, includes exceptions for countries that import less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia and are working to lessen their dependency.

Additionally, the bill includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior figures within the Russian government as well as banks and other financial institutions and Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions.

Senator Richard Blumenthal, a New York Democrat, previously described the legislation as "scorching sanctions" which would "throttle Putin's war machine".

Data from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, or CREA, shows that China accounted for 50% of Russian crude exports between December 2022 and August 2026, followed by India at 37%.

Turkey and the European Union each accounted for 5% during the same time period, although Russian energy exports to the EU have been decreasing.

Senator Graham had long sought to push the Trump administration to do more to punish Russia for the war that followed its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The bill also received the support of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who thanked Trump for signing the "critically important legislation".

"The best way to honour Lindsey's memory will be to implement the provisions of this law fully and swiftly," he wrote on social media.

"Senator Graham never doubted for a second that America has enough strength to stand up to dictators and achieve results if it acts the right way."

Graham, 71, died on 11 July of an "aortic dissection" caused by cardiovascular disease shortly after returning from a trip to Kyiv.

"He died doing the work he was born to do," Trump said at the time.

Prior to his death, he was widely considered one of Ukraine's fiercest allies on Capitol Hill, at a time when Republicans were bitterly divided over the extent of US involvement abroad and the amount of aid being given to Ukraine.

World.title: Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
World.content:
"What we are going to do, I have no idea," sobs Nokwanda Matshikiza, reflecting on the murder of her niece Dineo Motapane. "But something must give."

"For us, for all the other women. How many other bodies will be found before something happens?"

Nokwanda is speaking to the BBC from the family home near South Africa's main city, Johannesburg, just two days after relatives identified Dineo's body.

The 38-year-old mother-of-two was last seen alive on Sunday. Her battered and partly burned body was later found in the residential region of Ekurhuleni.

Nokwanda weeps as she describes how the family will have to face, at some point, the grim task of telling Dineo's daughter of her death.

"How do you explain that your parent was brutally murdered, dumped in a field, and just left there, discarded like a piece of rubbish.

"There's no coming to peace with it," she adds. "It's something that you can never reconcile yourself with, that you can never get over."

Dineo's death this week has come amid a series of comparable incidents in Ekurhuleni â her body one of three discovered there this week. In total, nine bodies of murdered women have been found in similar circumstances in the region since July.

The problem has always been there but this spate of grim discoveries has once again sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country â which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.

World.title: Shark attack prompts rare kill order in Western Australia as victim named
World.content:
A rare catch-and-kill order has been issued for a great white shark off the coast of Western Australia after 63-year-old swimmer Greg O'Neill was killed at a popular beach on Friday. His body has still not been found.

Authorities have said that beaches along the state's coast, including in the capital Perth, will remain closed until at least Sunday as the search for the shark continues.

It is the second shark attack in Western Australia (WA) this week, and the third fatal attack in the state this year.

The incident, at Sorrento Beach in Perth's north, has reignited debate about how to keep beachgoers safe in Australia.

In a statement, Greg O'Neill's family said they were "deeply shocked and devastated by the terrible tragedy."

"Greg loved the ocean and was known as a passionate swimmer, sports lover, dedicated worker and an all-round generous, witty guy."

On Saturday, his family visited the scene, where locals have been laying flowers.

Witness Jacqui Rapaic told the ABC that two men were swimming, but only one made it back to shore, and that she could see "a pool of blood" in the water.

Another witness told WAtoday that she saw the man being "mauled" as the shark "tossed him around like a fish". Members of the public reported seeing a 2.5m-long (8ft 2in) shark at around the same time.

Joondalup authorities, where Sorrento is located, said all beaches were closed "as a precautionary measure" and would remain so until at least midday on Sunday.

Pictures on Saturday showed the coastline being patrolled by a police boat and helicopter.

World.title: Millions without power as Cuba hit by latest major blackout
World.content:
Millions in Cuba were left without power on Friday as the country was plunged into yet another major blackout.

The country's entire electricity grid suffered "total disconnection" that triggered a nationwide outage, Cuba's energy ministry said.

Power was restored to some priority areas by late evening, including those near hospitals and water pumping stations in the capital Havana, grid operator UNE said.

It is at least the sixth partial or total blackout to hit Cuba this year, where ageing electricity infrastructure and chronic fuel shortages have been placed under further strain by a US blockade on oil shipments to the communist-run nation.

UNE said the outage started just before 14:00 local time on Friday (18:00 GMT) due to a transmission fault coupled with poor weather conditions in central Cuba.

Protocols to begin the "gradual restoration" of power were activated, the operator's national load dispatch director Felix Estrada said, with the process ongoing on Saturday.

Cuba relies heavily on fuel imports, meaning tight US sanctions and an oil blockade since the start of the year have exacerbated existing shortages.

Food and medicine have also become more scarce, with hospitals struggling to function normally and schools and government offices having to close.

"Lately, it's becoming a habit," Havana resident Frank Lorenzo told news agency Reuters on Friday.

"Before it happened less frequently - once a monthâ¦ just yesterday we were 24 hours without electricity, they turned it on for just an hour and it went down again."

"It's one thing after another: no water, no gas for cooking, no electricity," 36-year-old schoolteacher Lidia Fernandez told news agency AFP. "Honestly, I don't know how we haven't gone crazy."

Francisco Rodriguez, 78, said his home had already gone without power for 28 hours on Friday and feared he would not have light "for several days".

The repeated blackouts have prompted rare protests in Cuba, where unauthorised demonstrations are illegal and those who defy the ban risk being jailed.

Havana has blamed its fuel crisis on the Trump administration and denounced all of its sanctions - including a new round announced in August - which are part of a wider pressure campaign against the Caribbean island's leadership.

Cuba's regional ally Venezuela was believed to have sent it around 35,000 barrels of oil a day - about half of its oil needs - until Venezuela's own supplies were cut off following the US seizure of its President NicolÃ¡s Maduro in January.

US President Donald Trump has threatened tariffs on countries shipping oil to Havana, and a number of such shipments have been seized by the US.

Washington meanwhile attributes Cuba's energy crisis to poor internal management and has accused it of posing a "national security threat". Trump has openly discussed toppling its leadership, including threatening a "friendly takeover" in March this year.

World.title: At least 21 killed after vehicle loaded with explosives rams Pakistan mosque
World.content:
A car-bomb attack on a mosque at a police compound in north-western Pakistan has killed at least 21 people and injured more than 100, officials say.

Fifteen police officers and a four-year-old child are among those killed in the suicide attack, which also involved gunmen firing on the police facility in the city of Kohat in the province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan's APP news agency reported.

Video found by BBC Verify shows the site covered in rubble and people tending to casualties.

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Police suggested a faction of the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), also known as the Pakistani Taliban, carried out the attack.

A car loaded with explosives rammed into the entrance of the mosque at about 13:15 local time (08:15 GMT), police say. Friday prayers were taking place at the time.

At least six of the attackers were killed in the explosion and the gun battle that followed, according to a Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Police spokesperson.

In a post on X, the force said it was "determined to foil the nefarious designs of Fitna-al-Khawarij" - the designation used by officials to refer to the Pakistani Taliban.

The group was set up in 2007 with the aim of enforcing its strict version of Islamic law and is allied with al-Qaeda and the Afghan Taliban.

Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari expressed "his best wishes for the swift recovery of those injured in the explosion" in a statement, and called for the "complete elimination" of foreign-backed terrorists.

World.title: 20 NSCDC officers suspended over deaths of detained suspected illegal miners
World.content:
The federal government has suspended 20 officers of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in connection with the death of 37 suspected illegal miners in the corps’ custody in Niger State.

The Minister of Interior, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, announced the suspension on Saturday, alongside the suspension of the Niger State NSCDC Commandant, Suberu Aniviye.

The officers are suspended pending the outcome of an independent investigation into the deaths.

The affected officers include those responsible for station guard duties, arrests and investigation, intelligence, legal services, day/night duty and custody.

They include SC Usman Isah Ndamaka, ASCI Hassan Mohammed, CCA Bala Mohammed, CSC Oluwadare Sunday, DCC Obafemi Elvis, CSC Annas Shitto Lamino, DCC Philip Ajayi, ACC Barrister Stephen Tsado, ASCI Alhassan Mohammed, IC Abdullahi Sale, IC Mohammed Sonfada, CAI Liman Abubakar and CAI Bala Usman.

Others are IC Mohammed Jiya, DSC Isah Suleiman, CAI Ahmed Wushishi, IC Sale Adamu, IC Haruna Mohammed, ASCI Aliyu Sallah and CAI Isah Sanusi.

The suspension also affects the state commandant, Mr Aniviye.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The affected officers include personnel assigned to station guard, arrest and investigation, intelligence, legal, day and night duty and other custodial responsibilities.

The federal government has also ordered an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the deaths to establish the cause of death and determine whether there was negligence or misconduct.

The development follows a national outrage over the deaths, with authorities appealing for calm as investigations continue.

World.title: JPMorgan struggles to forecast oil price as Iran war deepens Nigeria’s petrol concerns
World.content:
JPMorgan, one of the world’s largest investment banks, says it no longer has a clear baseline view for the global oil market as the prolonged US-Israeli conflict with Iran continues to disrupt energy supplies.

The bank’s latest assessment marks the first time since the conflict began that it has abandoned a baseline scenario for oil markets.

“We simply don’t know how to model the endgame,” Reuters quoted JPMorgan analysts as saying in a note published on Thursday.

The warning comes as Nigeria grapples with another increase in petrol prices, with pump prices rising above N1,400 per litre in several parts of the country.

The latest increase followed an N85 adjustment in the gantry price of petrol by Dangote Petroleum Refinery, from N1,265 to N1,350 per litre, amid a surge in international crude prices.

A survey of filling stations in Abuja on Saturday morning showed significant variations in pump prices. At some outlets, petrol was selling at about N1,400–N1,450 per litre, compared with prices in the N1,200–N1,300 range in the previous month.

At the Rainoil filling station within the Lugbe axis of airport road in Abuja, petrol is sold at N14350/per litre as against N1,200 to N1,300 range it was sold for in the previous month. At Danmarna, fuel is sold at N1,4100/litre, while Cone oil is selling at N1,405/litre. BOVAS is selling at N1,4100 while NNPC is selling at N1,430.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The increase has come despite earlier easing in fuel prices following expectations that the Middle East conflict would de-escalate and that restrictions affecting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz would ease.

Nigeria exposed to global oil shock

Although Nigeria is a major crude oil producer, the country is not insulated from international oil-market disruptions.

Changes in global crude prices affect the domestic petroleum market through the cost of crude feedstock, refined products, freight and other supply-chain expenses.

The recent increase in Dangote Refinery’s wholesale price has consequently translated into higher pump prices at filling stations.

Brent crude, the benchmark for Nigerian oil, has remained above $100 per barrel amid continuing uncertainty over supplies from the Middle East. Brent closed at $104.87 per barrel on Friday, according to Reuters.

The prolonged disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has become a major concern for global energy markets because the waterway is a critical route for oil and refined-product shipments.

For Nigeria, the effect is being transmitted from the international oil market to the domestic cost of transportation, logistics, electricity generation and other economic activities that depend on petroleum products.

Oil outlook uncertain

JPMorgan said it had initially assumed there were economic “red lines” that the Trump administration would be unwilling to cross.

Six months into the conflict, however, the bank said many of those assumptions had been overtaken by events.

“Many of those lines have been crossed, yet the exit strategy is less clear, not more,” the bank said, according to Reuters.

JPMorgan said oil prices had risen above $100 per barrel, while US gasoline prices reached $4.37 per gallon. US diesel prices also climbed to a record $6.31 per gallon as inventories fell to historic lows.

The bank estimated Brent’s fair value at about $90 per barrel for September, compared with market prices around $106, suggesting that investors were pricing in the possibility of further supply losses.

It estimated that about 10 million barrels per day of supply had already been disrupted.

JPMorgan also pointed to risks affecting other strategic energy routes, including the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, attacks affecting Saudi export infrastructure, continued attacks on Russian refining infrastructure and the broader geopolitical tensions surrounding global energy supplies.

Despite the scale of the disruption, however, oil prices have not risen as sharply as the bank had initially expected.

JPMorgan said global inventories of crude and refined products had fallen by about 555 million barrels since the conflict began — roughly one-third of the decline it had projected earlier in the year.

At the same time, global oil demand has been about 4.4 million barrels per day below year-earlier levels, helping to offset part of the supply losses.

“By leaning much more on demand destruction and much less on stock draws, the market has been able to absorb an extraordinary supply disruption without a sustained rise in crude prices,” the bank said.

Since the conflict began, Brent has averaged about $94 per barrel, JPMorgan said.

The warning comes as oil executives increasingly question the assumption that the disruption will be temporary.

Chevron Chief Executive Officer Mike Wirth and other oil industry executives have warned that a global fuel crisis has arrived as supplies tighten and commercial fuel inventories fall.

The comments contrast with continued assurances from US officials that the disruption will eventually prove temporary.

World.title: Hoodlums kill popular Enugu opposition politician
World.content:
Some armed hoodlums have killed a chieftain of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) in Enugu State, Ikechukwu Oloto.

PREMIUM TIMES learnt that Mr Oloto was killed by the hoodlums who invaded his residence on Thursday evening at Odenigbo, Nsukka Local Government Area of the state.

Sources said the politician was stabbed repeatedly by the armed men during the attack.

When contacted on Saturday morning, the police spokesperson in Enugu State, Daniel Ndukwe, confirmed the incident to PREMIUM TIMES.

Mr Ndukwe, a superintendent of police, said the command received a report at about 5:45 p.m. on 17 September that Mr Oloto was “found in a pool of blood” in his residence.

“Operatives promptly responded and found him with deep suspected machete cuts to his head and stomach.

“He was rushed to a hospital, where he was confirmed dead by the attending doctor,” he said in a short message forwarded to this newspaper via WhatsApp.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The spokesperson said the body of the deceased had been deposited at a mortuary for preservation and autopsy.

The police, he said, have launched a manhunt for the attackers.

‘We’re on top of the situation,’ Nsukka LG

Reacting in a Facebook post on Friday, the Chairman of Nsukka Local Government Area, Chinedu Asogwa, described the killing as “an act of pure wickedness.”

Mr Asogwa, who condemned the attack, vowed to track down the killers.

“To the family of Mr Oloto, I share in your pain. This administration stands with you in this moment of grief.

“To the good people of Nsukka, be assured: we are on top of the situation, and we will not rest until the perpetrators of this heinous act are tracked down and brought to justice,” he said.

“Every instrument of government at our disposal, security personnel, intelligence networks, and community partnerships, will be deployed to protect lives, restore confidence, and ensure that criminals have no hiding place in Nsukka.”

From APC to ADC

Mr Oloto was a top member of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in February this year.

Recall that in October 2025, Governor Peter Mbah of Enugu State, alongside others, moved from the Peoples Democratic Party to the APC.

By February this year, some APC members protested against the outcome of the party’s local government congress, alleging that the “old APC” members were shortchanged in the sharing of leadership positions.

Mr Oloto was among a horde of aggrieved APC members who defected to the ADC in protest.

World.title: NASD appoints Arese Ugwu as acting MD, nine years after SEC suspension
World.content:
The National Association of Securities Dealers (NASD) appointed Arese Ugwu as its new Acting Managing Director, after serving a five-year regulatory suspension from capital market activities.

The over-the-counter market and self-regulatory organisation disclosed the appointment in an X post on Thursday, noting that it is subject to the approval of the Securities & Exchange Commission.

“The Board of Directors of NASD PLC has appointed Ms. Arese Ugwu as Acting Managing Director. Her appointment to act in this capacity is subject to the approval of the Securities & Exchange Commission,” NASD said.

Ms Ugwu succeeds the immediate past Managing Director, Eguarekhide Longe, who recently retired after years of service in the organisation.

Responding to her appointment, she vowed to make NASD the market where Nigeria’s great growth businesses find the capital they need to scale.

“My vision is to make NASD the market where Nigeria’s great growth businesses find the capital they need to scale and where investors can participate in the value they create,” she said.

SEC Ban

Ms Ugwu was among the directors of Partnership Investment Company suspended for a period of five years from engaging in capital market activities and banned from holding directorship positions in any public company in Nigeria by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in 2017.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

SEC said the suspension was for the said period and ordered her to pay a penalty of N100,000 for breaching Rule 1 (iii) of the Code of Conduct for Capital Market Operators and their Employees.

In the same statement, the apex regulator also barred the Managing Director of Partnership Investment Company Plc and Partnership Securities Limited, Victor Ogiemwonyi, from holding directorship positions in any public company in the country.

The sanctions followed alleged unprofessional conduct in the capital market.

NASD did not respond to calls seeking clarification on Ms Ugwu’s appointment as of the time of filing this report.

Ms Ugwu founded Smart Money Africa and is the author of The Smart Money Woman (2016), which was produced as a Netflix/Africa Magic series.

World.title: Sixty years of the written word, By Ezra Angai
World.content:
Six decades after International Literacy Day was established, the global campaign has therefore entered a different phase. The challenge is no longer simply to increase the number of people who can read and write, but to ensure that children and adults acquire the wider competencies required to participate in contemporary society… Nigeria’s challenge is especially urgent because of the scale of its out-of-school population and the disparities in educational opportunity.

Literacy at the Last Mile, and what a Nigerian state can teach us about reading in the age of Artificial Intelligence.

On 8 September UNESCO marked the sixtieth International Literacy Day in San Cristóbal de las Casas, Chiapas, Mexico. The day was proclaimed in 1966, following a 1965 conference of education ministers in Tehran, with the ambition of eradicating illiteracy within a generation. Six decades later, that objective remains unfinished, while the meaning of literacy has expanded considerably.

For much of the twentieth century, literacy meant the ability to read and write a short, simple statement about everyday life. That definition was useful for measuring progress, but it described only a basic threshold. Today, literacy encompasses reading, writing, numeracy, digital competence and the ability to find, assess and use information.

The change reflects the demands of modern life. A person may be able to read a printed sentence yet remain functionally excluded if unable to interpret a data table, complete a digital form, assess an online claim or identify a fraudulent communication. Literacy is increasingly a prerequisite for participation in economic, social and civic life.

The global challenge remains substantial. UNESCO estimates that at least 739 million young people and adults still lack basic literacy skills, with women accounting for nearly two-thirds of that population. Progress, however, has been significant. Global adult literacy has increased from roughly 65 per cent in the mid-1970s to about 88 per cent today, while youth literacy has risen from approximately 75 per cent to 93 per cent.

Yet access to school has not always translated into learning. About four in ten children worldwide still fail to attain minimum reading proficiency. The greatest difficulties remain concentrated in communities affected by poverty, conflict, insecurity and inadequate educational financing.

Nigeria presents one of the more difficult cases. The country has one of the world’s largest populations of out-of-school children, with widely cited estimates exceeding 18 million. National literacy figures conceal sharp regional and gender disparities. While literacy rates in parts of southern Nigeria are comparatively high, some northern communities record extremely low levels. Girls face barriers including early marriage, domestic responsibilities, poverty and unsafe journeys to school. Boys, too, are frequently withdrawn from education for farming, transport and informal labour.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Federal Government’s response under the Renewed Hope Agenda has placed education at the centre of its development strategy. The Federal Ministry of Education, led by Dr Tunji Alausa, has organised reforms under the Nigerian Education Sector Renewal Initiative, with emphasis on teacher quality, technical and vocational education, science and technology, digital skills, improved data and reducing the out-of-school population.

The renewed focus on technical and vocational education is particularly relevant to the changing definition of literacy. In an economy increasingly influenced by technology and automation, the ability to operate equipment, acquire a trade, understand technical information and use digital tools is part of the basic competence required for productive citizenship.

The government has also placed greater emphasis on evidence-based education planning, including a national digital education management information system and renewed learning assessments. The principle is important: educational policy cannot be effectively designed or evaluated without reliable information about who is learning, where the gaps are and what interventions work.

The project began with a household enumeration covering 360,319 homes. It identified 187,719 out-of-school children aged six to 17, including 2,305 children with disabilities. The survey also challenged assumptions about the gender composition of educational exclusion. Boys account for nearly 57 per cent of the identified out-of-school population, often because they enter agriculture, transport and other forms of informal work early. Girls face different barriers, including early marriage, domestic responsibilities, and safety concerns.

Financing remains a central issue. At the National Advancement Forum in September, the Education Minister argued that government funding alone could not sustain Nigeria’s universities and called for greater use of endowments, research grants, alumni contributions, philanthropy and industry partnerships. The broader lesson is that educational reforms require sustainable financing and institutions capable of maintaining gains after individual programmes end.

Kaduna State provides a useful case study of how such policies can be translated at subnational level.

For three consecutive years, the state has allocated roughly one-quarter of its annual budget to education: 25 per cent in 2024, 26.14 per cent in 2025 and 25 per cent of its ₦985.9 billion 2026 budget, equivalent to about ₦246.5 billion. The spending has supported free basic education, reduced tuition in state-owned tertiary institutions, scholarships and student assistance, classroom construction, learning materials, and teacher development.

The state has also expanded technical and vocational training. In August, the Kaduna State Institute of Vocational Training and Skills Development graduated its first cohort of 4,050 trainees, who received National Skills Qualifications, with many also receiving start-up support. The Federal Ministry of Education has adopted Kaduna’s technical and vocational training manuals as reference material for the national curriculum.

Data has been another area of emphasis. A statewide household survey provided a more reliable basis for estimating the number of out-of-school children, replacing conflicting earlier estimates. Such data is not merely statistical: it determines where resources are directed and whether progress can be measured.

That approach underpins the Reaching Out-of-School Children Project, or ROOSC, a $62.8 million multi-donor initiative supported by the Islamic Development Bank and its solidarity fund, the Kuwait Fund, the Global Partnership for Education, Education Above All, UNICEF and Save the Children International. Its target is to bring 100,000 out-of-school children into learning across Kaduna’s 23 local government areas.

The project began with a household enumeration covering 360,319 homes. It identified 187,719 out-of-school children aged six to 17, including 2,305 children with disabilities. The survey also challenged assumptions about the gender composition of educational exclusion. Boys account for nearly 57 per cent of the identified out-of-school population, often because they enter agriculture, transport and other forms of informal work early. Girls face different barriers, including early marriage, domestic responsibilities, and safety concerns.

The response, therefore, uses several pathways into education. The Accelerated Basic Education Programme provides intensive foundational literacy, numeracy, and life skills for older children who have never attended school. Catch-Up Clubs offer remedial support and prepare learners for formal schooling. Integrated Qur’anic and Tsangaya Education incorporates literacy and numeracy into existing Islamic learning environments, while radio-based instruction provides an alternative where insecurity makes conventional classrooms difficult.

The project also addresses practical barriers that can prevent children from remaining in school. More than 44,000 children have received learning materials, while girls have received menstrual-hygiene support. Thousands of learners have undergone medical assessments, and more than 4,000 assistive devices, including wheelchairs, spectacles and hearing aids, have been provided to children with disabilities. More than 4,000 teachers have received training.

Child protection forms another component. The programme has established trained caseworkers, referral mechanisms and case-management systems for children facing neglect, exploitation or abuse. The objective is to ensure that educational access is accompanied by the protection necessary to sustain it.

International Literacy Day began as a commitment to open the written word to those excluded from it. Sixty years later, the task has widened. The objective must now be to equip people not only to read, but to understand, evaluate and use the vast flow of information that increasingly shapes their lives.

Infrastructure is being expanded alongside these interventions. The project is constructing 102 schools and rehabilitating 170 others, providing 272 facilities in all. Accessibility is incorporated into their design, while Tsangaya and Qur’anic learning centres are included as legitimate education spaces. These centres receive trained facilitators and teaching materials, allowing the programme to work through institutions already accepted within their communities.

ROOSC also invests in the systems that must remain after donor funding ends. Its work includes strengthening education planning, school-based management committees, local government education structures and digital data systems. That institutional component is important because the long-term measure of any externally supported programme is whether it strengthens the public system, rather than creating a parallel one.

The stakes are higher now because the children entering these learning centres will grow up in an economy and information environment increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence. Traditional literacy remains essential: people must be able to read medicine labels, health advisories, official notices and other information on which everyday decisions depend. But they must also be able to assess information, recognise manipulation, distinguish evidence from falsehood and use digital and AI tools responsibly.

This is the next frontier of literacy. It is not enough to decode words; citizens must understand what they read, question its reliability and make informed decisions about it.

Six decades after International Literacy Day was established, the global campaign has therefore entered a different phase. The challenge is no longer simply to increase the number of people who can read and write, but to ensure that children and adults acquire the wider competencies required to participate in contemporary society.

Nigeria’s challenge is especially urgent because of the scale of its out-of-school population and the disparities in educational opportunity. Kaduna’s experience suggests that progress depends on several elements working together: credible data, sustained financing, multiple pathways into learning, teacher development, inclusion, infrastructure and stronger public institutions.

The lesson is straightforward. Literacy policy must begin with the child who is not in school, identify the reason for exclusion, provide an appropriate route to learning and ensure that the learner remains supported once inside the system. In an age of artificial intelligence, that foundation is more important, not less.

International Literacy Day began as a commitment to open the written word to those excluded from it. Sixty years later, the task has widened. The objective must now be to equip people not only to read, but to understand, evaluate and use the vast flow of information that increasingly shapes their lives.

The quality of Nigeria’s response will depend on whether that broader definition reaches the children at the margins of the education system. Kaduna’s effort offers one practical example of what that can look like.

Ezra Angai is the project coordinator of the Reaching Out-of-School Children (ROOSC) project, a multi-donor-funded initiative of the Kaduna State Government tackling the out-of-school children crisis. He writes on education access, financing and reform.

World.title: Delta records full spending on N50 million court project, chief judge says funds never accessed
World.content:
A N50 million court construction project in Erho-Abraka, Ethiope East Local Government Area of Delta State, has presented a disturbing discrepancy between the state government’s budget performance records and the state judiciary’s account.

The Delta State Government’s 2024 approved budget provided N50 million for the construction of a magistrate court at Erho-Abraka under the High Court of Justice. The project code is 13100123031100.

The state’s 2024 fourth-quarter Budget Implementation Report subsequently recorded the project as fully implemented, according to PREMIUM TIMES’ review of the document.

However, a response from the office of the Chief Judge of Delta State to a Freedom of Information request by Tracka, a service-delivery promotion arm and project-tracking platform of BudgIT, says the money was never accessed.

Tracka visited the court premises in Erho-Abraka and reported no evidence of construction or renovation corresponding to the N50 million project.

Court officials interviewed by Tracka also reported being unaware of the project. The magistrate at the court reportedly said the existing benches in the courtroom were provided by the community.

The physical condition of the facility further raises questions about the reported implementation. Parts of the court roof are reportedly pulling away, while bushes have overgrown substantial portions of the compound.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

‘N50m remained unaccessed’

In a letter dated 8 June 2026 and signed by the Chief Registrar, Eloho Okodiya-Onoriose, on behalf of the Chief Judge of Delta State, Tessy Diai, the judiciary acknowledged that N50 million was appropriated in the 2024 Delta State Appropriation Law for construction of the magistrate court at Erho-Abraka.

But the judiciary said the project was never awarded. It said no payment voucher, fund requisition or withdrawal request was raised against the allocation.

“The entire N50,000,000.00 … as appropriated remain unaccessed throughout the 2024 fiscal year or thereafter,” the letter stated.

The chief registrar rejected Tracka’s claim that the N50 million had been spent on the project, describing the assertion as “totally incorrect and misleading.”

The letter said the project allocation elapsed because it was not awarded within the 2024 financial year or subsequently.

The response creates a direct conflict with the expenditure position contained in Delta State’s budget implementation records.

What Delta’s budget records show

PREMIUM TIMES independently examined Delta State’s 2024 fiscal documents.

The approved 2024 budget shows N50 million allocated to the construction of the magistrate court at Erho-Abraka, under the High Court of Justice.

The project was also listed in the state’s first-quarter 2024 Budget Performance Report with a N50 million allocation but zero implementation at that stage.

The second-quarter report similarly showed N50 million for the project and 0 per cent performance.

By the third quarter, the project was still recorded at zero per cent implementation, with the N50 million allocation intact.

But the position changed in the fourth-quarter report, which recorded the project as having achieved 100 per cent implementation, according to PREMIUM TIMES’ review.

That means the state’s own quarterly records show the project moving from zero implementation through the third quarter to full implementation by the end of the year, even though the chief judge’s office says the project was never awarded and no money was accessed.

The discrepancy is particularly noteworthy because the 2024 audited accounts published by the Delta State Auditor-General include the consolidated budget report for the year ended 31 December 2024 as part of the audited financial documentation.

PREMIUM TIMES reviewed the 2024 audited financial statements but did not find a corresponding capital expenditure line item that independently clarified the N50 million expenditure.

Project predates Oborevwori’s administration

The Erho-Abraka court project is not a new proposal. PREMIUM TIMES traced the project through earlier Delta State budgets and found that it had appeared in the state’s budgetary plans years before the 2024 allocation.

In the 2019 budget, for instance, Delta provided N25 million for the construction of the magistrate court at Erho-Abraka.

According to PREMIUM TIMES’ review of subsequent budget documents, the project received a N50 million provision in 2021 but no funding was released for it between 2021 and 2023.

It was not provided for in the 2022 budget, while N20 million was budgeted in the 2023 revised budget.

The 2024 allocation represented another attempt to fund a project that had remained on the state’s books for years. Yet, according to the chief judge’s office, the 2024 allocation was never accessed.

No evidence on procurement portal

PREMIUM TIMES also checked the Delta State Government’s procurement portal for evidence of the project.

The project was not listed among the 132 completed projects, 171 ongoing projects or 127 new projects displayed on the portal, according to the newspaper’s review.

The absence of the project from the procurement records further complicates the state’s reported 100 per cent implementation of the N50 million allocation.

If the project was fully implemented as the fourth-quarter budget report indicates, questions arise about the procurement process, contractor, payment records, certification and physical delivery of the project.

Conversely, if the chief judge’s office is correct that the allocation was never accessed, then the state’s budget implementation record requires explanation.

‘Where is the N50m?’

Tracka in its post on X raised the issue publicly after receiving the response from the chief judge’s office.

The organisation said the response raised an important accountability question because the budget implementation report and the judiciary’s records appeared to tell different stories.

“If the funds were not accessed, how did the expenditure appear as fully implemented in the Budget Implementation Report?” Tracka asked.

It called for the relevant authorities to reconcile the figures and explain what happened to the allocation.

The organisation also asked the office of Governor Sheriff Oborevwori, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission and the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission to examine the discrepancy.

Yet, the issue moves beyond whether a court was constructed. What is now at stake is the reliability of public financial records and the whereabouts of the funds as reported in the fiscal documents as being spent.

A budget implementation report is expected to provide citizens with a picture of how appropriated public resources were used. Where an expenditure is recorded as 100 per cent implemented but the agency responsible for the project says the allocation was never accessed, the discrepancy requires a documented explanation.

Government keeps mum

PREMIUM TIMES sought clarification from the Delta State Government on the apparent contradiction.

The Commissioner for Information, Charles Aniagwu, did not respond to calls from our reporter.

The newspaper also sent a media enquiry to Mr Aniagwu via WhatsApp on 18 September and followed it up on the morning of 19 September. He had not responded as of the time of filing this report.

PREMIUM TIMES asked the government to explain how N50 million could be recorded as 100 per cent implemented if the chief judge’s office says the money was never accessed.

The newspaper also asked whether the money was released, accessed or expended by any government agency, department or contractor and, if so, requested details of the contractor, contract and certificate of completion.

It further asked whether the government had commenced any process to reconcile the seeming difference between its budget implementation records and the position of the chief judge’s office.

Delta State’s official 2024 financial records are publicly presented as part of the state’s fiscal reporting framework, while its audited accounts were signed off through the Auditor-General’s reporting process.

However, the immediate reality appears different from the paper record as the court remains in a visibly dilapidated condition, while the N50 million allocated for its construction remains the subject of conflicting official records.

The conflict leaves unanswered questions: how did a project whose implementing authority says was never awarded or funded become 100 per cent implemented in Delta State’s 2024 budget performance records?

World.title: JUST IN: Ebonyi governor sacks commissioner after recall from suspension
World.content:
Governor Francis Nwifuru of Ebonyi State has sacked the state’s Commissioner for Works, Stanley Mbam.

Mr Nwifuru announced Mr Mbam’s sack in a statement by his spokesperson, Monday Uzor, on Saturday.

The governor’s decision came months after he recalled the commissioner from his initial suspension over alleged dereliction of duty.

Mr Nwifuru directed Mr Mbam to immediately hand over all government property in his possession, including his official vehicle, to the Secretary to the Ebonyi State Government.

He was also directed to transfer his responsibilities to the permanent secretary in the Ministry of Works.

No reason was given for the removal of the commissioner.

“The governor assured residents of the State that his administration remains focused on delivering effective governance and improving public infrastructure,” the statement added.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Series of suspensions

This is not the first time Mr Mbam has faced disciplinary action under Mr Nwifuru.

On 28 July 2025, the commissioner was among about 85 government officials suspended by the governor for allegedly failing to attend an important government function.

The officials were recalled about a week later.

Mr Mbam was again suspended indefinitely on 28 February 2026, alongside the Commissioner for Infrastructure Development for Concession, Ogbonnaya Abara.

At the time, Governor Nwifuru cited alleged dereliction of duty, slow project delivery and lapses in the Ministry of Works for the suspension of the officials.

Three days after that suspension, Mr Mbam publicly apologised and appealed to the governor for another opportunity to serve.

He accepted responsibility for what he described as “unmet expectations” and asked for a second chance.

On 3 May 2026, Mr Nwifuru recalled Mr Mbam and other suspended officials during a Father’s Day service at the Government House Chapel in Abakaliki.

Mr Mbam subsequently returned to his position as works commissioner.

This is the third disciplinary action against him as works commissioner under Governor Nwifuru.

The state government has not announced a replacement for the commissioner.

World.title: Calabar Shooting: Police arrest suspected cult leader, launch manhunt for accomplices
World.content:
The Police Command in Cross River State has arrested a 24-year-old student over a viral video allegedly showing suspected cult members firing shots from a moving vehicle in Calabar.

The command, in a statement issued on Saturday by its spokesperson, Sunday Eitokpah, said the incident occurred in the early hours of 17 September.

Mr Eitokpah, an assistant superintendent of police, said the arrest followed the directive of the Commissioner of Police, Ajo Ordue, for the immediate identification and apprehension of those involved in the incident.

According to him, the deputy commissioner of police in charge of operations and operatives of the Violence Crime Response Unit commenced an intelligence-led operation at about 11:30 p.m. on 17 September.

“The operation led to the identification and tracking of the vehicle captured in the viral footage, and resulted in the arrest of its driver.

“Information obtained during the operation assisted the police in tracing a key suspect to a hotel in Calabar, where he was arrested.”

The spokesperson identified the suspect as a student of the University of Cross River, who allegedly identified himself during interrogation as a leader of the Vikings Confraternity.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said the suspect admitted to being the person seen firing the shots in the viral video.

Mr Eitokpah quoted the suspect as saying that he participated in a sign-out activity on the day of the incident and that another suspected member of the group handed him the pistol allegedly used in the shooting.

The spokesperson said efforts had been intensified to identify and arrest other persons connected with the incident.

He said the circumstances surrounding the possession of the firearm and the movement of the vehicle were still being investigated.

READ ALSO: Police arrest 60 over assault of officer

He quoted the police commissioner as directing that the investigation be conducted professionally and comprehensively, with all persons found to have participated in or facilitated the alleged act brought to justice.

The police commissioner warned that the unlawful discharge of firearms in public places posed a serious security concern and urged residents to report suspicious movements, illegal possession of firearms, and cult-related activities to the police.

(NAN)

World.title: Kingmakers elect Gbadebo Adeusi as Oloba of Oba- Ile
World.content:
By Dayo Johnson Akure

The stool of the Oloba of Oba-Ile in Akure North Local Government Area of Ondo State has a new occupant-elect, following the emergence of Prince Gbadebo Adeusi Aladetoye after a keenly supervised selection process.

Gbadebo, from the Orioge Royal House, was chosen after Ifa divination and voting by the kingmakers, conducted in the presence of government officials and security operatives.

Head of the kingmakers and Elemo of Oba-Ile, Chief Oluwatimileyin Gbemisayo, said the exercise was carried out in line with government directives.

He disclosed that an Ifa consultation held on Thursday, September 17, identified Adeusi among five contestants, but government representatives insisted on an election.

“Five out of the six kingmakers voted for Gbadebo Adeusi. I have declared him our king-elect. The government representative witnessed the election,” he said.

Officials of Akure North Local Government, the councillor representing Oba-Ile Ward, Hon. Adesoye Fagoroyo and security personnel witnessed the exercise.

The head of the Kingmakers, Chief Gbemisayo, described the outcome as victory for the community, adding that a reconciliation committee would be set up to unite the other contestants.

The community now awaits official recognition and presentation of staff of office by the Ondo state government before traditional installation rites commence.

Also speaking,the Agba Akin of Oba-Ile, Chief Olugbogi Olushola, appealed to the other aspirants to support the monarch-elect for peace and development.

Olushola said that “Many people contest for a position, but only one person will emerge successful.

” We have chosen our king, and that is the will of our people. I appeal to the other contestants to work with him,” he said.

The new monarch, studied Linguistics in France and later worked in Germany and the United Kingdom, where he studied Human Management and Elderly Care at the University of Sunderland. End

World.title: Meet Rosaline Ogunro, Nigerian-born woman who became mayor of Islington
World.content:
Rosaline Ogunro, a Nigerian-born councillor, has become the mayor of Islington in London, adding another prominent name to the growing number of Nigerians making their mark in British public life.

Ogunro, who represents St Peter’s and Canalside Ward, was officially sworn in as Mayor of Islington for 2026/27 on Wednesday, May 27, 2026.

Her emergence came a year after Nigerian-born Jason Jackson became the first Nigerian-born mayor of Islington, a milestone that brought attention to the increasing presence of people of Nigerian descent in British civic leadership.

From Nigeria to Britain

Ogunro was born in Issele-Uku, Delta State, Nigeria, as the first of seven children. She moved to the United Kingdom in 2001.

She later studied English law and obtained an LLB Honours degree from The Open University in London. She also attended the College of Law in London for a part-time legal practice course while working full-time at the London Symphony Orchestra.

Before entering elected office, Ogunro developed experience across broadcasting, community work and the voluntary sector.

She worked with organisations including Islington Citizens Advice Bureau, where she has served as a part-time adviser, and also worked in the marketing department of the London Symphony Orchestra as a customer service and office coordinator.

She was also a member of the orchestra’s community choir for more than 20 years.

Her journey into politics

Ogunro was first elected as a councillor for St Peter’s and Canalside Ward in May 2022.

During her time on Islington Council, she has served on several committees, including the Homes and Communities Scrutiny Committee, the Children and Young People Scrutiny Committee, and the Planning and Licensing Committees.

She also served as deputy mayor before taking over the mayoral office.

Islington Council’s official profile describes her as someone with a long-standing interest in helping and serving members of the community.

‘It means the world to me.’

Speaking about becoming mayor, Ogunro said the position would give her an opportunity to engage with communities across Islington beyond her own ward.

“It means the world to me,” she said, explaining that the role would allow her to meet people from different backgrounds and communities across East Islington.

She said she looked forward to meeting people of different ages and backgrounds and getting to know Islington better.

Ogunro also reflected on her history of volunteering and advocacy for women.

She has been involved with Soroptimist International of Great Britain and Ireland, an organisation that uses professional networks to support and uplift women.

She also recalled her experience in broadcasting and the changes she witnessed in the industry, particularly regarding women’s participation.

Another Nigerian in Islington’s mayoral office

Ogunro’s inauguration follows Jason Jackson’s historic tenure as Mayor of Islington in 2025/26.

Jackson became the first Nigerian-born mayor of Islington since the borough was established in 1900. He was elected a councillor in 2022 and subsequently became Chair of the council’s Homes and Communities Committee.

The succession means two Nigerian-born councillors have held the mayoral office in consecutive years.

NiDCOM congratulates Ogunro.

The Nigerians in Diaspora Commission also congratulated Ogunro on her emergence as Mayor of Islington.

NiDCOM Chairman and CEO Abike Dabiri-Erewa described her achievement as a proud moment for Nigeria and attributed her emergence to dedication, excellence and community service.

Dabiri-Erewa also highlighted Ogunro’s work in community development and advocacy, describing her as a worthy ambassador of Nigeria in the UK.

Ogunro’s appointment adds to a growing list of Nigerians and people of Nigerian descent occupying prominent positions in British public life, including elected and civic leadership roles.

World.title: Kalu orders, media team, supporters to focus on his record
World.content:
Orji Uzor Kalu

Senator Orji Uzor Kalu, representing Abia North Senatorial District, has directed his media team, supporters, political associates and affiliated groups to stop mentioning or responding to other candidates seeking the senatorial seat in the 2027 election.

Kalu, in a statement issued by his office, said his re-election campaign should focus strictly on his record of representation, legislative performance, infrastructural interventions and human capital development across the five local government areas in the district.

He directed members of his media team and supporters to refrain from personal attacks, political exchanges and responses to provocation involving other candidates.

According to him, the people of Abia North are capable of assessing all candidates based on verifiable records, performance and capacity to deliver.

The statement highlighted the senator’s interventions in education, infrastructure, healthcare, youth empowerment and other areas as part of his record in the district.

It said Kalu had facilitated the construction and renovation of more than 100 school blocks and classrooms, alongside the provision of desks and other educational facilities across communities in Abia North.

It also said more than 70 road projects had been attracted to the district, while educational and learning materials, including STEM textbooks, school bags, sandals and uniforms, had been distributed to pupils.

The statement added that more than 50 youths and other beneficiaries from the district had benefited from overseas scholarships, international training and capacity-building opportunities.

It further listed empowerment programmes through which thousands of constituents had received equipment, tools and other forms of economic support.

In healthcare, the statement said Kalu’s interventions included access to free healthcare services for vulnerable constituents, while communities affected by erosion, flooding and other environmental challenges had benefited from federal interventions attracted to the district.

On his legislative record, the senator’s office said he had, since his election to the Senate in 2019, sponsored and advanced bills covering education, security, taxation, agriculture, healthcare, transportation, environmental protection, energy, social welfare, justice and economic development.

Among the bills listed were the Coastal and Inland Shipping (Cabotage) Act Amendment Bill, National Tax Crimes Commission Bill, National Food Bank Establishment Bill, Compulsory Free Universal Basic Education Act Amendment Bill and National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency Amendment Bill.

Others include the Armed Forces Act Amendment Bill, Federal College of Education (Technical), Arochukwu Bill, Federal Polytechnic Abiriba Bill, Federal University of Medical Sciences and Biomedical Technology, Umunna, Bende Bill, Federal University of Technology, Ovim Bill, Federal College of Agriculture, Isiochi Bill, Nigeria Chinese Language Village Bill, Nigeria Women Trust Fund Bill and Social Welfare Service Bill.

The statement said Kalu had also sponsored motions on the rehabilitation of the Eastern Rail Line, rural water supply in Abia North, banking infrastructure in the district, decentralisation of Nigeria’s electricity grid, healthcare access for vulnerable Nigerians, renewable energy for health centres, compulsory use of body-worn cameras by law enforcement agencies, crude oil theft, illegal mining, maritime development, research and innovation.

Kalu therefore directed his supporters and media team to allow his achievements, ongoing projects, legislative record and plans for the future to speak for him.

“The campaign must remain focused on issues, development and service to the people,” the statement said.

It added that there should be no insults, personal attacks or responses to provocations, while directing the senator’s media office and supporters acting on his behalf not to mention other candidates in statements, campaign materials or commentaries.

Kalu expressed appreciation to residents of Arochukwu, Bende, Isuikwuato, Ohafia and Umunneochi for their support, saying the 2027 election should provide an opportunity for the people to evaluate his stewardship based on verifiable achievements and his record in the National Assembly.

World.content:
Gov Nwifuru

By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki

World.title: Nigeria’s indigenous languages to face extinction within 70 years – Linguists
World.content:
Linguists estimate that if current non-transmission trends persist, many of Nigeria’s more than 500 indigenous languages could face severe endangerment or extinction within 50 to 70 years.

Children, parents and experts said urban lifestyles had reduced children’s exposure to indigenous languages and weakened intergenerational transmission.

Maimuna Egigogo, 12, a resident of Kubwa, said that she understood Nupe but could not speak it because her parents communicated with her mainly in English.

She said she frequently interacted with her grandparents, aunt and uncle before moving from Bida, Niger, to Abuja three years ago.

“But since I came to Abuja, everyone around me, including my parents, speaks only English, so I think that is why I cannot speak my dialect,” she explained.

Amina Bello, a mother of three, said she did not speak Ebira with her children because she believed English would give them educational and social advantages.

Benjamin Mitu, from Plateau, said he and his wife adopted English at home because they spoke different indigenous languages and feared confusing their children.

“I do not want a situation where I speak my indigenous language while my wife speaks hers and the children end up learning neither language well,” he said.

Stephen Adeniyi, another child, said he spoke only English because his parents worked long hours, leaving him mostly with school and domestic staff who communicated in English.

“My parents do not have the time to teach me our indigenous language because of work, so I do not really blame them,” he said.

Rebecca Ibrahim said preserving her indigenous language was a deliberate family policy, adding that she spoke her local dialect with her children at home.

She said she also encouraged her children to visit their grandparents during holidays to strengthen their understanding and use of their indigenous language.

“My parents taught me our indigenous language and they are still helping me to teach my children,” Ibrahim said.

Emmanuel David, an Itsekiri, said he would struggle to converse with his parents if they stopped speaking English and switched completely to their indigenous language.

Michael Peter recalled growing up where indigenous-language use, was compulsory, while folktales, songs, proverbs and regular visits to ancestral communities strengthened cultural knowledge.

Peter urged parents to become more intentional about preserving cultural identity by encouraging regular use of indigenous languages and passing traditions to younger generations.

Prof. Chinwe Anunobi, Chief Executive Officer of the National Library of Nigeria, expressed concern over the global decline of indigenous languages during the 2026 International Mother Tongue Day event.

Anunobi warned that many indigenous languages faced extinction because of neglect and reduced intergenerational transmission, threatening cultural identity, traditional knowledge and community diversity.

She advocated education in indigenous languages, saying it could improve literacy, comprehension and academic performance while helping children maintain connections with their cultural heritage.

Educationist Funmi Soyoye dismissed concerns that teaching children indigenous languages could undermine English proficiency, saying multilingual exposure could strengthen communication and language-learning abilities.

“The brain is not a bucket. Learning a second language does not push out the first. The brain is like a muscle,” Soyoye said.

She said children could transfer sentence construction, storytelling and vocabulary skills acquired in indigenous languages to English, especially when encouraged to read and communicate bilingually.

“When a child learns how to build a sentence, tell a story or use a proverb in Igbo, they transfer that skill to English,” she said.

Soyoye said that children needed exposure to quality English and indigenous languages, warning that poor use of both languages, rather than bilingualism, could affect effective communication.

World.title: What to know about Denmark’s deal with Trump over Greenland
World.content:
Aerial view taken by Mads Schmidt Rasmussen and handed out by Arctic Creative shows people as they take part in a demonstration that gathered almost a third of the city population to protest against the US President’s plans to take Greenland, on January 17, 2026 in Nuuk, Greenland. Photo by Mads Schmidt Rasmussen / various sources / AFP.

Denmark on Saturday hailed a “binding” deal announced by US President Donald Trump to give Washington “permanent control” over Greenland’s security and bar Russian and Chinese bases from the Arctic territory.

Read Also: US appeals court puts brakes on third-country deportations

Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly insisted that Washington needed to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and sparking fierce pushback from the alliance.

Denmark and Greenland – an autonomous Danish territory – both hailed the deal and said they would sign it on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York next week.

Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said Saturday the potential signing meant “next week could be a good week”.

“A long period of uncertainty will hopefully be replaced by a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and North Atlantic,” the foreign minister said in a social media post.

The deal respected Denmark’s “red lines” and was “important” in light of a changed security situation, he said.

‘Permanent control’

While the terms are still unclear, Denmark maintains that its sovereignty remains intact.

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the agreement “recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination”.

Trump meanwhile hailed it as an “‘Infinite Life’ Agreement, there is no end!” and said Washington would immediately start building up a large military presence in the territory.

“From now on, no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval.”

While Trump presented the deal as a major triumph, Danish commentators said he had not really gained anything, noting that Washington was already able to ramp up its military presence on the island provided it informs Denmark and Greenland in advance, under a 1951 defence pact updated in 2004.

“Shhh. Don’t tell Trump that it’s the Kingdom of Denmark that has prevailed,” US correspondent Jacob Heinel Jensen wrote in the Danish newspaper Berlingske on Saturday.

“Donald Trump gets out of it that he can appear as a winner. He has been a good businessman who has pushed Denmark and Greenland into something new,” Marc Jacobsen, a researcher at the Royal Danish Defence College, told AFP.

Trump has repeatedly warned of Russia and China trying to establish a foothold in Greenland as a strategic battle for supremacy in a warming Arctic unfolds, and the State Department left no doubt that they would not be allowed to do so.

“This agreement guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors,” a State Department official said.

Frederiksen said Friday she was “pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States,” adding that it was “good for NATO and Europe.”

Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the deal with the United States “strengthens” the territory’s security.

NATO tensions

Trump gave no details about how the deal would work.

But several media outlets have reported that the United States wants to open three new military bases in southern Greenland, in addition to the Pituffik base it already has in the north of the territory.

At the height of the crisis, Trump would not rule out using force to seize the territory of 57,000 inhabitants, sowing anxiety within the EU and NATO.

Since then, tensions have cooled somewhat, and in an apparent move to assuage Trump, NATO launched a new mission to bolster security in the Arctic.

Danes strolling in Copenhagen on Saturday were cautiously optimistic about the deal.

“I hope this is a definitive and sound deal once the details are known but I wouldn’t be surprised if we have to take a step back again and then hopefully two steps forward,” Soren, a 52-year-old IT executive, told AFP.

He feared the announcement was “maybe a little bit premature”.

Katrine Rasmussen, a 47-year-old lawyer, said she hoped the agreement would be the last word.

“It would be nice if we could end these discussions, at least that would be a good outcome, so we can move on.”

Vanguard News

World.title: High flood to hit Lagos, Delta, Imo, 12 other states in 7 days – NiHSA
World.content:
File image or flood-ravaged community.

…asks affected people to relocate

By Gabriel Ewepu, ABUJA

The Nigeria Hydrological Service Agency (NiHSA) has said a seven-day high flood will hit Imo, Cross River, Lagos and 12 other states.

The Director General (DG) and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of NiHSA, Arch Umar Mohammed, made the disclosure on Friday in a National Flood Advisory, saying the flood is expected to occur from September 19 to 25, 2026.

Mohammed said schools, healthcare facilities, markets, farms and religious buildings, among others, will be affected.

He also called on affected state governments to urgently move their people to safer and higher ground ahead of the flooding.

He said, “High riverine flood risk forecast for the next 7 days across Imo, Cross River and 13 other states. Rising river stages are expected to cause flooding.

“Communities on the floodplain should prepare to move to higher ground. Stations: Obubra on the Cross River, Itigidi on the Cross River, and Epento on the Cross River.”

According to the advisory, several communities and critical facilities across the affected states are exposed to the risk of flooding.

In Imo State, the affected local government areas are Aboh-Mba, Ahizu-Mb, Ehime-Mb, Ezinihit, Ideato No, Ihitte/U and Ikeduru. The agency identified 958 communities, 1,022 schools, 553 healthcare facilities, 161 markets and 198 religious buildings as exposed to the flood risk.

In Cross River, the affected local government areas include Abi, Akamkpa, Akpabuyo, Biase, Calabar, Calabar South, Ikom and Obubra. NiHSA listed 2,471 communities, 703 schools, 344 healthcare facilities, 145 markets, 453 religious buildings and 854 hectares of farmland as exposed.

The agency also identified Abakaliki, Afikpo, Afikpo South, Ebonyi, Ezza North and Ezza as affected local government areas in Ebonyi State, with 2,574 communities, 1,064 schools, 422 healthcare facilities, 480 markets, 629 religious buildings and 1,882 hectares of farmland exposed.

In Benue, Buruku, Gboko, Guma, Katsina-Ala, Logo and Ukum are among the affected local government areas. The exposure includes 303 communities, 100 schools, 48 healthcare facilities, 32 markets, 151 religious buildings and 55 hectares of farmland.

For Anambra State, the affected areas include Aguata, Anambra East, Anambra West, Anaocha, Awka North, Awka South and Ayamelum. The advisory put the number of exposed communities at 1,314, with 1,308 schools, 1,089 healthcare facilities, 280 markets, 610 religious buildings and 1,529 hectares of farmland also at risk.

In Akwa Ibom, the affected local government areas are Abak, Eket, Etinan, Ibeno, Ibesikpo Asutan, Ibiono Ibom, Ika and Ikono. NiHSA identified 249 communities, 323 schools, 211 healthcare facilities, 74 markets and 289 religious buildings as exposed to the anticipated flooding.

Meanwhile, the agency identified Edo, Bayelsa, Enugu, Kogi, Delta, Abia, Taraba and Rivers among other states expected to experience severe impacts from the forecast flooding.

World.title: Scotland proposes 3 visa routes to attract Nigerian, other foreign workers
World.content:
Scotland

By Mmesoma Goodness

The Scottish Government has proposed three tailored immigration routes to attract foreign workers and graduates to Scotland as the country tackles population decline, an ageing population and labour shortages.

The proposals, contained in a new policy paper titled “Migration: supporting the future of Scotland’s economy and communities,” are designed to help Scotland attract and retain international talent while supporting its economy, public services and rural communities.

The Scottish Government said migration will play an increasingly important role in addressing demographic pressures, as deaths are expected to outnumber births in the coming decades while the working-age population declines.

However, the proposed routes are not currently available visa schemes. Immigration remains a reserved matter for the UK Government, meaning the proposals would require agreement and cooperation with Westminster before they could be implemented.

1. Scottish Visa

The proposed Scottish Visa would be a person-centred immigration route not tied to a specific employer.
