World.title: The ‘problem’ with Mexico’s 44% growth in exports: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
A recent headline took just about everyone by surprise: Mexico’s export revenue in July of this year hit US $81 billion, up 44%. Think about that for a moment — an annualized run rate of nearly $1 trillion of export revenue for the country. Last year, exports hit a record $665 billion on 7.6% growth, up from $417 billion in 2020. So far this year through July, exports are up an impressive 27.7%. As a result, Mexico is now firmly the largest exporter to the United States, far surpassing No. 2 Canada and No. 3 China. China had been the leader for years until Mexico overtook it in the years following the COVID pandemic.

One would think that a 44% growth in exports would be exceptional for Mexico and its economy … but is it really as good as it sounds? Let’s dig a bit deeper into the numbers for a better understanding:

1. Most of the growth has come from the category of electrical and electronic equipment and appliances, which increased by a massive 134% in July. For the first time in that month, Mexico’s exports in that category exceeded the category of auto and auto parts. That category had previously led Mexico’s export revenue figures for decades. I recently wrote about that development here: The hottest product on the planet is increasingly made in Mexico: A perspective from our CEO. Automotive exports have been roughly flat year-to-date, and oil exports are actually down. In other words, the vast majority of the export growth is not coming from a diverse set of industries but rather this one segment.

2. Import growth is also booming. Year-to-date, imports are up 25.6%, and in the month of July, imports exceeded exports. Mexico actually had a rare trade deficit in July as imports grew by 45.7%.

3. Mexico has begun to import a massive amount of products from Taiwan, growing by over 200% so far this year and hitting nearly US $40 billion in the first half of the year. For some perspective, Mexico only imported $14 billion from Taiwan in the same period last year. Mexican imports of Taiwanese products increased by only $2 billion in the first six months of 2025, compared to 2024.

4. The massive year-to-date import and export growth numbers are not resulting in an economy that is growing as much as would be expected or hoped. One would think that such a huge increase in exports would dramatically increase production capacity investment and domestic consumption. But neither is happening. Estimates vary, but Mexican GDP is generally only expected to grow in the 1.2%-1.5% range — only half of what is expected in the United States this year.

So what is going on here?

It’s important to look deeper into what is actually happening to these imports and exports, specifically analyzing two measures related to value added:

Domestic value added embodied in the exports (How much Mexican labor is going into the exports?) Mexican-origin content (How much Mexican product is going into the exports?)

What we see is that the rapidly growing electronics category is extremely low in both measures. Said differently, given the high value of the products, the actual amount of Mexican labor and Mexican-origin content going into them is minimal. It is estimated that less than 3% of the exported value of products in this category is Mexican added value — just 3 cents on the dollar! A cynic might say that Mexico is doing little more than receiving the product from Taiwan, adding a “Made in Mexico” sticker and then exporting it — and that cynic wouldn’t be too far from the current reality!

For some perspective, that is barely a tenth of the value that Mexico adds to products in the vehicle segment. Engineering, design, parts manufacturing and assembly in Mexico are all common in that industry. And here is where the real opportunity for Mexico comes in. If Mexico could capture more of the added value in the massive, fast-growing electronics category, it would be hugely impactful on employment in the country. So how can that happen?

Enter the USMCA negotiations. Mexico and the United States have had many rounds of discussions on the updated trade agreement, and despite clear disagreement in certain areas (I’m looking at you, Mexican tomatoes!), increased local content or value added requirements in areas like electronics seems to be an area of agreement and alignment. It is in both countries’ interests to shorten the supply chain and further “de-risk” from China and Taiwan. And it is in both countries’ interests to have more control of the production and supply of such a critical product line.

So will it happen? I am optimistic for a positive outcome given that both countries have similarly aligned interests. Stay tuned to MND as we bring you the developments in this critically strategic area.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Using US intelligence, Mexican Army downs drone and arrests its operator in Tijuana
World.content:
After receiving information from U.S. officials, the Mexican Army successfully deactivated a drone that crossed the border into Tijuana and arrested the operator in Mexican territory.

The Defense Ministry (Defensa) on Thursday provided details of the Monday operation, explaining that the drone was being used by a criminal group to monitor human trafficking routes.

En Tijuana, Baja California, como parte de la “Operación Águila Alta” y mediante el intercambio de información con autoridades de Estados Unidos, elementos de @Defensamx1 detectaron e inhibieron un dron utilizado por un grupo delictivo para vigilar rutas destinadas al tráfico… pic.twitter.com/xiRtDrlljY — Gabinete de Seguridad de México (@GabSeguridadMX) September 18, 2026

The drone operator was apprehended and found to be in possession of a handgun, ammunition and the aircraft control system.

Defensa said the Tijuana operation resulted from information-sharing with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) after its representatives met with CBP agents in the border city.

On Friday, Defense Minister General Ricardo Trevilla confirmed that four drones have been disabled as a result of Operation High Eagle, a joint, binational anti-drone security operation being carried out in the Tijuana-San Diego border area, with each force operating within its own territory.

The current deployment featuring approximately 800 military personnel from both countries encompasses a 5-kilometer area. It relies on ground patrols and the use of anti-drone equipment capable of inhibiting these types of aircraft within a 3-kilometer radius.

Trevilla said representatives from both countries met on Tuesday to assess the results of Operation High Eagle, which was organized after U.S. officials said its agents had shot down more than 300 drones linked to organized crime in the past year.

Defensa said coordination with U.S. authorities aims to strengthen border security under principles of reciprocity, shared and differentiated responsibility, mutual trust and respect for the sovereignty and territories of both countries.



The second phase of the operation, which began on Sept. 7, is scheduled to end on Sept. 21.

On Wednesday, U.S. President Donald Trump acknowledged Mexico’s security efforts but called for greater commitment.

“Mexico’s current investments in its security forces are insufficient to sustain and expand its campaigns against narcoterrorists, their finances and their criminal networks,” Trump said, adding that Mexico must do more to “expose corrupt public officials who have aided and abetted the cartels and betrayed their own country’s security and sovereignty.”

Also Wednesday, Trump sent a document to the U.S. Congress, blaming Mexico for the illicit substances entering the United States.

President Claudia Sheinbaum responded by saying she would like to see a report about what the U.S. government is doing to reduce drug use in its own country and combat drugs and weapons trafficking.

With reports from El País, LópezDóriga.com and El Mañana

World.title: Puerto Vallarta chosen for cruise ship homeport status, potentially doubling its dock capacity
World.content:
Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco, has been selected to develop a cruise ship homeport that would allow vessels to begin or end cruises at the Pacific Coast resort city rather than simply making brief stopovers.

Currently, Puerto Vallarta primarily receives cruise ships as a port of call, with passengers disembarking to sightsee, shop or eat before returning to the ship the same day to continue their journey. A homeport arrangement, however, would allow travelers to arrive in Vallarta to board the ship or to disembark there upon completing the voyage.

¡Tenemos una gran noticia! La licitación para construir un Home Port en Puerto Vallarta ya fue publicada, con este proyecto nuestro principal destino turístico podrá recibir y despedir cruceros internacionales de las principales navieras como @CarnivalCruise, @RoyalCaribbean,… pic.twitter.com/SK8I9y1CoH — Pablo Lemus Navarro (@PabloLemusN) September 15, 2026

“Imagine a cruise ship that starts in Puerto Vallarta, then continues to Los Cabos and ends in Los Angeles,” Jalisco Gov. Pablo Lemus said Wednesday in a video posted on his official social media channels.

Lemus noted that the construction needed for the new status is scheduled to begin in 2027 and be operational by 2029.

“This is great news that will transform Puerto Vallarta’s tourism economy for years to come,” Lemus said.

The homeport project could boost the economy of hotels, restaurants, transport providers, tour operators, businesses, and local suppliers. According to Lemus, cruise passengers could add an average of two nights of accommodations to their stay — either before boarding or after disembarking — in addition to spending on meals and tourist experiences.

Lemus also said that beyond tourism spending, supplies for the cruise ships would be sourced locally.

The governor told the newspaper El Infomador that the project aims to help Puerto Vallarta recover from a drop in visitor numbers, mainly due to the weaker dollar relative to the peso and the events surrounding the capture and death of drug lord Nemesio “El Mencho” Rubén Oseguera Cervantes on Feb. 22.

Local media also reported that the National Port System Administration (Asipona) of Puerto Vallarta has issued an international tender to build and operate the terminal, following a competitive process that also included proposals from Mazatlán, Los Cabos, and Nayarit.

The call for bids allows for the participation of Mexican and foreign companies with experience in operating cruise ship and nautical tourism terminals.

As for the financial requirements, interested parties must demonstrate net worth or subscribed equity of at least 200 million pesos (US $11.65 million) as of the end of 2025.

World.title: Azcatitlan Codex returns to Mexico after 186 years, on loan from France
World.content:
A monumental illustrated account of Aztec history — from the Mexica migration to the Spanish conquest of Tenochtitlán — is back in Mexico for the first time in 186 years under a loan agreement with France’s national library.

The centuries-old Azcatitlan Codex, on loan through Dec. 6, chronicles the origins, expansion and collapse of the Mexica world. Tenochtitlán was the island capital of the Mexica empire, built on Lake Texcoco where Mexico City now stands.

The document left Mexico in 1840 and remained in Europe through a succession of private and institutional collections. It has been held by the National Library of France since the 1890s, making its temporary return a rare cultural and diplomatic event for Mexico.

The loan is not a repatriation — unlike Mexico’s 2024 recovery of three 16th-century codices and Spain’s 2023 return of a Tlaquiltenango Codex fragment, which was expected to fetch more than US $100,000 at auction before Spain’s Civil Guard withdrew it.

But it comes as Mexico continues to seek the return of pre-Hispanic and colonial-era objects that left the country in earlier centuries, and after President Claudia Sheinbaum described codices in France as a top priority for recovery before French President Emmanuel Macron’s 2025 visit.

Instead, Sheinbaum and Macron agreed to a temporary, reciprocal exchange to honor the 200 years of diplomatic relations between their two countries.

Where to see the Azcatitlan Codex

The Azcatitlan Codex arrived in Mexico City this month for an exhibition at the National Museum of Anthropology, while Mexico has sent the Boturini Codex to Paris for display at the French national library.

The exchange is part of the Great Franco-Mexican Festival, a binational cultural program featuring nearly 200 activities, according to a joint release from Mexico’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Culture Ministry and National Institute of Anthropology and History.

The Azcatitlan Codex is a significant record of the Mexica, the Nahuatl-speaking people often called Aztecs. “Aztec” is widely used for the empire centered on Tenochtitlán, while “Mexica” more specifically identifies the people who founded and ruled it.

Created in the Valley of Mexico in the late 16th or early 17th century, the manuscript combines Mesoamerican pictorial writing with European paper, bookbinding and Spanish text.

The manuscript is divided into three broad sections: the Mexica migration from Aztlán; the reigns of Tenochtitlán’s rulers; and the 1519 arrival of Spanish forces led by Hernán Cortés, the conquest and evangelization.

The codex’s images have made it a particularly vivid source. One scene depicts Cortés and Spanish conquistadors, accompanied by Indigenous people carrying loads. Another depicts Mexica warriors defending Tenochtitlán’s great pyramid.

Tres grandes momentos atraviesan las páginas del Códice Azcatitlan: la migración desde Aztlan, la historia de Tenochtitlan y los primeros años de la Nueva España. En el marco de la Gran Fiesta Franco-Mexicana, el Museo Nacional de Antropología presenta por primera vez en México… pic.twitter.com/wF8hjc3PO3 — Secretaría de Cultura (@cultura_mx) September 18, 2026

The museum is exhibiting the original under low light, opened to pages four and five. They depict eight Indigenous groups setting out to find the site where Huitzilopochtli instructed them to found Tenochtitlán, El País reported.

Photographic reproductions of the remaining pages are displayed on the wall of the anthropology museum, located in the capital’s Chapultepec Park.

The exhibition also includes 25 archaeological and ethnographic objects and facsimiles of nine manuscripts, including the Codex Mendoza, the De la Cruz-Badiano Codex and the Boturini Codex.

The Boturini Codex, also known as the Tira de la Peregrinación, traces the Mexica journey from Aztlán to Tenochtitlán. It belongs to Mexico’s National Library of Anthropology and History and is due to return from France in December, when the Azcatitlan Codex will also return to Paris.

The temporary exchange is part of wider efforts to preserve, digitize and recover Indigenous documentary heritage, such as the digital public release of the Florentine Codex, a 12-book encyclopedia of Mexica life compiled by Nahua scholars in the 16th century.

With reports from BBC.com, El País and Deutsche Welle

World.title: Peso slides toward 17.3 to the dollar after US Fed’s first rate hike since 2023
World.content:
The peso depreciated on Friday morning and was on track for its worst weekly performance since March, as traders continued to react to the U.S. Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates.

The tightening of U.S. monetary policy has eroded the appeal of assets denominated in local currency, a trend that became evident as soon as the Fed announced its decision on Wednesday morning.

The peso had weakened to 17.32 to the dollar Friday morning, and hovered at 17.229 to the dollar by 2:00 p.m., down nearly 6 centavos from Thursday’s close of 17.1706. Market analysts projected a trading range of between 17.08 to 17.28 pesos per dollar for Friday’s session.

The Fed’s decision on Wednesday to raise its benchmark rate by 25 basis points, bringing it to a range of 3.75% to 4%, interrupted an eight-month pause that saw the U.S. rate remain between 3.50% and 3.75% since December.

The peso lost 0.58%, or 10 centavos, against the dollar that same afternoon.

Gabriela Siller, director of Financial Analysis at Banco BASE, said the fall of the peso is directly linked to the Fed decision, as well as the possibility of another rate cut in the United States this year.

“This is relevant because of carry trade operations, where the interest rate differential between Mexico and the U.S. is important,” she said.

The carry trade is an investment strategy in which investors borrow money in a currency with a low interest rate to invest in another currency or asset with a higher rate.

“With the rate cut, traders get a lower return, because the rate differential is the net return after paying off the loan,” Siller explained.

The Fed’s decision reduced the interest rate differential between Mexico and the U.S. to 250 basis points, a historic low not seen since December 2015. Mexico’s benchmark rate sits at 6.5% and the Bank of Mexico is expected to hold the rate steady at its meeting next week.

If the Fed announces another rate hike before the end of the year, as anticipated, this differential will be at 225 points, representing even lower returns for investors.

As such, the peso’s value would be impacted by the relative unattractiveness of peso-denominated investments.

These expectations are also related to the recent inflation trend in Mexico.

As of August, inflation stood at 3.26%, remaining within the central bank’s target range, a situation that contrasts with the United States, where inflationary pressures remain more persistent, suggesting the Fed will continue with a more aggressive posture.

With reports from El Economista, Forex.com and El Financiero

World.title: 59 million liters of stolen fuel seized in Guanajuato state, the largest such bust in Mexican history
World.content:
Listen to this article

Authorities confiscated 59 million liters of stolen fuel, the largest single-site seizure in Mexico’s history and five times larger than the March 2025 bust in Tamaulipas that led to 14 arrests, including six members of the Navy.

The operation, which was triggered after a July 3 arrest involving a tanker truck loaded with stolen fuel, occurred at a property located in the small community of La Fragua in the San José Iturbide municipality, Guanajuato state, alongside Federal Highway 57.

Las indagatorias para combatir a redes delictivas vinculadas al contrabando de combustible llevaron a la #FGR a cumplimentar órdenes de cateo que derivaron en el hallazgo de más de 59 millones de litros de hidrocarburo en #Guanajuato. Más ▶️ https://t.co/1aA8iguFlJ pic.twitter.com/D6A7lUbh4n — Guanajuato (@FGR_Gto) September 18, 2026

State and federal agents seized 10 tanks containing suspected fuel (diesel, regular gasoline and premium gasoline), three tanker trucks, containers used to transport fuel, and documentation. No arrests had been reported as of Friday morning.

State officials said the amount of hydrocarbon material discovered — roughly equivalent to the amount seized in all of 2025 — is so large that its identification and handling will have to be carried out by specialized personnel to prevent spills and fires.

The July 3 incident in which a person was arrested while unloading approximately 30,000 liters of stolen fuel at a gas station in San Luis de la Paz, Guanajuato, prompted an investigation that led to another arrest weeks later at an LP gas dispensing station in Dolores Hidalgo.

As the suspects were unable to provide documentation establishing traceability, a judge issued a search warrant after investigators identified the storage facility in La Fragua as the likely source.

Guanajuato Security Minister Juan Mauro González Martínez said that the seizure goes beyond the volume confiscated.

“Investigating possible irregular fuel operations allows us to reduce the risk of fires, explosions and spills, while also protecting our communities and the environment,” he said. “It also disrupts potential sources of funding for criminal organizations.”

The facility was equipped with access roads, both asphalt and metal, for the movement of trucks and rail vans, as well as large-scale containers with a capacity for up to 80 million liters. All materials have been turned over to the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR).

For now, the authorities have not publicly established the origin of the 59 million liters seized, a task the FGR will undertake.

Prosecutors will also seek to determine who was in charge of the mega-operation, which is located just outside La Fragua, a community of fewer than 400 people. Current ownership remains unverified.

A small fuel storage facility was authorized there in 2013. Ownership changed hands several times by 2020, by which time it had expanded and was legally established as a Petroleum Products Storage and Supply Terminal.

At the time, the facility was operated by Gas Natural del Noreste, in partnership with ExxonMobil and Grupo Gasolinero Orsan and had been granted permits from the Environment Ministry and the federal Agency for Safety, Energy and Environment.

This latest bust is the fifth this year in Guanajuato related to stolen fuel, though the previous four pale in comparison:

55,000 liters of fuel were seized during a Feb. 25 joint operation across three towns;

Twin operations in Apaseo el Grande on March 31 netted 99,000 liters of fuel.

State police seized a tanker truck carrying 21,000 liters of fuel near Pénjamo on Aug. 27.

A clandestine tunnel providing access to a Pemex pipeline was discovered and neutralized.

With reports from El País, La Jornada, Zeta, El Financiero and Periódico Correo

World.title: El Jalapeño: National Palace overrun by feral cats, Sheinbaum admits
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — In an unexpected admission during a routine morning address, President Claudia Sheinbaum confirmed that the National Palace’s administrative functions have been severely disrupted by an unmanaged population surge of its feline residents.

While the palace was originally reported to house 16 felines — all legally classified under Mexican law as “living fixed assets” — unregistered stray populations have ballooned, leaving cabinet members, visitors and security personnel navigating a sprawling feline hierarchy that operates outside government oversight.

The crisis reportedly escalated when an attempt to introduce a newly adopted puppy, Rollo, aimed at providing emotional well-being support to palace staff, was immediately thwarted by a coordinated blockade of senior orange tabbies occupying the primary garden corridors.

“We attempted to establish a balanced workspace for all four-legged personnel,” Sheinbaum explained, adjusting her podium microphone to avoid disturbing a sleeping calico. “However, the current asset distribution leans approximately 98% feline, and they have made it clear that additional canine integration will require extensive inter-departmental negotiation.”

Palace officials admitted that several key historic rooms have effectively been ceded to the animals. The famous courtyards now run on cat schedules, with high-level diplomatic meetings routinely paused to accommodate lap inspections by roving kitties. Staff members trying to process official paperwork report that several desktop keyboards remain indefinitely occupied by napping felines.

Despite the territorial challenges, the administration confirmed it has no plans to evict the current residents, citing their permanent legal protections. Instead, the government is considering creating a specialized feline mediation task force to negotiate shared corridor access before upcoming foreign dignitary visits.

World.title: Argentina’s Top Power Firm Sells Silver Stake for Six Times What It Paid
World.content:
Argentina · Markets

Key Facts — The story. Central Puerto sold its 9.9% stake in miner AbraSilver for US$163.1 million. — Why it matters. Argentina’s largest private power producer is paying the proceeds straight to shareholders. — The background. AbraSilver’s Diablillos silver project won Argentina’s RIGI investment tax breaks in May. — The numbers. The stake cost US$25.5 million, so the gain is about US$137.6 million. — The catch. An opposition deputy questions the timing, but no authority has found wrongdoing. — What comes next. A dividend of 247.3 billion pesos (US$163.6 million) is due on 25 September.

Argentina’s mining push has turned a tax-break regime into a magnet for investment and for political suspicion. The country’s biggest private power producer has now sold a silver-mine stake at six times its cost.

A historic power station building in the port area of Buenos Aires. Illustrative image. Photo: Horacio Cambeiro / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Central Puerto, Argentina’s largest private electricity generator, said on 16 September 2026 that it had sold its entire stake in AbraSilver. The Canadian-listed miner owns Diablillos, a silver and gold project in the northwest, and the sale raised US$163.1 million.

Why This Matters Beyond Argentina

Central Puerto runs thermal, hydro and renewable plants with about 7,115 megawatts of capacity, according to El Cronista. Its shares trade in Buenos Aires and in New York, so the deal reaches foreign portfolios directly.

In 2024 the company began buying into mining, whose exports reached a record US$6.037 billion in 2025. Gold made up about 68% of that total, followed by lithium and silver, official data compiled by Panorama Minero show.

The sale matters to investors because nearly all the cash is going straight back to shareholders. It matters politically because the project won benefits under RIGI, a tax-break regime approved by Economy Minister Luis Caputo.

Opposition figures now question whether that approval drove the gain, a claim no authority has examined or upheld. Peso figures use the central bank’s reference rate of 1,512.33 pesos per dollar for 18 September 2026 (BCRA Communication A 3500).

What Central Puerto Sold

Central Puerto held the shares through Proener, a wholly owned subsidiary, according to its February 2025 release. It bought a first block of about 4% in April 2024 for US$7.1 million, iProfesional reported.

A second purchase of US$18.4 million in January 2025 lifted the holding to 9.9%, making it AbraSilver’s largest shareholder. In total the stake cost US$25.5 million and sold for US$163.1 million, a gain of about US$137.6 million.

That is roughly 6.4 times the money invested, in less than two and a half years. The company said it had reviewed the investment and concluded the holding had ceased to be strategic, EFE reported via Infobae.

The buyer or buyers of the shares were not named in the announcement. Central Puerto keeps a 35% stake in 3C Lithium, which is developing the Tres Cruces lithium project in Catamarca.

How the Special Dividend Works

Central Puerto’s board approved paying out the sale proceeds as an extraordinary cash dividend. The payout totals 247.3 billion pesos (US$163.6 million), according to iProfesional and the company’s dividend notice.

That works out at 164 pesos (US$0.11) per ordinary share, according to the notice as summarised by Panabee. El Cronista put the payout at about US$1.08 per New York share.

Shareholders on record on 18 September qualify, and payment is due on 25 September. Foreign holders may ask for payment in US dollars if the company can use the MULC, the official currency market, that day.

The deadline to make that request through a financial intermediary is 22 September, according to the notice. A 7% income-tax withholding applies to the payment, the notice says.

How Argentina’s RIGI Regime Works

RIGI, the Large Investment Incentive Regime, was created by Law 27,742, the omnibus reform known as Ley Bases. Projects above a threshold, generally US$200 million, pay a flat 25% income tax instead of the standard graduated rate.

They also receive 30 years of regulatory stability and pay no export duties from the third year. Their freedom to keep export dollars rises in steps, reaching full access in the fourth year, the Economy Ministry says.

By mid-August, 21 projects had been approved with combined investment of US$46.7 billion, La Nación reported. Another 23 projects worth about US$152.3 billion were awaiting a decision, according to the same report.

Mining and oil and gas dominate the approved list, with projects concentrated in San Juan, Río Negro, Catamarca and Salta. For a mine not yet built, such terms change expected after-tax returns rather than current earnings.

Diablillos and Its Tax-Break Approval

Diablillos sits on the high Puna plateau between Salta and Catamarca provinces, about 160 kilometres southwest of Salta city. AbraSilver said on 2 March 2026 that Caputo had confirmed the project’s RIGI approval on 27 February.

The formal approval came in Resolution 562, published in the Official Bulletin on 11 May 2026, EconoJournal reported. It covers an initial investment of US$481.7 million, with US$352.4 million to be spent in the first two years.

Infobae reported that operations are scheduled to start in July 2029, with 2,013 direct and indirect jobs expected. AbraSilver’s feasibility study, as summarised by iProfesional, puts capital spending near US$760 million and after-tax value near US$3 billion.

Reserves stand at 183.5 million ounces of silver and 1.76 million ounces of gold, according to the same summary. “Securing RIGI approval is truly a transformational milestone for Diablillos,” AbraSilver’s chief executive said in March.

The Criticism and the Caputo Question

Rodolfo Tailhade, a Kirchnerist opposition deputy, publicly questioned the deal after the announcement. He pointed to what he called a coincidence between RIGI, the AbraSilver sale and gains of US$138 million, radio station LU17 reported.

La Arena, a newspaper in La Pampa province, reported that he called the deal a “pasamanos”, meaning a quick handoff. La Política Online, a political news site, described Central Puerto as linked to businessman Nicolás “Nicky” Caputo, calling him the minister’s cousin.

La Nación reported in December 2022 that Nicolás Caputo had sold his stake of nearly 3% in Central Puerto. No court, regulator or prosecutor has found wrongdoing by Luis Caputo, Nicolás Caputo or Central Puerto.

The Company’s Side

Central Puerto has presented the sale as a portfolio decision, saying the stake was no longer strategic. LU17, summarising the company’s position, noted that mining valuations move with permits, feasibility work and construction readiness.

The same report said available documents do not support attributing the whole gain to RIGI benefits. Bank of America and Citi rate the stock a buy, with targets of US$28 and US$22, El Cronista reported.

How the Market Reacted

Central Puerto’s New York shares traded at US$13.65 when El Cronista published its analysis. They fell 7.04% on Friday 18 September, the dividend record date, amid a broad sell-off in Argentine stocks.

Pampa Energía lost 5.76% the same day and the Argentina fund ARGT fell 1.50%, Rio Times market data show. It is not clear how much of the drop reflected the payout rather than wider selling.

What It Means If You Hold Argentine Assets

Registered holders receive a one-off payout worth about 7.5% to 8% of the share price, El Cronista estimated. Foreign holders should ask their broker before 22 September whether dollar payment through the MULC is available.

The sale does not involve Central Puerto’s power plants, so it has no direct bearing on electricity supply. The RIGI approval was granted to AbraSilver’s local project company, Pacific Rim Mining Corporation Argentina, not to Central Puerto.

La Arena reported that opposition lawmakers had proposed five-year limits on share transfers in RIGI projects, which were rejected. Stake sales in other approved projects may therefore face similar political questions, but not legal limits.

What Is Not Yet Known

Central Puerto has not said who bought the shares or at what price per share. It is not known whether the new owners will play any role in building Diablillos.

Central Puerto has not disclosed how much tax, if any, it will pay on the gain. Luis Caputo has not publicly addressed the criticism in the reports reviewed by The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does this sale matter? Argentina’s largest private power producer made about six times its money on a mining stake in under three years. It is paying nearly all of it to shareholders while opposition figures question a tax-break approval. How big is the dividend? It totals 247.3 billion pesos (US$163.6 million), or 164 pesos (US$0.11) per share. It is payable on 25 September to holders on record on 18 September. What is RIGI? It is Argentina’s Large Investment Incentive Regime, which offers a 25% income-tax rate and 30 years of stability. Diablillos was approved in May 2026 for a US$481.7 million investment. Has anyone been found guilty of wrongdoing? No. No court, regulator or prosecutor has found wrongdoing, and the allegations remain political claims reported by the press.

World.title: Brazil’s Helbor Moves Closer to Leaving the Stock Market After HBR Vote
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts — The story. Shareholders of Brazil’s HBR Realty approved a takeover offer for sister developer Helbor. — Why it matters. Helbor, a São Paulo homebuilder since 1977, would leave the stock exchange. — The background. Helbor shares have lost about 95% since their 2013 peak, Seu Dinheiro reported. — The numbers. HBR offers 0.8155 shares per Helbor share, worth R$2.52 (US$0.49) in July. — The catch. More than two-thirds of Helbor’s qualifying minority holders must still accept. — What comes next. The securities regulator must register the offer before a stock-exchange auction.

Brazil’s mid-sized listed homebuilders have spent years squeezed by some of the world’s highest interest rates. On Friday, shareholders backed one family’s plan to merge two of its listed property firms and delist one.

Mogi Shopping in Mogi das Cruzes, São Paulo state, one of HBR Realty’s malls. Photo: Tet / Wikimedia Commons (CC0)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

Shareholders of HBR Realty, a São Paulo shopping-centre and office owner, approved on 18 September 2026 a share-swap offer for developer Helbor. Both companies are controlled by the Borenstein family, and Helbor would become a wholly owned HBR subsidiary.

Why This Matters

Helbor is one of Brazil’s older residential developers, founded in 1977 in Mogi das Cruzes, near São Paulo. It listed on the stock exchange in 2007 and says it has delivered 46,000 homes in 30 cities.

Its shares traded at R$50.79 (US$9.85) at their 2013 peak and R$2.36 (US$0.46) before the offer, Seu Dinheiro reported. That is a fall of about 95% in little more than a decade.

Brazil’s benchmark Selic rate, set by the central bank, held at a peak of 15% from June 2025 to March 2026. High rates raise mortgage costs for buyers and borrowing costs for developers, who build with debt.

Seu Dinheiro said Helbor could become the latest company to leave B3 and its Novo Mercado. That is the top governance tier of B3, the São Paulo stock exchange.

Brazil also votes for president, governors and Congress in a first round on 4 October 2026. Dollar figures use the Central Bank’s PTAX selling rate of R$5.1575 per dollar on 18 September 2026.

What Shareholders Approved on Friday

HBR held an extraordinary shareholder meeting on Friday, 18 September, Money Times reported. Holders of 65.94% of HBR’s voting capital attended, and 64.71% voted in favour of the offer.

Holders of 1.23% of the voting capital voted against, according to the same report. The vote allows HBR to pursue the offer, but it does not complete the takeover.

HBR’s chief executive, Alexandre Nakano, said the deal combines companies with complementary roles in property development. HBR itself will stay listed on B3, while Helbor would leave the Novo Mercado.

The next steps are registration with the CVM, Brazil’s securities regulator, and the exchange offer itself. Money Times did not report a date for the auction on B3.

How the Offer Works

In Brazil, a public offer to buy shares is called an OPA, short for oferta pública de aquisição. HBR’s offer is a share swap rather than a cash bid, so Helbor holders would receive HBR stock.

Each Helbor share would be exchanged for 0.81553398 ordinary HBR shares, according to the companies. The ratio was set using 90-day weighted average share prices, Seu Dinheiro reported.

The deal was valued at R$2.52 (US$0.49) per Helbor share when it was announced in early July. Bloomberg Línea reported that this reference value will be adjusted by the Selic rate until settlement.

HBR must end up with at least 50.1% of Helbor’s voting capital, according to Bloomberg Línea. More than two-thirds of Helbor’s qualifying minority shareholders must also accept, Seu Dinheiro reported.

One Family on Both Sides

The Borenstein family controls both companies, holding about 51% of each, according to Money Times. Its holding company, Hélio Borenstein S.A., owns 38.56% of Helbor and 49% of HBR, Bloomberg Línea reported.

Family members Henrique and Henry Borenstein are co-controllers, according to the same report. The family has irrevocably committed to hand over its Helbor shares if the minimum thresholds are met.

Because one family controls buyer and target, the minority threshold gives outside Helbor investors a direct say. Bradesco BBI, the investment bank of Bradesco, provided a fairness opinion, and BTG Pactual acts as intermediary.

Two Businesses With Different Cycles

HBR was created in 2011 as the Borenstein family’s rental-income arm, according to its investor relations site. It owns Mogi Shopping and Suzano Shopping near São Paulo, and Patteo Olinda in Pernambuco state.

Its website also lists the HBR 3A office project and the W São Paulo hotel among its assets. Helbor builds and sells apartments, and over half its land bank targets upper-middle to luxury buyers, ADVFN reported.

“One of HBR’s greatest challenges is sourcing its primary raw material, land,” Nakano said, according to Seu Dinheiro. Helbor holds land for projects with a potential sales value of about R$12 billion (US$2.3 billion).

About 83% of that land bank is in the city of São Paulo, Money Times reported. The companies expect annual savings of R$10 million to R$20 million (US$1.9 million to US$3.9 million) from shared governance.

Why the Shares Fell After the Announcement

The market reaction in July was negative for both companies. Helbor shares were down 19.07% at R$1.91 (US$0.37) around midday on 6 July, Seu Dinheiro reported.

HBR shares were down 17.76% at R$2.11 (US$0.41) at the same time, according to the same report. In a share swap, a fall in the buyer’s stock also cuts what the target’s holders will receive.

At the time, Bloomberg Línea put Helbor’s market value at R$316 million (US$61 million). It put HBR’s market value at R$267 million (US$52 million), well below the R$2.05 billion (US$397 million) valuation at its 2021 listing.

Helbor reported net debt of R$1.67 billion (US$324 million), equal to 59% of its equity, Bloomberg Línea said. First-quarter profit attributable to controlling shareholders fell 74.5% to R$1.9 million (US$368,000), Seu Dinheiro reported.

Interest Rates and the Housing Market

The Central Bank’s monetary policy committee, Copom, began cutting the Selic in March 2026. On 16 September it cut the rate by 0.25 percentage point to 13.75%, its fifth consecutive cut, Poder360 reported.

The committee did not signal its next move, and its next meeting is on 4 November, Jornal do Brasil reported. The rate had stayed at its 15% peak for about nine months before the cutting cycle began.

The housing market has split in two, according to data from Abrainc, the developers’ association, and research institute Fipe. In the 12 months to March 2026, unit sales under the state-backed Minha Casa Minha Vida programme rose 12.2%.

Unit sales in the mid- and high-end segment, the one most relevant to Helbor, fell 12.2% over the same period. The programme’s name translates as “My House, My Life”, and it targets lower-income families.

What It Means If You Hold Shares or Invest in Brazil

Helbor minority shareholders will have to choose between taking HBR shares and staying in a company leaving the Novo Mercado. Their decision matters because the two-thirds minority threshold can block the deal.

For HBR shareholders, management expects daily trading volume to rise from R$1 million (US$194,000) to R$3.5 million (US$679,000). For foreign investors, the deal shows how Brazil’s small listed companies are consolidating or leaving the exchange.

The pace of Selic cuts after the 4 October election will shape demand for the mid- and high-end homes Helbor sells. Anyone holding either stock should read the final offer notice once the CVM registers it.

What Is Not Yet Known

The CVM has not yet registered the offer, and no auction date has been published. It is not known whether enough of Helbor’s minority shareholders will accept the share swap.

The final value of the offer will depend on HBR’s share price and the Selic adjustment at settlement. The reports reviewed do not say how Helbor’s net debt would be managed inside HBR.

No shareholder group has publicly announced opposition to the offer in the reports reviewed by The Rio Times. It is also unclear how the election result will affect interest rates and property demand next year.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does the Helbor takeover matter? It would take one of Brazil’s older homebuilders off the stock exchange after a 95% share-price fall. It also comes as high interest rates weigh on small listed property firms. Is the deal done? No. HBR shareholders approved the offer on 18 September, but the CVM must register it and Helbor’s minority shareholders must accept. How much is HBR offering? It offers 0.81553398 of its own shares for each Helbor share. The deal was valued at R$2.52 (US$0.49) per share when announced in July. Who controls the two companies? The Borenstein family controls both HBR and Helbor, with about 51% of each. That is why minority approval is a key condition.

World.title: Colombia’s Election Runner-Up Backs Union Protests Against New President
World.content:
Colombia · Politics

Key Facts — The story. Opposition leader Ivan Cepeda pledged firm support for protests against Colombia’s new government. — Why it matters. Unions have set a national protest calendar against President Abelardo de la Espriella. — The background. De la Espriella, a right-winger, beat Cepeda with 49.66% to 48.70% in June. — The numbers. Over 1,500 union and social delegates set a national march for 14 October. — The catch. The march is weeks away; no route or turnout target has been announced. — What comes next. Unions plan a national strike in November, on the 11th or the 20th.

Colombia’s new right-wing government is six weeks old and already faces a union protest calendar. On 18 September, the runner-up in June’s election pledged his backing to the coming protests.

Union members march in Bogotá during the national strike of 28 May 2025, under the previous government. Archive photo. Photo: ProtoplasmaKid / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Ivan Cepeda, the left-wing senator who lost Colombia’s presidential runoff, said on 18 September that social protests are being prepared. He wrote on X that the mobilisations would have his party’s “decided support” against President Abelardo de la Espriella.

Why This Matters

Street protest has shaped Colombian politics before, most recently in a 2021 national strike against a tax reform. Abelardo de la Espriella, a right-wing lawyer and businessman, took office as president on 7 August 2026.

He beat Cepeda in the runoff on 21 June with 49.66% of the vote against 48.70%. That narrow margin means close to half of runoff voters backed the candidate now supporting protests.

Cepeda holds the opposition seat in the Senate, reserved by law for the presidential runner-up. His running mate, indigenous leader Aida Quilcue, took a matching seat in the House of Representatives.

The unions say they are defending reforms of left-wing ex-president Gustavo Petro against the new government. For investors, the calendar of marches and a possible national strike adds a new domestic risk to watch.

What Cepeda Said

Cepeda posted his message on X on 18 September, Semana, a national news magazine, reported. “Comienzan a prepararse ya las movilizaciones sociales que contarán con nuestro respaldo decidido,” he wrote.

That translates as “social mobilisations are now being prepared, and they will have our decided support”. He said that, a month into the new government, many sectors feel their rights are severely affected, Infobae reported.

He listed earthquake survivors, peasant farmers, conflict victims, teachers, students and public-sector workers. He also named indigenous and Afro-Colombian communities, young people, former guerrillas in reintegration and LGBTIQ+ people.

Judges, artists and critical journalists were on the list as well, according to Infobae. Semana and El Universal, a Cartagena daily, both noted that the post named no date or city.

The Protest Calendar Set by the Unions

The dates come from a gathering held in Bogota on 11 and 12 September, before Cepeda spoke. More than 1,500 delegates from unions, social movements, peasant groups, ethnic organisations and parties attended, Vanguardia reported.

The main organisers are Fecode, the national teachers’ union, and the CUT, Colombia’s largest trade union federation. They defined Wednesday 14 October as a national day of mobilisation against the De la Espriella government, Semana reported.

A national strike is planned for November, with 11 or 20 November under discussion. El Tiempo, a Bogota newspaper, reported that the exact strike date had not yet been confirmed.

Petro’s coalition, the Historic Pact, also joined the call, according to Infobae. Routes and meeting points for the October march have not been announced, Vanguardia reported.

What the Protesters Want

The declaration names eight themes, including sovereignty, democracy, peace, labour rights, public education and public health. The groups also defend Petro-era reforms on labour, land for peasant farmers and negotiated peace, Infobae reported.

They oppose what they describe as plans to privatise state assets, including oil company Ecopetrol and pipeline operator Cenit. Minuto60, a news site, reported that Grupo Bicentenario, the state holding company, and Inpec, the prison service, were also named.

The CUT also cited the economic and social emergency after the 10 August earthquake, El Tiempo reported. The magnitude 7.4 quake, centred in the western department of Choco, killed 331 people, according to La Republica.

The Labour Bill Behind the Anger

A specific trigger is a new Labour Statute bill, presented by Labour Minister Natalia Lopez on 10 September. It would compile the 1950 labour code, later reforms and case law into a single law, El Tiempo reported.

The government says it settles a “historic debt” owed since the 1991 constitution required such a statute. It says the bill covers rural work, domestic work, delivery platforms and the self-employed.

Informal work stood at 54.5% of employment in April to June 2026, Infobae reported. The CUT says the bill was filed without the tripartite wage and labour commission, which brings together government, employers and unions.

“We cannot talk about dialogue while decisions that directly affect workers’ rights are taken unilaterally,” said CUT president Fabio Arias. The bill needs four debates in Congress before it can become law.

How Street Protest Works in Colombia

Peaceful protest is a constitutional right in Colombia, but national strikes have turned violent before. In 2021, weeks of road blockades caused shortages; the government counted 26 deaths, NGOs about 75.

Petro later replaced the riot police unit, known as ESMAD, with a unit focused on dialogue called UNDMO. In July, De la Espriella’s defence minister-designate, Jorge Eduardo Mora, announced that ESMAD would return.

Mora said the Petro-era rules had “tied the hands” of the security forces, El Colombiano reported. He added that the force would respect human rights and that peaceful protest would be protected.

On 11 September, masked people damaged a university library during a march towards the US embassy in Bogota. La FM, a radio network, reported four staff needed attention and the Universidad Nacional evacuated its campus.

The Government’s Side

De la Espriella responded to that unrest with a security package announced on 13 September. It would let police enter public universities during violent protests, and he said autonomy “is not a licence for impunity”.

Analisis Urbano, a Medellin outlet, reported that the government says it respects peaceful protest. The same report said the government promised action against violence or disruption of public order.

The Rio Times found no direct government reply to Cepeda‘s post by the morning of 19 September. Neither Semana nor Vanguardia reported any government response to the union calendar.

Cepeda Under Scrutiny Himself

Cepeda makes his call while facing a preliminary inquiry by the Supreme Court, Colombia’s top criminal court for lawmakers. The court opened it on 14 September into the financing of the Historic Pact primary held on 26 October 2025.

El Espectador cited a complaint that a Barranquilla firm with zero capital gave 600 million pesos (US$190,000) in services. Dollar figures use Colombia’s official market rate of 3,151.73 pesos per US dollar on 18 September 2026.

The firm’s owner denied any link to Cepeda, and the Historic Pact denied any irregularity. A preliminary inquiry establishes no responsibility, and Cepeda has not been charged with any offence.

What It Means If You Live, Travel or Invest in Colombia

Residents and visitors in Bogota should expect road closures and slower transport around 14 October. The 11 September march in Bogota already forced a campus evacuation, a sign that marches can disrupt normal routines.

Businesses should plan for a possible national strike on 11 or 20 November and watch for a final date. Investors should note the protests target what unions call privatisation plans at Ecopetrol, the state-controlled oil company.

Fecode represents public-school teachers, so parents should watch for school closures on protest days. Travellers should check local news and embassy alerts before moving between cities on those dates.

What Is Not Yet Known

It is not known how many people will join the 14 October march or which cities will see the largest crowds. The exact date of the November national strike has not been confirmed.

It is unclear whether ESMAD will be back in service by October, and under which rules. The government has not said whether it will negotiate on the labour bill before the protests.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does Cepeda’s announcement matter? He won 48.70% in June’s runoff and now leads the opposition in the Senate. His backing gives the union protests the support of the main opposition figure. When are the protests? Unions have called a national march for 14 October 2026. A national strike is planned for November, on the 11th or the 20th. What do the protesters want? They defend Petro-era reforms and oppose privatisations and the new Labour Statute bill. They also cite rights and public services. Is Cepeda under investigation? The Supreme Court opened a preliminary inquiry on 14 September into financing of his party’s 2025 primary. He has not been charged, and his coalition denies wrongdoing.

EXPATS IN BRAZIL · BRAZIL, 19 SEPTEMBER 2026

Key Facts —A single person needs about R$3,900–5,000 per month (US$755–970) to live in Brazil’s big cities in 2026; smaller capitals in the North and Northeast run lower —São Paulo has Brazil’s most expensive advertised rents: R$65.36 per square meter in August 2026 (FipeZAP); the national average is R$54.47 —The basic food basket costs R$915 in São Paulo and R$855 in Rio de Janeiro (Dieese, July 2026) — and it got cheaper in 26 of 27 state capitals that month —Inflation is easing: consumer prices rose 4.22 percent over 12 months in August 2026 (IBGE), inside the central bank’s target band —The real has gained about 6 percent against the US dollar this year (PTAX R$5.16 per dollar on 18 September 2026, Banco Central) — dollar earners feel Brazil getting pricier —The national minimum wage is R$1,621 per month in 2026 (Decree 12,797/2025) — the anchor of local purchasing power

What does it cost to live in Brazil in 2026? A single person spends between R$3,900 and R$5,000 per month (US$755–970) all-in in the major cities, while smaller capitals in the North and Northeast come in well below that — this guide adds up verified rents, food, transport and utility prices, city by city.

The Short Answer, With the Exchange Rate Attached

Brazil is a country of about 214 million people and at least four different cost worlds: the São Paulo–Rio axis, the southern capitals, the cheaper Northeast, and the interior. Most expat budgets land between R$3,900 and R$5,000 per month for one person renting a one-bedroom apartment, cooking at home most days, and using public transport. Comfortable expat life outside the premium districts of São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro is realistic on US$1,500 per month — about R$7,740 at the current rate.

Every dollar figure in this guide is converted at the PTAX reference rate of the Banco Central: US$1 = R$5.1575, and €1 = R$5.9126, both from the closing bulletin of 18 September 2026. One caution for dollar earners: the real has strengthened about 6.3 percent against the dollar since the last trading day of 2025, when the PTAX stood at R$5.5024. Brazil is measurably more expensive in hard currency this year than it was in January.

Housing: Rents by City in 2026

The most current national picture comes from the FipeZAP Residential Rent Index, which tracks advertised asking prices for apartments in 36 Brazilian cities. In August 2026 the national average stood at R$54.47 per square meter, up 9.16 percent over 12 months and 6.56 percent since January — rents are rising more than twice as fast as consumer prices. One-bedroom units carry the highest per-meter price of any category, at R$72.41 per square meter nationally. Our markets desk covered the underlying trend in this week’s IGP-M rent report.

City Advertised rent (R$/m², FipeZAP) Estimated 45 m² one-bed Note São Paulo R$65.36 (Aug) ≈ R$2,940 Most expensive capital in the index Recife R$64.11 (Jul) ≈ R$2,885 A surprise second place Florianópolis R$60.84 (Jul) ≈ R$2,740 Island premium, top safety ranking Rio de Janeiro ≈ R$55 (2026, expat areas) ≈ R$2,475 Rents +11.04 percent Jan–Aug (FipeZAP) Belo Horizonte R$50.14 (Jul) ≈ R$2,255 Mid-range, strong services sector Curitiba R$48.91 (Jul) ≈ R$2,200 Cooler climate, lower prices Fortaleza R$41.66 (Jul) ≈ R$1,875 Beach city at a discount Teresina R$32.51 (Aug) ≈ R$1,465 Cheapest capital in the index

Rio de Janeiro deserves a note of its own. Advertised asking rents in the city rose 11.04 percent in the first eight months of 2026 (FipeZAP), and FipeZAP-based market surveys put asking prices in the expat-sought South Zone neighborhoods around R$55 per square meter. Prime districts such as Leblon and Ipanema sit far above the city average; outlying zones sit far below it.

Two budget lines catch newcomers. First, most apartment buildings charge a monthly condominium fee (condomínio) for security and shared facilities; market practice adds roughly 20 to 50 percent on top of the base rent, so ask before you sign. Second, these tables describe the formal market. Millions of Brazilians live in favelas, a parallel housing system with its own economics — our explainer What Is a Favela? Brazil 2026 covers how that market actually works.

Food: The Basic Basket, City by City

The most grounded food-cost measure in Brazil is the cesta básica, the basic food basket that the inter-union research body Dieese prices monthly with the national supply company Conab. It contains the 13 staple items defined by law to feed one adult for one month. In June 2026, São Paulo posted the most expensive basket in the country at R$965.47, followed by Cuiabá (R$937.93), Rio de Janeiro (R$920.94) and Florianópolis (R$918.42). The cheapest baskets were in the North and Northeast: Aracaju at R$630.40, São Luís at R$654.73.

July brought relief: the basket got cheaper in 26 of the 27 state capitals. São Paulo fell to R$915.01 and Rio to R$855.37, a monthly drop of 7.12 percent. The honest counterpoint sits in the 12-month column: carioca beans cost 43.83 percent more than a year earlier, whole milk 13.53 percent more, and first-grade beef 12.67 percent more. Tomatoes, rice, coffee, sugar, butter and soybean oil got cheaper over the same period. Brazilians argue about food prices for a reason — the direction depends on which shelf you are looking at.

Eating out stays affordable by rich-country standards. Crowd-sourced Numbeo data from mid-2026 put a three-course mid-range meal for two at about US$38–48 (R$195–250) in São Paulo and Rio, and less in the Northeast. A per-kilo lunch buffet, the everyday Brazilian institution, costs less still.

Transport, Utilities and Connectivity

City bus fares for 2026: São Paulo R$5.30 (metro and commuter rail R$5.40, since 6 January), Rio de Janeiro R$5.00 for bus, BRT and light rail (since 4 January), Belo Horizonte R$6.25, Fortaleza R$5.40, Florianópolis R$6.20 on the citizen card. Rio’s metro holds the country’s highest single fare at R$7.90, unchanged this year; the SuperVia suburban train stayed frozen at R$7.60. A commuter making 44 single trips a month spends R$220–275.

For an average apartment, basic utilities (electricity, water, garbage) run about US$80 per month, broadband internet about US$20, and a mobile plan about US$13 — all crowd-sourced Numbeo estimates from mid-2026, so treat them as orientation, not tariffs. Electricity is the volatile line: air conditioning in the coastal summer pushes bills up, and Brazil’s power tariffs have outrun inflation for two decades, as our long-read on Brazil’s 401 percent electricity price rise over 20 years documents.

Three Example Monthly Budgets, One Person Each

Monthly line São Paulo Rio de Janeiro Florianópolis Rent, 45 m² one-bed (FipeZAP average) R$2,940 R$2,475 R$2,740 Food (Dieese basket + eating out) R$1,190 R$1,110 R$1,170 Transport (44 single rides) R$233 R$220 R$273 Utilities, internet, mobile R$583 R$583 R$583 Total (US$ at PTAX 18 Sep 2026) R$4,946 (≈US$959) R$4,388 (≈US$851) R$4,766 (≈US$924)

How we built these budgets: rent = the city’s FipeZAP advertised average per square meter times 45 m² (Rio: R$55/m² from FipeZAP-based market surveys of expat areas); food = the city’s Dieese basket plus 30 percent for meals out; transport = 44 single fares; utilities, internet and mobile = Numbeo mid-2026 estimates (US$113) converted at R$5.16. Condominium fees, health insurance and leisure are not included — add them for your own plan.

The Honest Downsides

Brazil is cheap for people who earn abroad, but it is not cheap everywhere, and it is not cheap for everything. Imported electronics, cars and branded goods carry a heavy tax stack and routinely cost far more than in the US or Europe. Private health insurance, which most expats choose on top of the free public system, gets expensive with age and varies widely by insurer. And in the big cities, security is a real budget line: buildings with doormen and gated parking cost more, and many residents price that in without thinking about it.

Two macro trends also cut both ways right now. Rents are climbing more than twice as fast as inflation (FipeZAP +9.16 percent over 12 months against IPCA +4.22 percent in August), so housing costs are eating a bigger share of budgets each year. And the strong real — up about 6 percent against the dollar in 2026 — quietly shrinks the purchasing power of dollar and euro incomes. The long view helps: consumer inflation of 4.22 percent is calm by Brazilian standards (2024 closed at 4.83 percent, and the country has lived through far worse), and a strong currency is a phase of the cycle, not a permanent state. Budget in reais, not in the exchange rate of the month you arrive.

What We Could Not Confirm

Neighborhood-level rents: FipeZAP publishes city averages, not district tables, and real asking prices vary sharply within cities. A single official price for private health plans does not exist — the regulator ANS approves annual adjustments but each insurer sets its own tariffs by age band. And the Numbeo figures used for utilities, meals and phone plans are crowd-sourced estimates, which is why they appear here only as secondary reference points, never as the backbone of a number.

Related Reading

→ IGP-M Second Preview Jumps 1.47% and Lifts Brazil Rent Adjustments

→ Brazil’s Electricity Bills Rose 401% in 20 Years — Far Above Inflation

→ What Is a Favela? Brazil 2026

→ Brazil Population Reaches 214 Million in 2026

→ Brazil News and Analysis

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Brazil expensive to live in for foreigners?

Not by rich-country standards. Numbeo’s June 2026 index places Brazil 125th of 151 countries for cost of living, and its crowd-sourced data put everyday costs roughly half of US levels. The exception is the premium housing market of São Paulo, Rio and Florianópolis, where rents behave like a separate economy.

How much money do I need per month to live in Brazil?

A single person renting a one-bedroom apartment in the big cities needs about R$3,900–5,000 per month (US$755–970). Outside the premium districts of São Paulo and Rio, US$1,500 per month (≈R$7,740) covers a comfortable life including leisure, and smaller capitals in the North and Northeast cost less still.

What is the cheapest major city in Brazil?

Among the state capitals tracked by FipeZAP, Teresina had the lowest advertised rent in August 2026 at R$32.51 per square meter, with Campo Grande and Aracaju also near the bottom. The cheapest basic food baskets are in the Northeast: Aracaju posted R$630.40 in June 2026 (Dieese).

Is Rio de Janeiro or São Paulo more expensive?

São Paulo, on most measures. It has the country’s highest advertised rents (R$65.36/m², August 2026) and its most expensive basic food basket (R$915 in July). Rio runs about 10 percent cheaper in our single-person budget (≈R$4,390 against ≈R$4,950), though its metro fare of R$7.90 is the highest in Brazil.

Does the exchange rate change the answer for foreigners?

Yes, materially. The real has gained about 6 percent against the US dollar in 2026, so a dollar income buys fewer reais than it did in January. At the PTAX of 18 September 2026 (US$1 = R$5.1575), a US$2,000 monthly income converts to about R$10,315 — against roughly R$11,000 at the end of 2025.

Can I live in Brazil on US$1,500 a month?

In most of the country, yes — that is about R$7,740 at the September 2026 rate, well above our big-city single budget. It is also the monthly income floor for Brazil’s digital nomad visa. In São Paulo’s or Rio’s premium districts, the same amount requires compromise on location or apartment size.

Is healthcare free in Brazil?

The public system, SUS, is free at the point of service for everyone in the country, including foreign residents. Most expats add a private plan for faster access and wider choice; prices vary by age and insurer, and no single official tariff exists.

World.title: Sacsayhuamán Graffiti Cleaned Off Rock as Peru Vows Complaint
World.content:
Peru · Heritage

Key Facts — What happened Two names were painted in red and pink on a carved rock inside the Saqsaywaman Archaeological Park above Cusco.

— Where exactly At Lanlacuyoq, a site inside the Saqsaywaman park above Cusco, and not on the famous zig-zag megalithic ramparts.

— Who found it The park’s own surveillance staff; Peru’s Ministry of Culture made the case public on 18 September 2026.

— The catch No one has been identified or detained, and the ministry has said only that it will file a complaint.

— What the law allows Attacks on pre-Hispanic archaeological monuments carry three to six years in prison plus a day-fine, Andina reports.

— Cleaning the rock The Cusco culture directorate says the pigment was removed; Andina reported on 18 September 2026 that cleaning had begun.

Two names in red and pink paint on a carved rock above Cusco have prompted Peru’s Ministry of Culture to announce a criminal complaint. Its Cusco office says the pigment has been removed.

The Plaza de Armas in Cusco, the city below the Sacsayhuaman site (Photo: Rio Times media library)

Sacsayhuamán graffiti has struck one of the best-known Inca sites in Peru. Two names were painted in red and pink on a carved rock above the city of Cusco.

Peru’s Ministry of Culture made the case public on 18 September 2026. Its office in Cusco said specialists had removed the pigment.

No one has been identified or detained. The ministry said it would lodge a formal complaint to find whoever was responsible.

What Sacsayhuamán is

Saqsaywaman, written Sacsayhuamán in most English guidebooks, stands on the heights above Cusco in the southern Peruvian Andes. It was an Inca ceremonial and military complex.

Construction began under Pachakuteq, the ninth Inca ruler. Work continued under Topa Inka Yupanqui, Huayna Qhapaq and Huascar Inka, according to the Cusco culture directorate.

All of that is pre-Hispanic, meaning it was built before the Spanish reached the Andes. The site is registered as national cultural heritage of Peru.

Its most famous feature is a line of zig-zag megalithic ramparts. These are defensive walls assembled from stone blocks of enormous size, and they are what the site is known for.

The park is much bigger than those walls. It covers close to 3,000 hectares and contains 96 archaeological sites, the directorate says.

Those sites include Q’enqo, Tambomachay, Kallachaca and Patallaqta. The monumental zone holds the Baluartes, Muyuqmarca, El Rodadero and Chinkana.

The rock that was painted

The Sacsayhuamán graffiti was not sprayed on the famous ramparts. It was found at Lanlacuyoq, a separate site within the same park.

The target was a carved limestone rock, not a built structure. Two names were painted on its surface in red and pink pigment.

Further inscriptions on the middle and lower parts of the rock were illegible. That account comes from the ministry’s own notice and from the broadcaster RPP.

The damage was spotted by the park’s own surveillance personnel. Neither the ministry nor the outlets covering it have said when the paint was applied.

Colonial arcades in central Cusco, in an undated archive photograph (Photo: Rio Times media library)

How the pigment came off

The Sacsayhuamán graffiti was taken off the stone by specialists from the directorate’s physical-chemical laboratory. They used specialised materials and tools so the rock’s original surface was not altered.

That account comes from the Cusco directorate, whose notice describes the work as completed. The state news agency Andina described the cleaning as under way on 18 September 2026.

No figure has been published for the cost of the cleaning. Nor has the ministry said whether any permanent mark remains on the rock.

Who looks after the park

The complex is managed by the Ministry of Culture through its Decentralised Directorate of Culture in Cusco. That office, known by its Spanish initials DDC, handled the Sacsayhuamán graffiti case.

Francisco Solís, an archaeologist, directs the Saqsaywaman National Archaeological Park. He appealed to residents of Cusco and to visitors to help protect the heritage and avoid such attacks.

The directorate said it would reinforce surveillance at archaeological sites across the region. It added that protection, conservation and monitoring of national heritage would continue.

Heritage status came through a national directoral resolution in 2006, with the park boundaries fixed in 2011. The park perimeter runs to just over 62 kilometres.

The site sits on the edge of Cusco, a city placed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1983. That inscription names Qoricancha, Aqllahuasi, Sunturcancha and Kusicancha, not Sacsayhuamán.

What Peruvian law provides

Peru’s Penal Code gathers crimes against cultural heritage in Title VIII of its second book. The legal publisher LP Derecho places them in articles 226 to 231.

Attacking a pre-Hispanic archaeological monument carries three to six years in prison. It also carries a day-fine of 120 to 365 days, the state news agency Andina reported.

A day-fine is counted in days of the offender’s income rather than as a fixed sum. The amount therefore varies with the person convicted.

Inducing or organising such an act carries three to eight years plus a day-fine, according to Andina. The code sets separate offences for damaging, altering or exporting cultural property.

Which of those provisions would apply to paint on a rock has not been stated. Neither the ministry nor the Cusco directorate has named an article.

No charge has been brought over the Sacsayhuamán graffiti. The ministry has said only that it will lodge a complaint so the case can be investigated.

Earlier cases in Cusco

The Sacsayhuamán graffiti is not the first such case in the region. Infobae published a round-up on 11 July 2026 of earlier vandalism in Cusco.

That piece set out earlier cases in which people were detained and prosecuted over damage to Inca walls. Infobae also reported a separate case earlier this year.

Vandal paint on the ceremonial zone of the Cheqtaqaqa huaca was reported in March 2026. A huaca is an Andean sacred place or shrine.

That record is the backdrop to the directorate’s promise of tighter surveillance.

What it means for visitors

The Sacsayhuamán graffiti has brought a promise of tighter surveillance at archaeological sites across the region. The rock has been cleaned, the directorate says, and the park stays under Ministry of Culture management.

For foreign travellers the other point is the legal exposure. Peru’s Penal Code punishes attacks on pre-Hispanic monuments with prison terms.

More: Peru coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly was damaged at Sacsayhuamán?

A carved limestone rock at Lanlacuyoq, a site inside the Saqsaywaman Archaeological Park above Cusco. Two names were painted on its surface in red and pink pigment, with further illegible inscriptions on the middle and lower sections. The Ministry of Culture’s own notice and the broadcaster RPP both describe the object as a carved rock.

Were the famous zig-zag walls hit?

No. The Sacsayhuamán graffiti was found at Lanlacuyoq, a separate site within the park, not on the megalithic ramparts that most photographs show. The park covers close to 3,000 hectares and takes in dozens of separate sites, among them Q’enqo, Tambomachay, Kallachaca and Patallaqta.

Has anyone been arrested?

No one has been identified or detained. The Decentralised Directorate of Culture in Cusco said it would lodge a formal complaint so those responsible could be identified and investigated, and that it would reinforce surveillance at archaeological sites across the region. No charge has been announced.

Is Sacsayhuamán a UNESCO World Heritage site?

It is registered as national cultural heritage of Peru, and it sits on the edge of Cusco, a city inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1983. The text of that inscription names Qoricancha, Aqllahuasi, Sunturcancha and Kusicancha, and does not mention Sacsayhuamán.

Sources: The Cusco culture directorate on the cleaning of the painted rock, RPP on the planned criminal complaint, El Popular on the red and pink paint, The Cusco culture directorate on the park and its 96 sites, LP Derecho on the Penal Code heritage offences, Andina on the prison terms and day-fines, UNESCO on the inscribed City of Cuzco, Infobae on earlier Cusco vandalism cases, Infobae on the Cheqtaqaqa huaca

World.title: Colombia’s President Rules Out ELN Hostage Exchange
World.content:
Colombia · Security

Key Facts — What happened President Abelardo De la Espriella rejected a Colombia ELN hostage exchange on 17 September 2026, the same day it was raised.

— Who is being held Three DIJIN police officers and one civilian, taken on the Ocaña-Cúcuta road in Norte de Santander on 17 August 2026.

— The catch The ELN has not published what it wants in return, and its exchange language was conditional rather than a formal offer.

— Why it matters InSight Crime calls the ELN the last remaining guerrilla insurgency in Colombia, after 62 years of continuous armed activity.

— Where talks stand De la Espriella ended all dialogue with the ELN on 11 September 2026, calling the process a false peace.

— The military answer With the rejection on 17 September 2026 he ordered military and police operations against the group to be intensified.

Colombia’s new president has refused to swap prisoners for three police officers and a civilian seized in August. The peace talks that might once have handled this no longer exist.

Colombia’s armed forces. The government has ruled out an exchange with the ELN (Photo: Rio Times media library)
