World.title: Shakira returns to Spain in fire, tears and 'Waka Waka'
World.content:
At 20:49 on Saturday 18 September, Spanish time, Shakira stepped onto the stage of the Madrid stadium that bears her name. The setlist of 25 songs spread over two hours opened with 'La fuerte', her collaboration with Bizarrap from her latest album, and continued with 'Girl like me' and a medley of 'Las de la intuición' and 'Estoy aquí', her first international hit.

 

"Good evening, Madrid, I can't believe I'm here", the artist said after the first few songs, before referring, without mincing her words, to her private life: "You'll be thinking, the face I left with and the face I've come back with." She added that "there is nothing like a she-wolf being reunited with her pack".

To the reggaeton beat of her latest work came 'Te felicito' and 'TDG', with Rauw Alejandro and Karol G respectively, as well as 'Don't Bother' and 'Can't Remember to Forget You', her collaboration with Rihanna.

Amid costume changes and images of water and fire projected onto the screen, the set also included 'Copa vacía', 'La bicicleta' and 'La tortura', along with 'Hips don't lie' and 'Chantaje', the latter coinciding with the end of the concert's first hour.

The second half opened with 'Loca' and a personal confession from the singer: "When a family breaks apart, as mine did, you feel as if you have lost your compass, until you realise that you can get through it and start to see single life as an opportunity." Those words were followed by 'Soltera', performed beneath a giant S on stage.

Songs such as 'Ojos así', 'Pies descalzos' and 'Antología' revisited her earliest years as an artist. "The most important years of my life I lived here, in Spain. It was here that I became a mother. You saw me arrive, fall, get back up and return. Thank you for walking with me for more than 30 years", she told the audience.

Near the end, 'Waka, waka' rang out, now also turned into an anthem for the 2026 World Cup, and the concert closed with 'BZRP Music Sessions #53', amid confetti and fireworks.

Macondo Park, a temporary city next to the concert

The concert venue, named Macondo Park in tribute to the town invented by Gabriel García Márquez in 'One Hundred Years of Solitude', opened its doors this Friday at around 17:00, albeit with an hour and a half delay. The space, carpeted with coloured artificial grass, comprises eight pavilions dedicated to different facets of Hispano-American culture under the Es Latina project.

Before Shakira's performance, Guitarricadelafuente played on one of the venue's stages, alongside Maro, Virtual Diva and Santos Bravos, who all declared themselves admirers of the Colombian star.

The album that lends its name to the tour, 'Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran' (2024), is the singer's twelfth studio record and, judging by its lyrics, deals with her break-up with former footballer Gerard Piqué. Macondo Park will close its doors on 11 October, after the last of the 12 concerts scheduled in Madrid.

World.title: Ed Sheeran set to resume tour after Macklemore was controversially dropped for making pro-Palestine comments
World.content:
Ed Sheeran is set to resume his tour on Saturday, possibly solo, after all his supporting acts withdrew in solidarity with opening-act Macklemore, who was dropped after making pro-Palestinian comments on-stage.

 

It remains to be seen how Sheeran will handle the performance at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field given the departure of his opening acts and supporting band.

Sheeran has performed much of his Loop Tour concerts solo, but he had been joined for several songs at each stop by the Irish folk band Beoga. Macklemore, Sheeran’s original US opener, had been replaced by Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe before they backed out.

Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year before he too dropped out earlier this week.

Sheeran has not said anything publicly since losing the artists' support. As of Friday, tickets were still available for Saturday's show, and his website did not list any replacement acts. A coalition of pro-Palestinian organisations plan to protest outside the show on Saturday afternoon.

The show comes after a tumultuous week that opened with Macklemore being dropped in response to exclaiming “Free Palestine” during a 5 September show in New Jersey.

Side-by-Side, American Rapper 'Macklemore' and English singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran at the premiere of the film "F1 The Movie" in London on June 23, 2025 AP Photo/undefined/AP Photo/undefined

Sheeran has said he was not responsible for the decision, which came at the urging of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft. His company owns a stadium where Sheeran’s tour was scheduled to play on Friday. Within hours of Sheeran's statement Tuesday, his supporting acts withdrew.

Macklemore said on Wednesday he is donating $1 million (€871m) to support Palestinian relief efforts and called on Kraft to match the gift, a spokesperson for Kraft has said the billionaire and Sheeran have each agreed to donate $2 million (€1.74m) but have not specified where the money will be directed.

Sheeran’s Loop Tour was the highest-grossing in the world, with an average box office gross of over $7 million (€6m) per city, Pollstar said in May. Through the end of 2025, Sheeran was the third-highest earning concert act since 2021.

Sheeran has said the tour promoter was ultimately responsible for the decision to drop Macklemore.

The Grammy winner was adamant in his Tuesday statement that he wouldn't be drawn into discussion of the war in Gaza, arguing that his fans don’t come to his shows to hear about these issues.

He also said he “spoke with the venues at length all week to try to build a bridge” before Macklemore was dropped. He insisted he would never willingly let down his fans or abandon the touring crew and others who rely on him to make a living.

While promoters and venues wield great power over concert tours, experts say an artist of Sheeran's magnitude generally has the final say about what happens concerning the shows.

World.title: Sweeping raids leave Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community fearing what comes next
World.content:
Turkey has jailed dozens of people pending trial as a sweeping crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups widens, prompting international condemnation and protests outside Turkish embassies on Friday.

Advertising

By Thursday, courts in several provinces had jailed at least 82 people following raids on LGBTQI+ organisations, clubs, cafes and homes.

The cases include LGBTQI+ activists and members of rights groups as well as people accused of prostitution, drug offences and other crimes. Not everyone jailed is accused of gay rights advocacy.

The United Nations human rights office has called on Turkey to uphold human rights without discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity and to immediately release anyone arbitrarily detained.

Protests were held outside Turkish embassies in cities including Paris, Brussels, London, Oslo and Washington on Friday.

The crackdown began on Saturday, when police carried out coordinated raids targeting nine LGBTQI+ organisations. Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said legal action was being taken against 162 people, nine associations and 13 businesses in 15 provinces.

Turkey arrests dozens in ongoing crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups

Mass detentions

The raids prompted protests across Turkey, including outside Istanbul’s main courthouse on Tuesday. Police broke up the demonstration and detained more than 100 people, including journalists. They were later released.

“I am here because I want to say that LGBTQ+ friends are not alone in this country,” said Ayse, a protester who asked to be identified only by her first name.

“I want to support them and to stay in solidarity with them, which is not easy these days in Turkey, but they are not alone, and we are not alone, and we will be here until the end.”

Opposition DEM Party parliamentarian Ozgul Saki remained at the protest, protected from arrest by parliamentary immunity.

“This oppression against LGBTQ+ people is an attempt to compress society into a single type; to build an Islamist, Turkish, racist society,” Saki said. “Those who are here say, 'No! Society will live equally, freely and honourably with all its diversity,' and that's why they were all detained.”

The operations have been defended by Gurlek, from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s conservative Justice and Development Party (AKP).

“No criminal organisation, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated,” Gurlek posted on social media.

Among the organisations affected was Istanbul-based SPoD, which provides psychological support to LGBTQI+ people.

“As a community, we were expecting that such an operation would come one day. But we didn't imagine it as that violent, that much unlawful,” said a SPoD representative who asked to remain anonymous.

“They raided our office; I think four or five have been detained, and they are still in custody. What will happen to the LGBTQ+ community after this day? Like they can implement a kind of informal criminalisation upon our community, so my personal feeling is an immense feeling of uncertainty.”

Surge in anti-LGBTQ disinformation targets Pride in Europe

Obscenity allegations

Homosexuality has been legal since the foundation of the Turkish republic in 1923, but authorities are using an obscenity law as part of the crackdown.

“All of our board members are detained due to the allegations of obscenity,” said Yildiz Tar of Ankara-based KAOS GL, Turkey’s leading LGBTQI+ news portal.

“They look into our social media account, and our news articles are seen as obscene because, for example, there is one picture of two women kissing, and they see that it's obscene. So that is why they have been detained.”

The measures resemble actions taken against LGBTQI+ communities in Russia and Egypt, Tar said.

“It's very similar to Russia and Egypt, like the things they want to do is very similar to anti-gay propaganda laws, and there were huge operations, and people got detained,” Tar said.

“So it's very similar to both countries. And actually, like the Turkish government is very fond of Putin's way of dealing things.”

The crackdown has also drawn condemnation from the European Union and international human rights groups.

“It's an attempt to show LGBTQ+ people as immoral and against the family. But in fact, none of this does anything to protect the family at all,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb, who leads Human Rights Watch’s Turkey office.

“It's all about discrediting and stigmatizing people for their sexual orientation or gender identity.”

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Wider crackdown

The arrests form part of a broader crackdown on people regarded as opposing the government, Sinclair-Webb said.

“This operation should be set in the context of a very wide crackdown on anybody who is regarded as oppositional to the government, whether in terms of being politically or in terms of their lifestyle or their outlook… there is a general attempt by the government to impose as well as, you know, ideological conformity on people, lifestyle,” Sinclair-Webb said.

President Erdogan routinely refers to LGBTQI+ people as perverts and has stepped up his rhetoric ahead of much-rumoured early elections. Gurlek has called on prosecutors to increase investigations into the LGBTQI+ community, fuelling fears of further arrests.

The crackdown has also prompted condemnation across Turkish civil society, with trade unions, doctors’ associations and opposition parties voicing their opposition.

For Tar, that support offers some hope amid fears over what could follow for Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community.

“If this attack won't be stopped, it would mean a lot of maltreatment and torture; it can also cause hate crimes; it incites hatred inside the country too,” Tar said. “And it will mean that you cannot be openly queer; if they succeed in their operation, that is a really, really hellish scenario.”

World.title: A doubleheader feast!
World.content:
This week on The Sound Kitchen it’s a doubleheader: you’ll hear the answers to TWO quiz questions, as well as TWO “Listener's Corner" with Paul Myers, and of course, Erwan Rome’s “Music from Erwan”. So sit down, relax, and join the banquet! Just click the “play” button above to join the feast.

Advertising

Hello everyone!

As noted on the show, I am retiring on 1 October. Unfortunately, The Sound Kitchen is retiring too – I will not be replaced.

We’ve had a great time together all these years, haven’t we?

Click here to listen to past Sound Kitchen podcasts.

I know you will all stay loyal to RFI English – our service has so much to offer. We’re small, but my colleagues are firebrands!

For example, we have wonderful podcasts: Spotlight on France, with journalists Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas; Melissa Chemam’s insightful Spotlight on Africa, and our International Report, usually sent to us by one of our foreign correspondents. We also have an award-winning bilingual series – an old-time radio show, with actors (!) – to help you learn French, called Les voisins du 12 bis.

Remember, podcasts are radio, too! As you see, sound is still quite present in the RFI English service. Please keep checking our website for updates on the latest from our team of journalists. You never know what we’ll surprise you with!

To listen to our podcasts from your PC, go to our website; you’ll see “Podcasts” at the top of the page. You can either listen directly or subscribe and receive them directly on your mobile phone.

And don’t forget, in addition to our audio bilingual series, you can also learn French through our website “Le Français facile avec rfi”. In addition to online lessons, there are news broadcasts in slow, simple French, with exercises to practice what you’ve heard.

Go to their website and get started! At the top of the page, click on “Test level”, and you’ll be advised on the best-suited activities for your level, according to your score.

Do not give up! As Lidwien van Dixhoorn, the head of the “Le Français facile” service, told me: “Bathe your ears in the sound of the language, and eventually, you’ll get it”. She should know – Lidwien is Dutch and came to France hardly able to say “bonjour,” and now she heads this key international award-winning RFI department – so stick with it!

For the quiz on 24 January: I asked you a question about the Africa Cup of Nations, and an article sent to us by Paul Myers, who was there. You were to re-read his article “Senegal outwit Morocco to claim 2025 Africa Cup of Nations”, and send in the answer to this question: At the 2026 World Cup, which took place in the United States, Mexico, and Canada in June, in which group did Morocco play, and in which group did Senegal play?

The answer is, to quote Paul’s article: “Morocco will play in Group C against Brazil, Scotland and Haiti.

Senegal will feature in Group I with France, Norway, and the team that emerges from the intercontinental play-off in March.”

In addition to the quiz question, there was the bonus question: “What is your favorite day of the year? Why? What is it about that day that makes it your favorite?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Dipita Chakrabarty from New Delhi, India. Dipita is also the bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners this week are Muhammed Naved, a member of the International DX Radio Listeners Club in West Bengal, India; Muhammad Abdullah, a member of the RFI Online Visitors Club in Sahiwal, Pakistan; RFI Listeners Club member Rodrigo Hunrichse from Bio-Bio, Chile, and last but not least, RFI English listener Sakila Musarrt from Chapainawabganj in Bangladesh.

Congratulations winners!

For the quiz on 31 January: You were to listen to our podcast “Spotlight on France”, the brainchild of my colleagues Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas. I hope you listen to it regularly, it’s really quite good.

On their programme number 138, Alison reported on La Ménardière, an alternative living arrangement for seniors in the village of Bérat, close to the southern French town of Toulouse. The aim of the project is for seniors to live and grow old together, contributing to society for as long as possible, and to delay – or avoid – the moment when people are forced into institutional care.

The answers you were to send in were: How many residents can live at La Ménardière, and what is the selection process?

The answer is, to quote Alison: “La Ménardière can house up to 20 residents. The selection process to become one is rigorous. Candidates stay for trial weekends and, if they decide to join, they must then complete a six-month probation period.”

The bonus question you answered that week – suggested by Murshida Parvin Lata, the co-chairman of the Sonali Badhan Female Listeners Club in Bogura, Bangladesh – was: “Which daytime temperature do you prefer: cold or hot? Why?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Father Steven Wara, who lives and serves in the Cistercian Abbey in Bamenda, Cameroon. Father Steve is also the winner of this week’s bonus question.

There’s long-standing RFI Listeners Club member Zenon Teles, who is also the president of the Christian – Marxist – Leninist – Maoist Association of Listening DX-ERs in Goa, India, as well as another faithful Sound Kitchen listener – and club member – Radhakrishna Pillai from Kerala State, also in India.

Moving over to Bangladesh, Anjana Parvin – she’s the secretary of the very active Shetu RFI Listeners Club in Naogaon. And last but not the least, club member and my fellow dinosaur, Alan Holder, from England’s Isle of Wight.

Congratulations winners!

Here’s the music you heard on this week’s programme: “Take the A Train” by Billy Strayhorn and Duke Ellington, performed by Duke Ellington and his orchestra; the “AFCON 2025 Official Intro Theme – Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2025” by Othmane Laaouina; “What a Wonderful World” by Bob Thiele and George David Weiss, sung by Louis Armstrong; “The Cakewalk” from Children’s Corner by Claude Debussy, performed by the composer, and “Étincelles”, Op. 36, No. 6 by Moritz Moszkowski, played by Alexander Zhou.

I’ll talk to you next week, 26 September, for our final Sound Kitchen together. You’ll hear the answers to the questions about the Grammy Awards Lifetime Achievement Awards and the Benin Bronzes, as well as your responses to the bonus questions on "The Listener’s Corner" with Paul Myers, so be sure and tune in.

Until then, fare thee well!

World.title: A city at the crossroads of history: Unearthing Gaza's ancient heritage
World.content:
Before Gaza became synonymous with conflict, it was a place where merchants sold wine from local vineyards, pilgrims crossed continents, fishermen set out before dawn, and generations of families lived between sea and desert. RFI explores its deep history.

Advertising

Sitting on the coastal corridor linking Egypt, the Levant, the Arabian Peninsula and the Mediterranean, the port city has always been a strategic crossroads.

Like many places around the Mediterranean, Gaza's identity wasn't built by a single people or culture. It was shaped by generations of arrivals, departures and exchanges.

As the Mid-East Junction podcast returns from a six-year hiatus, we'll trace the city's history from the age of the Philistines until the creation of Israel in 1948.

In this first episode of season 3, a Gazan archaeologist, a historian, and a professor of contemporary Arab people shed light on Gaza’s little-known yet fascinating ancient history.

Mid-East Junction is produced by RFI's English-language service. This episode was mixed by Vincent Pora.

World.title: Thousands protest Kennedy Center demolition fears
World.content:
Protesters took part in a "Hands Around the Kennedy Center" human chain. The demonstration comes amid fears the Trump administration could tear the arts hub down.

Thousands of people have demonstrated at the Kennedy Center in Washington D.C. amid fears President Donald Trump's administration could demolish the arts hub.

Crowds of people gathered in the Foggy Bottom area of the US capital city, many carrying signs as they joined in "Hands Around the Kennedy Center."

Some of those gathered held hands and formed a human chain around the center.

Protesters waved placards reading "hands off Kennedy Center" and sang songs close to where workers removed Trump's name from the building in June following a court order.

Actor Lynda Carter, a vocal Trump critics, addressed the rally on Friday Image: Jose Luis Magana/AP Photo/picture alliance

Protesters, residents condemn move to demolish Kennedy Center

"It makes me sick to my stomach," the AFP news agency quoted Neal Racioppo, a Washington resident who runs marketing and communications for a theatre, as saying.

Trump "can't get his name on this cherished building, so he is depriving the world of what it could be."

"He does not have a right to decide that an institution, a living memorial to a past president, can be demolished," another protester told AFP.

"The Kennedy Center is vital to the arts in Washington. We need it. We need this,” said local arts community member Bud Wilkinson.

"This is not just about putting the president's name on the Kennedy Center. It's about censoring the performances and the programming," Wilkinson said.

Trump and the Kennedy Center

The Kennedy Center — inaugurated in 1971 following the assassination of US President John F. Kennedy — has been a focal point of Trump's plans for Washington since 2025.

Trump has been pushing for major renovations and claims the building was left in a severe state of disrepair by those previously in control.

Trump's handpicked Kennedy Center board voted last year to rename the institution the Trump-Kennedy Center.

In May, a judge ruled that his name was illegally added and ordered it removed.

The Kennedy Center board voted last year to rename the institution the Trump-Kennedy Center Image: Cliff Owen/AP Photo/picture alliance

What has Trump said about the Kennedy Center?

On Wednesday, Trump appeared to imply that the Kennedy Center could be torn down if his administration did not receive "recognition."

"For the Trump administration, for me to get involved and to take that on long term and to carry it or to raise money to carry it, I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition, because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close," Trump said.

"It'll end up being ripped down. It's in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape," Trump told reporters.

World.title: Oktoberfest 2026: Everything you need to know
World.content:
This year, AI will be used to manage overcrowded situations. Find all the numbers surrounding the fest — including the price of water!

On Saturday, September 19, at noon, Oktoberfest will once again open with the ceremonial tapping of the keg, during which the mayor of Munich drives a tap into the first wooden barrel of beer and calls out "O'zapft is," a Bavarian phrase that translates to "It's tapped."

His call will be followed by 12 gunshots, a signal that lets all festival tents know that they can start serving beer.

More than 6 million people are expected at the world's largest Volksfest, which runs this year through October 4.

Oktoberfest: What to know about 'the best party in Germany' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Expanded security measures to prevent overcrowding

The festival grounds are enormous: Oktoberfest takes place on Munich's Theresienwiese, a 34.5-hectare site roughly the size of 48 soccer fields.

But crowds can swell, especially on weekends — sometimes to dangerous levels.

Last year, officials had to temporarily close the entrances.

One reason is that nearly all 38 beer tents operate in two or three reservation shifts. When one group of guests leaves and the next arrives at the 14 large tents — which each accommodate several thousand people — huge numbers of visitors end up trying to enter and exit at the same time.

That's how, on one Saturday afternoon at last year's Oktoberfest, the crowds became so dense that movement temporarily came to a standstill. The crush caused some visitors to panic.

To prevent that from happening again, the city of Munich has overhauled its security plan for this year's festival.

Twenty-six new cameras, in addition to 56 police cameras, will monitor the grounds, while an AI system will analyze visitor flows and issue alerts if areas become overcrowded.

Around 300,000 people were at Oktoberfest simultaneously on the second Saturday of the festival in 2025 Image: Frank Hoermann/SVEN SIMON/picture alliance

A newly established coordination center is also intended to improve communication between security agencies and event organizers.

Organizers and police have drawn up a plan to defend against drones over the grounds, though no details have been disclosed.

In addition, 600 police officers will be deployed on site.

Oktoberfest is famous worldwide, but most visitors are local

Oktoberfest may be known around the world as an international tourist attraction, but most of its visitors don't travel very far to get there.

A study commissioned by the city of Munich last year found that the festival remains overwhelmingly regional.

Statistically speaking, two international guests sit at every 10-person table in the festival tents Image: Maryam Majd/REUTERS

In 2025, 41% of visitors came from Munich, another 25% from the surrounding area and 9% from elsewhere in the region. In all, three-quarters of Oktoberfest's roughly 6.5 million visitors came from Bavaria. Another 4% came from elsewhere in Germany.

About 21% of visitors — roughly 1.35 million people — traveled from abroad. Americans made up the largest group of international visitors, accounting for just under 20% of the total, or more than 270,000 people. Italians were next, at just over 13%.

Beer prices rise again

Cannabis is banned throughout the festival grounds.

Alcohol, on the other hand, is available in whatever quantities visitors are willing — and able — to pay for. A Mass, the traditional 1-liter mug of beer served at Oktoberfest, costs between €14.80 and €15.90 ($17-$18.25) this year, only slightly more than last year.

A liter of table water comes in at a hefty €11, although the grounds also have several free drinking water fountains.

Visitors planning to enjoy one of Oktoberfest's many rides would be wise to stay relatively sober. Tickets cost anywhere from just under €5 to €14.

Germany's traditional fairground culture was officially added to the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2026, and that tradition remains very much alive at the 191st Oktoberfest. According to organizers, about 90% of the festival's more than 130 fairground operators can trace their roots back to the 19th century.

The festival remains decidedly traditional when it comes to payment, too: Many vendors still accept cash only. Visitors caught without any can withdraw money from ATMs on the grounds.

Dirndl or lederhosen for Oktoberfest?

Then there's the question of what to wear.

Bavarians who take pride in doing things properly generally show up in local traditional dress.

Traditional garb can be seen at the annual breweries' parade Image: Felix Hörhager/dpa/picture alliance

The dirndl is the traditional dress worn by women and girls, which consists of close-fitting bodice with a low neckline, a blouse worn under the bodice, a wide high-waisted skirt and an apron.

Men wear lederhosen, the traditional leather shorts or knee-length breeches with suspenders.

For those who are not Bavarian, lederhosen and dirndls are certainly an option, but they're by no means required. Munich's event marketing department, Simply Munich, advises first-time visitors to consider renting traditional garb rather than buying it.

Be aware that locals find cheap imitations of traditional dress off-putting, as Simply Munich points out: "If you want to avoid wry looks, steer clear of Seppl hats, 'leather pants' made of cloth and garish mini plastic dirndls. With jeans and a checkered shirt, you'll definitely be more suitably dressed."

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Ed Sheeran continues US tour amid Palestinian controversy
World.content:
Pro-Palestinian protests are expected at Ed Sheeran's first gig since Macklemore was dropped from the tour. The US rapper shouted "Free Palestine" at a concert in New Jersey.

Protesters were expected to gather in Philadelphia on Saturday at Ed Sheeran's first show since US rapper Macklemore was removed from the tour for making Pro-Palestinian comments during a performance.

Sheeran, one of the best-selling musical artists of all time, has denied responsibility for dropping the US rapper from the lineup, saying the promoter made the decision.

Ed Sheeran tour drops Macklemore after Gaza speech To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why was Macklemore dropped from Sheeran's tour?

Earlier this month, while performing at the opening of Sheeran's US Loop Tour in New Jersey, Macklemore expressed pro-Palestinian sentiments.

"One of the reasons why I wanted to come on this tour was because I wanted to stand up here on stages and stadiums across America and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine,'" the rapper said on stage.

Macklemore's comments were fiercely criticized by supporters of Israel in the US and led to him being removed from the tour.

His removal sparked a backlash that saw support acts quitting and Sheeran facing a stream of criticism.

Irish folk band Beoga, Sheeran's backing act, announced it was leaving the tour. In an Instagram statement, the band said it "fully supported" Macklemore's message.

Macklemore, real name Benjamin Haggerty, was removed from the line-up over pro-Palestinian comments he made on stage Image: Jack Plunkett/Invision/AP Photo/picture alliance

Sheeran says he is 'not complicit' in Macklemore's removal

Sheeran released a statement on Tuesday laying out his apolitical stance on the matter.

"I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine. The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy," Sheeran said.

The 35-year-old British performer said, "Upcoming tour dates had communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting."

Sheeran added that American billionaire Robert Kraft, who owns Gillette Stadium near Boston where he was due to perform, was among those demanding Macklemore be cut from the tour.

"I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care," he said on Instagram on Tuesday.

"Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum," the English singer-songwriter added.

Kraft said in a statement on Monday that the decision to remove Macklemore from the tour was a result of the rapper's recent comments "and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery."

Pro-Palestinian rally planned

Local groups have planned a pro-Palestinian rally near the concert venue on Saturday afternoon.

The AFP news agency cited local police as saying there would be an "appropriate police presence" to "help ensure the safety of concertgoers, employees and neighborhood residents."

Sheeran began his tour in Auckland, New Zealand, in January and is set to wrap up in Mexico City, Mexico, in December, with shows still scheduled across North and South America.

World.title: Rebels, workers, radicals: The making of 'Red Berlin'
World.content:
Berlin has a reputation for being unruly. When Joseph Goebbels was appointed the Nazi Party's district leader in 1926, he described Berlin as "the reddest city in Europe besides Moscow." From the Tailors' Revolution of 1830 and the barricades of 1848, to the rise of a vast industrial working class later in the 19th century, revolution, protest and rebellion run deep throughout the city's history.

While the future German philosopher and revolutionary socialist Karl Marx was still in high school in the small town of Trier in Prussia's Rhine Province, Berlin was fast becoming a center of the country's labor movement. It was during the March Revolution of 1848, a failed attempt to create a democratic German nation-state, that the General Workers' Brotherhood was founded, one of the first workers' organizations to become active in Germany.

In March 1848, Berliners fought for basic freedoms and German unity Image: United Archives International/IMAGO

By the 1870s and 1880s, major industries from mechanical and railway engineering to ready-made clothing were located in the city. As the working-class population grew, this, in turn, impacted the city's political culture.

"It became more populist in a positive sense: moving away from the traditional, elitist politics of the bourgeois liberals who had long dominated Berlin, and toward the inclusion of ordinary people, since at least men were now also important voters," Axel Weipert, a historian and author of the book "Red Berlin" (2019), tells DW.

Emergence of a radical labor movement

Berlin's labor movement became increasingly radical, partly in response to heavy-handed repression under the Chancellor Otto von Bismarck. Although Bismarck created the first modern welfare state to try and undercut the rising popularity of the socialist movement, he also introduced laws banning socialist and communist organizations, newspapers and public gatherings, as well as independent trade unions.

A memorial to Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, who co-authored 'The Communist Manifesto' in 1848, still stands close to Berlin's city hall Image: Jürgen Ritter/IMAGO

After Bismarck resigned in 1890, the anti-socialist laws were repealed, and the ideas of Karl Marx and his fellow revolutionary socialist Friedrich Engels became the ideology of what Weipert describes as a "genuine mass movement" in Berlin. The Social Democratic Party (SPD), Germany's oldest political party, was formed out of a merger between the General German Workers' Association and the Social Democratic Workers' Party in 1875. Before World War I, the SPD was able to win far higher vote shares in Berlin than elsewhere in the country.

In 1914, the labor movement was seriously discredited when the SPD leadership and the trade unions decided not to oppose the war pushed by Kaiser Wilhelm II. But from 1916 onwards, Berlin became the center of mass labor strikes against the war. One of the earliest strikes was against the trial of anti-war socialist campaigner Karl Liebknecht. Together with Rosa Luxemburg and other left-wing radicals, Liebknecht founded the Spartacus League in Berlin, an underground group that later became the Communist Party of Germany (KPD).

Karl Liebknecht (left) and Rosa Luxenburg were murdered by right-wing paramilitary soldiers of the Freikorps in Berlin Image: akg-images/picture-alliance

Triggered by war-weariness, severe food shortages and economic ruin, around half a million Berlin workers joined the January Strike of 1918. Supported by the Spartacus League, the anti-war strike was led by the Revolutionary Stewards, a clandestine network of factory workers and trade unions from large munitions and metal-working factories. The same group became a core organizing force behind the overthrow of the Kaiser in Berlin on November 9, 1918.

From left-wing unity to division

In the chaotic, war-torn city gripped by violent revolution, the Spartacist Uprising of 1919 was launched to overthrow Germany's provisional government and establish a republic of workers' councils. Its violent suppression, which resulted in scores of deaths — Liebknecht and Luxemburg were both murdered by soldiers of right-wing paramilitary militias — permanently fractured the political left.

Spartacist revolutionaries armed with machine guns aimed to establish a communist state Image: Cola Images/IMAGO

As the capital of the newly founded Weimar Republic, Berlin remained a hotbed of radical politics in the interwar period. This was especially true in neighborhoods with large numbers of tenement buildings, such as Wedding, Kreuzberg and Neukölln, where thousands of factory workers lived in squalid conditions. Berlin's many large factories also created shared interests and laid the groundwork for collective action.

"Bloody May" in 1929 saw brutal attacks on illegal May Day demonstrations, which left over 30 people dead. The SPD police president of Berlin had issued a ban on all public demonstrations for May Day, which the KPD defied. In response, the police opened fire on protestors in the streets and also shot through windows in residential buildings, primarily in the working-class districts of Wedding and Neukölln.

'Bloody May' inspired the labor movement song 'Red Wedding' by Hanns Eisler and Erich Weinert Image: Atlantic Photo-Co/SVT/TT/IMAGO

During the Great Depression era, the SPD lost much of its support between 1929 and 1933, as joblessness ravaged the city. "Unemployment is critical — it meant that men were no longer attached to the SPD-led factory floor and trade union and the social bonds of these spaces and organizations," explains Pamela Swett, a historian at the University of Rhode Island. "Unmoored from the rhythm of daily life, men sought new bonds — new ways to feel self-respect and camaraderie with others." Some joined the KPD, which became known as the "Party of the Unemployed." Others joined far-right paramilitary groups such as the Nazi stormtroopers.

From student sit-ins to the housing crisis

After the Nazis took power in 1933, many of the labor movement leaders were killed or exiled. Then, in the aftermath of World War II, Berlin was divided into two separate political systems. East Berlin became the capital of the communist German Democratic Republic. Isolated from the Federal Republic of Germany, West Berlin deindustrialized, the labor movement weakened, and the SPD moved to the right.

During the Cold War, many left-leaning young men moved to West Berlin to evade military service. This intensified the student movement, the center of which was Berlin's Free University (Freie Universität). It was there, in leafy southwest Berlin, that historic sit-ins were held to protest the perceived authoritarianism of the government and the presence of former Nazi officials in positions of power. The fatal shooting of student Benno Ohnesorg by a police officer during a demonstration against the visiting Shah of Iran in 1967 radicalized a generation that led the widespread protests of 1968.

The fatal shooting of student, Benno Ohnesorg, by police during protests against the Shah of Iran's visit in 1967 radicalized a generation Image: dpa/picture alliance

In the early 1970s, a housing shortage led parts of the student movement, as well as apprentices and young migrant families, to squat in West Berlin's empty buildings.

"You have migrant laborers and young laborers participating, so this was part of working-class rebellion against capitalist housing," says Ralf Hoffrogge, a labor movement historian at Berlin's Free University.

Today, as gentrification sweeps the city, Berlin is home to the strongest and most radical tenants' movements in Germany. In a 2021 referendum, 59% of voters in the city approved the expropriation of property from private real-estate companies. Hoffrogge was part of the campaign, and his 2025 book "Loud Berlin" ("Das laute Berlin") explores how the housing crisis has become a catalyst for a "socialist renaissance" in the city.

"It's not Berlin tenants against Berlin landlords. It's tenants against global capital. I think people have started to realize these contradictions, and this is why class-based policy concepts are becoming popular again."

'Housing is not a commodity': Berlin's housing crisis and rapid gentrification have triggered new political initiatives in the city Image: IPON/IMAGO

Edited by: Brenda Haas

World.title: Oktoberfest opens as Munich mayor taps first beer keg
World.content:
Thousands of visitors streamed onto Munich's Oktoberfest grounds as the world-famous beer festival got underway. Some spent the night outside the gates to secure coveted places in the festival tents.

The 191st Munich Oktoberfest officially opened at noon on Saturday, with the city's new mayor tapping the festival's first barrel of beer.

The annual ceremony, which takes place at midday, is always an eagerly awaited event, with no beer served until it has taken place.

Relief for Munich's new mayor

Green Party politician Dominik Krause needed just two strikes of the mallet for his first ceremonial tapping before handing the first liter mug of beer to Bavarian Premier Markus Söder of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU).

Krause had practiced for the occasion with a personal tapping coach. The 36-year-old had said he hoped to open the barrel with two or three strikes. His predecessor, Dieter Reiter of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), had set a high standard by regularly opening the first barrel with two strikes.

After the tapping, Krause then presented the first liter of beer to Bavarian Premier Markus Söder of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU). It's the first time Söder has received the ceremonial drink from a Green mayor.

Cannon fire then signalled that beer may be served throughout the festival grounds.

Revelers race to grab drinking spots

Crowds had earlier rushed onto the Oktoberfest grounds in the southern German city of Munich shortly after the gates opened at 9 a.m on Saturday.

Some visitors ran toward the beer tents to claim the best seats after waiting for several hours. Members of the first group in line said they had arrived at 7 p.m. on Friday with camping chairs, sleeping bags and emergency blankets.

Organizers briefly held back sections of the crowd at the entrance, allowing people onto the grounds in stages and preventing a more concentrated rush.

How big is Oktoberfest?

More than 6 million people are expected to attend the 191st Oktoberfest, which runs for 16 days until October 4.

The festival, known locally as the Wiesn, features beer tents, fairground rides, traditional Bavarian food and live music.

Opening day was expected to bring blue skies and temperatures of up to 24 degrees Celsius (75 degrees Fahrenheit).

Oktoberfest: What to know about 'the best party in Germany' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How much is an Oktoberfest beer?

A 1-liter (1.8-pint) beer costs between €14.80 and €15.90 ($17–$18.27) this year.

The average price has risen by 2.38% compared with last year to €15.61.

An analysis found that the average price has almost quintupled since 1985, when a liter of beer cost about 6.25 deutschmarks — equivalent to €3.20 at the fixed conversion rate. Consumer prices have risen by about 120% over the same period.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: US court rejects Trump policy on third-country deportations
World.content:
The Trump administration has deported more than 25,000 people to countries other than their own. Now a federal appeals court has put the brakes on the policy.

A US federal appeals court has largely upheld a ruling blocking the Trump administration from rapidly deporting migrants to third countries without giving them a meaningful chance to raise safety concerns.

The three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit in Boston said Friday that migrants must receive effective notice of their intended destination and an opportunity to challenge removal if they fear persecution or torture there.

What did the court say about the DHS policy?

The case challenges a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) policy allowing migrants with final deportation orders to be sent to countries other than their own, provided authorities have diplomatic assurances they will not face persecution or torture.

The court said the policy could deny protections to migrants sent to unfamiliar countries without notice.

The Trump administration is expected to appeal the ruling to the Supreme Court.

DHS General Counsel James Percival said on X that the policy remains in force because Friday's ruling has not yet taken effect.

"If you claim fear in your home country, DHS has the right to send you elsewhere," Percival wrote.

The order comes as two men deported by the US to Equatorial Guinea were arbitrarily detained, with police covering their heads with bags, beating them and holding them at gunpoint in a hotel turned into a detention center, the AP reported.

More than 25,000 deported to third countries

Since US President Donald Trump returned to office, his administration has sent more than 25,000 migrants to at least 29 third countries, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a project run by Refugees International and Human Rights First.

Some of the third countries immigrants are being deported to are:

South Sudan

Eswatini

Uganda

Equatorial Guinea

Liberia

Central African Republic

The third-country deals have drawn criticism from human rights groups, as several participating nations have notoriously repressive governments and poor human rights records.

World.title: India news: British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal granted bail after 9 years in detention
World.content:
Skip next section More uncertainty for Indian workers as Trump extends $100,000 H-1B visa fee

09/19/2026 September 19, 2026 More uncertainty for Indian workers as Trump extends $100,000 H-1B visa fee

Indians make up the largest share of people on the H-1B visa program Image: ANI News/IMAGO

US President Donald Trump has extended the $100,000 fee on H-1B visa petitions through September 2027, the White House has said — a move that will be strongly felt in India, the largest source of H-1B recipients.

The extension, announced on Friday, keeps a policy first introduced in September 2025 in place. It excludes visa renewals and student visa holders transitioning to H-1B status.

Trump also signed a proclamation directing tighter scrutiny of applications, instructing agencies to weigh employers' recent layoffs of American workers when reviewing petitions.

The policy remains under legal challenge, with an appeals court reviewing a June ruling that found the fee unlawful.

The stakes are high for India: USCIS data for fiscal year 2025 showed Indian nationals accounted for 69.9% of approved H-1B petitions, far ahead of China's 12.1%.

When the fee first launched last year, it caused panic among Indian travelers, including passengers who deboarded a Delhi-bound flight fearing they'd be barred from returning.

Opposition Congress party leader Pawan Khera criticized the extension on social media, warning it would make it "harder for Indian students to enter the US workforce" and could drive a "talent drain" toward the UK, Canada and Australia.

He also targeted Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his perceived camaraderie with Trump, adding: "Modi bent over backwards to appease Trump. Trump got the appeasement. India took the humiliation and the hit."

World.title: Russia votes for new parliament in controlled elections
World.content:
Russia is holding its first State Duma election since invading Ukraine, with voting also imposed in occupied Ukrainian regions. President Vladimir Putin's party is expected to dominate the tightly controlled contest.

Russians were casting their ballots on Saturday to elect a new lower house of parliament, on the second day of a round of voting that President Vladimir Putin's party is all but guaranteed to win.

It is Russia's first parliamentary election since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Parties that support Putin's war in Ukraine are the only ones registered to run, and the opposition is barred from taking part.

Russia's opposition party, Yabloko, was struck from the party list last month Image: Pavel Bednyakov/AP Photo/picture alliance

Despite expectations of an easy win for Putin, the elections are widely being viewed as a referendum on the continuation of his military campaign — now in its fifth year.

The polls are taking place at a time when public sentiment is starting to shift against the war over rising prices, internet crackdowns, fuel shortages and rumors of another mobilization drive following the elections.

More than 110 million Russians are eligible to vote for 450 members of the lower house of the Russian Parliament, known as the State Duma.

Putin's United Russia party currently controls over two-thirds of the seats and is expected to retain its dominance, allowing it to continue the military campaign despite ebbing public support.

Voting held in occupied Ukrainian regions

For the first time in a Russian parliamentary election, Moscow is conducting voting in occupied parts of the Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson.

Russia claimed to annex the four regions in September 2022, although it does not fully control any of them. The annexations are not internationally recognized.

Russian authorities say the occupied territories have more than 3.5 million eligible voters. Balloting began there and in some Russian border areas in late August, earlier than elsewhere, with officials citing security concerns.

Ukraine has strongly condemned the voting in occupied eastern areas Image: Dmitry Yagodkin/TASS/picture alliance

Footage from a polling station in occupied Donetsk showed voters casting ballots while an armed Russian soldier stood nearby.

Ukrainian officials condemned the voting as illegal and urged foreign governments and international organizations not to recognize either the election or its results.

Kyiv also warned that helping organize the vote could result in criminal prosecution.

Edited by: Natalie Muller and Karl Sexton

World.title: La Fiscalía investiga abusos y vejaciones en los centros de menores de Ceuta
World.content:
A las ocho de la noche del miércoles, el campo de fútbol del barrio ceutí de El Príncipe enciende las luces para iluminar a los que aún apuran el partido. También a un pequeño círculo de chicas que habla junto a las gradas, apretadas, muy serias. De pronto, una joven rebasa la verja de entrada corriendo en dirección a ellas, llega llorando, tropezándose. Las otras salen a su encuentro y chillan: “¿Cómo te has escapado?”, se abrazan, se le unen en el llanto. Ella se ha fugado de uno de los centros de menores que la ciudad autónoma ha habilitado en Ceuta para alojar a los menores no acompañados que cruzaron a finales de julio. Tiene 17 años y es la cuarta chica en este campo en escaparse, la séptima en total. Antes de la medianoche se unirá Nadia, la octava. Sus nombres han sido cambiados para proteger su identidad.

Todas estas migrantes, de origen marroquí, fueron alojadas en los centros de menores a inicios de septiembre tras más de un mes viviendo en los campos informales levantados con la solidaridad de los vecinos, como este de El Príncipe o el de Sidi Embarek, aún en funcionamiento. Se las reubicó en dos instalaciones gestionadas por dos entidades distintas (Samu y Engloba), ubicadas una al lado de la otra, dentro del polígono de las Naves de El Tarajal. Según han relatado en una denuncia a la Policía, a los pocos días comenzaron a sufrir malos tratos por parte del personal a su cargo, insultos, vejaciones y falta de atención médica. También castigos físicos y amenazas constantes con expulsarlas a Marruecos. Contactadas por este periódico, ninguna de las dos empresas ha querido hacer declaraciones.

Un grupo de menores, tras escaparse del centro de menores y refugiarse en la barriada de El Príncipe. Mònica Torres

“Nos llaman putas constantemente, nos golpean, nos castigan si pedimos usar el móvil o una almohada”, cuenta Fatima, acelerada. Ella escapó el martes junto a otras dos compañeras, y se atropella al tratar de resumir lo sucedido. Tiene un moratón en el muslo, que, asegura, es producto de una paliza por parte del personal del centro. El resto también tiene magulladuras y heridas de diverso tipo, que han fotografiado e incorporado al atestado policial. “Nos hemos escapado nosotras, pero hay muchas más que siguen dentro y no lo han conseguido. Lo hacemos también por ellas. Cuando tenemos algún problema de salud, no nos llevan al médico, y nos insultan para que nos aguantemos. Hay una chica que aún está dentro y ni siquiera cuando vomitó sangre la asistieron”, cuenta. Según su relato, a esa menor en concreto las vejaciones y los insultos se los profieren por su orientación sexual.

Uno de los episodios de mayor gravedad que refieren sucedió el pasado 10 de septiembre, durante la noche. Dos hombres con uniforme de seguridad entraron en el recinto donde dormían las jóvenes, las despertaron y pronunciaron insultos de índole sexual y amenazas explícitas de violación. “Yo ese día no trabajaba, esa noche no estuve, pero las chicas me lo contaron. Traté de enterarme de quiénes eran y lo comuniqué”, cuenta una de las auxiliares del centro. Asegura que en su presencia no se han producido esos episodios de abuso, aunque está al tanto de lo que relatan. “Yo trato de tranquilizarlas cuando quieren escaparse, les explico que en la calle no van a estar mejor”, explica. La auxiliar refiere que son frecuentes las peleas entre las jóvenes, y que en su presencia hay castigos, pero no de índole física.

Una de las menores que se ha escapado del centro de menores tras denunciar los abusos. Mònica Torres

Fue precisamente en una de esas peleas este martes cuando un grupo de cuatro menores aprovechó que el personal de seguridad se desplazó a la planta de arriba para intervenir, y escaparon. Salieron tras ellas, pero se dispersaron en el polígono. En su huida, Karima, de 16 años, se cruzó con una voluntaria de Médicos del Mundo, que mantiene su unidad móvil en el recinto para asistir a las decenas de migrantes que viven en asentamientos informales de la zona. “Apareció con una crisis de ansiedad, con magulladuras y una contusión en la espalda”, explica la sanitaria. Le realizaron un informe psicológico y otro de las lesiones, y ambos fueron incorporados a las denuncias. Según detallan fuentes de la organización, estaban al tanto de episodios de este tipo en los centros de menores habilitados, pero hasta esta semana no habían tenido una constatación porque no les está permitido el acceso. Apuntan a un problema de falta de formación del personal de estos centros y a una ausencia de atención sanitaria integral para las menores, muchas de ellas en situación de gran vulnerabilidad.

Investigación en curso

El jueves, la Fiscalía de menores de Ceuta recibió un informe con la denuncia policial, los informes médicos y psicológicos. Se tomó declaración a las jóvenes, y esa misma mañana el área de menores de la ciudad, que ostenta su tutela, intervino. Se identificó a los dos hombres de seguridad del episodio del 10 de septiembre y se los relevó de sus cargos, estableciéndose que fueran sustituidos por mujeres, ahora y en adelante. También se identificó a una de las educadoras a las que las menores acusan de golpearlas de manera reiterada.

Paralelamente, se buscó una nueva ubicación para las denunciantes y pasaron la noche en otra instalación habilitada para menores no acompañados. “Nosotros no podemos volver a acogerlas, no podemos estar otra vez como al inicio”, cuenta Ahmed Enfed-Dal, presidente de vecinos de El Príncipe. Hasta su campo llegó el grupo que se escapó el miércoles, aprovechando una salida del centro programada para que las chicas salieran al exterior. “Volvieron aquí contando lo que había pasado y a mí se me rompe el corazón, pero no podemos volver a montar aquí el campamento, porque eso no es solución. Nosotros no tenemos la tutela, se tienen que encargar ellos”, explica.

A pesar de eso, Hafida Mustafa, otra de las vecinas que levantó el campamento improvisado en agosto, busca soluciones. Al menos para esa noche. Ella acogerá en su casa a una de las chicas, y trata de reubicar a las demás hasta que a la mañana siguiente tengan que ir a declarar. “Mira cómo viene esta, tiene una infección en el pie”, dice, señalando una herida en el empeine de Nadia. “Ni cuando estaban aquí y dormían en el suelo estaban en estas condiciones”, critica. Las que huyeron del centro el jueves, como Fátima y Nadia, llegan sin sus teléfonos móviles ni ninguna de sus pertenencias. Se fugaron con lo puesto y regresaron al lugar anterior, que las refugió durante casi un mes al inicio de la crisis. “Pero eso no se puede volver a repetir, esto tiene que parar”, insiste Hafida, en vano. Un día después, en el campo aparecieron tres menores más, también del mismo centro.

Cuatro de las menores migrantes denunciantes, retratadas en la barriada de El Príncipe. Mònica Torres

Zineb también se fue, pero no regresó a El Príncipe: cruzó la frontera, otra vez. “No podía con más humillaciones, entre nosotras hay quienes llevan hiyab y quienes no, pero igualmente te insultan, te golpean. No pude más, volví a Marruecos, aunque no estoy contenta aquí con esta situación en la que estoy ahora, en la calle, pero no tengo qué hacer”, escribe desde allí. El sábado 12 de septiembre fue al puesto fronterizo y retornó voluntariamente. “Yo no tenía que volver a Marruecos, yo tenía que salir adelante y hacer mi futuro allí, porque tengo un hermanito pequeño allí al que tengo que apoyar y cuidar”, explica. Según sus compañeras de centro, es una de las cuatro que ha retornado voluntariamente, una opción que, según confiesan, cada vez ponderan más. Mientras tanto, la investigación sigue en curso.

World.title: Carlos Villar (Protos): “Bad Bunny salía en un vídeo cocinando en su casa con nuestro vino. Le escribí, pero no me contestó”
World.content:
El director general del grupo bodeguero tiene un método particular para sus vacaciones: cada mes y medio se toma cinco días de desconexión

Pertenece a la cuarta generación de una familia bodeguera. Carlos Villar (Valladolid, 54 años) estudió Ingeniería Técnica Agrícola y comenzó su carrera como director de Exportación en Bodegas Santa Eulalia. Posteriormente asumió la dirección general del Grupo Frutos Villar, con presencia en Ribera del Duero. En 2004 recibió la llamada de Bodegas Protos para incorporarse como director de Exportación. Durante cuatro años recorrió el mundo impulsando la internacionalización de la compañía, que pasó de exportar a 25 países a estar presente en 85 mercados.

En 2008 abandonó la empresa y el sector del vino para ponerse al frente de la Dirección de Comercio Exterior de la Cámara de Comercio de Valladolid. Apenas un año después recibió la llamada que marcaría su carrera: Protos le ofrecía la dirección general del grupo bodeguero, integrado por 270 accionistas. Desde entonces, la compañía ha registrado una etapa de fuerte crecimiento. El pasado ejercicio facturó 54,1 millones de euros y obtuvo 16 millones de beneficio. “El 40% del ebitda (beneficio bruto de explotación) lo reinvertimos y lo destinamos también a remunerar a toda la cadena de valor. Pagamos un 30% más de media que en la zona. Somos líderes en Ribera del Duero”, asegura, aunque no detalla el número de botellas vendidas. Villar también fue presidente de la Cámara de Comercio de Valladolid entre 2014 y 2016. Elige el restaurante Sacha, en Madrid, para mantener esta conversación.

Pregunta. ¿Notó el cambio de trabajar en una empresa familiar a hacerlo por cuenta ajena?

Respuesta. Tuve que aprender mucho, sobre todo porque cuando llegué a Protos me incorporé a una compañía que hasta entonces apenas había vendido fuera y tuve que empezar a desarrollar la exportación. A cualquier hora del día y de la noche. Era lo normal. Triplicamos las ventas, pero no porque yo fuera mejor, sino porque ya venía haciéndolo en una empresa familiar. Es muy sano trabajar fuera de la familia. No tomo decisiones que no tomaría para mí mismo. Fue más fácil que en la empresa familiar, porque estaba claro qué era la bodega y qué quería ser. Había una marca, y eso era lo que marcaba la diferencia. El desafío siempre es decir que no a cosas que pudieran perjudicarla.

P. ¿Qué rasgos cree que son los más importantes dentro de una compañía?

R. La honestidad y la lealtad. Parece que son lo mismo, pero no es así. Van juntas hasta que se separan. La lealtad es más importante.

P. ¿Viaja mucho?

R. Ahora menos que cuando era director de Exportación. Viajo, pero como apoyo. Lo que sí me encanta es viajar por placer. Soy motero y me gusta hacer viajes aventureros.

P. ¿Recuerda alguno en especial?

R. Mauritania, antes de que empezaran los secuestros. Me encanta la alegría de su gente. He recorrido Nepal en moto y el próximo viaje será a Nicaragua. Mi gran afición son las motos. Tengo cuatro: una de campo, una de trial, una scrambler y ahora me acabo de comprar otra de campo para enseñar a mis hijos.

P. ¿Le preocupa el descenso del consumo de vino entre los jóvenes?

R. Afortunadamente, los que tenemos marca estamos creciendo en ventas, pero nos preocupa el descenso del consumo. Si la crisis dura mucho, nos tocará. Las marcas, cuando llegan momentos difíciles, vendemos más que en épocas de bonanza.

P. ¿Y eso cómo es?

R. Durante la crisis de 2008 a 2014, los restaurantes dejaban solo los vinos líderes de cada zona, porque sabían que se vendían. La gente prefería lo que conocía.

P. Hay una corriente que desaconseja tomar vino. ¿Usted bebe vino?

R. Es de lo que más bebo. Mi vida es muy intensa y el mejor vino es el que me tomo cuando me relajo al llegar a casa. El mejor es el que te tomas en soledad.

P. ¿Cómo se mantiene en forma?

R. A las 6.30 de la mañana voy al gimnasio. Es el mejor momento. Antes salía a correr, pero ahora hago bicicleta y senderismo de montaña con mi mujer. Me encanta el deporte; me sirve para desconectar. Soy muy aeróbico. Sin saberlo, hago ayuno intermitente. Solo tomo un café cortado con sacarina por las mañanas, y mi mujer me aconsejó que le quitara la leche. De esta manera, hago el ayuno.

P. ¿Desconecta en vacaciones?

R. Mis vacaciones son atípicas: cada mes y medio me gusta tener cinco días de desconexión. Si me cojo muchas vacaciones seguidas, noto que tengo que estar pendiente de todo y no desconecto. De esta manera, durante esos cinco días no pienso en nada más que en descansar.

P. Por trabajo, tendrá que visitar muchos restaurantes.

R. Suelen llevarme, más que elegirlos yo, sobre todo a sitios donde tengo el vino y donde debo tenerlo. Al menos tres días laborables a la semana como en restaurantes.

P. ¿Alguno que le haya sorprendido?

R. Soy poco de parafernalias y más de producto. En Madrid me gusta ir a sitios de toda la vida: Zalacaín, Sacha, Rubaiyat o El Qüenco de Pepa. En Valladolid, me gusta la autenticidad de La Parrilla de San Lorenzo. También frecuento Trigo y Suite 22, que es de un cocinero que iba para ingeniero informático.

P. ¿Se mete en la cocina?

R. Nada. Hice una primera cosa mal y no volví a cocinar nada más. Eso sí, soy muy agradecido.

P. ¿Con los vinos es exigente?

R. Sé distinguir bien y soy exigente si el vino lo pago yo. España es un país de buenos vinos, y quien hace malos vinos es porque quiere. Soy exigente en cuanto a esas modas raras de premiar los defectos de un vino. No creo en eso. En el vino está tu identidad y no hay que variar nada para seguir modas. Creo que hay que valorar la elegancia, la finura y no perder esa identidad. No creo que las modas se beban, aunque sé que a los prescriptores les gusta hablar de cosas nuevas. Pero considero importante valorar a los restaurantes y a las bodegas por su trayectoria, por el paso del tiempo, y no solo por las modas.

P. Si le invitan a comer en una casa, ¿siempre lleva vino?

R. Sí, casi siempre. Suelo regalar alguna botella rara o desconocida para mí y para quien la recibe.

P. ¿Qué otras aficiones tiene?

R. Intento cultivar la familia y los amigos. Me pongo recordatorios para llamar a mis hermanos y a mis amigos, para ver qué tal están. Creo que es importante cuidar mucho estas relaciones.

P. ¿Qué le gusta leer?

R. Leo para dormir y elijo cosas sencillas. Acabo de leer La paciente silenciosa. Un tercio de lo que leo es para ser más listo, para aprender de diferentes disciplinas, algo que va en contra de las lecturas pensadas para conciliar el sueño. Duermo entre seis y siete horas y el 80% del tiempo duermo bien. Me voy a dormir a las 22.45 y leo durante unos 40 minutos.

P. ¿Es disciplinado?

R. Mucho. Mis amigos lo dicen y creo que me ha ido bien valorando la disciplina. En ese sentido, soy muy parecido a mi padre, siempre recto y estricto. Además, soy muy puntual. En una ocasión perdí un avión y llegué tarde a una cita con un alemán que no me atendió. Perdí una posible venta. La puntualidad es respeto. Soy de los que creen en dar ejemplo. Soy muy estricto conmigo mismo y menos con los demás.

P. ¿Escucha música?

R. Mucho, sobre todo rock. Antes iba a conciertos, pero ahora no porque me agobia que haya tanta gente. Los últimos a los que fui fueron los de AC/DC y Loquillo. Con Bad Bunny tengo una anécdota muy buena.

P. Cuente, cuente...

R. Hay un vídeo en las redes sociales en el que aparece cocinando en su casa de Puerto Rico con una botella de Protos. Fue en mayo de 2020. Le escribí, pero no contestó. En Puerto Rico nuestra marca es muy importante.

P. ¿Se ve trabajando el resto de su carrera en la misma compañía?

R. Sí, cuando termine mi carrera profesional, me gustaría hacerlo en Protos. Es una empresa que me ha dado la oportunidad de hacer cosas increíbles. Además, es una gran compañía española en la que nadie es propietario único de ella. Hemos invertido más de 50 millones de euros para hacerla crecer y ese sigue siendo nuestro objetivo. Tomamos decisiones pensando en el largo plazo, y eso redunda en beneficio de la empresa.

World.title: El millonario negocio de la devoción religiosa en Bolivia
World.content:
Los milagros en Bolivia no se compran, pero el dinero es la vía por la que se solicita o se agradece por uno. Los devotos son el motor principal de los 60 y 90 millones de dólares (70 y 103 millones de euros) que pueden llegar a generar las fiestas religiosas más importantes: la del Jesús del Gran Poder y la del Carnaval de Oruro, respectivamente. Miles de bailarines invierten hasta más de 1.000 dólares para participar en un desfile de danzas que rinde homenaje al Jesús del Gran Poder y la Virgen del Socavón, cimas del sincretismo religioso —ritualismo andino y creencia católica— que impera en el país sudamericano.

Minoika Crespo baila desde hace años en ambas fiestas, al menos 15 veces lo hizo en el Carnaval de Oruro. Dice que la devoción y el agradecimiento a los santos son fundamentales en su decisión de bailar, pero también su pasión por la danza. “Cuando la virgencita quiere que llegues a sus pies, de alguna forma llegas. Te llega el dinero”, cuenta. Los cuatro kilómetros que dura el recorrido de la entrada folclórica en Oruro —reconocida como patrimonio de la humanidad por la Unesco, al igual que la del Jesús del Gran Poder— concluyen en la basílica de la Virgen del Socavón. Algunos de los bailarines llegan arrodillados; todos se conmueven hasta las lágrimas. “Un año me invitaron a bailar y me fue muy bien en la prueba de ingreso. Un año antes tenía las ganas y el dinero, pero me lastimé la rodilla. Cuando la Virgen te pone muchos obstáculos es por algo”, cuenta Crespo. El gasto comienza desde la inscripción para las pruebas; el costo depende del tipo de baile, la antigüedad de la fraternidad o la posición a ocupar dentro del cuerpo de danza. La morenada, que es lo que baila Crespo, tiene un valor de 30 dólares. La milenaria danza es una satirización de la colonización española y se caracteriza por los pesados trajes y máscaras de los bailarines y por la ornamentación lujosa de las bailarinas.

Una vez aprobado el examen de ingreso, la cuota para la fraternidad —se cuentan por decenas— puede llegar a 170 dólares. A la hora de alquilar o comprar el traje, el rango de precios se amplía: los hay sencillos o de diseñadores de renombre que pueden cobrar 1.200 dólares. “Pueden participar hasta 10 personas en la elaboración de un traje. En los más exclusivos, en vez de lentejuelas, te ponen piedras preciosas”, precisa Crespo. Los participantes que quieren destacar suelen portar barriles de plata, mantas de vicuña, sombreros de fibra animal, maquillaje exuberante o joyas de oro hechas a mano.

El flujo monetario no acaba, sin embargo, en el desfile folclórico. Al Jesús del Gran Poder, por ejemplo, se le rinde pleitesía en fiestas populares durante todo el año. El alquiler de salones, la comida, las agrupaciones musicales, las bandas, el equipo de sonido y de amplificación y las misas son financiados por los llamados pasantes, personas o familias que pueden ser líderes o dueños de las fraternidades. Asumen voluntariamente la responsabilidad por un año y, a cambio, aumentan su prestigio y cimientan sus relaciones sociales en una dinámica que recuerda a la práctica aimara del ayni: quien recibe ayuda queda tácitamente comprometido a devolverla en el futuro.

Son justamente los burgueses aimaras —llamados qamiris—, importadores a gran escala que viajan regularmente a China, quienes conforman el grueso de los devotos. Cobran alrededor de 1.700 dólares por alquilar los salones de fiesta, con capacidad para hasta 5.000 personas, en ostentosos edificios que combinan motivos arqueológicos con cultura popular masiva, los cholets.

Pero no necesariamente la práctica de la devoción tiene que ir de la mano de eventos masivos o desfiles de danzas en un país cuya renta per capita solo llega a los 4.420 dólares anuales. Los Inturrias, por ejemplo, organizan en su casa cada conmemoración del Tata (padre en quechua) Santiago —apóstol relacionado en la cultura andina con el rayo y la lluvia—, una fiesta con familia, amigos y vecinos. El importe sobrepasa los 4.000 dólares, pero en este caso son varios los que la costean. “El aporte financiero depende del cariño de cada uno al Tata”, argumenta uno de los miembros de la familia.

World.title: 24 horas en Ayamonte, la ciudad de Huelva donde vivir uno de los mejores atardeceres de Europa
World.content:
Esta localidad onubense se define por su luz y por su condición fronteriza con Portugal. Hay que visitar su parte alta y la baja, a pie del río Guadiana, y aprovechar el viaje para ir al cercano paraje natural Marismas de Isla Cristina

Ayamonte es una localidad onubense que se define por su condición fronteriza. Su localización geográfica, en la desembocadura del Guadiana, es un punto estratégico en el que estuvieron fenicios, romanos, musulmanes y cristianos y en el que confluyen el mencionado río, el océano Atlántico, marismas, esteros, dunas y dos culturas: la local y la vecina portuguesa. En la orilla de enfrente, se encuentran los pueblos lusos de Vila Real de Santo António y Castro Marim. Las costumbres de unos y otros se filtran en ambas orillas de manera natural. Son humedades enriquecedoras, como ese fado del cantante Carlos Cano titulado María la portuguesa, que narra el trágico incidente de contrabando y amoríos que le costó la vida a un ayamontino en los años ochenta.

Esa posición geográfica aúna valor estratégico y estético. Localización que hizo que Ayamonte, desde el siglo XVI, tuviera un vínculo especial con la navegación, el comercio marítimo y la pesca del atún y de la sardina, actividades que hicieron que la localidad se desarrollara económica y socialmente. En el siglo XIX, tras el tsunami provocado por el terremoto de Lisboa de 1755 y que tanto afectó a Ayamonte, fue el turno de la industria conservera y salazonera. En 1991, se inauguró el Puente Internacional del Guadiana, lo que supuso un gran hito en la relación con Portugal, en la movilidad y en la economía.

Más información Cinco ciudades en España para comer muy bien más allá de Madrid y Barcelona

A su patrimonio histórico y arquitectónico se ha sumado el de la luz. El proyecto europeo Atlantic Sunset ha situado a Ayamonte entre los lugares del arco atlántico donde el sol se pone más tarde —los estudios científicos del proyecto lo han identificado como el lugar donde se produce el último atardecer de la España peninsular entre los meses de octubre y febrero—. Un espectáculo natural que suma otro motivo más por el que merece la pena el periplo hasta aquí. Por carretera se llega desde las ciudades de Huelva, Sevilla y Faro, en Portugal, donde se encuentra el aeropuerto más próximo a Ayamonte y principal puerta de entrada de muchos de los turistas extranjeros que se ven paseando por las calles y las plazas del Rosario, de La Laguna y de La Ribera. En estos escenarios tiene lugar en el mes de agosto Un paseo por el Arte, evento que tiene el fin de mostrar en la calle las obras pictóricas, escultóricas y fotográficas de cientos de artistas locales o con alguna vinculación con la ciudad.

La plaza de la Laguna, en Ayamonte. Vibrant Pictures (Alamy / cordon Press)

10.00 Una habitación con vistas

Si la de Virginia Woolf era una habitación propia, las del Parador Nacional de Ayamonte (1) lo son con vistas; al Guadiana, al Puente Internacional que lo cruza y a la ciudad. Aquí antes hubo un castillo de origen romano, reedificado por los musulmanes después y finalmente ocupado por los cristianos.

Desde lo alto de la colina se divisa el río, Portugal y Ayamonte, que está a sus pies. El pueblo tiene una zona plana, a orillas del Guadiana, y otra alta, donde está el parador. Aia, en árabe, significa zona elevada. Cuando llegaron los cristianos, se encontraron un pueblo que se llamaba Aia y ellos le añadieron el sufijo “monte”. La parte más baja del pueblo se encuentra a unos tres metros sobre el nivel del mar, en las zonas cercanas al estuario; la parte más elevada es la del parador, a 63 metros de altura.

11.00 Antes y después del terremoto

A mediados del siglo XIII, Ayamonte pasó de manos portuguesas a las castellanas. A partir de ese momento, creció al amparo de la familia Guzmán y se vertebró en torno a dos partes: La Villa, la parte alta, donde se concentraban los edificios administrativos y religiosos, y La Ribera, la parte baja, donde se concentraba la vida marítima y comercial.

La Villa está llena de calles estrechas, miradores, fachadas tradicionales, balcones floridos y pequeños rincones con encanto. En este barrio se encuentran templos como El Salvador (2), San Francisco (3) y San Sebastián (4), además de antiguos palacios y casas señoriales. Uno de los edificios más emblemáticos es el antiguo Palacio de los Marqueses (5), junto al “Patio de la Jabonería”.

La iglesia de El Salvador, en la localidad onubense. Felipe Rodriguez (Alamy / cordon Press)

En La Ribera están las casas blancas, el paseo fluvial y el ambiente que evoca su origen marinero. Destacan el Centro Cultural Casa Grande Manuel Rivero “El Pintado” (6), el Ayuntamiento (7), las plazas de la Laguna y de La Ribera, conventos como el de las Hermanas de Santa Clara (8) y la capilla de San Antonio (9) las iglesias de La Merced (10) y Las Angustias (11). La Casa Grande es la única casa que se conserva anterior al terremoto de Lisboa de 1775. Seísmo que derivó en un tsunami que afectó gravemente a Ayamonte y otras localidades de Huelva, como Isla Cristina. Destruyó muchos edificios y hubo que reconstruir gran parte de su casco urbano. Las fachadas que hoy se ven datan de aquella época.

La plaza de La Laguna —aquí antes había una— es el corazón histórico y social de la ciudad. En ella hay una la réplica de La pesca del atún en Ayamonte, obra de Joaquín Sorolla integrada en la colección Visión de España que la Hispanic Society de Nueva York encargó al pintor. La plaza de La Ribera la diseñó el arquitecto José Granados, inspirada en las obras de Aníbal González, arquitecto sevillano que hizo la plaza de España. En la misma hay cerámica y ladrillo mudéjar forjado en las farolas, los bancos...

14.00 Geografía en el plato

Puesto de mercado y marisco en el mercado central de Ayamonte. Marcos del Mazo (Alamy / cordon Press)

La gastronomía, como el turismo y la pesca, son algunos de los sectores que forman parte de la economía azul, esa que se nutre de los recursos marinos de manera responsable, generando un crecimiento económico y empleo al tiempo que preserva la salud de los ecosistemas acuáticos de la zona. El abanico de delicias que se pueden degustar incluye la gamba blanca de Huelva, el choco, el atún, la sardina, la caballa, el arroz marinero y la mojama, el jamón del mar.

Estas delicias se preparan desde hace 60 años en el Restaurante Casa Luciano (12). El negocio hoy lo lleva el hijo del marinero que lo abrió, Luciano Ramos. El menú depende de lo que se coja en el día. En la carta, unos días hay y otros no, morro de atún, gambas a la plancha, cazón seco con tomate, cocido de garbanzos con rape, etcétera. Mucha de esa materia prima viene de Isla Cristina, donde se encuentra la principal lonja de Andalucía y la segunda más importante de España, después de la de Vigo. Cerca de la misma se puede comer en el Bar Marinero (13) y en Doña Lola (14), a orillas de la ría Carreras.

17.00 Parajes naturales

“Un lugar con tanta riqueza ecológica, como Ayamonte y sus alrededores, tiene un gran potencial como destino de viaje responsable”, sentencia Margarita Arjona, directora de Healing Planet, consultora de turismo sostenible. Alrededor de Ayamonte hay dunas y las marismas del Guadiana y el paraje natural Marismas de Isla Cristina, bañado por la ría Carreras, donde se encuentran Las Salinas del Alemán (15). Es una explotación artesanal, entre esteros y caños, que tuvo como primer propietario a un espía germano que envió el gobierno nazi en 1939 a la zona, Hans Burghard (o Juanito el alemán, para los lugareños), y que en la década de los ochenta se puso al frente de las mismas Manuel Gómez, al que le siguieron su hija (Manuela) y sus nietas (Estefanía y Sabina).

El paraje natural Marismas de Isla Cristina. Sonia Bonet (Alamy / cordon Press)

Además de esta sal por aquí hay salicornia o espárrago de mar, una planta que nace en las marismas y que el proyecto Marshfood produce de manera pionera. Cocineros como Ángel León, Martín Berasategui y Quique Dacosta la han usado.

18.30 La luz como fuente de orgullo

Si en Ayamonte el Guadiana es frontera, la luz es un orgullo. El pasado mes de enero esta localidad acogió una jornada divulgativa en el marco del proyecto europeo Atlantic Sunset que sitúa al municipio onubense entre los enclaves del arco atlántico donde el sol se pone más tarde. Es decir, es uno de los mejores escenarios europeos para ver el atardecer. Algo que se puede ver en tierra firme o a bordo de una embarcación, ya sea la que hace una travesía por el Guadiana o la que lo cruza con destino la orilla portuguesa.

El Puente Internacional del Guadiana, que conecta Ayamonete con la localidad de Castromarín, en el distrito de Faro (Portugal), al atardecer. juampiter (GETTY IMAGES)

20.30 Una cena de sabores allende los mares
