World.title: EU urges US to reconsider visa denial to Palestinian UN assembly delegation
World.content:
The European Union says it regrets Washington's decision to deny visas to Palestinian officials seeking to attend the UN General Assembly.

The US State Department said it was refusing to grant visas to Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas and other members of his delegation ahead of next week's meeting in New York.

Spokesman for the EU's diplomatic service, Anouar El Anouni, said the EU had urged the US to rethink the move, referencing the White House's similar decision last year.

The UN is needed now more than ever When Anthony Albanese and Penny Wong attended the UN General Assembly 12 months ago, it felt like something significant might be happening. This year, things feel like they will be a bit more... prosaic.

"In light of its existing headquarters agreements with the UN and its obligations as host state, we urge the United States for this decision to be reconsidered," Mr Anouni said.

US President Donald Trump's administration denied visas for the Palestinian delegation last year, forcing Mr Abbas — a regular at the UN General Assembly — to address the body by video.

The General Assembly voted 152-3 on Thursday for Mr Abbas to be able to appear virtually once again this year.

On Friday, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres also expressed regret at Washington's decision, adding he was concerned about its impact "on the ability of the State of Palestine to participate fully in the work of the United Nations".

As it stands, only members of the Palestinian mission to the UN will be able to attend the meeting, which begins on Tuesday.

The General Assembly voted in favour of Mahmoud Abbas appearing virtually again this year. (Reuters: Remo Casilli)

US at odds with UN members recognising Palestinian state

The US and Israel have objected to the Palestinian Authority's (PA) historical payments to families of imprisoned or slain Palestinians, including those who carried out attacks against Israelis.

The PA recently reformed this system, allocating welfare payments to families on a needs basis rather than political affiliation or prisoner status.

Sources say Australia withdrew from West Bank sanctions talks European diplomats say they were surprised and disappointed that Australia baulked at joining a UK-led move to impose trade sanctions on West Bank Israeli businesses.

The State Department said Washington also opposed Palestinian "actions to internationalise the Israeli-Palestinian conflict including through the International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ), seeking to bypass negotiations through seeking unilateral recognition".

They accused them of "continuing to pay stipends to terrorists and to glorify acts of terrorism and terrorists in public pronouncements and school textbooks".

The US is at odds with the 142 UN member states that recognised a Palestinian state at the United Nations last year.

The decision to deny Mr Abbas a US entry visa comes as violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinians has escalated in recent months in the West Bank.

AFP

World.title: Russia reports cyber attacks on voting system during parliamentary election
World.content:
Russian authorities have reported multiple attacks on voting systems and communication lines across the country, as Russians head to the polls in a three-day parliamentary election.

The online voting system in Moscow was subjected to a strong attack overnight, but the situation remains under control, the Interfax news agency cited the Central Election Commission's head as saying on Saturday.

The attacks were continuing, but all were being successfully repelled, Ella Pamfilova said, according to state media.

A banner of Mr Putin with a quote reading: "Today, our entire country is one team. And that is undoubtedly the reason for the success of all our endeavours." (Reuters: Alexey Pavlishak)

Separately, Russia's digital ministry said it had registered a sabotage attempt on communication lines in the country's Far East, but that the attack had been thwarted and all communication had been restored, state media reported.

President Vladimir Putin earlier accused Ukraine of trying to interfere with the vote, without providing evidence.

Voting in Russia's parliamentary election runs from September 18 to 20.

Election triggers diplomatic row with Moldova

Russia's parliamentary election has triggered a diplomatic row with Moldova over plans to open polling stations for Russian nationals in the separatist Transnistria region.

Moscow says 220,000 residents of pro-Russian Transnistria, a sliver of land which broke away from Moldova in 1990 at the end of Soviet rule, hold Russian passports and are entitled to vote on Sunday in the election for the State Duma.

Moldova's pro-Western government says Russians may vote only in a single polling station in the Russian embassy in the capital Chisinau.

It contests the 220,000 figure and opposes any polling station in Transnistria, where it has no control over procedures.

Moldovan authorities this week denounced the Kremlin's 15 planned polling stations as "unacceptable and hostile".

Putin's new incentives to recruit soldiers in Transnistria The Kremlin is trying to recruit more soldiers for its war in Ukraine but an analyst says at the rate of casualties, "Russia cannot replace recruits fast enough to keep the 'meat grinder' fed."

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova urged Moldova to drop its objections and halt actions that "run against democracy, international law and common sense".

Moldovan Foreign Minister Mihail Popsoi told Moscow "not to interfere with Moldova's plans for peaceful reintegration" of the breakaway territory.

Flags of Transnistria and Russia fly in a square in Moldova's breakaway region of Transnistria. (Reuters: Vladislav Bachev)

Meanwhile, former Russian federal official Marat Kambolov was elected president of South Ossetia, a Russia-backed breakaway region of Georgia, in a vote Moscow hailed on Saturday as a sign of the territory's desire for closer ties with Moscow.

Election shadowed by war

The Kremlin is likely to cite the election result as evidence of widespread public support for Mr Putin's policies, in particular the invasion of Ukraine — Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II, now in its fifth year.

Most anti-war candidates have been barred from participating.

The second day of voting came after a New York Time report this week, citing two people close to the peace talks, that the White House is now considering signing business deals with Russia before it stops fighting in Ukraine.

Democrats probe Trump Jr wedding parties Two lavish post-wedding parties for Donald Trump Jr and his wife, held in the Bahamas in May, were funded by Russian businessman Umar Kremlev, who has strong ties to President Vladimir Putin, according to a report by US media outlet ProPublica.

"I don't know anything about such signals, and it would be strange to receive them, because we still hear exactly the opposite stance, namely, 'Let's agree on Ukraine and move forward, and everything else later,'" Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov told the RIA state news agency on Saturday.

Also on Saturday, Poland said it conducted a preventative military air operation during Russian strikes on Ukraine — though concluded their was no violation of Polish airspace.

Russian forces struck a Ukrainian cargo ship and a tanker located in the Black Sea and in one of Ukraine's ports, the Interfax news agency reported on Saturday, citing the Russian Defence Ministry.

ABC/Wires

World.title: Roosters power into prelim as Sharks insist they are not in rebuild mode
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters are 80 minutes away from their first NRL grand final in seven years after fighting past Cronulla in a 46-10 semifinal win.

Trent Robinson's men will play the Dolphins in a preliminary final after being made to work for victory against the Sharks at Sydney Football Stadium.

Halfback Daly Cherry-Evans was placed on report for tripping Cronulla's Teig Wilton on Saturday and, aside from the fitness of Sam Walker, is likely to be the only question mark heading into next Friday's meeting with the Dolphins.

Queensland number seven Walker underwent ankle surgery less than a month ago but coach Trent Robinson said the team is "pretty confident" he will be back to face the Dolphins.

"He hasn't trained with us yet but he's had really good progressions," Robinson said.

Just as everything fell into place for the Roosters, who also welcomed back Angus Crichton from a long injury lay-off on Saturday, just about everything fell apart for Cronulla.

Halfback Nicho Hynes failed a head injury assessment after copping a bang en route to Lindsay Collins' second-minute opening try.

Nicho Hynes was ruled out due to a second-minute head knock. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

And then centre Mawene Hiroti went off with a knee injury after 20 minutes after crashing over the dead-ball line.

It was little wonder the Roosters put a depleted Sharks outfit to the sword, piling on 24 points in the final half an hour.

Cronulla is now one of just two teams in the NRL era to reach five straight finals series without making a grand final, and has not been returned to the last game of the season despite making the top eight in nine of 10 seasons since.

"We've been up for five years now with the same group of guys and a good portion of those are leaving," Sharks coach Craig Fitzgibbon said.

Cameron McInnes, Sione Katoa, Siosifa Talakai, Jesse Ramien and Mawene Hiroti are some of the core members of the team on their way out, but Fitzgibbon said it would not be a complete rebuild for the club.

"Everyone thinks we need a reset or rebuild; we'll just keep going, we've got some guys ready to go," he said.

"We won't be going anywhere."

Look back at all the action in our live blog below and check out all the stats in the full ScoreCentre.

World.title: Broncos blitz Knights to set up derby preliminary final
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Defending NRLW premiers Brisbane have destroyed Newcastle in a 40-16 win to set up a preliminary final against Gold Coast.

The Broncos led 34-0 at half-time at Langlands Park on their way to clinching a fourth straight win.

But there were some concerns for the Broncos, with Bree Spreadborough sustaining an ankle injury.

Lock Lillian Yarrow was also put on report for a lifting tackle.

It took the Knights until the 16th minute to complete a set of six as they were blown off the park by a rampant Broncos outfit.

Raiders end Tigers' NRLW fairytale The Raiders claim a first-ever NRLW finals win, downing the Tigers 6-0 to end Wests' fairytale season.

Broncos trio Tamika Upton, Jesse Southwell and Romy Teitzel tormented their former club in masterclass displays.

Upton, who was given an early mark 20 minutes from full-time, probed and dazzled from fullback.

Southwell was the chief puppeteer at number seven with a pinpoint kicking game, and Teitzel was dominant in the right edge second-row spot.

The Broncos had a dream start with a try after just 56 seconds, brought about by perfect execution in all aspects of play.

Knights fullback Lucy Spain dropped the ball after a Southwell bomb, with Teitzel picking up the scraps to storm over.

Robinson weaved over five minutes later and barnstorming prop Shannon Mato was unstoppable close to the line.

Teitzel's second try was followed by Upton's four-pointer.

Upton laid one on with a crafty grubber for centre Georgia Bartlett to finish, and it was already a cakewalk before the half-time siren.

Broncos prop Brianna Clark crashed over after the break before Knights backs Mercedez Taulelei-Siala, Shanice Parker and Sidney Taylor got the visitors on the board in an improved second-half performance.

AAP

World.title: 'Western values' and 'national pride' underpin Coalition's education reform plans
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The Coalition has unveiled its plan for "root and branch" reform of Australia's education system, that would include subjects on "Western values", and less time spent on Indigenous history.

Speaking in Sydney's west, Shadow Education Minister Julian Leeser said the reforms would also see the Australian flag flown in all schools to foster more national pride.

He declared that the Coalition's policy would "restore excellence" in education, amid plummeting academic standards.

"Our academic performance is worse than ever. Our boys are disengaged and falling behind, our classrooms are disrupted and, in some cases, dangerous," Mr Leeser said.

To address rising classroom disruption, Mr Leeser floated the idea of teaching pathways for military veterans.

"When I think about the need for better classroom behaviour and more discipline in our classrooms, and the need for more support for Australian values, it seems to make sense," he said.

Make Indigenous history 'discrete' subject

Mr Leeser, who is also the shadow minister for Indigenous Australians, said children should learn about Indigenous heritage, "just like they learn about our British foundation and multicultural character".

Global results show Aussie students' struggles Australian students have recorded their lowest-ever scores in maths and reading in international testing, but improved on their science results.

Advocating for a shorter national curriculum that "returns time to teachers", he said the Coalition would remove cross-curricular priorities — which are areas of learning embedded across the curriculum, rather than as separate subjects.

These include Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories and culture, Asia and Australia's engagement with Asia, and sustainability.

"All three topics are important … but that doesn't mean they should be delivered thematically to our children as cross-curricular priorities," he said.

"Teach them as discrete, carefully planned topics that fit properly within geography or history or science classes."

'Western values' to underpin curriculum

The Coalition's curriculum overhaul also calls for students to "specifically learn" about Western values and culture.

"That includes basics like democracy, the rule of law, a fair go, the development by Australians of our system of constitutional monarchy and federation," Mr Leeser said.

"But I would also like to see Australian students taught and exposed to …classical works of literature, art, music and philosophy that underpin and enrich the ideas that have shaped our country."

The shadow minister said the Coalition's "root and branch" reforms would build a sense of national pride, which he said was lacking.

"Let every school have a flag and let every student take pride in it, its history and the values for which it stands."

Faster pathways for teachers

In addition to potentially streamlining teaching pathways for soldiers, a Coalition government would also slash qualification timelines.

Coalition's teacher claims spark backlash A teacher's union has fired back, labelling remarks by Angus Taylor and Matt Canavan "fundamentally incorrect".

Mr Leeser pledged a Coalition government would support a return to a one-year teacher accreditation system.

"Until the early 2010s, teachers in Australia were generally accredited on the basis of one-year teacher training courses," he said.

"In 2023, the NSW Productivity Commission released data showing that the shift to the longer qualification led to 9,000 teachers not entering the profession between 2015 and 2022."

The Coalition's policy would also include a framework to help all Australian schools develop "a clear statement of behavioural expectations" for students, amid rising instances of abuse towards teachers.

World.title: Mother charged over hidden recording device in son's clothing
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A Gippsland mother has been charged by police after allegedly sewing a recording device into her non-verbal son's clothing after he began refusing to go to school.

Skye Cooper says her seven-year-old son came home from school one day last year with what looked like bruises.

He had been attending Churchill Primary School in the state's east since February 2025, but it was only around a month into his time there when he began acting distressed during the morning school run.

"He would not get out of the car. He started screaming, he started begging for me," Ms Cooper said.

"He just got more and more emotionally distressed… [and] would not be left in a room with anyone other than me. He was traumatised."

Her son has severe epilepsy, autism level three, global development delay and severe language delay. He is also non-verbal.

Ms Cooper said she was prompted to act when she noticed bruising on her son's arm. (ABC News: supplied)

Ms Cooper said she had multiple meetings with the school to express her concerns about her son's experience but didn't feel that her concerns were being addressed.

Worried, Ms Cooper approached a disability advocate for advice and was advised to sew a recording device into his clothes.

Each night, she listened back to the audio — until she heard an aide telling her son "you hurt me, I'll hurt you".

"Once I heard her on the recording threatening him, saying that she'll hurt him … I ended up pulling him out [of the school]," Ms Cooper said.

Charges laid over recording device

The alleged use of a recording device was reported to police and Ms Cooper has since been charged with Regulation of Installation, Use and Maintenance of a Listening Device.

She said she is shocked by the turn of events.

"I was trying to protect my child," she said.

"I just couldn't make sense of it, that … the tables have been turned on me."

She said she's been told by police that if she admits to the charges and makes a donation of $300 to a suitable charity, she won't have a criminal record.

Ms Cooper is receiving legal advice over her next steps.

She has also started a petition calling for the aide's removal and for the Education Minister to push for change in the Surveillance Devices Act to protect parents who use covert recording devices in suspected cases of abuse.

Ms Cooper doesn't believe her concerns have been addressed. (ABC News: Danielle Kutchel)

Earlier this year Ms Cooper received a formal written apology from the aide, which said she did "not specifically recall the exchange" but was "extremely remorseful that such a statement was made".

"I take full responsibility for the language used and am using this as an opportunity to reflect on my communication style under stress," the letter said.

"I clearly used words that I should not have used. While they would not have been intended as a threat or a literal statement, I recognise that language expressed that way is inappropriate."

Recording device 'only recourse you've got'

Julie Phillips is the disability advocate who has been assisting Ms Cooper and who recommended placing a recording device in the child's clothes.

She said she would still recommend it to others, while also warning of the possible consequences.

"But if there's no other way of finding out, what else can you do?" Ms Phillips said.

Julie Phillips advised Skye Cooper to use a recording device. (ABC News: supplied)

She said Ms Cooper's descriptions of her son's behaviour during his time at the school immediately raised red flags.

"One of the common issues with kids who can't use speech to communicate is when their behaviour deteriorates and there is bruising, usually something is going on that's traumatic for them," she said.

"Obviously it shouldn't be that [using a recording device] is the only recourse you've got, but with non-verbal people it is the only recourse you've got.

"The consequences have been experienced by a mother whose number one priority is the safety of her child, who can't communicate with her. If that's not completely backwards, I don't know what is."

Ms Phillips said abuse of children with disabilities in schools is extensive.

"When you take away any options that parents have to find out what is going on at school, your children are in a very dangerous position," she said.

She believes Ms Cooper's use of a listening device was justified and could even be legally defended if it can be proven that there was a threat to assault her son.

"If children can't be safe in government schools, it's a sad reflection on our society."

Ms Cooper said the Disability Workers Commission is investigating the issue.

World.title: Victorian Greens MP Tim Read dies aged 64
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Victorian Greens MP Tim Read has died aged 64, following a high-profile battle with metastatic cancer.

Dr Read, who announced his retirement from the Victorian parliament in January, used his final year as the Member for Brunswick to fight against the Allan government's decision to close VicHealth, described as the world's first health promotion foundation.

The former general practitioner told the ABC in January that VicHealth had helped pioneer sun safety messaging that could have helped him reduce his cancer risk if promoted when he was younger.

Mr Read delivered his valedictory speech to the Victorian parliament earlier this year. (AAP: James Ross)

Paying tribute to Dr Read on social media today, Victorian Greens leader Ellen Sandell said the Brunswick MP was the most liked MP in the state parliament.

"Tim was a brilliant local MP, doctor and scientist — but to those who knew him, he was also the kindest, funniest and most fundamentally decent of people," Ms Sandell said.

"Tim never held back from speaking truth to power, whether it was getting arrested for spray-painting health messages on tobacco billboards prior to getting elected or taking it up to the Premier in Question Time.

"Yet, he was also the most liked MP in state parliament, respected across the community for that rarest combination in a politician: conviction, integrity, wit and genuine humility."

Ms Sandell said Dr Read's advocacy led to legislative reforms over pill testing, tobacco licensing, the abolition of public drunkenness laws and a statewide plan to eradicate congenital syphilis and HIV transmission.

She said his work also led to gay men being allowed to donate blood, and a statutory ban on solitary confinement in prisons.

Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said he spoke with Dr Read earlier this week and was "deeply touched by that conversation".

"We spoke about something on which we have always agreed: integrity in public life and the need for reform," Mr Carroll said.

"Despite his health challenges, he was positive and optimistic for a better world.

"I always valued his intelligent and humane contributions to the public debate."

Victorian Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said Dr Read "was a man of conviction and a thoroughly decent person".

"He brought sincerity, compassion and a strong sense of public duty to his work, earning respect across the parliament," she said.

The Greens MP was a doctor before being elected to the Victorian parliament eight years ago. (ABC News: Simon Tucci)

"His commitment to integrity in public life was unwavering. Through his leadership of parliament's Integrity and Oversight Committee and his advocacy for stronger anti-corruption laws, Tim worked to ensure those entrusted with power were held accountable."

Ms Wilson said parliament often required negotiation and compromise.

" I always enjoyed working with Tim. He was an honest broker, someone who listened, engaged in good faith and approached every discussion with respect and integrity. "

Born in 1962, Dr Read completed a PhD while working as a medical practitioner in a public HIV and sexual health clinic.

His research included HIV prevention and treatment and how best to treat antibiotic-resistant sexually transmitted infections.

Dr Read's political activism started in his early 20s, as a participant in the Billboard-Utilising Graffitists Against Unhealthy Promotions group, comically known as BUGA-UP.

Medical students including a young Tim Read took part in a graffiti campaign in the mid-1980s, when cigarette advertising was still legal on public billboards. (Supplied)

The politician first ran for a parliamentary seat at a federal level, running as the Greens candidate at the 2013 election in former prime minister Bob Hawke's seat of Wills, which overlaps with the state electorate of Brunswick.

The following year, he stood as the Greens candidate for Brunswick in the Victorian election before ultimately winning the seat on his second attempt in 2018.

The Greens hold the inner suburban constituency with a two-candidate preferred margin of 13.7 per cent against Labor.

A by-election for the Brunswick electorate will not be necessary as Victoria is already scheduled to go to the polls on November 28.

Last year, Dr Read told the ABC he had noticed his leg was swollen while getting ready for work.

Scans revealed cancer had spread throughout his body. Dr Read first had a melanoma removed from his leg seven years ago.

His initial diagnosis was grim, forcing the Brunswick MP to retire ahead of the November state election.

Victorian Premier John Cain established VicHealth in 1987. (ABC News)

In January, Dr Read said closing VicHealth would create a "false economy" — an apparent saving that would in fact lead to more spending.

"We need to be strengthening health promotion, not weakening it," he told the ABC.

VicHealth was set up in 1987 by Labor premier John Cain and his health minister David White with bipartisan political support.

The policy banned outdoor tobacco advertising and used taxes from cigarette sales to promote health, including warning about the dangers of cigarettes.

Revenue was used to fund the arts and sport, which until then had relied heavily on tobacco sponsorship.

In his valedictory speech, Dr Read called for stronger NSW-style anti-corruption oversight in Victoria and bolstered rental controls, similar to those of the Australian Capital Territory.

"Despite the theatrics, most of us are here for the right reasons," he said.

"Politicians are unfairly maligned, and for me, politics is the work you do to improve people’s circumstances, not just now but in the future.

World.title: Demons claim top spot as Cats maintain winning ways
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Melbourne is the only unbeaten side after six rounds of the AFLW season, producing a statement 34-point win over Carlton at Casey Fields.

But the Demons may count the cost of Saturday's 8.10 (58) to 3.6 (24) win after star forward Georgia Gall limped off in the third quarter with an ankle injury.

A day after Hawthorn manufactured an upset to topple defending premiers North Melbourne, the Demons knew a win over the Blues would lift them into top spot on the ladder and establish a 6-0 (win-loss) start to their campaign.

The Blues were spirited in the opening half, but Melbourne slotted four straight goals in the third quarter to set up the victory.

Midfielder Olivia Purcell (26 disposals) was at the centre of the blitz, slotting two majors, while Jorja Livingstone scored on debut in the final quarter.

Tyla Hanks (32 disposals, one goal) also excelled, but it came as Gall sustained her injury.

It is the second consecutive loss for the Blues (4-2) and dents their top-four aspirations, although midfielder Claudia Whitfort was typically busy with 24 disposals.

Cats in fifth straight win

Aishling Moloney produced a goal-of-the-year contender to help Geelong to a 14.6 (90) to 7.7 (49) triumph over Collingwood at Victoria Park.

Knowing a victory would shore up their position inside the top eight, the Cats (5-1) were given a scare when the winless Magpies levelled scores minutes after the main break.

But the visitors flicked a switch, finding six goals in an electrifying third quarter to take a 31-point lead into the final break.

One of those majors was from Moloney, who booted the ball from halfway before it took a favourable flurry of bounces and crept into the goal.

The Cats tightened the screws in the final quarter, keeping Collingwood goal-less to seal their fifth straight win.

Midfielders Nina Morrison (30 disposals), Mikayla Bowen (29 disposals) and Georgie Prespakis (12 clearances) were prolific for the Cats, while Moloney and Chloe Scheer grabbed three and four majors respectively.

While the loss kept the Magpies (0-6) winless, they enjoyed a highlight when half-forward Olivia Lewis booted a goal on her AFLW debut after shifting from Super Netball's Melbourne Mavericks to the Magpies.

Lewis was a late call-up on Saturday morning because midfielder Bri Davey was ill.

Swans move clear in top four

Chloe Molloy continued her glittering goal-scoring form, spearheading Sydney to a 14-point victory over Port Adelaide.

Chloe Molloy played a starring role for the Swans. (Getty Images: Mark Brake)

The Swans (5-1) knew a win at Alberton Oval would move them four points clear of the fifth-placed Blues.

Molloy was instrumental in helping the visitors secure the precious 5.11 (41) to 3.9 (27) victory, booting three goals.

Her dazzling display came despite the Power keeping Sydney's usually dynamic attack at bay in the first half, with the scores locked at 16-16 at the main break.

The Swans stepped up in the third quarter, with Molloy booting a crucial goal, although a late major by Gemma Houghton kept the Power in the contest.

Leading by four points at three-quarter time, young Swans forward Cynthia Hamilton snagged a settling major, before Molloy kicked another to open up a match-winning advantage.

Swans defender Zippy Fish was typically influential, picking up 26 disposals, while midfielder Montana Ham had 16 possessions.

Midfielder Abbey Dowrick was a shining light for the Power (2-4), racking up a match-high 27 disposals and 415 metres gained.

Triumphant Bulldogs

The Western Bulldogs held firm to claim a 6.4 (40) to 4.6 (30) victory over Fremantle.

Looking to jump into the top eight, the Bulldogs (4-2) were kept scoreless in the opening term in Perth but kicked four unanswered majors in the second quarter to lead by 11 points at half-time.

The Dockers tightened their defence in the third quarter, holding the visitors to just one point as they surged back after Hayley Miller and Kiara Bowers found goals.

But just 17 seconds into the final quarter, a series of slick handballs led to Bulldogs forward Heidi Woodley slotting a major, before Sarah Hartwig nailed a goal to help her team move up to seventh on the ladder.

The Dockers (3-3) missed an opportunity to cement themselves inside the top eight, although Bowers (23 disposals, eight tackles and one goal) was busy, while midfielders Gabrielle Newton and Aisling McCarthy posted 24 possessions each.

Defender Jess Fitzgerald (25 disposals) shone for the Bulldogs, and midfielder Isabelle Pritchard jagged 21 disposals and a goal.

AAP

World.title: NZ’s ski capital is fast becoming a summer destination
World.content:
Australians love to chase the sun on holiday. But as temperatures rise and summer heat makes some traditionally popular destinations less appealing, could the lure of cooler climes start heating up?

Certainly, New Zealand’s Queenstown would love that. Australians have long flocked to Queenstown for the ski season, but increasingly the destination is courting them year-round. And there are signs the strategy is working: international traffic through Queenstown Airport is at record levels, while trans-Tasman travel connecting Queenstown with Australia’s eastern seaboard has reached 145 per cent of pre-pandemic levels.

The Kawarau Gorge Trail is set to open for cycling this month. iStock

Tourism New Zealand research also suggests Australians are open to travelling outside the traditional peak: 67 per cent of Australians actively considering a New Zealand holiday say they would consider an off-peak visit. Asked which seasons they would consider, spring came out on top at 42 per cent, followed by summer at 35 per cent, autumn at 29 per cent and winter at 24 per cent.

Queenstown is, of course, synonymous with skiing for many Australians, but there’s an ever-growing list of reasons to visit without skis.

World.title: ‘Confident’: Walker eyes remarkable return as DCE sets up storybook Dolphins clash
World.content:
The Roosters are “confident” Sam Walker will return from injury alongside veteran Daly Cherry-Evans in his storybook showdown with the Dolphins after the Tricolours first outmuscled, then outgunned Cronulla 46-10 at Allianz Stadium.

The Sharks lost their own million-dollar No.7 Nicho Hynes within 90 seconds to a head knock and conceded the first try of the evening just two tackles later.

Loading

But even with centre Mawene Hiroti (knee) also ruled out of the contest when he collided with the advertising boarding, reducing Cronulla to 15 fit players for an hour, Craig Fitzgibbon’s side hardly wilted.

Instead, it took another piece of out-and-out Mark Nawaqanitawase magic to truly spark the Tricolours, along with a superb solo act from Cherry-Evans himself to ensure neither departing Rooster was playing their last game for the club.

As is the way when this star-studded side is on a roll, the rugby-bound Nawaqanitawase finished with a double. Cherry-Evans helped himself to three try assists.

The Redcliffe-based Dolphins and a sold-out Suncorp Stadium in next Friday night’s grand final qualifier now await.

Loading

It is a tantalising scene on so many levels. Not least because Cherry-Evans, 37 and now playing every game because it can well and truly be his last on Australian soil, took his first furtive steps in rugby league as an eight-year-old for Redcliffe almost 30 years ago, where his dad and uncle both played as well.

With another week to heal from the syndesmosis surgery that was feared to have ended his season, superstar No.7 Walker will do everything in his power to play as well.

“I’m pretty confident with what I’ve seen,” Robinson said of Walker, who is eyeing a four-week return in the preliminary final.

“He’s had really good progression, but we’ll get a good gauge on Monday or Tuesday.

In front of 39,147 at a heaving Allianz Stadium, the Roosters held an 18-10 half-time lead, yet two ugly unforced errors after the break set a tone Roosters fans know and fear all too well.

Enter Nawaqanitawase. With the kind of audacious flick pass he produces so often it is somehow in danger of becoming ho-hum, he and Rob Toia set in motion a rambunctious try that went through several sets of hands before Connor Watson dived over.

Loading

“It’s been probably five to six weeks since I’ve seen us flick the ball and pass the ball and that’s a signature of ours when we’re humming,” Robinson said. That was a big play in the context of our game.”

The coach wasn’t wrong. This was the four-pointer that truly gave the Roosters breathing room. Cherry-Evans’ 27th-minute stepping, swivelling effort from close-range didn’t hurt either.

Not when Braydon Trindall and Blayke Brailey had threatened enough through the ruck to engineer two Sharks tries in three minutes, even without Cronulla’s recognised halfback.

Even after Watson’s try, the Sharks kept coming. A tight, but technically correct double movement call denied Teig Wilton. A desperate try-saving tackle from Billy Smith shot down Trindall when the line beckoned.

And then, the Roosters weren’t just coming. They were gone. Cherry-Evans set up a couple. He was placed on report for tripping Wilton but won’t face anything more than a fine. Skipper James Tedesco joined the party after making 11 tackle breaks, as did Rob Toia after his own excellent outing.

Watson and Reece Robson were fantastic through the middle too, while the Sharks didn’t deserve to have so many points put on them or have their season end so brutally.

Cherry-Evans knows all too well he’s every chance of not getting his ultimate farewell premiership fairytale either.

But a showdown with the Dolphins – where it all started for him three decades ago – isn’t a bad place to start next Friday.

World.title: ‘He apologised’: It was another night of finals misery for Nicho Hynes. This time it was different
World.content:
Analysis SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘He apologised’: It was another night of finals misery for Nicho Hynes. This time it was different Tom Decent September 19, 2026 — 10:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Of all the weeks to not cop a head knock in the first two minutes of a match, the penultimate weekend in September would be very high on Nicho Hynes’ list. To then watch his opposing halfback, Daly Cherry-Evans, set up a try and kickstart a thumping 46-10 Roosters win at home, only made it harder to take. Loading Hynes’ night lasted just 90 seconds, cut short in cruel fashion after he failed a head injury assessment following a tackle gone wrong on Cronulla’s fourth of the night. It ended with him apologising to teammates and coach Craig Fitzgibbon. Rightly or wrongly, Hynes is arguably the most maligned player in the NRL. For all his sharp work in the regular season – he has a 67 per cent winning record across his NRL career – he is judged on finals form and criticised for an inability to deliver the Sharks to a grand final.



What’s worse, though: having a bad game or barely being able to be involved? Both are awful propositions for professional athletes who obsess over success, but the latter was Hynes’ sad reality as he stared blankly towards the Allianz Stadium turf from the bench during the first half. Nicho Hynes leaves the field early on Saturday night. Getty Images Not because of the sore head from a tackle gone wrong with Salesi Foketi. But because he was left wondering whether this was going to be the anticlimactic end to another season as the Sharks’ marquee million-dollar man. “He went head first into the first collision he could get and got the timing wrong,” Fitzgibbon said. “It’s a sign of how much he wanted it and went after it. It cost him dearly.



Hynes on the sideline. Getty Images “He apologised, and he knows that he had an opportunity tonight, which was important for him and us. It went wrong, but you can handle that … when you are that committed.” Hynes’ finals record is quickly wheeled out whenever Cronulla stumble in September – four wins from 10 matches as a starting halfback since 2022 – but Saturday’s match cannot count against him. Cameras panned to Hynes at half-time, with his side trailing 18-10, and he looked understandably glum. It brought back memories of the day Wallabies star Matt Giteau was pulled off 25 minutes into the 2015 World Cup final, a match Australia went on to lose 34-17 to the All Blacks. It was Giteau’s last chance to lift the Webb Ellis Cup.



Giteau gave his coach that day, Michael Cheika, a gobful in the sheds at half-time. On Saturday, Cheika sat in the Roosters’ coaching box alongside Trent Robinson, knowing full well the significance of Hynes’ absence as the Roosters powered towards a preliminary final against the Dolphins next Friday. Nicho Hynes chats to Daly Cherry-Evans at full-time. Getty Images If there is a silver lining for Hynes, as insignificant as it may feel, at least he won’t be blamed for the Sharks’ failure to make a third preliminary final in as many years. He has grown tired of the narrative that dogs him, but that comes with the territory when you are the million-dollar halfback at a club desperate to turn consistency into a premiership.



This will hurt in a different way than the straight-sets exit of 2022, or the back-to-back preliminary final heartbreak of 2024 and 2025. Most clubs would kill for such consistency. The Sharks would trade plenty of it for another premiership, 10 years after their breakthrough triumph. Cronulla No.6 Braydon Trindall was superb in Hynes’ absence, but Cherry-Evans fired his bullets when they mattered. His long, looping pass for Mark Nawaqanitawase’s 62nd-minute try put the result beyond doubt and made the final quarter a tough watch for a Sharks contingent far greater than the one that turned up for last week’s clash with Newcastle at the same venue. With Mad Monday plans potentially beginning to creep into the mind, the Sharks wilted as the Roosters unleashed their attacking weapons at frightening speed.



Loading When the passes stick, and defenders are left bamboozled, the Roosters are a joy to watch. Nawaqanitawase’s swan dive for his second try, nine minutes from full-time, was straight out of the rugby playbook. Even Giteau would have been impressed. His impending switch back to rugby will have to wait another week. Maybe two, if his Roosters teammates continue to hold up their end of the bargain. Cam McInnes’ final touch for the Sharks – he is heading to the York City Knights – was a knock-on. It summed up their night.



Cronulla’s roster is evolving and there will inevitably be questions about whether their premiership window is beginning to close. One could argue it certainly has. Related Article Sydney Roosters 46 Cronulla 10

NRL 2026 ‘Confident’: Walker eyes remarkable return as DCE sets up storybook Dolphins clash “There’s only been two teams who have won the comp in the last five years,” Fitzgibbon said. “We’re not that far off. We haven’t got there, so that’s a fair criticism and it’s frustrating. “We’ve got to work out how and what we do with what we’ve got to get there.” Hynes, though, is contracted until 2029. He will dust himself off and come back for another crack.



It was just a shame that he had to shake Cherry-Evans’ hand at full-time wearing a crisp Sharks polo rather than a dirty jersey. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Hawthorn v Brisbane Lions player ratings: The four players who score a perfect 10 in a September classic
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Hawthorn v Brisbane Lions player ratings: The four players who score a perfect 10 in a September classic

Loading

It’s so often said that September is the time the biggest and best step up most, and Saturday’s thriller at the MCG in front of a shade under 98,000 people was proof of that. In a match that had nail-biter written all over it, both the Hawks and Lions had their chances, but it was the two-time reigning premiers who did just enough when it mattered most. The time will come for Sam Mitchell’s group, which is stacked with match-winning talent in its own right, but to be the best, they’ve got to beat the best. Four-time AFLW premiership player Libby Birch (Hawthorn) and reporter Jon Pierik (Brisbane Lions) run their eye over a preliminary final that will live long in the memory of all who saw it. Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell and gutted superstar Nick Watson after an MCG classic to remember. AFL Photos



Hawthorn (1) Harry Morrison: Provided good early spread and a reliable outlet on the wing, but faded after half-time and conceded two costly turnovers by foot in the third quarter that handed Brisbane momentum. Huge smother on the boundary with 2 mins to go. 6/10 (2) Mitch Lewis: Set the tone with a strong inside-50 tackle and two first-quarter goals in quick succession, producing a career defining mark in the 4th. 8.5/10 (3) Jai Newcombe: His bump on Lachie Neale at the opening centre clearance appeared to rattle him, and he conceded several early free kicks, before working his way back into the contest. 6/10



(4) Jarman Impey: Had Conor McKenna deployed as a defensive forward on him for much of the night and lacked his usual damaging influence from half-back, although he worked desperately to shift momentum after half-time. A holding the ball call could haunt him forever. 6/10 (5) Nick Watson: Is this just about the best finals performance we have seen? He was elite all game, first in his match-up with Ryan Lester, drawing him high up the ground and repeatedly beating him back towards goal, while kicking the opener with a classic soccer finish from Hawthorn’s first inside 50 and influencing centre clearances as the Harry Potter music fittingly rang out. 10/10 View post on X (6) James Sicily: Produced several important early spoils and intercept marks to steady Hawthorn, before Sam Mitchell’s inspired move to the wing and a courageous intercept mark running back with the flight underlined his influence. 7.5/10 (8) Dylan Moore: Started superbly, using his running power to create handball chains down the wing, and remained a consistent connecting presence while trying to lift Hawthorn at every stage of the game with his offensive presence. 9/10



(9) Connor Macdonald: Worked high as a linking half-forward and pushed up to provide coverage around stoppage. 6/10 (10) Karl Amon: Quiet early before his precise ball use came to the fore in the second quarter, but he was unable to stem the influence of the Lions’ small forwards once momentum shifted after half-time. Had a huge moment in the fourth to push the momentum the Hawks’ way. 6/10 (12) Will Day: He impacted early with important tackles and showed composure with ball in hand, a very strong performance. 7/10 (15) Blake Hardwick: Went searching for Charlie Cameron’s body too early in aerial contests, allowing him to get out the back and punish Hawthorn twice in the second quarter, while his decision-making looked unusually uncertain. Still worked hard in defence. 4/10 (16) Massimo D’Ambrosio: Collected 12 disposals by half-time, worked hard to support the defence and took two important marks in the third quarter in a solid performance. 6/10



(17) Lloyd Meek: He clearly won the ruck battle, consistently giving Hawthorn’s midfielders and forwards first look while remaining exceptionally clean at ground level, looking like an extra midfielder in a career-best performance. 9/10 (18) Mabior Chol: Had no impact in the first half and was beaten in several contests, then failed to provide the aerial presence Hawthorn desperately needed after the main break as the Lions’ defenders marked too easily. 4/10 Hawthorn champion Jack Gunston stepped up yet again. AFL Photos (19) Jack Gunston: Reached 50 career finals goals, was always in the right place at the right time. The evergreen veteran was a massive presence in the last quarter. 8/10 (23) Josh Weddle: Shifted to half-back when Sicily moved onto the wing in the second quarter and again served as Sam Mitchell’s versatile utility, influencing the game at both ends of the ground. He got shifted forward in the last and had some big moments. 7/10



(24) Josh Battle: Outplayed both Oscar Allen and Logan Morris, keeping both forwards quiet and completing his defensive role effectively. 7/10 (25) Josh Ward: Very clean early, he was Hawthorn’s best midfielder, maintaining a consistent contribution across all four quarters. He had some huge game defining clearances in the fourth quarter as the Hawks charged. 10/10 Josh Ward and Josh Dunkley were men inspired on Saturday. AFL Photos (28) Cam Mackenzie: He found plenty of space on the outside and collected nine disposals by half-time, but faded after the break. 5/10 (33) Jack Ginnivan: Was uncharacteristically quiet on the big stage, but always tried to pressure and create havoc wherever he went. He had some great composure late when the game was on the line. 5/10



(37) Tom Barrass: Positioned himself well behind the ball, winning several important early contests and providing a strong last line of defence. He took what could have proved to be the game-saving mark with two minutes to play. 9/10 (40) Max Beattie: He had little influence as a small forward and struggled to become involved in the game. 3/10 (42) Bailey Macdonald: He offered limited run and carry and had little influence, aside from one strong first-half tackle and some strong aerial contests. 4/10 Brisbane Lions



(1) Kai Lohmann: Wow, what a third term, the flashy forward leaving football Siberia in the first half for the warm waters of Florida after the main break. He did not have a touch in the first term, and it took until he won a contentious free kick late in the second term to have an impact, converting a set shot. But his third term was match-turning, delivering three goals, including a stunning set shot from just inside the right boundary, as the Lions booted seven goals to one for the term. 7/10 Editor's pick AFL 2026 Dusty v Ashcroft: The Lions’ whiz kid on a fast track to matching Martin (2) Sam Draper: The former Essendon ruckman didn’t have the best of games against the Crows last week, but was solid around the ground against Meek. He botched a crucial set shot in the second term, but was active all evening. 7/10 (3) Jaspa Fletcher: The reliable defender struggled to regain his best form early in the season, but regained touch, and continued that here with 11 disposals to half-time. Worked hard after the main break. 7/10 (4) Oscar Allen: The former West Coast captain was busy early, pushing up field to have an influence with four marks in the first term. He did not take another, and will need to lift next week. 4/10



(5) Josh Dunkley: There have been few better at the coalface than this man over the past decade, his attention to detail impeccable. That was the case when he went to Day and held the Hawks star to two touches in the first term, and six to the main break. While Day was more productive after the main break, Dunkley, who also spent time on Newcombe, won this battle. 8/10 (6) Hugh McCluggage: Must now be dubbed “Mr Cool” after his goal-kicking heroics in the final term. The pressure he was under was just enormous. This was another superb performance from the hard-running midfielder and big-time finals performer, who slotted two goals when the contest was in the balance. He had another important kick in the third term. He still appeared to be nursing a calf issue, but finished with 23 disposals nonetheless. 10/10 Cometh the moment, cometh the man: Hugh McCluggage put the dagger through Hawthorn hearts. AFL Photos (7) Jarrod Berry: The dynamic onballer, who missed last year’s grand final because of injury, struggled to get involved in the first half, held to only six touches on a wing. He came to life with a 60m bomb in the third term which cut the Hawks’ lead to 10 points. 7/10 (8) Will Ashcroft: Put simply, the dual Norm Smith medallist was involved in everything. This man has an astonishing finals record, and was at his brilliant best with a super running goal and nine touches in the first term. He finished with 28 disposals, 10 inside 50s and eight clearances in another finals masterpiece. Just call him “Mr September”. 10/10



View post on X (9) Lachie Neale: The dual Brownlow medallist took a high hit at the opening centre bounce when floored by Newcombe, and – oddly – did not immediately leave the field for assessment. He had five clearances to half-time, the Lions winning this battle 24-17 to the main break. Neale was typically robust after the break, finishing with 26 touches, and extending his Lions career by a further week. 8/10 (10) Levi Ashcroft: The younger of the two Ashcrofts has had a charmed run in his two seasons, and began this contest well after a chip pass from his brother, and goal. Didn’t exert much influence after that, but delivered a crucial spoil with 10 minutes remaining. 6/10 (13) Logan Morris: The All-Australian and brilliant young forward was well held to half-time by Battle with only three touches, and had only two marks to three-quarter-time. But he burst into action in the final quarter, booting two early goals to give his team what seemed to be a match-winning lead. 5/10 (15) Dayne Zorko: The cheeky veteran had the job on Ginnivan, and held the former premiership Magpie goalless and to only seven touches to half-time. He provided his typical dash from half-back with six rebound 50s, in what will be remembered as a classic preliminary final. 7.5/10



(16) Cam Rayner: The robust half-forward knows how to pump up his team with a moment of brilliance, but wasn’t able to do that in the first half. Had the semi-defensive job of negating James Sicily after the main break, but the Hawks’ co-captain took a pivotal mark which almost saved the day for the Hawks. 6.5/10 (22) Ty Gallop: The man who played in the 2025 premiership in just his sixth game held his spot ahead of Noah Answerth, but had nowhere to hide when tackled by Lewis, conceding a first-term goal. He battled seriously hard. 6.5/10 View post on X (23) Charlie Cameron: Was in the play early when he marked strongly on the lead and converted. While he had only five touches to half-time, two of them were goals. He delivered more dash after the main break, and was crucial to the victory. Perhaps next week he needs to persuade the MCG to let rip Take me Home, Country Roads. 7.5/10 (26) Conor McKenna: The man with a Gaelic title and AFL premiership began as a defensive forward on rebounding half-back Impey, and delivered one of the goals of the year, a trademark soccer poke off the outside of his boot. Held Impey to only two touches in the first term, and provided speed all evening. 7/10



(27) Darcy Gardiner: The no-fuss, no-frills defender had the job on Gunston, and it was a tough night at the office. Gunston finished with five goals, but Gardiner did have his important moments. 5/10 (30) Eric Hipwood: The veteran forward missed last year’s premiership because of injury gave the Lions their first lead of the evening with a brilliant left-foot snap. He was quiet at times, but gave the Lions a target all night, and finished with three. 7/10 View post on X (31) Harris Andrews: The Hawks needed to find a way to curb Andrews’ intercept marking, and they did this by making the star defender accountable. Lewis did just that with three goals before half-time, but Andrews was back to his best after the main break with marks and spoils, although Lewis hauled in a huge pack mark late. 7.5/10 (32) Darcy Fort: The dual premiership ruckman was typically solid and dependable, although he needlessly held on to Weddle at a throw-in and conceded a goal in the second term. 6.5/10



(33) Zac Bailey: This is a man who knows how to step up in finals. He was a non-factor in the first half, rated “poor” by Jonathan Brown at half-time. However, he got moving after the break, finishing with 18 disposals, albeit goalless. 7/10 (35) Ryan Lester: The unheralded defender, 34, had the imposing assignment on Watson, and began horribly when “the Wizard” booted the Hawks’ opening two goals. He regained his composure, but Watson was a star all night and almost dragged the Hawks to victory. 5.5/10 (44) Darcy Wilmot: The rebounding half-back failed to have the influence he wanted in the first half, and then coughed up a high free kick – and goal – to Nick Watson in the third term. Finished with four rebounds from defensive 50. 6/10 Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: One Nation’s bigotry is not redemption
World.content:
Parnell Palme McGuinness can write all the puff pieces she likes about One Nation candidate Warren Pickering. She even fantasises that his story is one of “redemption” (“Why Hanson’s candidate with a drug-taking past will win”, September 13). But she ignores what is truly significant about Pickering and other One Nation personalities: their belief in mad conspiracy theories and the obvious bigotry that comes with running under the One Nation banner. Perhaps McGuinness would do better to emulate the ethical integrity of Liberals like Andrew Hastie, instead of trying to “normalise” white supremacists and conspiracy loonies by saying they represent “a new aesthetic”. Steve Ellis, Canberra (ACT)

One Nation state candidate for Pakenham Warren Pickering and One Nation leader Pauline Hanson. The Age

Long wait for results

Paul Sakkal’s article quoting Bill Kelty highlights the federal government’s failure to “get the economy moving” and address the productivity malaise and decline in real wages (“Labor luminary unleashes over falling house prices, real wages”, September 13). After a productivity summit and a productivity budget, there is little evidence after the government entering its fifth year that any new ideas or urgency is being shown to address the accelerating decline in Australian living standards. Labor’s current majority probably means it will win the next federal election in 2028, regardless of the One Nation “threat”. It’s a sobering thought. Is federal Labor up to the task of delivering improved living standards? Unfortunately, we may have to wait five years to find out. Paul McGee, Cranebrook

Stand or fall

The civil population of Ukraine is now being terrorised by Russia, obviously in an attempt to weaken the resolve of the people against their dictatorial aggressor (“The new terror stalking Kyiv day and night,” September 13). The small nation is receiving some support from free countries, but certainly more is needed to prevent it being overwhelmed and its spirit broken. In the early 1940s we saw another small nation in a similar situation. Hitler’s Luftwaffe pounded London and other English cities in an attempt to break the will of the people. He failed, due to British courage and determination and the bravery of a small group of aviators. England stood alone against the aggressor. The support of Commonwealth countries and finally the might of American military power and industry saw that the Axis threat was defeated. This is a lesson for free nations of the world today. Unless they are prepared to bolster the Ukraine war effort, they might eventually have to face a more emboldened aggressor. Derrick Mason, Boorowa

World.title: AFL LIVE: McCluggage the hero as Lions break Hawks hearts; Bottles thrown at umpires despite right decision
World.content:
Ugly fan behaviour will come under scrutiny on Sunday after angry fans threw bottles at umpires as they left the MCG following a pulsating finish to the preliminary final between the Hawks and the Brisbane Lions.

The crowd erupted after a last-minute free-kick decided the match in the Lions’ favour, and the field umpires were booed as they left the arena.

TV images showed umpire Jacob Mollison stop his colleagues just moments before a crowd-propelled missile lands at their feet. He then pointed out a member of the crowd to nearby officials.

World.title: Minister orders shark to be destroyed as family shares grief over Perth swimmer’s death
World.content:
Updated NationalWASharks Minister orders shark to be destroyed as family shares grief over Perth swimmer’s death Rebecca Peppiatt Updated September 19, 2026 — 8:55pm ,first published 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The shark that killed a 63-year-old swimmer at Sorrento Beach on Friday will be caught and destroyed, in what Fisheries minister Jackie Jarvis said was “an extraordinary step”. Greg O’Neill was swimming “very close to shore” when he was witnessed being pulled underwater by a large white shark at approximately 10.30am on Friday. Lifesavers raced to rescue O’Neil but were unsuccessful in locating him. Loading A witness told this masthead there was blood in the water, while the swimmer who had accompanied the victim had to be consoled by rescuers once he got to shore. On Saturday morning, Jarvis said it was “an incredibly sad and distressing incident” before saying the shark was later located by water police and “positively identified as the shark involved in the incident”.



“WA Police requested that the shark be captured to assist with the recovery of potential coronial evidence,” she said. “Given the shark had been positively identified, remained in the vicinity following a fatal attack, and was considered to pose an ongoing threat, I authorised fisheries officers to destroy the shark if it could be captured.” Greg O’Neill, 63, left, has been identified as the victim of a shark attack at the popular Perth beach of Sorrento on Friday. O’Neill’s family shared their grief on Saturday, saying in a statement to 9News Perth they were “deeply shocked and devastated” by the tragedy that claimed the life of a much-loved, father, grandfather-to-be, brother, uncle, husband and friend.” “He was a generous, devoted family man that gave his children so much love, care and opportunity,” the statement read.



“Greg loved the ocean and was known as a passionate swimmer, sports lover, dedicated worker and an all-round generous, witty guy. “The kind thoughts and support from everyone who has reached out are deeply appreciated.” Jarvis said the circumstances of the attack were “exceptional” and that the rare catch and kill order was carefully considered, weighing up the safety of water police and fisheries officers involved in recovery efforts and the response to the incident. “Capture gear was deployed by fisheries officers yesterday,” she said. “However, at this stage, the shark has not been captured. A WA Police water police vessel remains on the water today. Police conducted a search of the shoreline this morning, and beaches in the area remain closed.”



Jarvis said the shark was not one of around 300 tagged sharks in WA waters before claiming the state has a comprehensive shark mitigation program. “We will never be able to mitigate all of the threats,” she said. “And people make an informed decision when they go into the water because it was so close to the shore, because of the circumstances, and because we were able to identify the shark, is why I have taken somewhat extraordinary step to issue a catch and kill authorisation for this shark.” She said the government’s shark mitigation plan had been added to in recent years with the inclusion of beach emergency number signs, increased tagging efforts and the SharkSmart app. “Of course, we will regularly review this, and we’ll see what more we can do,” she said.



Related Article Sharks Government must step in over escalating shark attacks in WA, experts warn “I cannot remove the risk of all apex predators in the ocean, but we want to make sure the public have as much information as possible, and we will of course review what we’re doing and seeing if we can do more.” The attack was the second in Western Australia in the space of a week, and the third fatal incident in the state this year. with 9News Perth

World.title: NZ’s ski capital is fast becoming a summer destination
World.content:
Australians love to chase the sun on holiday. But as temperatures rise and summer heat makes some traditionally popular destinations less appealing, could the lure of cooler climes start heating up?

Certainly, New Zealand’s Queenstown would love that. Australians have long flocked to Queenstown for the ski season, but increasingly the destination is courting them year-round. And there are signs the strategy is working: international traffic through Queenstown Airport is at record levels, while trans-Tasman travel connecting Queenstown with Australia’s eastern seaboard has reached 145 per cent of pre-pandemic levels.

The Kawarau Gorge Trail is set to open for cycling this month. iStock

Tourism New Zealand research also suggests Australians are open to travelling outside the traditional peak: 67 per cent of Australians actively considering a New Zealand holiday say they would consider an off-peak visit. Asked which seasons they would consider, spring came out on top at 42 per cent, followed by summer at 35 per cent, autumn at 29 per cent and winter at 24 per cent.

Queenstown is, of course, synonymous with skiing for many Australians, but there’s an ever-growing list of reasons to visit without skis.
